en: Oṃ,
the Chāndogya Upaniṣad belonging to the Sāmaveda.
Now begins the first chapter:
May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, as well as strength and all my senses, be nourished.
May everything that constitutes the Upanishadic Brahman not reject me, and may I not reject the Brahman. May there be no rejection; may there be no rejection for me.
Whatever virtues are contained in the Upanishads for one devoted to the Self, may those be in me; may they be in me.
Om. Peace! Peace! Peace!
The Commentary composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. Introduction:
"Om, this syllable... and so forth is the Chāndogya Upaniṣad consisting of eight chapters.

For those desiring to know its meaning in brief, this *Ṛjuvivaraṇa*, a commentary on the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad-bhāṣya* composed by the venerable Narendrapurī Yatīndra in a concise form, is now commenced.

Regarding its connection (*sambandha*): all ritual action (*karman*) previously understood—when accompanied by the knowledge of deities such as Prāṇa—is the cause for attaining the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) via the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*).
And when performed alone, it is the cause for attaining the world of the moon (*candraloka*) via the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādi-mārga*).

For those who follow their own nature and have fallen away from both paths, a miserable downward course is described; yet, in neither of these two paths is there an ultimate attainment of the human goal. Therefore, the Upaniṣad is commenced to set forth the knowledge of the non-dual Self, independent of karma, which destroys the causes of the three courses of transmigration.
Furthermore, the attainment of absolute supreme bliss does not occur apart from the realization of the non-dual Self;
for it will be stated: "Now, those who know otherwise than this have other rulers and their worlds are perishable; but upon the contrary, he becomes his own ruler."

Thus, it has been stated that for one who falsely identifies with the realm of duality, there is bondage—just as a thief experiences being bound and burned upon grasping a heated axe—and the attainment of the miseries of saṃsāra; whereas for one who truly identifies with the non-dual Self, like a non-thief, there is an absence of binding and burning upon grasping the heated axe, as well as liberation, which is the cessation of the miseries of saṃsāra.
Therefore, the vision of the non-dual Self does not coexist with ritual action (karman).

Because no subverting cognition can arise against such statements as "By the destruction of the distinctions between action, agent, and fruit, [the Self] is non-existent, one, and without a second; indeed, this all is the Self," [the Upanishads cannot be subordinate].
If it is argued that they are cognitions regarding ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*), we say no;

for ritual injunctions are prescribed only for one who possesses the notion of being an agent and an enjoyer, and who is possessed of defects such as attachment and aversion toward the fruits of action produced thereby.
If it is argued that ritual action (*karman*) is prescribed even for one who has realized the meaning of the entire Veda and possesses the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñāna*), we say no.

This is because the innate cognition of being an agent, an enjoyer, and so forth—which constitutes the domain of eligibility for ritual action—is sublated by the realization "Being alone is this, one without a second; all this is indeed the Self" (*sadekamevādvitīyam ātmaivedaṃ sarvam*).
Therefore, rituals are prescribed only for those who possess defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*).
Not for one who possesses the knowledge of non-duality (advaitajñāna).
For this very reason, he will say: "All these [practitioners] attain worlds of merit;
but he who is established in Brahman attains immortality."

In this context of the knowledge of non-duality (*advaita-vidyā*), meditations (*upāsanā*) that are means for attaining worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) are taught; these have as their fruit a result closely proximate to absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).

Furthermore, there are those whose objects are Brahman slightly modified by non-duality and so forth, which have the success of ritual action (*karma-samṛddhi*) as their fruit and are connected to the constituent parts of rituals.

Because of the commonality of being secret and the commonality of being mental modifications (*manovṛtti*), just as the knowledge of non-duality is merely a mental modification, so too are the other meditations of the nature of mental modifications; for such is the commonality between them.
What, then, is the distinction between the knowledge of non-duality (advaitajñāna) and the various forms of meditative worship (upāsanā)?
It is said:

the knowledge of non-duality is that which removes the innate cognition of distinctions—such as the agent and other factors of action, as well as actions and their fruits—which has been superimposed upon the actionless Self.

Just as in the case of a rope and the like, the determination of the true nature of the rope—which is characterized by the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of a snake and so forth—is caused by illumination;

however, meditation (*upāsana*), on the other hand, consists in producing a continuous flow of identical mental modifications (*cittavṛtti-santāna*) with respect to some object presented according to scripture, uninterrupted by cognitions of a different nature—this is the distinction.

These meditations are presented first because they purify the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*), thereby illuminating the reality of things (*vastu-tattva*) and thus assisting the knowledge of non-duality (*advaita-jñāna*); furthermore, because they have a specific object as their support (*ālambana-viṣayatva*), they are easy to accomplish.

In this regard, because the practice of ritual action has been firmly established, the surrender of the mind to meditation alone is difficult while abandoning such action; therefore, first of all, meditation is introduced as having the constituent parts of ritual action as its object:
"One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha, for one chants the Udgītha with 'Om'."
This is its further explanation.
Thus begins the introductory commentary: "One should meditate upon this syllable *om* as the *udgītha*.
This syllable *om* is the most proximate designation of the Supreme Self;
for when it is employed, He becomes gracious, just as a person in the world is pleased when his own dear name is uttered."
When the word "that" (*tad*) is employed as something else, the mere form of the word itself is perceived once its denotative function has been set aside;
thus, it becomes a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self, just like an image (*arcā*) and so forth.

In this way, it is understood in all the Vedāntas that the means for the meditation upon the Supreme Self is most excellent both by virtue of being a name (*nāman*) and by virtue of being a symbol (*pratīka*).
Its preeminence is well-established through its frequent application at the beginning and end of recitations (*japa*), ritual acts (*karma*), and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).
Therefore, one should meditate upon this very syllable—which consists of phonemes—as the *udgītha*, because it is a constituent part of the *udgītha* chant.
One should maintain a firm, one-pointed concentration of mind upon the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the ritual act and serves as a symbol (*pratīka*) for the Supreme Self.
The Śruti itself states the reason why the syllable *oṃ* is denoted by the word *udgītha*: "For one sings [the udgītha] with 'oṃ'.
Since one begins the singing with "oṃ," therefore the syllable *oṃ* is the *udgītha*; this is the meaning.

Its *upavyākhyāna*—that is, the detailed exposition of that syllable, consisting of statements such as "it is to be meditated upon in this way," "it has such power," and "it has such fruit"—is called the *upavyākhyāna*.
The words "it proceeds" are the completion of the sentence.
Of these beings, the earth is the essence;
of the earth, water is the essence;
of water, plants are the essence.
Of herbs, man is the essence;
of man, speech is the essence;
of speech, the Ṛg-veda is the essence.
The Ṛgveda has the Sāman as its essence;
the Sāman has the Udgītha as its essence.

Of these beings, both moving and unmoving, the earth is the essence, the goal, the ultimate resort, and the support. Of the earth, water is the essence; for the earth is woven like warp and woof within the waters, and therefore water is the essence of the earth. Of the waters, plants are the essence, because plants are a transformation of water.
Of these, man is the essence, because man is a transformation of food;
and of that man, speech is the essence,
for among the limbs of a person, speech is the most excellent.
Therefore, the essence of speech is said to be the person;
of that speech, too, the *ṛc* is the more essential essence;
of the *ṛc*, the *sāman* is the even more essential essence.
Of that Sāman as well, the Udgītha—being the subject under discussion—is the syllable Om, which is the most essential part.
This very Udgītha is the essence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth.
Thus, this very syllable *oṃ*, known as the Udgītha, is the "most excellent essence" (*rasatama*), being the most preeminent among the successive essences beginning with the elements;
it is "supreme" (*parama*) because it is the symbol of the Supreme Self; and it is "the highest goal" (*parārdhya*), for its place (*ardha*) is the highest.

"Parārdhya" means that which deserves the highest place (parārdha), namely half of that; the intention is that it is worthy of the station of the Supreme Self because it is to be meditated upon like the Supreme Self.
It is the eighth in the enumeration of the essences beginning with earth; it is that which is the Udgītha.
"What is the Ṛk? What is the Sāman? What is the Udgītha?"—thus it is investigated.
It has been stated that speech is the essence of the *ṛc*. Which is that *ṛc*, which is that *sāman*, and which is that *udgītha*?
The repetition "which—whichever" (*katamā katamā*) is for the sake of showing reverence.
But surely, the suffix *ḍatamac* is used when there is an inquiry regarding many members of a genus (*jāti*). Since there is no multiplicity of *ṛc*-genus here, how can there be the use of *ḍatamac*?
This is not a fault.

In the analysis *jātau paripraśnaḥ* (an inquiry regarding a genus), because a plurality of individual *ṛc*-verses is possible within that genus, the compound is not analyzed as *jāteḥ paripraśnaḥ* (an inquiry of the genus).
[Objection: But if the analysis were *jāteḥ paripraśnaḥ*, then examples such as "Which Kaṭha? would be appropriate; however, they are not suitable for the analysis *jātau paripraśnaḥ*.
Even in that case, there is no fault, because the question is intended to refer to the multiplicity of individual instances (*vyakti*) within the very class (*jāti*) such as "Kaṭha" and so forth.

If the question were directed toward the class itself, then an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) would have to be formulated for cases such as "which one? or "which [of the many]? [The phrase] *vimṛṣṭaṃ bhavati* means that a deliberation (*vimarśa*) has been performed.
Speech indeed is the Ṛk; breath is the Sāman;
the syllable "Om" is the Udgītha.
Now, this indeed is a union: speech and breath, as well as the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
For when an inquiry has been made, it is appropriate to provide a reply, namely: "Speech is the Ṛk, breath is the Sāman.

Although speech and the Ṛk are one, there is no contradiction regarding its being the eighth [member], because this constitutes a different sentence from the preceding one, intended to establish the quality of attainment (*āpti*), as in: "The syllable *Om* is the Udgītha.
Since speech and breath are the sources of the Ṛk and the Sāman, it is said that "speech is the Ṛk, breath is the Sāman."

For, by the sequential grasping of speech and breath as the sources of the Ṛg and Sāman, there would be the inclusion of all Ṛcs and all Sāmans; and with the inclusion of all Ṛcs and Sāmans, there would be the inclusion of all rites accomplished by the Ṛcs and Sāmans;
and with their inclusion, all desires would be included.
The doubt that the syllable "Om" is merely the *udgītha* in a figurative sense is dispelled.
By the words "That indeed is this," the couple is indicated.
To the question "What is that couple? he replies: it is speech and breath, which, being the causes of all *ṛc*s and *sāmans*, constitute the couple.
The phrase "the Ṛc and the Sāman" means that the words "Ṛc" and "Sāman" denote the causes of the Ṛc and the Sāman;
it does not mean that the Ṛc and the Sāman themselves constitute an independent couple.
For otherwise, there would be two couples: one consisting of Speech and Breath, and another consisting of the Ṛc and the Sāman.
And thus, the designation in the singular as "this pair" would be untenable;
therefore, the state of being a pair belongs only to speech and breath, which are the sources of the Ṛk and the Sāman.
This pair is united in this syllable "Om.
Indeed, when a couple comes together, they fulfill each other's desire.
This very couple, characterized in this way, is merged in this syllable *oṃ*.

Thus, the couple—distinguished by the quality of attaining all desires—is found merged in the *oṃkāra*; therefore, the *oṃkāra*'s possession of the quality of attaining all desires is well-established.

Since the *oṃkāra*'s nature as consisting of speech, its production by means of breath, its being merged with the couple, and the couple's capacity to fulfill desires are all well-known, this analogy is stated.
Just as in the world when a pair of sexual partners—a man and a woman—come together and unite through carnal desire, they then fulfill and attain each other's mutual longing;
so too, because the couple has entered into its own self, it is established that the syllable *oṃ* possesses the quality of attaining all desires. This is the intended meaning.
He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable as the Udgītha.

He says that even the *udgātṛ* who is a worshipper of that [syllable] comes to possess its qualities: "He indeed becomes the fulfiller of the desires of the sacrificer, who worships this syllable as the *udgītha* endowed with the quality of attainment (*āpti*).
The meaning is that for him, there is this aforementioned fruit, according to the Vedic revelation: "In whatever way one worships it, that very thing he becomes."
This, indeed, is the syllable of assent. For whatever one assents to, one says "Om" to that.
Assent is indeed prosperity.
He indeed becomes a fulfiller of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha.
The syllable *oṃ* possesses the quality of prosperity.
How so? This very thing is the primordial syllable of permission (*anujñā*), and that permission is itself the syllable. "Permission" means consent; the meaning is that it is the syllable *oṃ*.
How is it that this is permission? Scripture itself explains:
whatever knowledge or wealth one grants permission for—whether a wise man or a wealthy man gives his consent therein—he says "Om" to that.
And likewise in the Veda: "Thirty-three [gods]," "Om," he said, and so forth.
And likewise in the world, when someone says, "I take this wealth of yours," one replies, "Om.
Therefore, this very thing is prosperity—that which is permission; that which is permission is prosperity, because permission has its root in prosperity.
For one who is prosperous gives permission by saying "Om"; thus, the meaning is that the syllable Om possesses the quality of prosperity.

Because he is a worshipper of the quality of prosperity, being possessed of that nature, he indeed becomes a fulfiller of the desires of the sacrificer—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable as the Udgītha; and so on, as before.
By means of this, the threefold knowledge proceeds:
"Om," he says when calling for the response.
He praises with "Om";
he chants the Udgītha with "Om.
It is for the sake of honoring this very syllable, by means of its greatness and its essence.
Now, he praises the Imperishable (akṣara) for the purpose of generating interest, because it is to be meditated upon.

How so? By means of that aforementioned Imperishable, this triple knowledge (trayī vidyā)—characterized by the Ṛgveda and the others—[is established]; the meaning is that the ritual action prescribed by the triple knowledge [proceeds].
For it is well known that it is not the triple knowledge itself that proceeds through the acts of recitation and so forth, but rather the ritual action that proceeds in that manner.
From the indicative mark—"He utters 'Om' as the *āśrāva*, he recites 'Om' as the *praśaṃsā*, and he chants 'Om' as the *udgītha*"—it is understood that this refers to the Soma sacrifice.
And that ritual is for the sake of honoring—that is, for the purpose of worshiping—this very syllable;
for it is indeed a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self.
That worship is indeed directed toward the Supreme Self alone, according to the Smṛti: "By worshipping Him through one's own action, a human being attains perfection.
[This is done] by means of His majesty and essence.

Furthermore, it is by the greatness— that is, the majesty— of this very syllable, meaning by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the officiating priests and the sacrificer; likewise, it is by the essence (*rasa*) of this very syllable, meaning by the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) produced from the essences of rice,
barley, and so forth, that sacrifice, oblation, and other rites are performed through the syllable.
And that [offering] approaches the sun;
from that, through the sequence beginning with rain, vital breath (*prāṇa*) and food (*anna*) are produced;
and by means of the vital breaths and food, the sacrifice (*yajña*) is performed.
Therefore it is said: "They taste through the greatness of the Imperishable."
Therefore, both perform [the sacrifice]:
he who knows this thus, and he who does not know it.
But knowledge and ignorance are indeed different.
"Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful"—this indeed is the further explanation of this very syllable.
In this regard, it is established that one who possesses the knowledge of the syllable must perform ritual action; for, by means of the [sacrificial] vessel brought forward,
both perform the rite— the one who knows this syllable as explained above, and the one who knows only the ritual action but does not know the true nature of the syllable.
And since the fruit would arise from the very efficacy of those two actions alone, what is the use of the knowledge of the true nature of the syllables?
For it is observed in the world that when two people eat *harītakī*, purgation occurs for both, whether they know its taste or not.
This is not so.
But because knowledge and ignorance are indeed different, for knowledge and ignorance are distinct;
the word "but" (tu) serves to exclude the previous position.

Knowledge of the syllable Om as being merely a subordinate part of ritual action is not itself the knowledge endowed with the qualities of being the most savory, the attainment, and the prosperity; rather, it is something superior to that.
Therefore, the intention is that an increase in the result is logical due to the addition of those auxiliary factors (*aṅga*).
For it is observed in the world that between a merchant and a forest-dweller (*śabara*) selling rubies and other gems, the merchant achieves a greater result due to his superior knowledge.

Therefore, whatever action one performs while being endowed with *vidyā*—that is, with specialized knowledge—and while being full of faith through *śraddhā*, as well as being joined with the *upaniṣad*, meaning with yoga.
That very same action becomes more powerful— that is, it yields a greater fruit than the action of the ignorant—
by this statement regarding the superior power of the action of the knower, the intention is that the action of the ignorant person likewise becomes powerful.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the ignorant person lacks the qualification for performing action.
In the section concerning Uṣasti, since the performance of priestly duties is seen even for those who are ignorant,
there is one single meditation on the Imperishable (akṣara) as possessing the qualities of being the most flavorful, the attainment of prosperity, and abundance;
for no other effort is observed between these attributes.
Indeed, because this very syllable under discussion, known as the Udgītha, is to be meditated upon in many ways through numerous attributes, there follows its detailed exposition.
Thus ends the first section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Once, indeed, when the gods and the asuras,
both of them offspring of Prajāpati, were contending, the gods took up the Udgītha, thinking, 'By this we shall overcome them.'"
"Devas and asuras" refers to both the gods and the demons.
The "gods" (devas) are the functions of the senses illuminated by the scriptures, derived from the root *div*, meaning "to shine.

The "asuras" are those opposed to them; they are the natural functions of the senses consisting of darkness (*tamas*), which take delight (*ramanāt*) in their own vital breaths (*asu*)—the various objective fields of perception—and thus are contrary to the former.
The particles *ha* and *vā* are used here as indicators of a prior occurrence.
"Where" (*yatra*) refers to that occasion characterized by the mutual seizure of each other's domains.
Since the root *yat-* preceded by the prefix *sam-* has the sense of "struggle," the meaning is that they engaged in combat.

The natural functions of the senses, which consist of *tamas*, are the "asuras" that act to overpower the functions of light prescribed by the scriptures. Conversely, the "devas"—whose nature is the light of discrimination regarding the objects of scriptural meaning—act to overpower those asuras consisting of natural *tamas*.
Thus, in every body among all living beings, there is a battle between the devas and asuras, characterized by mutual subjugation and emergence, like a war.
The intention is that [this conflict] has been proceeding from time immemorial.

Here, it is recounted by means of a scriptural narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) for the sake of discerning knowledge regarding the origin and distinction between merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), with the aim of teaching the method for attaining purity of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, both the gods and the asuras are called "descendants of Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyāḥ*) because they are the offspring of Prajāpati.
Prajāpati is the person (puruṣa) who is qualified for ritual action and knowledge;
for another Vedic text states, "The Puruṣa himself is the Uktha; he indeed is the Great Prajāpati.
Indeed, his scriptural and natural functions of the organs, though opposed to one another, are like offspring because they originate from him.

On account of the specific causes characterized by the excellence or deficiency of those respective [elements], the gods took up—that is, they brought forth—the ritual function of the Udgātṛ, as indicated by its constituent part, the Udgītha.
Since it is impossible to bring forth that alone in isolation, the intended meaning is that they brought forth the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices.
To the question "For what purpose did they bring them forth?", it is said: they did so with the intention, "By means of this ritual action, we shall overcome these Asuras."
They meditated upon the breath of the nose as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, one smells both the fragrant and the foul with it.
For he has been pierced by evil.

And when the gods, desiring to take up that Udgītha rite, then meditated upon the nasal—the conscious breath located in the nose—as the performer of the Udgītha by means of the Udgītha-contemplation; the meaning is that they performed this meditation.
The meaning is that, by viewing the syllable *oṃ* known as the Udgītha through the perspective of the nasal breath, they meditated upon it.
For in this way, there would be neither the abandonment of the subject at hand nor the introduction of an irrelevant subject.
Indeed, the meaning is that they meditated upon the syllable *oṃ* as being of this very nature;
for in this way, there would be neither the abandonment of the subject at hand nor the introduction of an irrelevant subject.
But indeed, regarding this very syllable— since the syllable *Oṃ* was introduced as the object of meditation,
did you not just now say that they took up the ritual action characterized by the *udgītha*?
How then do you now state that they meditated upon the syllable *Oṃ* through the vision of the nasal breath?
This is not a fault.

For it is precisely in the act of the *udgītha* that the syllable *oṃ*—which is a constituent part of the *udgītha- bhakti*—is intended to be meditated upon as the deity Prāṇa viewed through the perspective of its agent; it is not independent. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate to say that they brought forth the ritual action for the sake of that [meditation].

When the Udgātṛ had been thus chosen by the gods, the Asuras—who are of the nature of primordial darkness—pierced that god, the Prāṇa in the nose, who is of the form of light, with their own inherent evil consisting of attachment to unrighteousness; the meaning is that they brought about contact [with him].
For that nasal Prāṇa became one whose discriminative knowledge was overcome by the attachment and conceit arising from the perception of pleasant odors.
By that defect, he became associated with evil. This is what was meant by the statement, "The Asuras pierced him with evil.
Because he was pierced by the evil of the Asuras, therefore, impelled by that evil, the sense of smell—the vital breath (prāṇa) that perceives foul odors—belongs to living beings.
Therefore, because he has been pierced by evil, the world perceives both— the fragrant and the foul-smelling. The mention of "both" is not intended to be exhaustive.

It is just as in the case of the scriptural passage, "Whose two oblations both meet with disaster," because of the scriptural statement in the same context: "Whatever here is unseemly, that he smells."
Then they indeed worshipped speech as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one speaks both the true and the false.
For she has been pierced by evil.
Then, they venerated the eye as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one sees both the beautiful and the ugly.
For this is pierced by evil.
Then they venerated the ear as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one hears both what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing.
For this is pierced by evil.
Then they venerated the mind as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one conceives both that which is to be conceived and that which is not to be conceived.
For this is pierced by evil.
This inquiry was initiated by the Śruti for the purpose of experiencing the purity of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) so that it may become an object of meditation.
Therefore, the deities of the eye and the other senses are examined in succession and set aside as they were pierced by the evil spirit (asura-pāpman). The rest is the same.
Then indeed, speech, sight, hearing, mind, and so forth [are mentioned].
Other deities, such as those presiding over the skin, the sense of taste, and the rest, though not explicitly stated here, are also to be understood;
for there is another scriptural passage stating, "In this way, these deities were indeed afflicted by evils."
Then, they meditated upon that very vital breath which is principal as the Udgītha.
When the Asuras struck at it, they perished, just as a clod of earth would perish upon striking a solid stone.

Because they were pierced by the Asuras, the deities of the sense of smell and the others withdrew; then, immediately thereafter, they began to worship as the Udgītha that which is well-known as the "principal" (mukhya) breath located in the mouth. When the Asuras reached it, just as before, they shattered it—that is, they destroyed it—merely by their intention.

Without having done anything at all to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), how did they perish? To this, he provides an illustration: just as in the world a stone that is "unbreakable" (*ākhaṇa*)—meaning it cannot be dug up even with spades and the like, nor can it be split, being indeed unbreakable (*akhaṇa*)—having encountered such a stone, by implication, a clod of earth (*loṣṭa*), a lump of dust, [is destroyed].

And from another scriptural passage: "Just as a stone thrown at another stone with the intention of splitting it might, without doing anything at all to that stone, itself shatter and split apart—so do they perish. This is the meaning.
Just as a stone, having struck a flint, is shattered, even so is he shattered who desires evil against one who knows this, and he who seeks to harm him; for such a person is like a flint-stone.

Thus, because he is pure and cannot be overcome by the Asuras, he is called "Prāṇa. For one who knows this and has become the self that is Prāṇa, the scripture declares this result: "Just as [a clod of earth] against a stone"—this is the very illustration. In this very way, he is utterly shattered and perishes.
Who is this? He says: whoever desires—that is, wishes—to do that which is unworthy, namely evil, against one who knows thus, i.e., one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) as described;
and whoever also seeks to injure him—that is, harms the knower of the vital breath by employing abuse, beating, and so forth—he too perishes in exactly the same way. This is the meaning.

Because this knower of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being of the nature of the vital breath itself, is like a stone-cake (*aśmākhaṇa*); that is to say, he is invincible. Now, one might object: "But the nasal breath (*nāsikya-prāṇa*) is also of the nature of air, just like the principal breath (*mukhya*). In that case, how is it that the nasal breath was pierced by evil while still being the vital breath itself, yet not the principal one?
This is not a fault.

However, it is logical that the *nāsikya* (the nasal sound), although its nature is air (*vāyvātmā*), is not "pierced" due to the defectiveness of its place and organ of articulation; because the presiding deity of the place is more powerful, it is not pierced.

Just as axes and other tools produce specific effects when held by a skilled person, but not when in the hands of another, so too the nasal deity is not the primary [agent], as it is "pierced" by being associated with a defective nose.
By this [breath] one perceives neither fragrance nor foul odor,
for it is free from evil.
Whatever it eats and whatever it drinks, by that it sustains the other vital breaths.
Indeed, having failed to find this even at the end, one departs;
for at the very end, one merely opens one's mouth.

Because the principal [organ] was not pierced by the Asuras, therefore one does not perceive either fragrance or foul odor by means of it; rather, the world perceives both of those by means of the sense of smell alone.

And because no effect of evil is seen therein, it is "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*); that is to say, evil has been struck away, destroyed, or removed from it, hence it is "free from evil," meaning it is pure.
Furthermore, while the nose and other organs are "self-supporting" due to their attachment to pleasant things and so forth, the principal organ is not like that; rather, it is for the sake of all.
How so? It is said: by that which one eats and drinks through that primary [prāṇa], the world protects and sustains the subsequent [organs] such as the nose;
for by it their stability is maintained—this is the meaning. Therefore, prāṇa is the supporter of all, and thus it is pure.
But how is it understood that their subsistence is primarily through what is eaten and drunk?
It is said: "This very primary breath" means that food and drink are the functions (*vṛtti*) of the primary breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*).

In the end, at the time of death, having failed to obtain or acquire [sustenance], the collection of vital breaths such as the sense of smell and so forth departs; this is the meaning. For one who is without vital breath is unable to eat or drink.
Therefore, the departure of the collection beginning with the sense of smell is well-established;
for during the act of departing, a desire to eat is observed in the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Hence, "he opens his mouth" means he performs the act of opening it wide.
For that is indeed the sign of one who has departed when food is not obtained.
Aṅgiras meditated upon that as the Udgītha;
it is indeed this Aṅgirasa whom they consider to be the essence of the limbs.
Some have established the connection that Baka meditated upon that chief vital breath (prāṇa) as "Aṅgiras"—that is, as having such qualities—as the Udgītha;
for it is stated, "They consider this very Aṅgirasa to be Bṛhaspati and Ayāsya.
This is indeed so, provided that the literal sense [of the names] is not possible.
However, it is possible that even in the case of the injunction by the seers (*ṛṣi*), it may be taken according to the literal text, as is the case with other scriptural passages (*śruti*).
Therefore, they call this very [breath] "the Seer of the Hundred Verses" (*śatarcin*), though he is indeed [the breath];
likewise, the scripture brings about the seers themselves—such as Mādhyma, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, and so forth—as the vital breath.

In the same way, he makes these sages—the Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, and Ayāsya—who are worshippers of the vital breath (prāṇa), into the vital breath itself for the sake of realizing their non-difference, just as in the passage, "The vital breath is indeed the father; the vital breath is the mother," and so forth. Therefore, the sage named Aṅgiras, being the vital breath itself, meditated upon himself as the Aṅgirasa vital breath, the Udgītha.
Since he is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the limbs and their essence (*rasa*), he is therefore called *Āṅgirasa*.
Therefore, Bṛhaspati meditated upon that Udgītha.
Indeed, they consider him to be Bṛhaspati;
for Vāk is the Great (Bṛhatī), and he is her lord (pati).
Therefore, he meditated upon that Udgītha as Āyāsya;
for they consider him indeed to be Āyāsya,
because he issues forth from the mouth (āsya).

Likewise, because he is the lord (*pati*) of the great (*bṛhatī*) speech, he is Bṛhaspati. Because he issues forth (*ayate*) from the mouth (*āsya*), he is the seer Āyāsya; the meaning is that he is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Similarly, another worshipper should meditate upon the self as the Udgītha—the vital breath endowed with qualities such as being Aṅgiras and so forth.
By means of this [knowledge], Baka Dālbhya came to know him.
He became the Udgātṛ priest for the residents of Naimiṣa;
he used to obtain their desires by means of chanting.
It was not only Aṅgiras and the others who paid homage to him;
Baka by name, the son of Dalbhya—known as Dālbhya—also came to know that Prāṇa exactly as it had been shown.
Having known it, he became the Udgātṛ priest for the performers of the sacrificial session (sattra) at Naimiṣa.
And by the power of his knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa), he sang forth desires for these people of Naimiṣa; "he sang" means, it is said, that he indeed performed the singing.
"Verily, one becomes an attainer of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable as the Udgītha; this is with reference to the self."

Likewise, another who knows this also becomes a singer of the Udgītha who indeed attains his desires—he who, knowing thus, meditates upon the syllable *akṣara* as the Udgītha characterized by the qualities already mentioned. This aforementioned result is its visible fruit;
however, its invisible fruit—namely, "having become a god, he goes to the gods"—is established by other scriptural passages (*śruti*). Such is the intention.

This concludes the meditation on the Udgītha with reference to the self (*adhyātma*), which concerns the individual soul; this summary is intended to focus the mind for the meditation on the Udgītha with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*) that is about to be described.
Thus ends the second section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now, with respect to the deities:
one should meditate upon that very sun which shines as the Udgītha.
Rising up, he sings the Udgītha for the sake of all creatures;
rising up, he drives away darkness and fear.
Indeed, he who knows this becomes a dispeller of fear and darkness.

Immediately thereafter, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the deities—that is, having the deities as its object—is introduced for the purpose of showing that the *udgītha* is to be meditated upon in many ways, because it is to be meditated upon in various forms. "That which is yonder sun which shines—one should meditate upon that as the *udgītha*" means that one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the sun. To the question, "Since the word *udgītha* denotes a syllable, how can it apply to the sun?", it is said in reply: [The text continues: "He who knows this, even if he should be standing in the midst of a great forest, becomes fearless; he stands as one who has reached the highest light. [This is] the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the self—that is, having the self as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the vital breath. "He who knows this, even if his head should be struck off, his head is not struck off," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to speech—that is, having speech as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as speech," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of speech. "He who knows this, even if his speech should be cut off, his speech is not cut off," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to fire—that is, having fire as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as fire," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of fire. "He who knows this, even if his house should burn down, his house is not burned down," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the earth—that is, having the earth as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the earth," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the earth. "He who knows this, even if his earth should be taken away, his earth is not taken away," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the body—that is, having the body as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the body," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the body. "He who knows this, even if his body should be struck, his body is not struck," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the right eye—that is, having the right eye as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the right eye," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the right eye. "He who knows this, even if his right eye should be struck, his right eye is not struck," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the left eye—that is, having the left eye as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the left eye," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the left eye. "He who knows this, even if his left eye should be struck, his left eye is not struck," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the ether—that is, having the ether as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the ether," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the ether. "He who knows this, even if his ether should be pierced, his ether is not pierced," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the water—that is, having water as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as water," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of water. "He who knows this, even if his water should be drunk up, his water is not drunk up," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the food—that is, having food as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as food," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of food. "He who knows this, even if his food should be exhausted, his food is not exhausted," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the sound—that is, having sound as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as sound," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of sound. "He who knows this, even if his sound should be destroyed, his sound is not destroyed," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the mind—that is, having the mind as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the mind," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the mind. "He who knows this, even if his mind should be distracted, his mind is not distracted," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the intellect—that is, having the intellect as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the intellect," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the intellect. "He who knows this, even if his intellect should be confounded, his intellect is not confounded," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the seed—that is, having the seed as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the seed," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the seed. "He who knows this, even if his seed should be lost, his seed is not lost," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the offspring—that is, having offspring as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as offspring," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of offspring. "He who knows this, even if his offspring should perish, his offspring is not destroyed," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the progenitor—that is, having the progenitor as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the progenitor," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the progenitor. "He who knows this, even if his progenitor should die, his progenitor is not dead," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the self—that is, having the self as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as the self," meaning one should meditate upon the *udgītha* by means of the vision of the self. "He who knows this, even if his self should be struck, his self is not struck," etc.; this is the reward for the meditation on the *udgītha*. Now, the meditation on the *udgītha* with reference to the space between—that is, having the space between as its object—is introduced. "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*
Rising or ascending, he sings the Udgītha for the sake of creatures—that is, for the purpose of producing food for creatures.
For if he were not rising, there would be no ripening of rice and other grains; therefore, he "sings the Udgītha," as it were.
Just as the Udgātṛ priest sings for the sake of food, so too is the Sun the Udgītha; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, he who knows the Sun— who dispels the nocturnal darkness and the fear born from it for living beings—
indeed becomes a dispeller, a destroyer, of fear characterized by birth, death, and so forth, as well as of the darkness that is its cause, namely ignorance.
This one here and that one yonder are indeed the same:
this is warm, and that is warm.
They call this one "sound" (svara), and they call that one "echo" (pratyāsvara).
Therefore, one should indeed meditate upon this Udgītha and that [Udgītha].
Although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the sun (*āditya*) appear as if distinct due to the difference in their locations, nevertheless there is no difference in their essential nature (*tattva*).
How so? Because the vital breath is indeed the same as, that is, equal to, the sun in its qualities, and the sun is equal to the vital breath;
for this vital breath is warm, and the sun is also warm.
Furthermore, they call this breath "svara" (sound), meaning they speak of it as such;
and they call that sun "pratyāsvara" (the one who sounds back).
For the breath indeed "sounds forth" (svarati) and does not return once it has died.
Savitṛ, having set, returns again day after day;
therefore, on account of this quality as well as their names, Prāṇa and Āditya are similar to one another.
Thus, because there is no difference in their true nature, one should meditate upon this Prāṇa and that Āditya as the Udgītha.
Now, one should indeed meditate upon the vyāna breath as the udgītha. That which one breathes out is the prāṇa; that which one breathes in is the apāna.
Now, that which is the junction of the out-breath and the in-breath is the diffused breath;
that which is the diffused breath is speech.
Therefore, one utters speech without breathing out and without breathing in.

Now, indeed, in another manner, the meditation on the *udgītha* is being stated: one should meditate upon the *udgītha* as *vyāna* itself—that specific function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose characteristics will be described hereafter.

Now its true nature is being defined: when a person breathes out (*prāṇiti*), expelling air from the mouth and nose, that specific function of the wind called *prāṇa*; and when he breathes in (*apāniti*), drawing air inward through those same two [openings], that is [the function of *apāna*]. It is this [combined function]...
"Prāṇa" is the function designated as "out-breathing.
To the question "What follows from that?", it is said: now, that specific function which exists between prāṇa and apāna—those two whose characteristics have been described—is vyāna.
The intention is that what is well-known from the Sāṅkhya and other treatises is not this Vyāna, because its specific nature is defined by the Śruti.

But why, setting aside Prāṇa and Apāna, is the meditation on Vyāna alone enjoined with such great effort? It is because it is the cause of efficacious action; thus it says: "That which is Vyāna is speech."
Because speech is the effect of vyāna:
since speech is brought about by vyāna, therefore people utter—that is, pronounce—speech without breathing in or breathing out, that is, without performing the functions of prāṇa and apāna.
Speech is the *ṛc*; therefore, even while not breathing in or out, one utters the *ṛc*. That which is the *ṛc* is the *sāman*.
Therefore, one sings the Sāman without breathing in or breathing out.
That which is the Sāman is the Udgītha;
therefore, one chants the Udgītha without breathing in or breathing out.

The intention is that one accomplishes a specific speech-form as a Ṛc, the Sāman residing within the Ṛc, and the Udgītha which is a limb of the Sāman, by means of the vyāna alone, without breathing out or breathing in.
Therefore, whatever other vigorous actions there are—such as the churning of fire, the running in a race, or the drawing of a firm bow—one performs them without breathing in or breathing out.
For this reason, one should meditate upon vyāna itself as the udgītha.

Not only does he perform the utterance of speech and so forth from this [breath], but also other vigorous actions that are accomplished through a great effort— such as the churning of fire, running across a boundary, and the drawing back of a firm bow— he performs these without breathing out or breathing in.
Therefore, the *vyāna* is superior to the functions of *prāṇa* and the others;
meditation upon that which is superior is better because it yields fruit, like the worship of a king.
For this reason and for this cause, one should meditate upon the *vyāna* alone as the *udgītha*, and not upon any other function.
The fruit is the state of being more intensely endowed with the vigor of karma.
Now, indeed, one should meditate upon the syllables of the Udgītha as "Udgītha. The syllable *ut* is breath itself,
for by means of breath one rises up (*uttiṣṭhati*).
*Vāk* is *gīḥ*; for they call speech *giraḥ*. *Anna* is *tham*.
For by food indeed all this is sustained.

Now, one should indeed meditate upon the syllables of the *udgītha*, lest they be taken merely as the syllables of the word "bhakti. Therefore, he specifies them as "the *udgītha*," meaning the syllables of the name *udgītha*. Even when meditating on the syllables of a name, it is effectively meditation on the possessor of the name, just as in the case of saying, "Amuka-miśra. In the syllable *ut* of *udgītha*, one should perceive the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

How is the *udgītha* the breath (*prāṇa*)? He says: for everyone rises by means of the breath, since one observes the collapse of that which is breathless; therefore, there is a commonality between the *udgītha* and the breath.
Speech is the *gī*. For the learned call speech "the *gī*s."
Likewise, all this is established upon food; therefore, there is a similarity between food and the syllable *tha*.
Heaven is indeed the *ut*,
the intermediate space is the *gīḥ*,
and the earth is the *tham*.
Āditya is the *ut*;
Vāyu is the *gīḥ*;
Agni is the *tham*.
The Sāmaveda is indeed the *ut*;
the Yajurveda is the *gīḥ*;
the Ṛgveda is the *tham*.
Speech yields its milk for him who knows the milking of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food—
he who, knowing them thus, meditates upon these syllables of the Udgītha as "Udgī-tha."
The common characteristics declared by the Śruti for these three should, by that same analogy, be understood to apply to the remaining ones as well:
the sky is [the first], because it is situated high up; the intermediate space is [the second], O Gārgī, because it is the middle of the worlds.
The earth is [the syllable] *tha* because it is the support for living beings;
the sun is *u* because of its upwardness;
and the wind is *gī* because it swallows fire and the other elements.
The *Agni* [Veda] is so called because it abides in the sacrificial rites;
the *Sāmaveda* alone is so called because it is praised as heaven itself;
and the *Yajurveda* is so called because the gods swallow the oblation offered with the *yajus* formulas.

Because the Sāman rests upon the Ṛk contained in the Ṛgveda, the fruit of the meditation on the syllables of the Udgītha is now stated: "It yields for this practitioner"—for what [practitioner], and what milk? What is that Speech (vāk), and what is the milk (doha)?
What is this "milking"? It is the milking of speech;
the intention is that the fruit to be accomplished by the words of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth is the milking of speech. That milking of speech milks itself—it milks its own self.
Furthermore, one becomes possessed of food, having abundant food, and an eater of food, with a stimulated digestive fire.
He who, being a knower, thus meditates upon these syllables of the Udgītha as possessing the qualities just described, [meditates] on the Udgītha.
Now, indeed, there is the fulfillment of one's wishes.
One should perform the approach-rites;
one should attend upon that *sāman* with which one intends to chant the praise.
Now, indeed, this is stated so that there may be the fulfillment of blessings—the fulfillment of one's desires; such is the remainder of the sentence.
"Approaches" (upasaraṇāni) means those which are to be approached, to be resorted to, or meditated upon. How? One should worship (upāsīta) in this manner.

One should meditate in this manner: for instance, with whatever *sāman* or specific *sāman* the Udgātṛ priest is about to praise—that is, perform a hymn of praise—he should approach that *sāman*, draw near to it, and contemplate it through its origin and other such characteristics.
One should mentally approach that *ṛc* in which [the verse occurs],
that *ṛṣi* who is its seer (*ārṣeya*),
and that deity whom one intends to praise.
One should meditate upon that Ṛc in which the Sāman occurs by means of its deity and other attributes; one should meditate upon that Ṛṣi to whom the Sāman belongs;
and one should meditate upon that deity whom one intends to praise.
With whatever *chandas* one intends to praise, one should meditate upon that *chandas*; with whatever *stoma* one is about to praise, one should meditate upon that *stoma*.
One should meditate upon that *chandas* (meter), such as the *gāyatrī* and others, by means of which one intends to praise;
and upon that *stoma* (hymn-form) by means of which one will be praising.
The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the word "stoṣyamāṇaḥ" (intending to praise) is because the fruit of the subsidiary part of the *stoma* accrues to the agent.
One should run toward that hymn of praise.
Toward whichever direction one intends to offer praise, toward that direction one should run.
One should run toward whichever direction one intends to praise, [approaching it] with the presiding deities and so forth.
Having approached the Self at the very end, one should praise it while meditating on the desired object with vigilance.

Indeed, that desire for which one praises will quickly be fulfilled for him—for whatever desire one praises, for that desire it shall be so, for whatever desire one praises, for that desire it shall be so.

The Udgātṛ priest, having approached himself—his own form—by means of his lineage, name, and so forth, in due order, and finally approaching himself at the very end, should chant the Sāman and other hymns.

Meditating on his desire and remaining vigilant, not committing any error regarding the vowels, sibilants, consonants, and so on, then, for one who knows thus, that desire will quickly indeed reach fulfillment; it will attain success.
Who is this person? He is "one who has a desire" (yatkāmaḥ), meaning he is one for whom there is a desire; being such a person, he should praise.
The repetition is for the sake of showing respect.
Thus ends the third section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon this syllable "Om" as the Udgītha;
for one begins the chanting with "Om."
This is its further explanation.

The repetition of the syllable *akṣara* introduced at the beginning with "Om, this... is for the purpose of ensuring that the subject does not shift elsewhere due to being interrupted by other meditations on the syllables of the *udgītha*.
This section begins in order to enjoin the meditation on the very same *akṣara* as previously introduced, characterized by the qualities of immortality and fearlessness.
The passage beginning with "Om" has already been explained.
The gods, fearing death, entered the threefold knowledge;
they covered themselves with the meters.
Because they covered themselves with these, that is the "metrical" nature (*chandastva*) of the meters.
It is said what the gods did when they were afraid of death, the destroyer:
they entered the threefold knowledge—that is, the action prescribed by the three Vedas; the meaning is that they undertook Vedic ritual action, considering that to be a protection from death.
Furthermore, by performing recitations, oblations, and so forth with those meters and mantras not assigned to specific ritual acts, they concealed themselves within other rites;
because they concealed [themselves] with these mantras, the status of the meters as *chandas* (concealers) is indeed well-established.
Thereupon Death beheld them, just as one might see a fish in water, within the *Ṛgveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, and the *Yajurveda*.
Having discovered them, they rose above the *Ṛgveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, and the *Yajurveda*, and entered into the very tone (*svara*) itself.

There, Death beheld those gods devoted to ritual action, just as in the world a fisherman might see a fish in water that is not very deep, considering it capable of being caught by means of a hook and a flow of water; in this way, Death perceived—that is, saw—the gods as beings who could be overcome through the means of exhausting their merit. This is the meaning.
"Where did he see those gods? It is said: "In the Ṛk, the Sāman, and the Yajus"—meaning in the ritual acts connected with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Those gods, purified by Vedic ritual and being of cleansed soul, came to know what Death intended to do.
Having understood this, they turned away from ritual acts—that is, they rose up above the *Ṛg*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus* verses, as well as the rites connected with them.

Despairing of attaining freedom from the fear of death through those rituals, they cast them aside and entered—indeed, they had already entered—the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which possesses the qualities of immortality and fearlessness, and which is "Sound" (*svara*), denoted by the word *svara*.
They became devoted to the meditation upon the syllable *Oṃ*.
The word *eva* (indeed), being used for the purpose of restriction, serves to exclude conjunction;
the meaning is that they became intent upon the meditation on that [Brahman].
When one encounters a *ṛc*, one utters "Om" as its over-tone; likewise for the *sāman* and likewise for the *yajus*.
This very syllable is the tone (*svara*), which is immortal and fearless.
Having entered that, the gods became immortal.

How, then, is it said that the syllable (akṣara) is denoted by the word "sound" (svara)? When one encounters a Ṛg-verse, one utters "Om" as its over-tone; likewise for a Sāman and likewise for a Yajus.

This indeed is the sound (svara). What is this? It is this very syllable (akṣara), which is immortal and fearless. Having entered into that, the gods became, according to their respective qualities, immortal and fearless.
He who, knowing it thus, utters this syllable, enters this very syllable—the sound, the immortal, the fearless.
Having entered it, he becomes immortal, even as the gods are immortal.
Whoever else, like a god, knowing this syllable to have such qualities as immortality and fearlessness, praises it— that is,
offers worship to it (for "praise" here intends worship)—
he likewise enters this very syllable, which is sound, immortal, and fearless.

And having entered that royal palace, he does not become superior to those who have already entered—just as there is no distinction between the inner and outer circles of a king's attendants—nor is there any deficiency, nor any excess; the meaning is that his immortality remains exactly as it was.
Thus ends the fourth section of the first chapter in Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha.
Verily, yonder sun is the Udgītha, and he is the Praṇava.
For he goes forth sounding "Om."

Having restated the meditation on the *udgītha* as qualified by the vision of it being the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the sun, and having established the identity of the *praṇava* and the *udgītha*, the following section is now commenced to explain the meditation on the syllable (*akṣara*)—qualified by the vision of its distinction from the rays of the vital breath—which yields the fruit of many sons:
"Now, indeed, that which is the *udgītha* is the *praṇava* of the Bahvṛcas; and that which is the *praṇava* of them [the Bahvṛcas]..."
That very same [deity] is denoted by the word *udgītha* in the *Chāndogya*:
"Verily, that sun is the *udgītha*. He is also the one denoted by the word *praṇava* for the followers of the *Bahvṛca* [Ṛgveda], and none other.
How is it that the *udgītha* is the sun?
The syllable *oṃ* known as the *udgītha*— for this very reason, because he, while singing (*svaran*),
utters it; or alternatively, because he goes (*gacchan*) while singing (*svaran*)— therefore, this *udgītha* is the Sun (*savitṛ*).
"It was precisely this that I meditated upon; therefore you are my only son," Kauṣītaki said to his son.
"You must turn [the horse] toward the rays;
then indeed many sons shall be yours."
Thus with reference to the deities.

"I have approached this very one," that is, I have sung toward it face-to-face; the meaning is that I have performed meditation by effecting the non-differentiation of the solar rays [from the Sun]. For that reason, "you alone are my son," thus said Kauṣītaki—the offspring of Kuṣītaka—to his son.
Therefore, "you should turn around the rays and the Sun separately"; the meaning is: "turn them around."
"By virtue of you, thus indeed shall many sons be yours"— this is with reference to the deities.
Now, with reference to the self: one should meditate upon that very vital breath which is the chief as the *udgītha*.
For it moves along sounding "Om."
Immediately thereafter, the internal [meditation] is described:
"One should meditate upon that which is this primary vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgītha*," and so forth, as before.
Likewise, this vital breath goes along saying "Om"; for it is as if granting permission by saying "Om" for the sake of the functioning of speech and the other senses—this is the meaning of "it goes."
For those standing near a person about to die do not hear the utterance of the syllable *oṃ* by the departing breath;
on account of this similarity, the utterance of *oṃ* in the case of the sun should be regarded as a mere formal permission.
"It was precisely this that I sang to; therefore, you are my only one," thus Kauṣītaki said to his son.
"Sing to the breaths as the plurality, for then many indeed shall be mine."
"I have sung unto him alone," and so forth, as before.

Therefore, perceiving speech and the other organs, as well as the principal breath (prāṇa), as the Udgītha distinguished by its specific qualities, one should sing with the mind to the Infinite (bhūman).
The meaning is: "Repeat [the meditation] as before."
The meaning is that he has the intention, "Indeed, many sons shall be mine.

Since the meditation on the Udgītha as the identity of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the sun—which yields the fruit of having only one son—has been set aside as a defect, the necessity of performing the meditation on the distinction between the rays and the vital breaths is enjoined in this section for the sake of the fruit of having many sons.
Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha.
For from the seat of the Hotṛ priest, he indeed rectifies even a poorly performed Udgītha—yes, he rectifies it.

Now, indeed, this result can be brought about for one who has realized the identity of the *praṇava* and the *udgītha*, as stated in the passage beginning with "That which is the *udgītha*" and so forth.

What is that? Even if the *udgīta*—the singing performed by the *udgātṛ* priest—is "badly sung" (*durudgīta*), meaning his own ritual action has been flawed or injured, he "restores" (*anusamāharati*) it;
that is to say, he repairs it.
Just as medical treatment brings about the restoration of equilibrium when there is a disorder of the bodily constituents.
Thus ends the fifth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: This [earth] indeed is the Ṛg;
fire is the Sāman.
This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc.
This [earth] itself is that [Sāman].
Agni is the unassailable;
that is the Sāman.
Now, for the sake of attaining all fruits, another meditation on the *udgītha* is intended to be taught: this very earth is the *ṛc*;
one should perceive the earth as the *ṛc*.
Likewise, fire is the *sāman*.
The view of fire upon the *sāman*:
how is it that earth and fire possess the nature of *ṛc* and *sāman*? It is said in reply:
This very thing, this very Sāman called "Agni," is situated upon this earth as its *ṛc*— that is to say, it exists in a superior position over it,
just as the Sāman rests upon the *ṛc*.
For this very reason, even now, the Sāman is sung by the chanters of the Sāman as being supported by the *ṛc*.
And just as the *ṛc* and the *sāman* are not absolutely distinct from one another, so too these two—the earth and fire—have attained the status of being denoted by the single term "Sāman.
Therefore, the pair of earth and fire is not distinct from each other, being eternally conjoined like the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
And for this reason, the meaning is that the earth and fire possess the nature of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
Some maintain that this [mantra], "This indeed is she; Agni is he," is intended for the injunction of viewing the *sāma* and the syllables as the earth and fire, respectively.
The intermediate space is indeed the *ṛc*,
and the wind is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The intermediate space itself is the Sāman;
the wind is the Ama.
That is the Sāman.
The sky indeed is the Ṛg;
the sun is the Sāman.
Thus, this Sāman is supported upon that Ṛg.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The sky is indeed the Sāman;
the sun is the Am.
That is the Sāman.
"The intermediate space is the Ṛg, the wind is the Sāman," and so forth, as before.
The stars are the *ṛc*,
the moon is the *sāman*;
thus this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The stars are the Sāman;
the moon is the Āma.
That is the Sāman.
The moon is the lord of the stars; therefore, it is the Sāman.
Now, that which is the white light of the sun is the *ṛc*;
and that which is the blue, the exceedingly black, is the *sāman*.
This *sāman* is thus supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as being superimposed upon the Ṛc.
Now, that which is the white light, the white radiance of the sun, is the *Ṛk*.
And that which is the blue, the exceedingly black—meaning the extreme darkness—within the sun, is the *Sāman*;
for that is seen by one whose vision is perfectly concentrated.
Now, that which is the white light of this sun is indeed *sā*;
and that which is the blue, the exceedingly black, is *amaḥ*.
That is *sāman*.
Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, is entirely golden down to his very fingernails.
These two are indeed light (*bhās*) and shadow; that is *āma* and this is *sāman*.
Now, that which is within the sun—within the midst of the sun—is golden, as it were;
for it is not possible for the Lord to be an actual modification of gold.
Because [the qualities of] being the source of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajur-veda, and being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva) are impossible [in the sun];

for there is no possibility of the sun, which is golden and insentient, being subject to evil or the like such that it would need to be denied; and because [these qualities] are not perceived in the visual [sun].

Therefore, the word *hiraṇmaya* is indeed an elided simile (*luptopamā*), meaning "consisting of light" (*jyotirmaya*). The same application [of this interpretation] holds for the subsequent terms as well.
[The term] *puruṣa* [is so called] because he dwells in the city (*puri-śayana*) or because he fills the world with his own self.
He is seen by those whose eyes have turned away [from the external] and whose minds are concentrated, depending on the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth.
Since even for one who is radiant, the beard, hair, and other features might be dark, he specifies: "with golden beard, with golden hair.
The meaning is that his beard and hair consist of light itself.
From the very tips of the nails—meaning including the nails themselves, along with the extremities of the nails—the whole [body] is like gold, which means it is of the nature of light.
His eyes are like a lotus flower that is as yellow as a monkey's buttocks;
his name is "Ut" (the Arisen),
for he has risen above all evils.
He who knows this indeed rises above all evils.
Although he was thus entirely golden-colored, there was a specific feature regarding his eyes.
How so? His *kapyāsa*—the word *kapyāsa* being derived from *kapin* (a monkey) and *āsa* (the buttocks)—refers to the buttocks (*āsa*) of a monkey (*kapi*).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the root *ās*, which means "to sit."
The edge of the monkey’s back is where he sits;
his two eyes are like a lotus flower (*puṇḍarīka*) that has emerged from the monkey’s anus, being exceedingly radiant.
Because it is a comparison using a comparison, it is not a "deficient simile" (*hīnopamā*).

This is the secondary name of that very one who is distinguished by such qualities. How is it secondary? This god is [called "Ud"] because he has risen (*udita*) from all evils—that is to say, together with evil and its effects.
That which he will describe as "the Self free from evil" and so forth;
"udita" means risen or emerged;
therefore, his name is "Ud."
He who knows that very Uddālaka, endowed with such qualities, in the manner described, likewise rises up—indeed, he rises up—from all evils.
The two particles *ha* and *vā* are indeclinables used for emphasis;
the meaning is "he certainly rises up."
The Ṛk and the Sāman are his two singers;
therefore he is the Udgītha,
and for that very reason, the Udgātṛ priest.
For he is the singer of this [Sāman];
he is the lord of those worlds which are beyond that [sun] and of the desires of the gods.
Thus far with respect to the divine.

Since it is intended to show that this deity possesses the nature of the *udgītha*—just as [the qualities] of Āditya and others are intended [in other contexts]—the text says: "The *ṛk* and the *sāman* are his two joints (*geṣṇau*)," meaning the two sections characterized as earth and so forth.
For the deity is the self of all;
because he is the lord of the higher and lower worlds and of all desires, his having the earth, fire, *ṛk*, and *sāman* as his joints is logical.
And because it is the source of all;

since it is thus named and has the *ṛk* and *sāman* as its essence, therefore the state of being the *udgītha*—which follows from having the *ṛk* and *sāman* as its essence—is stated figuratively, because the God loves what is indirect; hence it is called the *udgītha*.
For that same reason, he sings "out" (*ud*) and "sings" (*gāyati*), and is thus the *udgātṛ*.
Because he is the singer (*gātṛ*) of this aforementioned "High Name" (*unnāman*), the designation "Udgātṛ" (the High Chanting Priest) is appropriately established for him.

This very deity, the "High Name," rules over those worlds which are higher than and beyond that Āditya—those worlds which go upward (*parāñcaḥ*) by virtue of their ascending nature—and not only does he rule them, but according to the word "and" (*ca*), he also sustains them, as stated in the mantra passage: "He has supported the earth and this heaven."
Furthermore, "he desires the objects of the gods"—this has been stated as the *adhidaivata*, the nature of the deity, with respect to the divine Udgītha.
Thus ends the sixth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now, with respect to the self:
Speech indeed is the Ṛk.
The breath is the Sāman.
This Sāman is thus supported upon this Ṛk;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛk.
Speech indeed is the *sā*,
breath is the *ama*;
that is the *sāman*.
Now, the internal [correspondence] is being stated:
Speech is the *ṛc* and breath is the *sāman*,
because of the commonality of their respective positions as lower and upper.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*), together with the wind (*vāyu*), is called the sense of smell;
speech itself is that *prāṇa*, "Ama," and so forth, as before.
The eye is indeed the Ṛg;
the self is the Sāman. Thus, this Sāman is supported upon this Ṛg.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The eye is indeed the Sāman; the self is the Ṛc.
That is the Sāman.
The eye itself is the *ṛc*, and the *sāman* is the self;
the "self" here refers to the shadow-self (*chāyātman*), for it is the *sāman* because it abides therein.
The ear is indeed the Ṛg,
and the mind is the Sāman;
thus this Sāman is supported upon this Ṛg.
Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being superimposed upon the *ṛc*.
The ear indeed is the *sā*, and the mind is the *ama*.
That is the Sāman.
The ear is indeed the Ṛg and the mind is the Sāman;
because the ear is the presiding authority over the mind, the mind possesses the nature of the Sāman.
Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the *ṛc*;
and that which is the dark, exceedingly black [light] is the *sāman*.
This *sāman* is thus supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as resting upon the *ṛc*. Now, that which is the white light of the eye is indeed the *sāman*;
and that which is blue-black is the *ama*.
That is the Sāman.
Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the Ṛg;
and that which is the dark, the deep black, like the sun—the locus of the power of sight—that is the Sāman.
Now, that person who is seen within the eye— he is indeed the Ṛg,
he is the Sāman, he is the Uktha.
That is the Yajus;
that is the Brahman. Of this very [Brahman], its form is the same as the form of that [sun].
Whatever are its two joints, those are the two joints;
whatever is its name, that is the name.
Now, as before, that person who is seen within the eye—
he is indeed the Ṛgveda, internally as speech and so forth, and externally as the earth and so forth.
Furthermore, it is well known that the *ṛc* consists of syllables bound into quarters;
likewise the *sāman*.
Or, by association with the *uktha*, the *sāman* is the *stotra*, while the *uktha* is the *śastra*.
Other than the *uktha*, as well as the *yajus*—including *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, and so forth—all speech is indeed *yajus*, and that is He alone.
For we have already stated that this is because He is the self of all and the source of all.
Since the context concerns the *ṛc* and the rest, "that Brahman" refers to the three Vedas.
The very form of this person in the eye is extended [to the other]—
that which belongs to that person in the sun,
beginning with "golden" and so forth, as was described in the context of the deities (adhidaivata).
Whatever are the two *geṣṇas* (places of singing) and the two joints (*parvan*) of that [Āditya], those very same are the two *geṣṇas* of this [Cākṣuṣa] as well;
and whatever is its name, "the Unfading" (*nādat*) and "the Udgītha," that indeed is its name.

If it is argued that there is a distinction between Āditya and Cākṣuṣa because of the difference in location, the transfer of form, qualities, and name, and the designation of a difference in their spheres of lordship (*īśitṛtva*), we say no.
Because it is impossible for a single entity to attain both natures by means of this very [act] or that [act].
If it is argued that it is possible through a twofold division, [we reply: no;
for he will state later, "He becomes onefold, he becomes threefold," and so forth. It is not so.
Because a single conscious entity, being partless, cannot logically undergo division,
there is therefore absolute identity between the internal (ādhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata).
As for the extension of form and other attributes that you mentioned as a cause for distinction, that is not intended to establish a difference.
Rather, it is for this purpose: so that no suspicion of difference might arise due to the difference in location.
He is the one who rules over those worlds that are on this side of him, and over the desires of men.
Therefore, when these people sing to the lute, they sing to him; hence they are winners of wealth.
This very person who is in the eye exercises control over those worlds that are below this internal self and have gone downward, as well as over the desires pertaining to human beings.

Therefore, when these singers sing upon the lute, they sing of him alone. Because they sing of the Lord, they are "winners of wealth"—meaning they are endowed with the acquisition of wealth, that is, they become wealthy.
Now, he who, knowing this thus, sings the Sāman, sings with both [worlds].
By that very [upper world], he attains those worlds which are beyond it, as well as the desires of the gods.
Now, he who, knowing this thus, knowing the aforementioned deity as the Udgītha, sings the Sāman—he sings both the one belonging to the eye and the one belonging to the sun.

The fruit for such a knower is stated: by means of that very sun, he attains those worlds which are beyond it; the meaning is that, having become the deity residing within the sun, he also attains the desires of the gods.
Furthermore, by this very means he attains those worlds that are on this side of it, as well as the desires of human beings;
therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows this should say:
"What desire shall I sing forth for you?
For he who, knowing this, sings the Sāman, is indeed capable of singing forth desires; he who sings the Sāman [is so capable].
Furthermore, by means of this very eye, he attains those worlds that are below it, as well as the desires of human beings; the meaning is that he becomes one who possesses the eye.

Therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows this should say to the sacrificer: "What desire of yours shall I bring forth through my singing? For this reason, the Udgātṛ is able—that is, capable—of accomplishing a desire through his singing by means of the *udgītha*.
Who is he? He who, knowing thus, sings the Sāman—sings the Sāman.
The repetition is intended to mark the completion of the meditation.
Thus ends the seventh section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"Now there were three who were skilled in the Udgītha: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, and Pravāhaṇa Jaibali.
They said, 'We are indeed skilled in the Udgītha; come, let us have a discussion regarding the Udgītha.'"
