Because the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be meditated upon in many ways, the text introduces another meditation with the fruit being the quality of being "higher than the high" (parovarīyastva) by means of a different method;
the historical narrative (itihāsa), however, is for the purpose of easy comprehension.
"Three" refers to the number three.
"Ha"—this is the meaning of the traditional report (aitihya). They became skilled and proficient in the Udgītha, that is, in the knowledge of the Udgītha.
The intention is that they were so when they had gathered together at a certain place, time, or occasion.
For it is not the case that in the entire world only three possess skill in the knowledge of the *udgītha* and so forth;
for Uṣasti, Jānaśruti, Kaikeya, and others are heard of as being almost omniscient.
As to who those three were, he says: Śālāvatya is by name Śilaka, the descendant of Śalāvat.
Caikitāyana is the descendant of Cikitāyana;
Dālbhya belongs to the lineage of Dalbha, or is a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (belonging to two lineages);
Pravāhaṇa by name is the descendant of Jīvala, thus Jaivali—these three said to one another, "We are indeed renowned as being skilled and proficient in the *udgītha*."

Therefore, "come now! If you have permission, let us discuss the Udgītha"—that is to say, let us engage in a formal debate (*vāda*) consisting of the presentation of arguments and counter-arguments based on knowledge of the Udgītha.
For in such a discussion with one who possesses that knowledge, there occurs the destruction of erroneous graspings, the arising of new understanding, and the cessation of doubt;
thus, association with one who possesses that knowledge must be undertaken—this is the purpose of the narrative.
For it is indeed seen in the case of Śilāka and others.
"So be it," they replied, and sat down together.
Then Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said,
"Let your honors speak first."
"I shall listen to the words of the two wandering mendicants as they speak."
Having said, "So be it," they sat down together; indeed, they had already taken their seats.
There, because of the king's audacity, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to the other two: "May your honors, the venerable ones, speak first.
From the use of the term "brāhmaṇau" (the two Brāhmaṇas), it is clear that this person was a king.
"I shall listen to the speech of you two Brahmins as you speak"—
others say this implies "speech devoid of meaning," because of the specific qualification "speech."
Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya, "Come, let me question you.
"Ask," he replied.
When these two had spoken, Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya, "Come now, if you will permit me, I would ask you a question. Being thus addressed, the other said, "Ask.
[Śilaka] asked, "What is the goal of the Sāman?
He replied, "The voice (svara)."
"What is the goal of sound?
"Breath," he said.
"What is the goal of food?"
"Food," he said.
"What is the goal of food?
"Water," he said.
Having obtained permission, he said: "Of what [is this the meditation]? Because of the context, it is of the *udgītha*;
for here the *udgītha* is the subject under discussion as the object of meditation.
And he will later say, "The udgītha is higher than the high. "Gati" means support or refuge;
thus questioned, Dālbhya said, "It is sound (svara)."
Because the Sāman consists of tone (*svara*), it is logical that whatever constitutes its essence is also its course and its support—just as a jar or similar object has clay as its support.
[The question arises: "What is the course of tone?"
"It is breath," he said.
"For the *svara* (vowel) is produced by breath; therefore, breath is the destination of the *svara*.
What is the destination of breath? "It is food," he said.
For life-force (prāṇa) has food as its support;
for there is a scriptural statement: "Life-force indeed withers without food," and also, "Food is the bond."
"What is the destination of food? "Water," he said;
for food originates from water.
"What is the goal of the waters?
"That world," he said.
"What is the goal of that world?"
"It would not lead one to the heavenly world," he said.
"We establish the Sāman upon the heavenly world;
for the Sāman is a hymn of praise directed toward heaven."
"What is the goal of the waters? "That world," he replied. "From that world, rain comes into being.
When asked, "What is the goal of that world? Dālbhya said: "No one should lead the Sāman beyond that heavenly world to another support," he said.
Therefore, we too establish the Sāman upon the heavenly world;
the meaning is that we know the Sāman as being established in the heavenly world.

It is "svargasaṃstāvam," for its *saṃstāva*—its praise—is by way of the heaven; that is, the Sāman is praised as being the heaven itself. For there is a Vedic scripture stating: "The heavenly world is indeed the Sāmaveda."
Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya, "O Dālbhya, your Sāman is indeed without a foundation.
If someone were to say to you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would surely fall off."

The other, Śilaka Śālāvatya, said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "The Sāman, O Dālbhya, is indeed [as you say] unestablished, unstable, and its course not yet completed in terms of being 'higher than the high' (parovarīyas). The word "vā" serves to recall the traditional teaching, and "kila" indicates that this is what was reported.
"O Dālbhya, such is your Sāman."

However, if someone who is intolerant and ignorant of the *sāman* were to say at this time, "The *sāman* is not established; it is established [only] in a contrary way," then for that offender who speaks thus, his head shall fall off—it will clearly fall off.
When told this, the head of that offender would indeed fall off in that very manner; there is no doubt. But my intention is not that I am saying this.

Now, if one has committed an offense deserving of having one's head fall off, then one's head would fall even if not told by another; if one has not committed an offense, it does not fall even if told.
Otherwise, there would be both the arrival of what was not done and the destruction of what was done.
This is not a fault, because the attainment of the fruit of a performed action— whether auspicious or inauspicious— depends upon place, time, and causal conditions.
This being so, even ignorance, which is the cause for the falling from the summit [of existence], depends upon the condition of another's speech.
"Ah, let me learn this from the Blessed One!
"Learn it," he said.
"What is the goal of that world?"
"This world," he said. "What is the goal of this world?
"One should not lead [the sacrifice] beyond the world that is the foundation," he said.
We establish the world as the foundation through the Sāman;
for the Sāman is indeed the praise of the foundation.
Thus addressed, Dālbhya said, "I would like to know this from your reverence: on what is the Sāman established? Being thus addressed, Śālāvatya replied, "Know it.
When asked by Dālbhya, "What is the goal of that world? Śālāvatya said, "This world.
For this world nourishes that world through sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and so forth.
For the Vedic scriptures declare, "The gods subsist upon what is given from here.
Indeed, it is directly perceived that the earth is the foundation for all beings;
therefore, it is logical that this world is likewise the foundation of the Sāman.
When asked, "What is the goal of this world? Śālāvatya replied:
"No one can lead the *sāman* beyond this world, which is its foundation;
therefore, we establish the *sāman* upon the world as its foundation."
The meaning is that because the *pratiṣṭhā-saṃstava*—that is, the Sāman praised as a support—is indeed praised as a support;
for there is the Vedic revelation: "This [earth] is indeed the Rathantara."
Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him:
"O Śālāvatya, your Sāman is indeed finite.
If someone were to say to you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would indeed fall off."
"Come, let me learn this from the Blessed One.
"Learn it," he said.
To him who had spoken thus, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said, "O Śālāvatya, your Sāman indeed has an end," and so on as before.
Then Śālāvatya said, "Come now, let me learn this from your reverence. The other replied, "Know it," and being thus permitted, he spoke.
Thus ends the eighth section of the first chapter in Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "What is the goal of this world?
"Space," he replied.
Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone;
they dissolve back into space.
For space is indeed greater than them.
Space is the ultimate resort.
"What is the goal of this world?
"Space," Pravāhaṇa replied;
for space is the supreme Self, according to the Vedic scripture: "Space, indeed, is its name."
For its function is the production of all elements,
and within it alone is the dissolution of the elements.
It emitted that light.
For it will later state, "The fire [is merged] in the highest deity.
Indeed, all these beings, both stationary and moving, arise from space alone through the sequence of fire, water, food, and so forth, by implication.

They merge into space at the time of dissolution by that same reverse order; for since space alone is greater—meaning more extensive—than all these elements, it is therefore the supreme goal, the ultimate resort, and the foundation of all beings throughout the three periods of time. This is the meaning.
This is that Udgītha which is higher than the high;
it is infinite.
For one who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Udgītha as the higher than the high, there becomes a result higher than the high, and he conquers worlds that are higher than the high.

Because he is higher than the high, more excellent even than the excellent—meaning that this Udgītha, having become the Supreme Self (paramātman), is both the highest and the most excellent; therefore, he is infinite (ananta), having no end. One who knows him thus as the infinite, as the Supreme Self, and as the Parovarīyas Udgītha, meditates upon that very Parovarīyas Udgītha. Regarding his reward, it is said: "The life of this knower becomes higher than the high, increasingly excellent, and more distinguished."
There is a visible fruit and an invisible one: he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Udgītha, conquers worlds that are progressively more excellent, reaching up to the world of Brahman-Ākāśa.
Atidhanvā Śaunaka, having taught this very Udgītha to Udaraśāṇḍilya, said to him:
"As long as they shall know this Udgītha among their offspring, so long shall there be for them a superior life in this world."
Furthermore, having taught this Udgītha to his disciple Udara-Śāḍilya, Atidhanvan by name— the descendant of Śunaka, a Śaunaka— said: "As long as they shall know this Udgītha in your lineage—
that is, in the continuity of your progeny— for that long their life will be *parovarīyaḥ*, meaning increasingly more excellent than these well-known worldly lives."
Life shall come from them.
"Likewise, there is a world in yonder world.
For him who, knowing this, meditates upon it, his life in yonder world becomes even more excellent, and likewise there is a world in yonder world—yes, a world in yonder world.
Likewise, even though the next world is not seen, Atidhanvan Śaunaka said to Śāṇḍilya, "There will be a world hereafter that is progressively more excellent.

This might lead to the suspicion that such a fruit belongs only to those of great fortune in former times and not to people of the present age; therefore, to dispel this doubt, he says: "Whoever, knowing it thus, now meditates upon this Udgītha—for him too, in this very world, there shall be a world that is progressively more excellent."
In that same way, there is life in this world and in the world beyond—world after world.
Thus ends the ninth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
When the Kurus had been devastated by hailstorms, Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa lived as a wanderer in the village of the elephant-keepers together with his wife Āṭikī.
In connection with the meditation on the *udgītha*, it must also be stated that there is a meditation concerning the *prastāva* and the *pratīhāra*; therefore, this section is commenced.
The narrative is for the purpose of easy understanding.
"When the Kurus were struck by hailstones"—*maṭacī* means hailstones; "struck" means destroyed; thus, it refers to when the crops of the Kurus were ruined.

Then, when a famine had arisen, Uṣasti by name—the son of Cakra (Cākrāyaṇa)—was wandering about in the village of the wealthy (ibhyagrāma), destitute due to the lack of food; [the village] belonging to one who deserves an elephant (ibhya), that is, a lord of elephants or an elephant-keeper. [The word *ibhya* is derived from *ibha*, meaning "elephant," with the suffix *yat* indicating fitness. [The root *drā* is used here in the sense of "going" with the prefix of contempt (*kutsā*). He was accompanied by his wife, an old woman who had not yet developed the physical characteristics of a woman, such as breasts.
"Having gone to a miserable state" means having reached the final stage [of life]; "he dwelt" (uvāsa) means he lived, having taken refuge in someone's house.
He begged from him as he was eating some sour gruel.
He said to him,
"There are no others than these which have been set before me."

While wandering for food, he happened upon a man at the merchant's house eating—that is, consuming—some *kulmāṣas*, which are inferior beans; having found him by chance, he begged (*bibhikṣe*) from him.
The merchant said to that Uṣasti:
"There are no other *kulmāṣas* than these [beans] which are being eaten by me from this heap of leavings."
And when he was asked, "What shall I do with these which have been placed and deposited by you in my heap? Uṣasti replied:
"Give these to me," he said.
He gave them to him.
"Now, here is a drink," [he added].
"I would indeed have drunk what is left over," he said.
The meaning of "these" is "these very ones.
He said, "Give them to me.
That Ibha gave them, having bestowed them upon him, Uṣasti.
When he was told, "Come, take this water nearby as a drink," he replied, "This water of mine would indeed become defiled if I were to drink it. To him who had spoken thus, the other replied:
"Are these not also leftovers?
"I would not have lived without eating them," he said.
"The well is my desire."

When asked, "Are these not indeed boiled beans [kulmāṣas], or are they leavings? Uṣasti replied, "No; had I not eaten them, I would not have lived—I would not have survived. He meant that he could obtain water for drinking at his own will or desire.

Therefore, the intention is that even for one who has reached such a state—possessed of knowledge, virtue, and fame, capable of helping himself and others—even performing this kind of action (eating leavings) does not involve the touch of sin.
The intention is that even for him, when there exists another blameless means of livelihood, this contemptible act leads to fault;
for one who performs it out of pride in his knowledge, a fall into hell will certainly occur,
as indicated by the mention of the word "perishing."
Having eaten them, he brought the leftovers to his wife;
she became well-supplied with food even before they had been consumed.
Having received them, she set them aside.
Having eaten those [beans], he compassionately brought the remainder that were left over to his wife.
At the very moment those beans were obtained, she became one who had received a "good alms" (subhikṣā)—meaning she had obtained excellent food—even though she had previously been destitute.
Nevertheless, out of the natural disposition of women, she did not despise those beans; having taken them from her husband's hand, she set them aside.
As he was rising in the morning, he said:
"If only we could obtain some food! We might obtain a measure of wealth;
for that king is going to perform a sacrifice."
"Let him choose me for all the priestly offices."

Knowing her deed, as he was rising at the time of dawn, leaving his bed or casting off sleep, he spoke while his wife was listening: "If only we could obtain even a small portion of food; having eaten that food, we might go out and obtain a measure of wealth—a small amount of wealth."
"Then our livelihood will be secured.
And as for the reason for obtaining wealth, he says: "That king will perform a sacrifice at a place not very far away.
Because he is the one performing the sacrifice (*yajamāna*), the *ātmanepada* ending is used.
And that king, having recognized me as a worthy recipient, might choose me for all the functions of the officiating priests—that is, for the purpose of performing the priestly rites.
His wife said to him,
"Come now, husband, here are these very beans.
Having eaten them, he went to that sacrifice which was being performed.
When he had spoken thus, Jāyā said, "Come, my husband, take these very groats which were placed in my hand by you.
Having eaten them, he went to that sacrifice spread out and performed by the officiating priests for the king.
There he sat down near the Udgātṛ priests as they were about to chant the hymns in the place of chanting.
He then said to the Prastotṛ:

Having gone there, he approached the Udgātṛs—the men who chant the Udgītha—and sat down near them, that is, he sat down in their vicinity, in the place of chanting (āstāva) where they were about to chant.
Having sat down, he spoke to the Prastotṛ.
"O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva, your head will shatter apart."
He addresses him as "O Prastotṛ" in order to draw his attention.

"If you, being ignorant of that deity which follows and is inherent in the Prastāva—the specific portion of the chant—should chant it in my presence, that is, while I am a knower; or even if it should fail in my absence, your head shall shatter. Thus, there would be no qualification for those who know only the ritual action to perform the rite.
And that is undesirable, because even those who lack knowledge are seen to perform ritual actions,
and because there is scriptural mention of the southern path;
furthermore, if they were ineligible [for the northern path], only the northern path would be heard of for those lacking knowledge.
Furthermore, the southern path is not caused by *smārta* (tradition-based) rites alone,
because of scriptural statements such as "by sacrifice, by charity," and so forth;

and because of the qualification "spoken by me," there is no disqualification from ritual action only in the presence of the learned, but rather [disqualification] from all [such acts], including the *agnihotra*, *smārta* rites, study, and the like.
Since authorization (anujñā) is seen in various places, it is established that even those who know only the ritual action have the qualification for the rite;
thus [the text says], "Your head shall fall off."
In the same way, he said to the Udgātṛ:
"O Udgātṛ, if you perform the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Udgītha, your head will shatter apart."
In the same way, he said to the Pratihartṛ:
"O Pratihartṛ, if you perform the Pratihāra chant without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Pratihāra, your head will shatter apart.
Terrified, they remained silent.
In the same way, he spoke to the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ; the rest is the same as before.

Having withdrawn from their ritual duties—that is, having desisted—those priests, beginning with the Prastotṛ, remained silent out of fear that their heads would fall, doing nothing else because of their desire [for life].
Thus ends the tenth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, the sacrificer said to him:
"I truly desire to know you, O Blessed One."
"I am Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa," he said.

Immediately after that, the royal sacrificer said to this Uṣasti: "I desire to know—that is, I wish to understand—the venerable one, the one worthy of honor. Thus addressed, Uṣasti replied: "I am Cākrāyaṇa; have you heard of me before? he said.
He said:
"I have indeed sought you, O Blessed One, for all these priestly offices;
it was because I did not know you that I chose others."

The sacrificer said: "It is indeed true that I have heard of you, O Blessed One, as one possessed of many virtues; I sought you out for the office of the officiating priests through all the duties of the *ṛtvij*s, and having searched, because I did not find you, O Blessed One, I chose these other seers."
"But let the Blessed One himself perform all the priestly functions for me.
"So be it," [the Blessed One replied].
"In that case, let these very priests, being fully authorized, perform the praise."
"As long as you would give wealth to these [priests], so much should you give to me.
"So be it," the sacrificer replied.
"Even now, let the Blessed One himself be my officiating priest for all the duties of the *ṛtvij*s," [Uṣasti] said; and [the King] replied, "So be it.
However, in that case, let these very priests whom you previously chose—and who have been fully authorized and permitted by me, being well-pleased—perform the praise;
as for this task, it must be done by you.
When he was told, "You should give me as much wealth as you give to all these others, such as the Prastotṛ and the rest," the sacrificer replied, "So be it."
Then the Prastotṛ approached him and said,
"Sir, you told me, 'O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Prastāva, your head will shatter.
Which is that deity?"
Then, having heard these words of Auṣastya, the Prastotṛ approached him; he came to Auṣastya with humility and said:
"O Venerable One, you previously said to me, 'Which deity...?
Which is that deity who is dependent upon the Prastāva portion?"
"It is breath," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings enter into breath alone,
and from breath they emerge."
This very deity is connected with the Prastāva.
If you had chanted the Prastāva without knowing her, your head would have fallen off, as was said by me.
When asked, he said, "Prāṇa. [The questioner said:
"It is appropriate that Prāṇa is the deity of the Prastāva.

How so? All beings, both stationary and moving, enter into Prāṇa alone at the time of dissolution; having aimed at Prāṇa, they emerge with Prāṇa as their very self—that is to say, they rise up from Prāṇa alone."

At the time of its origination; therefore, this very deity is inherent in the *prastāva*. If you had chanted it without knowing her—that is, if you had performed the *prastāvana*, the act of chanting the *prastāva* division—your head would have fallen off, it would have been severed, had I spoken thus at that time.
"Your head would have fallen off.
Therefore, you have acted rightly;
the intention is that because I forbade you, you brought that action to a halt.
Then the Udgātṛ approached him and said:
"Venerable sir, you told me, 'If you chant the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is associated with the Udgītha, your head will shatter.
Which is that deity?"
Likewise, the Udgātṛ asked: "Which deity follows and is inherent in the portion of the chant known as the Udgītha?"
"It is Āditya," he said.
"Indeed, all these beings sing to Āditya as he is high above.
This deity is connected with the Udgītha."
"If you, not knowing that, had risen with your face toward the north, your head would have fallen off, even though I had spoken thus to you."
When asked, he said, "The Sun.
The meaning is that all these beings indeed sing to, call out to, and praise the Sun as it exists high above.

Because of the commonality of the sound *ud* (as in *ucchabda*), and because of the commonality of the sound *pra* (as in *praśabda*), Prāṇa [is thus identified]; therefore, "this deity," and so forth, is to be understood as before.
Then the Pratihartṛ approached him and said:
"Venerable sir, you said to me, 'O Pratihartṛ, if you perform the Pratihāra chant without knowing the deity that is associated with the Pratihāra, your head will shatter.
Which is that deity?"
In the same way, the Pratihartṛ then approached him and asked, "Which deity is associated with the Pratihāra?"
"Food," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings live by taking up food alone.
This deity is dependent upon the Pratihāra."
"If you had carried it back without knowing this, your head would have fallen off—just as I have said, just as I have said."
When asked, he said, "Food. Indeed, all these beings live by bringing food toward themselves from every side as their very self.
This deity, because of its commonality with the word *prati* (toward), follows the *pratihāra* division of the Sāman.
The rest is the same as what was stated by me:
"One should meditate upon the sections of the *prastāva*, *udgītha*, and *pratihāra* with the vision of Prāṇa, Āditya, and Anna"—this is the collective meaning.
The fruit is either the attainment of Prāṇa and the others, or the success of one's ritual action (*karma*).
Thus ends the eleventh section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, therefore, follows the Udgītha of the dogs. Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya, as some say—went out to recite his private Vedic study.

In the preceding section, a state of hardship characterized by eating leftovers and stale food was described as being caused by the failure to obtain food. Lest that state should occur, the *śauva*—the *udgītha*, which is the chanting (*udgāna*) of the *Sāman* seen by dogs—is introduced hereafter for the sake of obtaining food.
Regarding this, there were two persons: one named Baka, the son of Dalbha (Dālbhya), and the other named Glāva, the son of Mitrā (Maitreya).
The word "vā" (or) has the sense of "ca" (and);
for he is indeed a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (belonging to two lineages),
since an option is inadmissible regarding a real entity, just as it is with actions.
For there are Smṛti texts stating that one may have two names or belong to two gotras; moreover, the partaking of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) from both sides is observed [in such cases].
This may be due to the sage having his mind fixed on the Udgītha, or perhaps out of disregard for the Ṛṣi.
The word *vā* is used for the sake of recitation (*svādhyāya*).
He went out from the village—that is, he departed—to a secluded place near water in order to perform his recitation.
From the indicative mark of the singular verb "he went out" (*udvavrāja*) and "he waited" (*pratipālayāñcakāra*), it follows that this seer was one.

The intention is that the sage’s performance of his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) is characterized by his desire for food, due to his waiting for the time of the *udgītha* chant on the following day.
For him, a white dog appeared.
Other dogs approached it and said,
"May the venerable one sing for us food."
"Or rather, it is hunger," he said.

The deity or the seer, gratified by his private recitation (*svādhyāya*), assumed the form of a dog—a white dog—and appeared before that seer for the sake of bestowing grace upon him; he made himself manifest.
Then other small dogs approached that white dog and said: "May the Blessed One procure food for us by means of singing," which means he should produce it through song.

It is entirely reasonable to understand it thus: either the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) or speech and the other senses, who subsist on food and were gratified by the recitation, took on this form and showed favor to him.
"We are indeed hungry; we are truly famished."
He said to them, "Come to me right here in the morning.
Then Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya, as some say—waited there.
When this was said, the white dog spoke to those small dogs: "Do not come near me here, in this very place, morning after morning.
The form *samīyāta* is used for metrical lengthening; or it may be a reading resulting from a lapse in memory (*pramādapāṭhaḥ*).
The performance of the rite at dawn is for the sake of ensuring the food is not stale;
or else, because the Sun, the giver of food, would not be facing him in the afternoon.
In that very place, the seer Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya, according to some—waited, meaning he remained there in expectation.
Just as those who are about to chant the Bahiṣpavamāna stotra here on earth move forward, holding onto one another, so did they move forward;
and having sat down together, they made the sound "hiṃ."

Those dogs, having gone right there into the presence of the sage, just as here the chanters of the *udgātṛ* priests— when about to chant the *bahis-pavamāna* hymn— stand closely joined together, each grasping the tail of the other with his mouth, so did they run around; that is to say, having moved about, they sat down together and, being seated, they made the sound "hiṃ," that is, they uttered the *hiṅkāra*.
Oṃ, let us drink! Oṃ, the god Varuṇa, Prajāpati, and Savitṛ have brought food here.
Oṃ, we give; Oṃ, we drink; Oṃ, the god [is so called] because of his shining.
Varuṇa is so called because he covers (vṛṇoti) the world;
Prajāpati because he protects (pāti) his progeny;
and Savitṛ is called Āditya because of his nature as the impeller (prasavitṛ) of all.
By these means, they said: "May that very Āditya, being such as he is, bring food here for us; may he bring it.
Having thus performed the *hiṃ* chant, they spoke again: "O Lord of Food (*annapate*)!
For he is the lord (*pati*) because he is the progenitor of all food."
For without its cooking, not even a minute particle of abundant food arises for living beings;
therefore, he is the Lord of Food. "O Lord of Food, bring food here for us, bring it! [he says].
The repetition is for the sake of showing reverence.
"Om. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the twelfth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
This world, indeed, is the syllable *hāu*;
the wind is the syllable *hāi*.
The moon is the syllable *atha*,
the self is the syllable *iha*,
and fire is the syllable *ī*.

Since the meditation on the object of devotion is connected with the constituent parts of the Sāman, other meditations concerning the *stobha* syllables belonging to other parts of the Sāman are taught immediately thereafter as a collective whole, because they are no different in being connected to the constituent parts of the Sāman: "This [earth] indeed is the *hā-ukāra* *stobha* in the *Rathantara* Sāman; for this [earth] is the *Rathantara*."

On account of this commonality of connection, one should meditate upon this stobha "hāu" as being the world; for Vāyu is the syllable "hā," and the syllable "hāi" is well known in the Vāmadevya Sāman.

Furthermore, because the connection between air and water is the source (*yoni*) of the *vāmadeva* sāman, on the basis of this similarity, one should meditate upon the syllable *dhī* with the vision of air.
The syllable *atha* is the moon;
one should meditate upon the syllable *atha* with the vision of the moon.
Indeed, this world is established upon food; the moon is the self of food,
because of the commonality of the letter *tha* and the vowel *ā*.
The syllable *iha* is the self (*ātman*).
For the self is designated as "here" (*iha*) because it is directly perceived;
thus, the interjection *iha* is the self.
Because of that similarity:
the letter *ī* is Agni;
and all Sāmans have *ī* as their finale (*īnidhana*) and are dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*). Therefore, it is because of that similarity.
Āditya is the syllable ū;
Nihava is the syllable e;
the Viśve Devās are the syllable auhoyi.
Prajāpati is the *hiṅkāra*;
breath is the *svara*;
food is the *yā*.
Speech is the Virāj.
The syllable *ū* is the Sun (*āditya*). Because they sing of the Sun as being high and above, and because this stobha is the syllable *ū*,
the stobha "ū" in the Sāman whose deity is the Sun is the syllable *ū* representing the Sun.
*Nihava* means an invocation; the *stobha* is the syllable *ehi*, because they say "come" (*ehi*) when invoking, due to that similarity.
The *viśve devāḥ* (All-Gods) are [represented by] the syllable *auho*, because this is seen in the *sāman* dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
Prajāpati is the *hiṅkāra*,
because the *hiṅkāra* is unmanifest due to its lack of specific definition;
breath is the *svara*.
"Svara" is a stobha;
it is so called because of the commonality of being the cause of sound for the vital breath (prāṇa).
"Yā yā" is a stobha; it is food (anna).
Because it moves by means of food, on account of that similarity,
the *stobha* is called "Speech" (*vāk*), or else it is the *virāj*— which is food— or a particular deity,
since the *stobha* is observed in the *vairāja* sāman.
The thirteenth stobha is the unexpressed, the moving *huṃ*-sound.

"Unspecified" (*anirukta*) means that because it is unmanifest (*avyakta*), it cannot be specified as "this" or "that"; therefore, it is a "wandering" one, meaning its specific form is being conceptualized.
To the question "What is this?", he says: "The thirteenth is the *stobha*, the syllable *huṃ*.
The intention is that since this is indeed unmanifest, it should be meditated upon precisely as having the nature of the unspecified.

Speech yields its milk for him who knows the milking of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food— whosoever knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Sāmans, indeed, knows the secret doctrine.
"Speech milks for him [the desired fruit]"—this and what follows has its meaning already explained.

The meaning is that for one who knows this Upaniṣad—the vision concerning the stobha-syllables which are parts of the Sāmans, characterized as previously described—there is this aforementioned result.
The repetition at the end is for the purpose of concluding the chapter.
Or rather, it is for the purpose of concluding the specific meditations concerning the parts of the Sāman.
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.
Now begins the second chapter. Om.
Indeed, the meditation on the entire Sāman is excellent.
For what is indeed excellent, they call "Sāman," and what is not excellent, they call "Asāman."
By the passage beginning with "The syllable Om," meditation (upāsana) concerning the constituent parts of the Sāman was taught as having manifold fruits;
immediately thereafter, meditation concerning the *stobha* syllables was mentioned.

In every respect, that [meditation] was indeed connected to a single part of the Sāman. Now, the Scripture begins with the intention: "I shall now describe meditations concerning the entire Sāman, pertaining to the whole of the Sāman."
For it is logical that after the meditation on a single part, the meditation concerning the possessor of those parts is taught;
that is to say, the meditation on the whole as characterized by all its parts, whether consisting of five or seven divisions. The particle *khalu* serves as an ornament for the sentence.
The meditation on the *sāman* as "the good" (*sādhu*) is intended to enjoin the perception of the "good" in the entire *sāman*.

Because its purpose is to prescribe this perception of the "good," the word "good" does not intend to disparage the meditations mentioned previously; rather, the word "good" signifies what is beautiful.
How is this understood? It is said: in common worldly usage, those who are skilled declare that which is "good"—meaning beautiful and irreproachable—to be the *sāman*.
That which is improper and contrary is what we do not approve of.
Regarding this, they also say: "He has approached him with *sāman*"; by this they mean "He has approached him with what is good.
They also say: "He has approached him without *sāman*"; by this they mean exactly that.
Regarding that very matter of distinguishing between what is beneficial and what is harmful, they also say: "He approached this king and the neighboring vassal with conciliation (*sāman*).
Who is he, from whom there is the apprehension of falling into unrighteousness?
Such is the intended meaning of the word "he" (*sa*).

With a noble intention, he approached him with what is good—this is what worldly people say in that case, not seeing any improper action such as binding and so forth. But where the opposite is true, and they do see an improper action such as binding and so forth, there they say, "He approached him with what is not gentle," or "He approached him with what is not good."

Then they also say: "O, we have attained *sāman*! when something is good; they mean to say, "O, it is indeed good! And: "O, we have not attained *sāman*! when something is not good; they mean to say, "O, it is indeed not good!"

Then they also said, "Alas! Our *sāman* has become self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*) to us," saying this out of compassion. By this they meant that when something good occurred, they would say, "Ah, how good! and in the opposite case, "Alas! Our *sāman* [is lost]!"
When something is not good, they say, "Alas, it is not good! Therefore, it is established that the words *sāman* and *sādhu* have the same meaning.
He who, knowing this thus, venerates it as "the good Sāman," will soon indeed find that good dharmas come to him and incline toward him.

Therefore, whoever meditates upon the Sāman as "good"—that is, as possessing the qualities of the good—knowing the entire Sāman to possess the qualities of the good, for him this is the fruit: "abhyāśo ha," meaning quickly indeed; "yat" is used here as an adverbial particle. Good (sādhavaḥ)—that is, auspicious qualities not contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti—will come (ā ca gaccheyuḥ) toward this meditator, and they will not only come, but will also bow down (upa ca nameyuḥ); the meaning is that they will present themselves to him as objects of enjoyment.
Thus ends the first section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds.
The earth is the *hiṅkāra*.
Agni is the Prastāva;
the intermediate space is the Udgītha;
Āditya is the Pratihāra.
"Heaven is the Nidhana"—
thus for those [vessels] that are upright.
What, then, are those [forms] which, distinguished by the vision of the virtuous (sādhudṛṣṭi), are all collectively to be worshipped?
These are said to be "the fivefold in the worlds" and so forth.
But is it not a contradiction that they are to be worshipped both through the vision of the worlds and through the vision of the virtuous? No.
Because the meaning of the word *sādhu*—which is the cause in effects such as the world—is pervasive throughout them, just as clay is in its transformations such as jars;
and because the object denoted by the word *sādhu*, whether it be *dharma* or *brahman*, is in every way pervasive throughout effects such as the world;
therefore, just as in any case where there is the perception of a jar or the like, that perception is necessarily pervaded by the perception of the clay or the like.
Likewise, the view of the world and so forth follows precisely from the view of the Sublime (sādhudṛṣṭi),
because the world and other such things are effects of the Dharma and so on.
Although the causality of Brahman and the Dharma is indistinguishable, [the former is not the direct cause].

Nevertheless, it is logical that *dharma* alone is denoted by the word "good" (*sādhu*), because the word "good" is applied to *dharma* in the statement: "One who performs good deeds becomes good. [Objection: Since the cause is inherent in effects such as the worlds and so forth, that perception [of the effect in the cause] is already established by implication; therefore, one need not say, "He should worship [the breath] as the 'Good' (*sādhu*) and the 'Sama' (*sāma*). [Reply: No, for that perception is to be understood through scripture (*śāstra*).
For in all cases, only those dharmas established by the Śāstra are to be meditated upon, and not even existing things that are outside the Śāstra.
One should meditate on the Sāman as fivefold—of five kinds according to the division of the fivefold devotion—perfectly complete within the worlds, such as the earth and so forth.
How?
The earth is the *hiṅkāra*. Regarding the phrase "in the worlds," that which is the seventh [case-ending] is transformed into the first [case-ending] in the reversed [formulas].
The sky is the *hiṅkāra*;
the sun is the *prastāva*;
the intermediate space is the *udgītha*.
Agni is the Pratihāra;
the Earth is the Nidhana.
Now, when the worlds have turned back and are facing downwards, the fivefold meditation on the Sāman is taught.
For the worlds are characterized by coming and going;
since they are perceived in that manner, the meditation on the Sāman is prescribed with reference to those worlds as they turn back.
The sky is the *hiṅkāra* because of its primacy;
the sun is the *prastāva*,
for when the sun has risen, the activities of living beings are set in motion (*prastūyante*).
The intermediate space is the *udgītha*, as before;
fire is the *pratihāra*,
because fire is brought forth (*pratiharaṇa*) by living beings.
The earth is the *nidhana*;
for those who have come from there, it is the *nidhana* here.
The worlds, both ascending and descending, become favorable to him who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds.
"They become capable" means they become able; "for him these worlds"—both those above and those below—become established as objects of enjoyment, characterized by coming and going.

This is the meaning: for one who, knowing this, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman as the entire "Good" (sādhu) distributed among the worlds—the application of this phrase is to be understood everywhere, both in the fivefold and the sevenfold [meditations].
Thus ends the second section of the second chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain:
the preceding wind is the *hiṅkāra*.
The cloud arising is the *prastāva*;
its raining is the *udgītha*;
its lightning and thundering are the *pratihāra*.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain.
Because rain is the cause of the stability of the world, it follows immediately [after the meditation on the earth].
The preceding wind is the *hiṅkāra*.
For rain begins with the east wind and ends with its cessation; just as a *sāman* chant begins with the *hiṅkāra* and ends with the *nidhana*,
therefore the east wind is the *hiṅkāra*.
Because it comes first:
the cloud arises; that is the *prastāva*.
For it is well known that when clouds arise in the rainy season, there is the "introduction" (*prastāva*) of rain.
It rains— that is the *udgītha*, because of its excellence.
It flashes and thunders— that is the *pratihāra*,
because it is drawn back (*pratihṛta*).
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in rain, takes hold of that finale and indeed causes rain to fall.
He grasps that finale because of the commonality of their completion;
he bestows the fruit of the meditation upon him according to his desire.
Likewise, he causes it to rain even when there is no rain;
"he who [does this]," and so forth, as before.
Thus ends the third section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters:
that which is the gathering of clouds is the *hiṅkāra*.
That which rains is the *prastāva*;
those rivers that flow eastward are the *udgītha*; those that flow westward are the *pratihāra*.
The ocean is the place of rest.

One should meditate upon the fivefold *sāman* in all waters. Since all waters are preceded by rain, there is a sequence of proximity: when a cloud gathers—that is, becomes dense through mutual union—it is said that the cloud "gathers" (*saṃplavate*). When the cloud rises, it is then said to "gather. That cloud is the beginning of the waters; it is the *hiṅkāra*.
That which rains is the *prastāva*,
for the waters have begun (*prastuta*) to pervade everywhere.
Those waters that flow eastward are the *udgītha*, because of their excellence.
Those [waters] which flow westward are the *pratihāra*, due to the commonality of the word "prati" (back/against).
The ocean is the *nidhana*,
because the waters have that as their final resting place (*nidhana*).
He does not perish in water; he becomes possessed of water—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters.
He does not perish in water;
if he does not desire it,
he becomes possessed of water as his fruit.
Thus ends the fourth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons:
Spring is the *hiṅkāra*.
Summer is the Prastāva;
the rainy season is the Udgītha;
autumn is the Pratihāra.
Winter is the Nidhana.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons. Because the establishment of the seasons has the aforementioned water as its cause, it follows immediately [after the meditation on water]. Spring is the *hiṅkāra*.
Because it comes first:
the summer season is the *prastāva*,
for the gathering of barley and other grains is commenced for the sake of the rainy season.
The rainy season is the *udgītha* because of its preeminence;
the autumn is the *pratihāra*,
because it brings back those who are ill and those who have died.
Winter is the end;
for living beings, there is death in the windless state.
The seasons serve him; he becomes possessed of the seasons, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons.
The seasons indeed become available as objects of enjoyment for this practitioner in accordance with the seasonal order;
the meaning is that he becomes endowed with the measures of the seasons and with the enjoyments pertaining to the seasons.
Thus ends the fifth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals:
the goat is the *hiṅkāra*.
Sheep are the Prastāva; cows are the Udgītha;
horses are the Pratihāra.
The Person is the Nidhana.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals.
Because the time for cattle is immediately following the seasons that have turned properly, there is a sequence:
the she-goat is the *hiṅkāra*.
Because of its preeminence or its primacy—
according to the Vedic revelation that "the goat is the first of animals"—
the sheep (*avayaḥ*) is the *prastāva*.

In the case of words such as *aja* (goat), [the plural form] arises from the observation of their association; for example, "cows" (*gāvaḥ*) refers to the *udgītha*. [The plural form] also arises from excellence.
The horses are the *pratihāra*,
because they carry away men;
the man is the *nidhana*.
Because animals have man as their refuge.
Cattle attend him; he becomes possessed of cattle, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in cattle.
The meaning is that cattle become his fruit; he becomes possessed of cattle, and he is endowed with the fruits of cattle, such as enjoyments, renunciations, and so forth.
Thus ends the sixth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman, which is progressively higher, as being in the vital breaths.
The vital breath is the *hiṅkāra*.
Speech is the Prastāva;
the eye is the Udgītha;
the ear is the Pratihāra.
The mind is the finale;
these [notes] are indeed progressively more extensive.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman as the vital breaths (prāṇas), which are progressively more excellent. The meaning is that one should meditate on the Sāman as characterized by the view of the vital breaths, which possess the quality of being successively superior. The nose is the *hiṅkāra*.
Because it is the first among those that become increasingly excellent in succession, speech is the *prastāva*;
for by means of speech everything is introduced (*prastūyate*).
Speech is superior to the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
for speech speaks even of that which has not been reached,
whereas the vital breath is the perceiver only of a fragrance that has already been reached.
The eye is the Udgītha.
Since the eye illumines a much wider range of objects than speech, it is superior to speech; therefore, it is the Udgītha because of its excellence.
The ear is the Pratihāra,
because it is drawn toward [objects];
and the mind is superior to the ear.
Because they pervade all objects of the senses,
even an object beyond the senses is indeed within the range of the mind;
for the reasons stated, these [elements], beginning with breath, are progressively more excellent.

"Superior and more excellent becomes his [state], and he conquers superior and more excellent worlds—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman as 'superior and more excellent' within the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Thus much for the fivefold [Sāman]."
"He who meditates upon the Sāman as distinguished by this view—the 'higher-than-high' (parovarīyaḥ)—his life becomes higher-than-high"; the meaning of this has already been explained.
This concludes the meditation on the fivefold Sāman, stated for the purpose of fixing the mind upon the subject about to be described regarding the sevenfold Sāman;
for one who is independent [of the lower] in the fivefold [meditation], [is likewise independent in the higher].
He intends to fix his mind upon what is about to be explained.
Thus ends the seventh section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, concerning the sevenfold [Sāman]:
one should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech.
Whatever in speech is "hum," that is the *hiṅkāra*; whatever is "pra," that is the *prastāva*;
whatever is "eti" (goes), that is the *ādi*.
Immediately after that, this meditation on the sevenfold Sāman in its entirety is properly commenced.
The locative case in "vāci" (in speech) is as before;
the meaning is that one should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman as characterized by the vision of Speech.

Whatever specific sound of speech there is, namely "hum," that is the *hiṅkāra*, because of the commonality of the letter *ha*. That form of sound which is "pra" is the *prastāva*, because of the commonality of the prefix *pra*. That which is "ā" is the *ādi*.
Because of the commonality of their forms;
"the first" refers to the syllable *oṃ*, because it is the beginning of all.
That which is "ud" is the *udgītha*;
that which is "prati" is the *pratihāra*;
that which is "upa" is the *upadrava*.
Whatever is the beginning, that is the end.
That which is "ut" is the Udgītha, because the Udgītha begins with "ut. That which is "prati" is the Pratihāra.
Because it corresponds to each [particular].
That which approaches is "distress" (*upadrava*), because distress involves being afflicted;
that which leads away is the "conclusion" (*nidhana*).
Because of the commonality of the word "ni".
Speech milks for him that which is the milk of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food—
he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech.
"He milks for him," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
Thus ends the eighth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, indeed, one should meditate upon yonder sun as the sevenfold Sāman.
It is always the same (*sama*); therefore, it is the Sāman.
Because it is "māṃ prati" (toward me), "māṃ prati" (toward me)—that is, equal toward all—it is therefore called *sāman*.
In the first chapter, the meditation on the Sun as Sāman was taught with respect to each individual part of the fivefold Sāman.
Now, however, one should meditate upon this very Sun as the sevenfold Sāman by superimposing it upon the Sāman as a whole, part by part.
But how, then, does the Sun possess the nature of Sāman?
It is said:
as there is a reason for the sun being the *udgītha*, there is likewise a reason for its being the *sāman*.

What is that? It is that it is always the same (*sama*), due to the absence of increase or decrease; by that reason, the sun is a *sāman*, because it produces an equal cognition [in people] such as "toward me, toward me."
Therefore, it is equal to all; thus, *sāman* means "on account of equality" (*samatvāt*).

Since the nature of being preceded by the *hiṅkāra* and so forth is understood from the very mention of the commonality of the *udgītha* division and from the commonalities stated regarding the worlds and so on, no specific reason for its being preceded by the *hiṅkāra* has been stated.
However, as for its being a *sāman*, the unstated reason for the Sun is not easily understood; therefore, its equality has been stated.
One should know that all these beings are dependent upon it.
That which is before sunrise is its *hiṅkāra*;
upon it, domestic animals are dependent.
Therefore, they utter the sound "hiṅ"; for they are partakers of the "hiṅ" of this Sāman.
One should know that all these beings about to be mentioned are dependent upon—that is, follow along with—that sun, by way of being its support.
How so? That form of the sun which exists before its rising is the *hiṅkāra* division; in this regard, there is a commonality:
the animals, such as cows and others, are dependent upon—that is, follow along with—the *hiṅkāra* division of that Sāman of the sun, meaning they subsist upon that form of its division.
Since this is so, therefore those animals utter the sound "hiṅ" before sunrise;
for they are partakers of the *hiṅkāra* of this Sāman called Āditya, and because it is their nature to participate in its divisions, they behave in this manner.
Now, that which occurs at the first rising [of the sun] is the *prastāva*;
human beings are dependent upon it. Therefore, they are fond of initiating things and fond of praise.
For these indeed are the participants in the introductory section (prastāva) of this Sāman.
Now, that form of the Sun which has just risen is the *prastāva* of this Sāman called Āditya; humans are dependent upon it, as before.
Therefore, they desire praise and exaltation, for they are partakers of the *prastāva* of this Sāman.
Now, that which is at the time of the gathering of cattle (saṃgava) is its beginning;
to it birds are attached.
Therefore, they fly about in the intermediate space, holding themselves without any support.
For these are the initial portions of this Sāman.

Now, as for the time of *saṅgava*: that period at which there is a coming together (*saṅgama*) of the rays of the cows, or when the cows come together with their calves—that is the time of *saṅgava*. At that time, the form belonging to Savitṛ is the first specific division, namely the syllable *Oṃ*; to this, birds (*vayāṃsi*) are attached. Because it is so, therefore those birds in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), being without support (*anārambaṇa*)—that is, without a hold—take hold of themselves alone, using the self itself as their support.
Having grasped it, they fall away and depart; because of this commonality of form, these [notes] indeed partake in the first division of this *sāman*.
Now, that which is exactly at midday is the Udgītha;
the gods are dependent upon it. Therefore, they are the best among the offspring of Prajāpati.
For they are indeed partakers of the *udgītha* of this *sāman*.
Now, that which is precisely at midday— meaning the straight midday— is the *udgītha* division; the gods are dependent upon that part of it,
because of the excellence of its radiance at that time.
Therefore, they are the best and most distinguished;
for among those belonging to Prajāpati—the offspring of Prajāpati—they are the sharers in this Sāman, the Udgītha.
Now, that which is after midday and before afternoon is the *pratihāra*.
To it are attached the embryos;
therefore, being held back (*pratihṛta*), they do not fall away.
For these indeed are the sharers of the *pratihāra* of this Sāman.
Now, that form of the Sun which exists after midday and before afternoon is its *pratihāra* (response). To it the embryos are attached;
therefore, being held up by the *pratihāra* as a portion of the Sun, they do not fall down—that is, they do not drop below—even though the door [of birth] is open.
For the embryos of this Sāman are indeed partakers of the *pratihāra*.
Now, that which comes after the afternoon and before sunset is the *upadrava*.
To it the forest animals are attached;
therefore, when they see a man, they flee into the brush or a hole, crying out, "An *upadrava*! (a danger).
For those who partake in this sāman are indeed subject to calamities.
Now, that which comes after the afternoon and before sunset is the *upadrava* (the "approach"); it belongs to these wild animals of the forest.

Therefore, when they see a man, being afraid, they "approach" (*upadravanti*)—that is, they go toward—the thicket, the forest, or the cave as a place free from fear; for because they approach [it] upon seeing him, they partake in the *upadrava* of this *sāman*.
Then, that which occurs at the first setting of the sun is the *nidhana* (the "conclusion").
His ancestors are dependent upon that;
therefore they place them down,
for they are the sharers in the *nidhana* of this *sāman*.
In this way, indeed, one venerates that sun as the sevenfold Sāman.
Now, when the sun has just set and is about to go out of sight, that is the *nidhana* (concluding note);

the ancestors are connected to this. Therefore, they lay them down—that is, they place them upon *darbha* grass in the form of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—or they establish those *piṇḍas* for that purpose.
For the ancestors partake of the *nidhana* (concluding syllable) because of their connection with the *nidhana* of this Sāman.

Thus, the remainder of the sentence is that for one who meditates upon yonder sun as the sevenfold Sāman divided into seven parts according to its constituent members, the result is the attainment of that [sun].
Thus ends the ninth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, one should indeed meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman, which is commensurate with the Self and transcends death:
*hiṅkāra* consists of three syllables.
"Prastāva" consists of three syllables;
that is equal.
The Sun is Death, because it causes the destruction of the world through time consisting of day, night, and so forth.

For the purpose of transcending that [Death], this meditation on the Sāman is taught; "now," indeed, immediately following [the previous instruction], [this meditation] upon the Sāman whose object is the Sun as Death is presented.
"Measured by the self" means measured by similarity to one's own limbs or measured by equality with the Supreme Self; it is "beyond death" because it is the cause for conquering death.

Just as in the first chapter the syllables of the name of the *udgītha* division were declared as objects of meditation under the name "udgītha," so here the syllables of the names of the sevenfold divisions of the *sāman* are collected and, by arranging them into groups of three, their nature as *sāman* (equality) is conceived and they are declared as objects of meditation.

By meditating upon that [Sāman], one reaches death through the commonality of the number of its syllables with those within the sphere of death; then, by means of the syllable exceeding that, one fashions a transition for the purpose of transcending that very death of the Sun.
One should meditate on the sevenfold Sāman as "beyond death," for it is called "immortal" (amṛtyu) because it has transcended death by virtue of the number of its excess syllables.

Of this, the syllables of the name of the first division (*bhakti*) are "Biṃ," which consists of three syllables; and since the division called *prastāva* also consists of three syllables, its measure is equal to the former.
"Ādi" consists of two syllables;
"pratihāra" consists of four syllables;
therefore, one [syllable] is added here.
That is equal.
"Ādi" consists of two syllables; the syllable *oṃ* is called "ādi" because it completes the count of the sevenfold *sāman*.
"Pratihāra" consists of four syllables.
Then, having subtracted one syllable from here, it is added to the two initial syllables;
by that means, it becomes exactly equal.

"Udgītha" consists of three syllables; "upadrava" consists of four syllables. With three syllables each, they become equal; one syllable remains over, making [the second word] three-syllabled. Thus, it is equal.

"Udgītha" has three syllables; "Upadrava" has four syllables. By means of the three [syllables] in each, they become equal, and one syllable remains over—it is redundant. Since this would result in inequality, for the sake of making the *sāman* equal, that [redundant] syllable, though being one, is treated as "a-syllable" (a negative particle), and thus it becomes exactly three syllables.
Therefore, they are equal.
"Nidhana" consists of three syllables;
thus it becomes equal.
These, indeed, are twenty-two syllables in total.
The word *nidhana* consists of three syllables, and thus it is equal [to the preceding].

Having thus established its quality as a *sāman* through this equality of three syllables, the syllables are counted exactly as they occur; these syllables of the names of the seven *bhaktis* amount to twenty-two.
He attains the twenty-first Āditya;
for that Āditya is the twenty-first from here.
By means of the twenty-second, he conquers what is beyond the Āditya.
That is the peak;
that is free from sorrow.
Therein, by the number twenty-one, one reaches the sun, which is death;
for from this world, that sun is the twenty-first in number.

According to the Vedic revelation: "Twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and that sun make twenty-one. By means of the remaining twenty-second syllable, one conquers—that is, surpasses—the supreme death beyond the sun. This is the meaning.
And what is that which is beyond the sun? It is *nāka*. *Ka* means happiness; its negation is *aka*, meaning that which is not happiness. Thus, *nāka* means that which is indeed happiness.
Furthermore, it is *viśoka*; because suffering belongs to the domain of death, *viśoka* means free from sorrow, i.e., devoid of mental distress.
"He obtains that."
He attains victory over the sun in this world;

indeed, his victory becomes even greater than the victory of the sun—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the sevenfold Sāman as commensurate with the self and transcending death—yes, he meditates upon the Sāman.

He states the summarized meaning of what has just been said: "By the number twenty-one, one attains victory over the Sun; for one who knows thus, there is a victory beyond the reach of death through this victory over the Sun"—the meaning is that it is by the number of syllables in the twenty-two-syllable [verse]. "One who knows this thus" refers to the meaning already explained starting with the verse beginning with *dvādaśa*.
"This is its fruit as previously described"—this repetition is for the purpose of concluding the sevenfold exposition.
Thus ends the tenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The mind is the *hiṅkāra*;
speech is the *prastāva*.
The eye is the Udgītha;
the ear is the Pratihāra;
the breath is the Nidhana.
This Gāyatra is woven upon the vital breaths.
The meditation on the fivefold and sevenfold *sāman* has been explained without mentioning their specific names.

Now, however, other meditations on the *sāman* with distinct fruits are described, preceded by the mention of the names Gāyatra and so forth, in the same order as they are employed in ritual practice.
The mind (*manas*) is the *hiṅkāra*, because the mind precedes all activities of the sense organs.
Then, because of their immediate succession, speech is the Prastāva; sight is the Udgītha because of its preeminence;
hearing is the Pratihāra because it is drawn back [to the self];
and breath is the Nidhana, because at the time of sleep, those aforementioned [faculties] find their support (nidhana) in the breath.
This Gāyatra Sāman is woven upon the vital breaths (prāṇas),
because the Gāyatrī has been praised as being identical with the vital breaths.
He who thus knows this Gāyatra woven upon the vital breaths becomes possessed of vital breaths;
he reaches a full lifespan.
He lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle;
he becomes great in fame.
One should be high-minded;
that is the vow.
He who thus knows this Gāyatra as woven upon the vital breaths becomes possessed of vital breaths; that is to say, he becomes one whose organs are unimpaired. He attains a full span of life.
According to the Vedic revelation that "the full lifespan of a person is a hundred years," he lives long and radiantly;
he becomes great through progeny and other such means, and great in fame.
This is the vow for one who worships the Gāyatrī: that he should be "great-minded," which means he should possess a mind free from meanness.
Thus ends the eleventh section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The rubbing [of the fire-drills] is the *hiṅkāra*;
the smoke that arises is the *prastāva*.
When it blazes, that is the *udgītha*;
when it becomes embers, that is the *pratihāra*;
when it subsides, that is the *nidhana*.
That which subsides is its dissolution;
this is the Rathantara [Sāman] woven into Agni.
The first rubbing is the *hiṅkāra*, because it comes first;
the smoke arising from the fire is the *prastāva*, because it follows immediately after;
the blazing is the *udgītha*, because of its connection with the oblation, for blazing is preeminent.
They become embers; it is a *pratihāra* because the embers have been brought forth (*pratihṛta*).
It is a state of subsiding (*upaśama*) because the fire still has a remainder.
It is a complete subsiding (*saṃśama*) because there is no remainder left. Because of the commonality of completion, this *nidhana* is the *rathantara* [sāman] woven into the fire.
For it is said that fire is produced by friction.
He who thus knows this Rathantara as woven into the fire becomes endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge and becomes an eater of food.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
He is great in fame.
He should not sip water facing the fire, nor should he spit;
that is his vow.
The passage beginning with "sa yaḥ" is as explained previously. *Brahmavarcasī* refers to the splendor (*tejas*) caused by one's conduct and Vedic study;
mere physical radiance, however, is simply *tviṭ*.
One who eats food possesses a kindled digestive fire.
One should not sip water while facing the fire, nor should one eat anything, nor spit, nor discharge phlegm; that is his vow.
Thus ends the twelfth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"He invites [the guest]; that is the *hiṅkāra*. He makes himself known; that is the *prastāva*."
He who lies with a woman is the *udgītha*;
he who lies facing a woman is the *pratihāra*;
that he passes the time is the *nidhana*.
It goes to the further shore; that is its dissolution.
This Vāmadevya [sāman] is interwoven in the couple.
He invites her and makes a secret sign; because it is the first act, that is the *hiṅkāra*.
He makes himself known and pleases her; that is the *prastāva*.
Sleeping together and mounting the same bed is the *udgītha*, because of its preeminence.
The facing toward the bed by means of the woman is the *pratihāra*.

When one reaches the end—that is, the completion—of the sexual act through copulation, that is the *nidhana*. This *Vāmadevya* chant is thus woven into the couple, due to the connection with the couple consisting of wind and water.
He who thus knows this Vāmadevya as woven upon the couple becomes a couple himself;
from every couple he procreates offspring.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
Great in fame;
he should not avoid anyone whatsoever—
this is his vow.
The passage beginning with "sa ya" and so forth is as explained previously.
"He becomes paired" means that he becomes inseparable [from his wife].
"From pair after pair he procreates" expresses the fact that his seed is never in vain.

One should not reject any woman whatsoever who has come to one’s own bed seeking union, because this is prescribed as an ancillary part of the meditation on the Vāmadevya Sāman; since the understanding of dharma arises from the authority of such scriptural statements, there is no contradiction between this and the prohibitive scriptures.
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: Rising is the *hiṅkāra*; having risen, it is the *prastāva*.
The midday is the *udgītha*;
the afternoon is the *pratihāra*;
and the setting [of the sun] is the *nidhana*.
This Bṛhat is interwoven in the sun.
The rising sun is the *hiṅkāra*, because it is the first appearance [of light]. The risen sun is the *prastāva*, because it is the cause for the commencement (*prastavana*) of ritual actions.
Midday is the *udgītha*, because of its preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*).

The afternoon is the *pratihāra*, because cattle and other animals are driven back (*pratiharaṇa*) toward their homes. That which sets is the *nidhana*, because living beings are placed (*nidhāna*) in their homes at night.
This *Bṛhat* [Sāman] is woven into the sun, because the *Bṛhat* has the sun as its deity.
He who thus knows this Bṛhat as woven into the sun becomes radiant, an eater of food,
and reaches a full span of life.
He lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle;
he becomes great in fame.
One should not revile one who is performing penance;
that is the vow.
"Whoever," and so forth, is as before;
"one should not revile the one who is performing penance"—that is his vow.
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The gathering of clouds is the *hiṅkāra*;
the formation of the rain-cloud is the *prastāva*.
When it rains, that is the *udgītha*;
when it flashes and thunders, that is the *pratihāra*;
when it ceases, that is the *nidhana*.
This Vairūpa [Sāman] is interwoven in Parjanya.
Clouds are so called because they bear water; a rain-cloud (megha) is so called because it sprinkles water.
The rest has already been explained.
This Sāman named Vairūpa is woven into Parjanya;
for Parjanya possesses a manifold form through clouds and other such phenomena, owing to his lack of a single, uniform nature.
He who thus knows this Vairūpa [Sāman] as woven into Parjanya acquires both deformed and well-formed cattle;
he reaches a full span of life.
He lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle;
he becomes great in fame.
One should not revile it when it rains;
that is the vow.
He acquires and obtains animals that are both deformed and well-formed, such as goats, sheep, and so forth; this is the meaning.
He should not revile one who is raining—that is his vow.
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
Spring is the *hiṅkāra*;
summer is the *prastāva*.
The rainy season is the *udgītha*;
the autumn is the *pratihāra*;
the winter is the *nidhana*.
This Vairāja [sāman] is interwoven within the seasons.
Spring is the *hiṃṅkāra* because of its primacy;
summer is the *prastāva*, and so forth, as before.
He who thus knows this Vairāja [sāman] as woven into the seasons shines forth with offspring, with cattle, and with the splendor of sacred knowledge.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
One should be great in fame;
one should not revile the seasons—
that is the vow.

This Vairāja [Sāman] is woven into the seasons; he who knows this shines like the seasons. Just as the seasons shine by means of their seasonal characteristics, so does the knower shine by means of offspring and other such blessings—this has been stated elsewhere.
One should not revile the seasons; that is his vow.
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The earth is the *hiṅkāra*;
the intermediate space is the *prastāva*.
The sky is the *udgītha*;
the quarters are the *pratihāra*;
the ocean is the *nidhana*.
These Śakvarī verses are interwoven throughout the worlds.
"The earth is the *hiṅkāra*" and so forth, as before.
"The *śakvarīs*" always takes the plural ending, just like the *revatīs*.
They are woven into the worlds.
He who thus knows these Śakvarī verses as interwoven in the worlds becomes possessed of the worlds, reaches a full lifespan,
and lives radiantly.
He becomes great in offspring and cattle;
he becomes great in fame.
He should not revile the worlds.
That is the vow.
One becomes a "worldly person" (lokī) because one is joined with the fruits of the world;
therefore, one should not revile the worlds—this is the vow.
Thus ends the seventeenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
The goat is the *hiṅkāra*;
the sheep is the *prastāva*.
Cows are the *udgītha*;
horses are the *pratihāra*;
man is the *nidhana*.
These Revatī verses are interwoven with the cattle.
"Goat is the *hiṅkāra*, etc., as before;
they are woven into the animals."
He who thus knows these Revatī verses as interwoven with cattle becomes possessed of cattle and reaches a full lifespan.
He lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle,
and great in fame.
One should not revile animals;
that is the vow.
One should not revile animals; that is his vow.
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Hair is the *hiṅkāra*;
skin is the *prastāva*.
Flesh is the *udgītha*;
bone is the *pratihāra*;
marrow is the *nidhana*.
This Yajñāyajñīya is interwoven into the limbs.
Body hair is the *hiṅkāra* because it is the first among the limbs of the body; the skin is the *prastāva* because it follows immediately after;
the flesh is the *udgītha* because of its excellence.
The bone is the *pratihāra* because it is held together;
the marrow is the *nidhana* because it is the final part. Thus, this Sāman named Yajñāyajñīya is woven into the limbs of the body.
He who thus knows this Yajñāyajñīya as woven into the limbs becomes possessed of limbs;
he does not become crippled in any limb.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
He is great in fame.
For one year he should not eat marrow;
that is his vow.
Or [he should think], "I shall not eat marrow."

"He becomes whole" means he possesses all his limbs; "he does not become deformed by a limb"— meaning he does not become crooked, lame, or withered— means he remains so for a year, that is, for the duration of one year, he shall not eat or consume marrow or flesh.
The plural number is used for the purpose of indicating fish in general;
his vow is that he should never eat marrow, or rather, that he should not eat it at all.
Thus ends the nineteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
Fire is the *hiṅkāra*;
Wind is the *prastāva*.
The sun is the *udgītha*;
the stars are the *pratihāra*;
the moon is the *nidhana*.
This royal power is interwoven within the deities.
Agni is the *hiṅkāra* because he occupies the first position;
Vāyu is the *prastāva* because of the commonality of being immediate [to the first];
Āditya is the *udgītha* because of his preeminence.
The constellations are the *pratihāra* because they are drawn forth (*pratihṛta*);
the moon is the *nidhana* because it is the final resting place for those who perform ritual acts.
This *rājana* chant is woven into the deities, because of the radiance of the deities.
He who thus knows this King woven into the deities attains the same world,
the same creation, and union with these very deities;
he reaches a full span of life.
He lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle;
he becomes great in fame.
One should not revile brahmins;
that is the vow.

The fruit for the knower of these very deities—Agni and the others—is *salokatām*, which means being in the same world; *sārṣṭitām*, which means having equal prosperity; and *sāyujyam*, which means union, that is, becoming one body and one soul with them.
Here, the word "or" (*vā*) is understood as elided, as in "or *salokatām*," and so forth, because a specific result arises from a specific mode of contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
He goes; he attains [the goal]. And because a cumulative collection is not possible, the vow is: "One should not revile Brahmins."
Since the scripture states, "These Brahmins are indeed the gods manifest before our eyes," reviling a Brahmin is equivalent to reviling a deity.
Thus ends the twentieth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
The triple Vedic knowledge is the *hiṅkāra*;
these three worlds are the *prastāva*.
Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya—that is the *udgītha*.
The stars, the birds, and the rays of light—that is the *pratihāra*.
The serpents, the Gandharvas, and the ancestors—that is the *nidhana*.
This Sāman is woven into everything.
The triple Veda is indeed the *hiṅkāra*.
The immediate sequence of the triple Veda after the Sāman beginning with Agni is due to the scriptural statement that the triple Veda is the effect of Agni and the others;
for the *hiṅkāra* comes first among all things to be performed.
These three worlds are the *anantara* (intermediate) because they are the effects of that [Brahman]; this is the introductory statement.
Fire and the others are the *udgītha* because of their excellence;
the stars and the others are the *pratihāra* because they are held back (*pratihatatvāt*).

Because of the commonality of the syllable *dhakāra* found in serpents and other such beings, this *sāman* possesses the quality of "death" (*nidhana*). Since there is no distinction in name, the word *sāman* refers to the entire collection of *sāmans*. Indeed, the constituent parts of the *sāman*, such as the *hiṅkāra* and so forth, are to be meditated upon through the vision of the threefold knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*) and others.
Even regarding the previously mentioned meditations on the *sāman*, whatever *sāman* is woven into each respective [object], that *sāman* is to be meditated upon through the vision of that object.
Because the ritual wife is to be consecrated by a specific gaze, just as clarified butter [is consecrated].
He who thus knows this Sāman as woven upon everything becomes everything indeed.
The meaning is that for one who knows the equality of all objects, everything indeed becomes his fruit; he becomes the Lord of All.
For if [the term "all"] were used in its literal sense, it would be impossible for him to receive offerings from those situated in every direction.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"That which is fivefold, three by three— there is nothing else superior or higher than that."
Regarding this matter, there is also this verse, which is a mantra:

"There is no other entity whatsoever that is greater than or more supreme than those fivefold triads—which are declared to be threefold in each of five ways through the divisions of the *hiṅkāra* and so forth, such as the three Vedas. There exists no other distinct reality that is superior or beyond them.
The meaning is that it does not exist;
for within that very [reality], everything is included.
He who knows that knows all;
all the quarters bring tribute to him.
One should worship with the thought, "I am all."
That is the vow, that is the vow.
The meaning is that he who knows the Sāman as having all things as its essence knows everything; he becomes omniscient.
All the quarters—that is, those situated in all directions—bring tribute, meaning they deliver enjoyments, to such a knower.
"One should meditate upon this Sāman as 'I am all, I become all. This indeed is its vow.
The repetition [of the concluding words] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the meditation on the Sāman."
Thus ends the twenty-first section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"I choose the resonant Sāman, which is beneficial for cattle"—this is the *udgītha* of Agni.
That which is undefined belongs to Prajāpati.
