The etymological derivation belongs to Soma;
that which is soft and smooth belongs to Vāyu;
that which is smooth and powerful belongs to Indra.
The *krauñca* [style] belongs to Bṛhaspati;
the *apadhvānta* belongs to Varuṇa;
one should practice all of them.
But one should certainly avoid that which belongs to Varuṇa.

In connection with the meditation on the Sāman, the excellence of the chanting and other qualities of the Udgātṛ priest are taught. Because of its connection with specific results, the word *vinardi*—meaning "possessing a special resonance" (*narda*) that is a particular tone resembling the lowing of a bull (*ṛṣabha*)—refers to the chant; this is the completion of the sentence.
And that [chant] belonging to the Sāman is beneficial for cattle (*paśavya*), belongs to Agni (*āgneya*), and pertains to the *udgītha*, which is the act of singing the *udgītha*.
"Therefore, I choose such a one," thinks a certain sacrificer or Udgātṛ priest.
It is "unspecified" (*anirukta*), meaning not distinguished as "such-and-such"; it belongs to Prajāpati—that is, its deity is Prajāpati—and that specific chant is not specified.
Because Prajāpati is unspecified, [the chant] is "specified" (*nirukta*) and clear for Soma.
The meaning is that the *udgītha* has Soma as its deity;
singing that is soft and smooth belongs to Vāyu, having Vāyu as its deity;
and singing that which is smooth yet forceful, endowed with excessive effort, belongs to Indra, having Indra as its deity.

The *krauñca* chant, which resembles the cry of the *krauñca* bird, belongs to Bṛhaspati; it is the *bārhaspatya*. The *apadhvānta* chant, which resembles the sound of cracked bell-metal, is this song of Varuṇa.
One may practice all of these or employ them, but one should avoid the *vāruṇa* alone.
"May I sing forth immortality for the gods," thus he should sing.

"May I sing forth the *svadhā* for the ancestors, hope for men, grass and water for animals, the heavenly world for the sacrificer, and food for myself"—meditating on these in his mind, he should chant with vigilance, thinking: "May I sing forth immortality for the gods; may I accomplish it."

"Let me sing forth the *svadhā* for the ancestors; let me sing forth hope for men—'hope' meaning a prayer, that which is prayed for; let me sing forth grass and water for the cattle; let me sing forth the heavenly world for the sacrificer; let me sing forth food for myself, for me. Thinking and meditating thus in his mind, being vigilant regarding vowels, sibilants (*ūṣman*), consonants (*vyañjana*), and so forth, he should chant the praise.
All vowels are the very self of Indra.
All the *ūṣman* sounds are the self of Prajāpati;
all the *sparśa* consonants are the self of Death.
If one should perceive him within the vowels, [he is protected].
He should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Indra; he will speak to you."

All vowels, beginning with *a*, are the selves (*ātman*) of Indra—that is, of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose function is strength—and they stand in the place of the limbs of his body. All sibilants (*ūṣman*), beginning with *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *h*, are the selves of Prajāpati, the Virāj, or Kaśyapa.
All consonants (*sparśa*), beginning with *ka*, are the selves of Death. If anyone should find fault with this Udgātṛ priest regarding the vowels...
Being thus reproached, "The accent was wrongly applied by you," he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Indra, the vital breath, the Lord;
as I am applying the accents, that very Indra will speak to you regarding what you have to say—he, the God, will give the answer. Thus one should speak to him.

Now, if someone should reproach him regarding the *ūṣman* sounds, he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Prajāpati; he will look after you. And if someone should reproach him regarding the *sparśa* consonants, [he should say the same].
"I have sought refuge in Death; he will consume you"—thus one should say to him.
Now, if they should reproach him regarding the vital heats (*ūṣman*) in that same manner, he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Prajāpati; he will look upon you and crush you to pieces.
And if they should reproach him regarding the objects of touch (*sparśa*), he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Death (*mṛtyu*); he will burn you up and reduce you to ashes."

All vowels should be pronounced with resonance and strength, thinking: "May I bestow strength upon Indra. All sibilants should be pronounced without being swallowed, without being expelled, and with the mouth wide open, thinking: "May I entrust my own self to Prajāpati.
All stops should be pronounced with slight, non-contacted articulation, thinking: "May I avoid my own self from Death."
Since the vowels (svaras), beginning with *a*, have Indra and the others as their selves, therefore all vowels should be pronounced resonant and strong, thinking:
"In this way, may I bestow strength upon Indra; may I impart strength.

Likewise, all the sibilants (*ūṣmans*)—unswallowed (not taken inward), not thrust out (not cast outward), and open (endowed with the effort of openness)—one should offer them up, giving them over, thinking: "May I surrender my self to Prajāpati."
All contacts should be described as slight, gradual, unpressed, and uncast down, as one who avoids himself from death slowly, like a child, thinking, "I shall avoid myself from death."
Thus ends the twenty-second section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
There are three branches of duty:
sacrifice, study, and charity—this is the first.
Austerity alone is the second; a student who dwells in the teacher’s family is the third, completely exhausting himself while living in the teacher’s family. All these attain worlds of merit.
Established in Brahman, one attains immortality.
The passage beginning with "There are three branches of duty" (*trayo dharmaskandhāḥ*) is commenced for the purpose of prescribing the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the syllable *Oṃ*.
It should not be thought that the fruit is obtained solely from meditating on the *Oṃ* that is a constituent part of the *Sāman*, characterized as the *Udgītha* and so forth.
What then? That fruit—immortality—which cannot be attained even by all the meditations on the *Sāman* or by ritual acts (*karman*), is obtained from the meditation on the *Oṃ* alone.
It is for the purpose of praising that [Dharma] that this is introduced in the section on the Sāmans.

"Three aggregates of Dharma" (dharmaskandhas) means three divisions of Dharma; the meaning is "categories of Dharma. He asks, "Which are they? and replies: "Sacrifice," such as the Agnihotra and so forth.
Study consists of the practice of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures according to the prescribed rules;
giving consists of the distribution of wealth to those who beg for alms outside the sacrificial altar according to one's capacity.
This is the first pillar of Dharma.

Because it is associated with the householder, it is designated by the householder who performs it; "the first" means "the one," not the sense of "the beginning," because of the mention of a "second" and "third.

Austerity itself is the second; "austerity" refers to the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth. One who possesses that is an ascetic (*tāpasa*) or a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), but not one who is established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*), for the latter is established merely in the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*).
This is because immortality is heard [in scripture] only for one who is established in Brahman.
The second aggregate of Dharma:
one whose nature it is to dwell in the family of a preceptor as a religious student is a "resident of the preceptor’s family.
The third aggregate of Dharma is one who, for the rest of his life, exhausts himself through observances while dwelling in the preceptor’s family, thereby wearing away the body.
From the qualification "absolutely" (*atyantam*) and so forth, it is understood that this refers to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).
For the student who returns home (*upakurvāṇa*), since his celibacy is for the purpose of mastering the Veda, he does not attain the worlds of merit through that celibacy alone.
All three of these types of ascetics, however, attain the worlds of merit by means of their respective duties as previously described.
Those for whom the world is meritorious are these "merit-worlders," namely the forest-dwellers (*āśramins*).

But the remaining one who has not been mentioned—the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) established in Brahman, meaning perfectly situated in Brahman—he attains immortality, which is distinct from the merit-world and consists of the state of non-death that is absolute; it is not relative like the immortality of the gods and others, because immortality is distinguished here as being separate from the merit-world.
And if immortality were merely a superior state among the worlds attained through merit, then it would not have been taught as distinct from the "worlds of merit.
Since it is taught as a distinct category, it is understood that this immortality is absolute.

Furthermore, the presentation here of the fruits of the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) is for the purpose of praising the practice of the syllable Om (praṇava), and not for the purpose of enjoining those fruits as ends in themselves.

For the sentence would be split if it were intended for the praise of the service of the *praṇava*, as well as for the injunction regarding the fruit of the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*).
Therefore, by restating the fruits of the stages of life as established in the Smṛti, the text praises the service of the *praṇava* by declaring immortality to be its fruit.
This is just as the service of Pūrṇavarman yields the mere reward of clothing for his devotees, whereas the service of Rājavarman yields a reward equal to sovereignty over a kingdom.
And the *praṇava* is that Truth, because it is the symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Brahman;

for the *Kāṭhaka* Upaniṣad records: "This very syllable is Brahman; this very syllable is the Supreme," and so forth. Therefore, it is logical that immortality results from its service, since there is no distinction among the four [classes] regarding their eligibility.

Furthermore, because there is no prohibition against being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃstha), and because the capacity for such establishment is possible even when one's own duties are interrupted; nor is the term "brahmasaṃstha" conventionally established (rūḍha) as referring specifically to the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), in the manner of words such as "barley" or "boar."
Because it proceeds by taking as its basis the state of being established in Brahman;
for conventional words do not depend upon a causal basis,
and the establishment of all things in Brahman is logically consistent.

Wherever a ground for the term "established in Brahman" exists, it is improper to restrict the word *brahmasaṃstha*— which denotes anyone possessing such a ground— to the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) alone, since there is no reason for such a limitation. Furthermore, immortality is not attained through the mere duties of the wandering mendicant stage of life.
Because it would follow that knowledge is purposeless.
If it is argued that only knowledge conjoined with the dharma of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is the means for attaining immortality, we say no;
because there is no distinction in their being dharmas belonging to [specific] stages of life (āśrama).
Furthermore, the claim that "dharma distinguished by knowledge is the means to immortality" applies equally to the duties of all stages of life (*āśrama*).
Nor is there any scriptural statement to the effect that liberation belongs only to the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) who is established in Brahman, and not to others.

Moreover, it is the established doctrine of all the Upanishads that liberation comes from knowledge. Therefore, whoever among those performing the duties prescribed for their own stage of life is established in Brahman, he attains immortality.
Injunctions regarding action proceed by saying, "Do this" or "Do not do that"; and that cause [of such injunctions] is not created by the scripture,
because it is observed among all living beings.

The cognition produced by the scriptures— of the form "the Self alone is this all, one without a second," and "Brahman alone is this all"— which constitutes true knowledge (*vidyā*), does not arise without first subverting the innate cognition of the distinction between action, agent, and fruit, which is the cause for the injunctions of ritual action.
This is because there is a contradiction between the cognition of difference and the cognition of non-difference.

For indeed, the cognition of the oneness of the moon and so forth does not arise upon the removal of the cataract without first subverting the cognition of the diversity of two moons and so forth produced by the cataract;
this is because there is a contradiction between the cognitions of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
This being the case, for whomsoever that cognition of diversity—upon which the injunctions for ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) are based—is subverted, [for him those injunctions no longer apply].

"That which is one alone, without a second, is the Truth; the differentiation of modifications is untruth"—by means of this cognition of unity produced by the authority of such scriptural statements, he desists from all ritual actions because the cause [for action] has ceased.
And that person, having desisted from action, is said to be "established in Brahman."
And that [person] must be a wandering mendicant alone, because no other state is possible.

For another person—one for whom the notion of difference has not ceased—thinks while seeing, hearing, thinking, and cognizing something else: "Having done this, may I attain that. For one who acts in this manner, there is no state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*).
Because modifications are merely verbal designations and are based on the false conviction [of duality],

once the cognition of difference has been shown to be unreal, the notion of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*)— such as "this must be done by this person" or "by me"— is no longer tenable. To the discerning person, it is like the perception of surface or impurity in space.

If, even when the notion of difference has been sublated, one does not desist from actions, then— as before— the statement that enjoins the realization of oneness would be rendered invalid despite the sublation of the notion of difference.
However, just as the validity of prohibitive statements regarding the eating of forbidden food and so forth is established, so too is the validity of the statement concerning oneness appropriate,
because all the Upaniṣads have that [oneness] as their ultimate purport.

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the ritual injunctions (karmavidhi) being invalid, we say no; for their validity is established with respect to persons who possess the cognition of difference that has not yet been sublated, just as cognitions in dreams are valid prior to waking. If it is argued that because the discerning (vivekin) do not perform [rituals], the validity of the ritual injunctions would be destroyed, we say no.
Because we observe that the injunctions for optional rites (*kāmyavidhi*) are not abolished.

For it is not the case that because those who know "being motivated by desire is not praiseworthy" cease to perform optional rites, the injunctions for optional rites are thereby abolished; rather, they are indeed performed by those who possess desire.

Similarly, although rites are not performed by those established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*), the knowers of Brahman, the injunctions for them are not abolished, since they are indeed performed by those who do not know Brahman.

If it is argued that, just as for wandering mendicants who have attained the realization of oneness through practices such as begging for alms, householders and others do not cease from performing rites like the *agnihotra* even after such realization has arisen—this is not so.
For when considering the authority of scripture, human behavior does not serve as a valid precedent.

Indeed, one does not observe anyone performing a prohibited act such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), simply because someone is seen doing so; thus, even a discerning person free from hatred toward an enemy would not perform such magic.

Furthermore, once the cognition of difference— the cause for engaging in the performance of ritual acts— is sublated, there remains no motivating cause for performing the *agnihotra* and other such rites,
just as hunger and so forth are the motivators for a wandering mendicant to go about begging.
If it is argued that here too, the fear of sin (*pratyavāya*) resulting from non-performance is the motivator, we say no.
Because the person characterized by the notion of difference is the one under discussion;
we have already stated that he who possesses the notion of difference—that is, whose cognition of difference has not been sublated by knowledge—is the one qualified for ritual action.

For there is sin (pratyavāya) in the non-performance of that action for one who is qualified for it, but not for one whose qualification has ceased, just as there is no sin for a celibate student (brahmacārin) in failing to perform the specific duties of a householder.
If it is argued that, in that case, everyone established in their own stage of life (*āśrama*) would be a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) once the cognition of oneness has arisen, we say no;
because the cognition of the distinction between "self" and "owner" has not ceased,
and because the other stages of life exist for the sake of ritual action (*karman*).

Furthermore, because of the Vedic injunction, "Then one should perform action," it follows that due to the absence of the relationship between property and owner, only the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is a wandering renunciant (*parivrāj*),
not the householder or others.

If it is argued that for a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), the practice of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) is untenable because the cognition of difference caused by ritual injunctions has been sublated by the cognition of oneness produced by the rule of [the knowledge of] oneness; we say no.
For hunger and the like arise even before the cognition of oneness, and thus there is a need for the purpose of their cessation.
Furthermore, this does not entail the performance of prohibited acts.
Because the notion of oneness has already been refuted even prior to its arising;
for one who has fallen into a well or upon a thorn at night does not fall into that very same place once the sun has risen.
Therefore, it is established that only the mendicant whose actions have ceased is "established in Brahman."
Furthermore, as for what was said— that for all those devoid of knowledge, there is the world of merit—
this is true. And as for what was said— that by the word "austerity" (tapaḥ), the wandering mendicant (parivrāj) is also included— [that too is true].
This is incorrect.
Why?
Because the state of being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthatā) is possible only for a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka).

For we have already stated that he alone is what remains; moreover, for one who possesses the knowledge of oneness, there is a cessation of asceticism (*tapas*), just as in the case of the *agnihotra* and other rites.
Indeed, the duty to perform asceticism would belong only to one who possesses the cognition of duality.

By this, the argument that the state of being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) is impossible during intervals between ritual acts, as well as the lack of prohibition [against such acts], has been answered.
Likewise, the argument that knowledge would be useless because only one who possesses knowledge and has ceased from action is a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) has been answered.
Furthermore, the claim that the term *brahmasaṃstha* is not a conventional designation (*rūḍha*) for a wandering mendicant—unlike words such as *yava* or *varāha*—has been refuted.
Because the state of being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthatā) is possible only for that [person] and not for any other;
as for what was further stated— that words established by conventional usage do not require a [specific] etymological cause—
that is not so.

Because we observe words such as *gṛhastha* (householder), *takṣan* (carpenter), and *parivrājaka* (wandering mendicant), these words— though they take as their basis causes such as residing in a house, wandering as a mendicant, or the act of carpentry— are seen to be conventional designations (*rūḍha*) for specific stages of life (*āśrama*) like that of the householder or the mendicant, and for a person of a particular caste like the carpenter; they do not apply wherever those causes may be found.
Because [the term] is not commonly established [in that sense].

Likewise here as well, the word *brahmasaṃstha* must apply to one who has desisted from all ritual actions and their means—the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) belonging to the highest stage of life (*atyāśramin*), known as the *paramahaṃsa*.
This is because the fruit of immortality is heard as being primary [for him].
Therefore, this alone is the renunciation (pārivrājya) declared in the Veda:
not the possession of the sacrificial thread, the triple staff, the water-pot, and so forth.
For the Śruti says, "Shaven-headed, without possessions, free from attachment," and in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, "The supreme purifier for those who have transcended [the world]," and so on.
This is also established by such Smṛti texts as "without praise, without salutation," and so forth;

and by such Smṛti texts as "therefore, ascetics who have seen the further shore do not perform ritual action," and "therefore, the knower of Dharma is without marks, with unmanifested marks," and so forth.
As for the renunciation of action accepted by the Sāṃkhyas,
that is false because they accept the reality of the cognition of distinctions between action, agent, and fruit;
and as for the non-agency accepted by the Buddhists due to their acceptance of emptiness (śūnyatā).
That too is incorrect,
because the one who accepts that [non-doership] must necessarily accept the existence of a being; furthermore, the acceptance of non-doership by the ignorant out of indolence is also invalid.
Because the notion of being an agent is not removed by any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*),

it is established that only for one who possesses the cognition of oneness produced by the Vedānta *pramāṇa* does there exist the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatva*)— which is characterized by renunciation (*pārivrājya*) and the cessation of ritual action (*karmanivṛtti*).
By this, it follows as a matter of course that when a householder possesses the realization of oneness, renunciation is necessarily established.

"Would not the wandering mendicant incur the fault of extinguishing the sacred fire, according to the Vedic scripture: 'He who lets the fire go out is indeed a slayer of the heroes among the gods'? No;
for it has already been extinguished by the Veda itself, since that fire is truly extinguished when the vision of oneness arises.
"From fire, the nature of fire has departed," according to the Vedic scripture; therefore, a householder who goes forth as a wandering mendicant does not incur any fault.
Prajāpati brooded over the worlds;
from them, thus brooded upon, the threefold knowledge issued forth.
He brooded over that.
From her, as she was being heated, these syllables flowed forth: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*.

In order to define that state established in which one attains immortality, Prajāpati—whether Virāj or Kaśyapa—directed his attention toward the worlds; with the desire to grasp their essence, he "heated" them, meaning he performed meditation, that is, austerity.
From those worlds thus heated, the triple knowledge (trayī vidyā), as their essence, flowed forth; the meaning is that it appeared within the mind of Prajāpati.
He brooded over her, as before;
from her, thus brooded upon, these syllables issued forth: *bhūr*, *bhuvas*, and *svar*—these are the vyāhṛtis.
He brooded over them;
from them, thus brooded upon, the syllable Om issued forth.
Just as all leaves are pierced by a pin, even so all speech is pierced by the syllable Om.
The syllable Om is indeed all this; the syllable Om is indeed all this.
He brooded over those syllables; from them, thus brooded upon, the syllable *oṃ* flowed forth—that is Brahman.
To explain what kind it is, he says: "Just as all leaves—that is, the entire collection of leaf-parts—are pierced, perforated, and pervaded by a stalk, meaning by the midrib;
even so, the entire collection of words is pierced by the syllable *oṃ*, which is Brahman and serves as the symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self."
Because of such scriptural passages as "The letter 'A' is indeed all speech," and because a modification of the Supreme Self is merely a name, it follows that "all this is indeed the syllable Om.
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
The purpose of explaining the accomplishment of the worlds and so forth is for the sake of praising the syllable Oṃ.
Thus ends the twenty-third section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The exponents of Brahman say:
"That which belongs to the Vasus is the morning libation."
The midday pressing belongs to the Rudras;
the third pressing belongs to the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas.

In connection with the meditation on the Sāman, having set aside the syllable *oṃ*—which, being subordinate to ritual action, was previously subject to cessation—and having magnified it as a symbol of the Supreme Self and a cause of immortality, [the author], desiring to teach the Sāman, the oblation, the mantra, and the rising up which are constituent parts of this very sacrifice under discussion, says: "The exponents of Brahman say: 'That which is the morning extraction belongs to the Vasus.'"
And by them—the Rudras who are the lords of the midday pressing—this world connected with the morning pressing was brought under control;
likewise, the intermediate world was brought under control by the Rudras who are the lords of the midday pressing;
and the third world was brought under control by the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas who are the lords of the third pressing.
Thus, there exists no other world remaining for the sacrificer.
"Where, then, is the world of the sacrificer?
"If one were not to know that, how could he perform it? Only one who knows it should perform it."

Therefore, where then is the world for the sacrificer, for whose sake he sacrifices? The intention is that there is no world at all, because of the Vedic scripture: "He who sacrifices sacrifices indeed for the sake of a world."

And in the absence of the worlds, that sacrificer who would not know—that is, would not understand—the means of acquiring those worlds, characterized by the Sāman, the Homa, and the Mantras; how could he, being ignorant, perform the sacrifice? In no way whatsoever is his status as an agent possible—this is the meaning. Since this passage is intended to praise the knowledge of the Sāman and so forth, it does not prohibit the agency of one who is ignorant of them but knows only the ritual action (*karman*).
For this sentence is divided [in its purpose]: for the sake of praising the knowledge of the Sāman and so forth, and for the sake of prohibiting the agency of one who is ignorant.
Regarding the first point, we have already stated the reason in the *Oṣastya-kāṇḍa* that ritual action exists even for the ignorant;
however, one who possesses knowledge should perform the means consisting of the Sāman and so forth which are about to be described.
Formerly, before the commencement of the Prātaranuvāka, having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire facing north, he sings the Sāman dedicated to the Vasus.

What is that which is to be known? He says: Formerly, before the commencement of the recitation of the *prātaranuvāka*, having sat down behind the *gārhapatya* fire facing north, he sings the *sāman* dedicated to the Vasus (*vāsava*).
Open the door of the world;
may we behold you, O King, with our eyes.
O Agni, open the door of this world of earth for the sake of attaining it; through that door may we behold you for the sake of sovereignty.
Then he offers the oblation:
"Homage to Agni, who dwells on the earth, who dwells in the world!
Find a world for my sacrificer!"
This indeed is the world of the sacrificer; I am this.

Immediately thereafter, he offers an oblation with this mantra: "Homage to Agni! We bow down before you, O dweller on earth—that is, to the one who resides upon the earth; O dweller of the world—that is, to the one who resides in the world of the earth. Find—obtain—a world for me, the sacrificer.
This indeed is my world, the sacrificer’s; I shall go to it."
At this point, the sacrificer says, "Svāhā! Beyond the span of my life! and having said, "Remove the bar," he stands up.
To him, the Vasus present the morning pressing.
"In this world, I, the sacrificer, having passed beyond my lifespan—that is, having died—[I offer]," he says; thus he offers with "Svāhā!
Having uttered the mantra, "Drive away, remove the crossbar—the bolt of the door to the worlds"—he stands up. In this manner, [he offers] to the Vasus.
The world connected with the morning pressing would have been ransomed; therefore, they hand over the morning pressing to the sacrificer.
Formerly, before the commencement of the midday pressing, he sits down behind the Āgnīdhrīya fire facing north and sings the Sāman dedicated to Rudra.
Open wide the door of the world!
May we behold you, O Vira, as the one who leads us forward.

Likewise, having sat down to the rear of the Āgnīdhrīya fire and behind the Dakṣiṇāgni, facing northward, the sacrificer chants the Raudra Sāman, which has Rudra as its deity, for the sake of attaining sovereignty.
Then he offers:
"Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space, who dwells in the world!
Find a world for my sacrificer!"
This indeed is the world of the sacrificer; I am in this.
Here the sacrificer says, "Beyond the span of life, Svāhā!
Remove the bolt," and having spoken thus, he rises;
the Rudras then hand over the midday pressing to him.
"Antarikṣakṣitaḥ," and so forth, is the same as before.
Formerly, before the commencement of the third pressing, sitting behind the Āhavanīya fire facing north, he sings the Sāman dedicated to Āditya and the Sāman dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
Open the door of the world;
may we behold you, O Self-radiant One! [With the words] "Come hither, come hither," one worships the Āditya.
Now follows the Vaiśvadeva [offering]: "May we behold thee with the Sāman; hūm! O Jyāya! (RV 10.127.1).

Likewise, having sat down facing north in front of the Āhavanīya fire, he sings the Sāmans dedicated to Āditya and to the Viśvedevas—namely, the Āditya and the Vaiśvadeva Sāmans—in succession for the sake of self-sovereignty and universal sovereignty.
Then he offers the oblation:
"Homage to the Ādityas and to all the gods who dwell in heaven, who dwell in the world!
Find a world for me, the sacrificer!"
"This indeed is the world of the sacrificer;
here I am, the sacrificer, beyond the span of life—svāhā! Having said, "Strike away the crossbar," he rises.
The rest is the same as beginning with "To those dwelling in heaven" (divikṣidbhyaḥ);
the only difference is the addition of the words "vindata apahatā" (find and drive away).
However, this belongs to the sacrificer (yājamāna).
This is because of the indicative mark [in the scripture] beginning with, "I am here, O sacrificer."
Therefore, both the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas grant him the third libation.
He indeed knows the measure of the sacrifice who knows thus, who knows thus.
This sacrificer, indeed, who knows thus—that is, who knows the measure and the true nature of the sacrifice as described, such as the Sāman and so forth—knows it exactly as stated.
The repetition, "He who knows thus, he who knows thus," is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa. Om.
Now begins the third chapter.
Yonder sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods;
of it, the sky is the cross-beam and the atmosphere is the cake.
The Marīcis are the sons.
The connection for the beginning of this chapter is as follows:

at the end of the immediately preceding chapter it was stated, "He knows the measure of the sacrifice," and various elements pertaining to the sacrifice—such as the Sāmans, oblations, mantras, and ritual postures—were taught as constituent parts of the sacrifice for the attainment of specific results.
And Savitṛ, whose nature is the accomplishment of all sacrifices, shines with great splendor.
This very [sun], which is the fruit of the karma of all living beings, is directly perceived and subsisted upon by all.

Therefore, immediately after the description of sacrifice, the Śruti begins with the words, "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods," etc., intending to enjoin a meditation on the Sun— the effect of that sacrifice— which yields the most excellent fruit among all human goals.
Because he gladdens the gods like honey, this Āditya is "honey" (madhu).
He will later explain that Āditya is the cause of joy for Vasu and the others, since he is the embodiment of the fruit of all sacrifices.
To the question, "In what way is he honey?", he says: of that honey, heaven itself is the horizontal bamboo frame, just as there is a horizontal bamboo frame for the honey of bees.

For the sky appears as if turned sideways, and the intermediate space (antarikṣa) hangs down like a honeycomb attached to the beam of the sky; thus, due to this similarity with a honeycomb, the intermediate space is called a "honeycomb" (madhvapūpa). Furthermore, it is because the intermediate space is the support of the honey, which is the Sun.

The rays are the light-beams, and the waters situated within those rays are the terrestrial waters drawn forth by the Sun; for it is known from scripture: "These indeed are the waters of the self-ruling one (Svarāj), namely the rays."

Because they are situated within the rays that stand in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), they appear like sons placed within honeycombs; thus they are called "sons" (*putra*). For the sons of bees are indeed placed within the cells of a honeycomb.
Those rays of his which extend eastward are his eastern honey-cells;
the *Ṛg* verses themselves are the honey-makers.
The Ṛgveda itself is the flower;
those are the immortal waters;
these indeed are the Ṛc verses.

Of that Savitṛ, who is the substratum of honey, those rays which go forward—that is, toward the eastern direction—are his "eastern honey-veins"; the meaning is that they are like honey-veins, being apertures that serve as the substrata for honey because they extend eastward.

In that context, the Ṛg-verses themselves are the honey-makers; they are called honey-makers because, like bees, they produce the honey that has Savitṛ as its substratum by taking up essences, just as bees produce honey by collecting juices.

The *Ṛgveda* is like the flower of that [tree]. Since the collection of *ṛks* and *brāhmaṇas* is designated as the *Ṛgveda*, and because it consists of mere sound, it is impossible for the flow of nectar in the form of objects of enjoyment to issue from it; therefore, by the word "Ṛgveda," the ritual action prescribed by the *Ṛgveda* is meant here, for from that action the flow of sweet nectar consisting of the fruit of the work can indeed arise.

Just as honey is produced by bees from flowers, so too, having taken the "water" from the ritual action prescribed in the Ṛgveda—which stands in the place of flowers—honey is produced by means of the Ṛks. What are those waters? They are the substances consisting of Soma, clarified butter, and milk, employed in the ritual; when cast into the fire and transformed through its cooking, they become "immortal" waters (amṛta), being exceedingly flavorful because they serve the purpose of immortality.
Taking up those essences, these very Ṛks are like bees that extract the juice from flowers. Thus, the Ṛks are the bees.
They brooded upon this Rigveda;
from it, thus brooded upon, there was born as its essence glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.

These *ṛks*—employed as constituent parts of the ritual such as the *śastra* recitations—when applied to the action prescribed by the *Ṛgveda*, performed an intense heating (*abhyatapan*) upon it, as it were;

for it is logical that the ritual being performed by means of these *ṛk* mantras yields a juice that produces honey, just as flowers being sucked by bees release their sap. This is what is meant by the phrase:
"of that *Ṛgveda* which was thus heated."
What is that essence which is said to have been extracted by the Ṛg-verse-bees from their heating?

It is fame, which is renown; splendor, which is the radiance residing in the body; the senses, which is the non-deficiency of the faculties endowed with capacity; vigor, which means capability or strength;

and food, which is both "food" (anna) and "that which is to be eaten" (ādya)—that by which, when consumed day after day, the sustenance of the gods occurs. This essence was produced from ritual action characterized by sacrifice and the like.
It flowed forth;
it took refuge around the sun.
This, indeed, is that which is the red form of the sun.
That [water], from fame (*yaśas*) down to food (*anna*), flowed out—that is, it issued forth in its various forms.
Having gone there, it took refuge on all sides, on the flanks, specifically in the eastern part of the sun; the meaning is that it resorted to that.

For people perform ritual actions for the sake of attaining results characterized by fame and so forth, thinking, "We shall enjoy the honey called the fruit of karma accumulated in that sun," just as one performs the work of preparing a field.
This is demonstrated before the eyes of farmers for the sake of instilling faith;
that is indeed this very thing: the red form which is seen of the rising sun.
Thus ends the first section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, those which are its southern rays are its southern honey-cells;
the Yajus formulas themselves are the honey-makers.
The Yajurveda itself is the flower;
those are the immortal waters.
Now, "those which are its southern rays," and so forth, is the same as before.
The *yajus* formulas themselves are the honey-makers, employed in the rites prescribed by the *Yajurveda*;
they are like honey-makers, as previously described.
The ritual action prescribed by the Yajurveda occupies the position of the flower and is thus called the "flower";
these very waters, such as Soma and the rest, are the nectar.
These very sacrificial formulas (yajus) heated this Yajurveda;
from it, thus heated, its essence was produced as glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.
That flowed forth;
it took refuge around the sun.
That indeed is this white form of the sun.
"These very Yajus formulas brooded over this Yajurveda," and so forth—all is the same [as before].
This "honey" is that white form of the sun which is seen.
Thus ends the second section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, those rays of his that point westward are its western honey-cells;
the Sāman chants themselves are the honey-makers.
The Sāmaveda itself is the flower;
they are those immortal waters.
These very Sāmans heated this Sāmaveda;
from it, thus heated, there was produced as its essence glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.
It flowed forth;
it took refuge around the sun.
That, indeed, is this black form of the sun.
Now, "those rays of his which are directed westward," and so forth, is the same [as before].
Likewise, there is the honey of the Sāmans.
This is the black form of the Sun.
Thus ends the third section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, those rays of his which point upward are its northern honey-cells;
the Atharvans and Aṅgirases are the honey-makers.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas are the flower;
they are the waters of immortality.
These very Atharvans and Aṅgirases brooded upon this Itihāsa-Purāṇa;
from it, thus brooded upon, there was produced as its essence glory, splendor, the senses, vigor, and food.
It flowed forth;
it took refuge around the sun.
That indeed is this very form of the sun which is intensely black.
Then, "those rays of his which go upward," and so forth, is the same [as before].
The *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ* are the mantras seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras; when employed in ritual action, they are the honey-makers (*madhukṛtaḥ*). The *Itihāsa-purāṇa* is the flower.
The application of these two—the Itihāsas and Purāṇas—as constituent parts of the ritual during the *pāriplava* nights of the Aśvamedha sacrifice is well-established.
This "honey" is the supreme black form of the Sun; that is to say, it is exceedingly black.
Thus ends the fourth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, those rays of his that point upward are its upward honey-cells;
the secret instructions are the honey-makers.
Brahman itself is the flower;
they are the immortal waters.
These secret instructions indeed brooded over this Brahman;
from it, thus brooded upon, glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food—these were born as its essence.
That flowed forth;
it took refuge around the sun.
That indeed is this which appears as if shimmering in the middle of the sun.

Now, "those rays of his which go upward," and so forth, is as explained previously. The secret, hidden, and esoteric instructions—namely the ritual procedures concerning the "door of the world" and other such rites, as well as the meditations (*upāsanā*) pertaining to the constituent parts of ritual action—are the honey-makers. Brahman alone, because of its connection with the word [in this context], is the flower called Prāṇa. The rest is the same [as before].
This honey of the sun, seen by one with concentrated vision in the midst of the solar orb, appears as if it were agitated or even quivering.
These, indeed, are the essences of essences;
for the Vedas are essences,
and these are their essences.
These, indeed, are the nectars of the nectars;
for the Vedas are nectars,
and these are their nectars.
These aforementioned specific forms, such as the red one and so forth, are the "essences of essences.

Of which essences? He says: because the Vedas are the "essences" (*rasa*) since they are the exudation of the world, these specific forms—the red one and so forth—are the essences even of those Vedas that have entered into the state of ritual action (*karman*); the meaning is that they are the ultimate core.
Likewise, the Vedas are indeed immortal, for they are immortal because of their eternity; these forms, such as the red one and so forth, are the immortals belonging to them.
The statement "the essence of essences" and so on is a praise of the action, meaning that he whose fruit consists of such distinguished immortals [attains it].
Thus ends the fifth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which is the first nectar, the Vasus subsist upon it through Agni as their mouth.
Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink.
Having seen this very nectar, they are satisfied.
Regarding the phrase "of form" (*rūpasya*): no, because fame and so forth are accessible to the ear and other senses;
fame is that which is apprehended by the ear.
The form of fire is that which is perceived by the eye.
The sense faculty is the capacity of the instrument, inferred from the effect of grasping its object.
Vigor is strength, the enthusiasm residing in the body, and the possession of vital breath.
Food, which is consumed daily and serves to maintain the body, is entirely of the nature of *rasa* (essence).
Seeing this, all the gods are satisfied; the phrase "seeing it, they are satisfied" means that having experienced it through their own senses, they are satisfied.
Abiding in the sun, they are free from the defects of the body and the senses, such as foul odors and the like.
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge.
Do they live upon the nectar without making any effort? No.
How then?
It is by perceiving this very form and realizing, "Now is not the time for our enjoyment," that they enter into it and remain indifferent.

When indeed the occasion for the enjoyment of that nectar arrives, then from this nectar—for the purpose of enjoying the nectar—they rise up; that is to say, they become full of enthusiasm. For it is not observed in the world that those who lack enthusiasm, who do not exert themselves, and who are indolent, attain the enjoyment [of their goals].
He who thus knows this immortality becomes one of the Vasus themselves; with Agni as his mouth, he beholds this very immortality and is satisfied.
He enters into this very form and rises from this form.
Whoever understands this exactly as it has been stated— that the bees are the Ṛg-veda, that the protection of the honey is the performance of rituals prescribed by the Ṛg-veda,

that the resorting to the sun is the attainment of the form of the *rohita* (red) light, that the nectar is situated within the channels of the rays extending toward the eastern direction, that it is to be enjoyed by the Vasus, and that the knower of this, having attained oneness with the Vasus, subsists through the mouth of Agni and finds satisfaction merely by the sight [of it] at the time of his own enjoyment— [attains that state].
He knows the rising when that time has passed and the reclining; he too experiences everything just like Vasu.
As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so long does he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Vasus.

It is now stated for how long that wise man subsists upon that immortality: "As long as the sun rises in the east, in the eastern direction, and sets in the west, in the western direction—for that long is the period of enjoyment for the Vasus;
for that same length of time he becomes one who traverses (paryetā) the sovereignty and self-rule (svārājya) of the Vasus. The meaning is that he goes around (parito gantā) it.
He does not remain like one who abides in the lunar orb—a mere performer of ritual actions, dependent on others, and serving as food for the gods;
rather, he attains sovereignty and the state of being a self-ruler.
Thus ends the sixth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, as for the second nectar, the Rudras subsist upon it with Indra as their mouth. Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink.
Having seen this very nectar, they are satisfied.
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge.
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Rudras, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar through Indra as his mouth.
He enters into this very form;
from this form he emerges.
Now, as for that second nectar, the Rudras subsist upon it; the rest is the same as before.

As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice that long it rises in the south and sets in the north; for so long does he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Rudras. As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice that long—double that duration—it rises in the south and sets in the north; such is the period of enjoyment for the Rudras.
Thus ends the seventh section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, as for that third nectar, the Ādityas subsist upon it with Varuṇa as their mouth.
Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink;
they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar.
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge.
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Ādityas himself, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar through Varuṇa as his mouth.
He enters into this very form;
from this form he emerges.

"As long as the sun rises in the south and sets in the north, twice that long it shall rise in the west and set in the east; for so long shall he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Ādityas"—thus ends the eighth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now, as for the fourth nectar, the Maruts subsist upon it with Soma as their mouth.
The gods indeed neither eat nor drink;
they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar.
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge.
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Maruts themselves, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar with Soma as his mouth.
He enters into this very form;
from this form he emerges.

"As long as the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, twice as long it shall rise in the north and set in the south; for so long shall he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Maruts"—thus ends the ninth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which is the fifth nectar, the Sādhyas subsist upon that with Brahmā as their mouth.
The gods indeed neither eat nor drink;
they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar.
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge.
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Sādhyas, becomes satisfied by beholding this very nectar through the mouth of Brahman alone.
He enters into this very form;
from this form he emerges.

"As long as the sun rises in the north and sets in the south, twice that long it shall rise above and set below; for so long shall he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Sādhyas"—thus ends the tenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Likewise, it shall rise in the west, the north, and above, and set in the opposite directions.
The view that [the duration] increases twofold for each successive period compared to the preceding one is not found in the Purāṇas.
For the authors of the Purāṇas have stated that the time of sunrise and sunset is equal for the Sun in the cities of Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma in the four directions,
because its circumambulation of Meru on the summit of Mānasottara is uniform.
Regarding this, the solution has been stated by the Teachers:
the evacuation of cities such as Amarāvatī and others occurs at intervals of successively doubling time.

Furthermore, what is called the "rising" of the sun is simply its coming within the range of vision for the living beings dwelling there, and its "setting" is the cessation of that; in the ultimate sense, there is neither rising nor setting.

Furthermore, in the absence of living beings residing there, even though [the sun] moves along that very same path toward them, it neither rises nor sets, because there is no occurrence of its entering the range of vision or its departure from it.

Likewise, the city of Saṃyamanī remains for twice the duration of time as Amarāvatī; therefore, with respect to the living beings residing there, it is said—relative to our own perception—that it rises as if from the south and sets in the north.
The same application [of the rule] applies to the northern cities as well;
for all of them, Mount Meru lies to the north.
When the sun has reached the meridian in Amarāvatī, it is seen rising in Saṃyamanī; when it has reached the meridian there, it is seen rising in Vāruṇī.
Likewise, in the north,
because the clockwise circumambulation is equal [to that of the other quarters],
for the inhabitants of Ilāvṛta, whose sunbeams are blocked on all sides by the mountain ramparts, the sun is seen as if rising directly overhead and setting directly below.
From the entry of the sun's light through the opening at the summit of the mountain,

it is inferred that the immortals— who subsist on the nectar of the Ṛg-veda and other Vedas— possess a doubling of power in each successive higher realm, as evidenced by the doubling of the duration of their enjoyment.
Furthermore, the rising, setting, and so forth of the gods, beginning with Rudra, are common to both them and the person who possesses knowledge.
Thus ends the eighth, ninth, and tenth sections of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, having risen from there upwards, he neither rises nor sets; he stands alone in the midst. Regarding this, there is this verse:

Having thus performed the favor toward living beings by means of their rising and setting for the purpose of their enjoyment of the fruits of their own karma, and having withdrawn those classes of living beings into himself upon the exhaustion of that enjoyment of karmic fruits, he then—
subsequent to that time of favoring living beings— having risen within himself and emerged, remains established in his own self due to the non-existence of those living beings for whom he had risen.
"He neither rises nor sets; he is alone, without a second, partless, and remains established in his own self in the midst.

Thereupon, a certain wise man—who shared the same conduct as Vasu and the others, who partook of the enjoyment of the immortals such as Rohita, and who, having approached the Sun as his own self according to the stated sequence, remained concentrated—saw this mantra, rose up, and spoke it to another who questioned him.

"Since you have come from the world of Brahmā, does the sun there also, revolving through day and night, exhaust the lifespan of living beings just as it does for us here? Being thus questioned, he replied.
Regarding that matter—both what was asked and what was said—there is this verse; this is the statement of the Śruti, spoken by the Yogin.
Truly, there it has never set,
nor has it ever risen;
by that truth, O gods, may I [be protected].
May I not offend the sacred word.
"Indeed, that which you ask about does not exist there, in that Brahma-world from which I have come.
For there the sun neither sets nor rises; it never, at any time, in any place, has gone down or risen from anywhere.
When told that the world of Brahmā is devoid of rising and setting, he accepted this as if it were true.

"O gods, you are witnesses; hear the true word as spoken by me. By that truth, may I not be at variance with Brahman—that is, with the one whose nature is Brahman—nor may I be opposed to Him; the meaning is: let there be no failure for me in attaining Brahman."
Verily, for him the sun neither rises nor sets;
for him it is always day,
who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman thus.

The Śruti says that what was spoken by him is true: "Verily, for this knower of Brahman as described, neither does the sun rise, nor does it set, nor does it go to its rest; rather, for this knower of Brahman, there is always, indeed, perpetual day, because of his own self-luminosity—he who knows this secret Upaniṣad of Brahman as described."
Thus, by means of the thread [of the Upanishadic discourse], one understands the triad beginning with the lineage, as well as the connection to the nectar and whatever else we have stated;
the meaning is that the knower becomes the eternal, unborn Brahman, which cannot be delimited by the times of rising and setting.
Brahmā told this to Prajāpati; Prajāpati told it to Manu; and Manu told it to his offspring.
A father taught this very Brahman to his eldest son, Uddālaka Āruṇi.

Now, this very knowledge of the honey (madhu-jñāna), Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha told to Virāj Prajāpati; he, in turn, told it to Manu; and Manu proclaimed it to the subjects beginning with Ikṣvāku. Thus, the text praises the knowledge as having come down through a distinguished succession starting from Brahmā.
Moreover, this very knowledge of honey (madhu-jñāna), his father taught to Uddālaka Āruṇi; indeed, a father should impart this Brahman-knowledge to his eldest son or to a worthy disciple.
This indeed is that which has been stated: one may also proclaim this Brahman to another who is an eldest son worthy of all affection, or to a beloved, competent disciple.
Not to anyone else whatsoever;
even if one were to give him this earth, surrounded by water and filled with wealth, this alone would be more than that.
One should not proclaim this to anyone else; two types of *tīrtha* (sacred recipients) are authorized: among the many *tīrthas* who have arrived, such as teachers (*ācārya*) and others.

Why, then, is there this restriction regarding the *tīrtha*? It is for the sake of redeeming the knowledge by giving wealth to the teacher in its entirety, provided with all enjoyments and possessions. This [wealth] is not its redemption, because even more than that gift, it is precisely this gift of the Madhu-knowledge [that truly redeems it].
The meaning is that it yields much more fruit;
the repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the eleventh section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Verily, this whole world that exists is Gāyatrī;
for speech is indeed Gāyatrī.
Speech indeed sings and protects this entire world that has come to be.
Since this knowledge of Brahman possesses such extraordinary fruits, it must be explained by yet another method; thus the passage beginning with "The Gāyatrī indeed... is commenced.
And it is taught by way of the Gāyatrī because Brahman—which is devoid of all distinctions and is to be understood through the negations "not this, not this" (neti neti)—is difficult to comprehend.
Although there are many meters (*chandas*), the *gāyatrī* alone is selected as the gateway to the knowledge of Brahman because of its preeminence.

The *gāyatrī* holds primacy in the sacrifice because it brought down the Soma, because it pervades the other meters by taking up their syllables, and because it extends throughout all the libations (*savana*).

Furthermore, since the Brāhmaṇa has the *gāyatrī* as his essence, just as one would not abandon a mother for anyone else, he does not find anything weightier than the *gāyatrī*; as it is said, "even Brahman [is not weightier]."
Because extreme reverence for her is well-established, Brahman is spoken of by means of the Gāyatrī alone. In the phrase "Gāyatrī indeed," the word *vai* serves the purpose of emphasis.
All this that has come into being, whatever is stationary or moving, all that is indeed the Gāyatrī.

It might be argued that it is impossible for that which is merely a metrical measure (chandomātrā) to be all beings; therefore, [the text] declares Speech to be the cause of the Gāyatrī, saying, "This is a cow," "This is a horse," and so forth; and it protects and guards [beings] by saying, "Do not fear from this," "What fear has arisen for you? and so on.
One who is being turned back from fear on all sides shall be saved by speech;
for that which has become speech both sings and saves, and thus the Gāyatrī itself both sings and saves, because it is non-different from speech.
It is called Gāyatrī because of its singing (gāna) and its saving (trāṇa).
That which is indeed the Gāyatrī is this very earth; for upon this all that has come to be is established,
and it does not exceed beyond it.
That Gāyatrī which has such characteristics and consists of the forms of all beings is indeed this very earth.
But how is it that this earth is Gāyatrī?
It is said [to be so] because of its connection with all beings.
How is there a connection with all beings?
For on this earth, every being—whether stationary or moving—is established; it does not exceed nor does it go beyond this very earth. This is the meaning.

Just as the earth is connected to the elements through its singing and protecting, so too the earth is connected to the elements because it is the foundation of the elements; therefore, Gāyatrī is the earth.
That which is indeed this earth is verily this body of the person here;
for upon this [body] these vital breaths (prāṇas) are established,
and they do not go beyond this.

That which is indeed this earth is this very Gāyatrī; what is that? It is this body within this person—this aggregate of causes and effects—which exists while living, because the body is composed of the element of earth.
How is it that the body is the Gāyatrī?
It is said: for in this [body] these vital breaths (*prāṇa*), which are denoted by the word "beings" (*bhūta*), are established.
Therefore, because it is the locus of the vital breaths denoted by the word "beings"—just as the earth is the locus of beings—the body is *gāyatrī*.
This is precisely because the vital breaths do not exceed this body.
That which is indeed the body in a person is truly this very thing, namely the heart within this person;
for upon this all these vital breaths (prāṇas) are established,
and they do not go beyond this.
Or rather, that which is the body in the *tatpuruṣa* is indeed this *gāyatrī*.
That which is the heart, called the lotus, within this person—that is the *gāyatrī*.
How so? He says: for in this [heart] these vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are established; therefore, like the body, the heart is the *gāyatrī*.
And the vital breaths do not exceed this very [breath].
The vital breath is indeed the father;
the vital breath is the mother.
Thus, according to the Vedic texts "not harming any living beings" and "all beings," the term "beings" (bhūta) refers to the vital breaths (prāṇas).
This very Gāyatrī consists of four feet and is sixfold;
concerning this, it has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:

This very Gāyatrī, being of the nature of a meter, consists of four feet with six syllables per foot; yet, being composed of the sixfold forms of speech, the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, and the vital breath (prāṇa), it becomes sixfold.
Although speech and the vital breath are mentioned for other purposes, they nonetheless constitute modes of the Gāyatrī, for otherwise the completion of the number six would be impossible.

Therefore, regarding this matter, this Brahman called Gāyatrī—which follows the Gāyatrī and has been explained by way of the Gāyatrī—is also proclaimed and illuminated by a Ṛk verse, that is, by a mantra.
Such is his greatness, and the Puruṣa is even greater than that;
all beings constitute one quarter of him, while his three quarters are the immortal in heaven.
Such is the greatness—the extent of power and manifestation—of this entire Brahman known as Gāyatrī;

that is, the extent of the four-footed and sixfold modification of Brahman which has been explained as "Gāyatrī is a foot. Therefore, beyond that Gāyatrī, which is characterized by modification and consists merely of a verbal handle (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), there is the Puruṣa, who is greater and more vast, whose nature is ultimate reality, who is non-modified, and who is called Puruṣa because he fills all things (*pūrayati*) within the city (*puri*).
And from the context of "resting":
"of this [Brahman], one foot is all beings"—that is, all things consisting of fire, water, food, and so forth, including both the stationary and the moving;
it has three feet, thus it is "tripāt."
The meaning is that the immortal three-quartered Puruṣa, who is the Gāyatrī-self as a whole, is established in the "heaven"—that is, in his own self which is luminous.
That which is indeed called "Brahman" is this very space that is outside of the person;
for that which is the space outside of the person is [Brahman].
That which was indeed described as the three-quarter immortal Brahman by way of the Gāyatrī—this is verily that; this very thing is it.
That which is well-known as the elemental space (ākāśa) outside the person—that is indeed the space outside the person which was mentioned.
This indeed is that very space which is within the person;
for that which is the space within the person is [the same as] this.
This indeed is that which is this space within the person in the body; for that which is the space within the person is [the same as] that [space].
This indeed is that which is the space within the heart; it is full and unchanging. He who knows this obtains full and unchanging prosperity.
This indeed is that which is this space within the heart, inside the lotus of the heart.
How can there be a threefold division of space, which is one?
It is said: in the space that is the waking state, the domain of the external senses, an abundance of suffering is observed.
Then, within the body—which serves as the locus of dream—there occurs a much milder suffering for one who is seeing dreams.
However, when [the mind] is situated in the space within the heart, one desires no object whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever.
Therefore, space, which consists in the cessation of all suffering, is the locus of deep sleep.
Therefore, it is logical to explain even a single [element] as having a threefold division.
Starting from the external person and effecting the contraction of space within the heart is for the purpose of praising the locus for the concentration of the mind;
just as, among all three worlds, Kurukṣetra is distinguished as superior.
"Just as it is said that Kurukṣetra is half [of the earth] and Pṛthūdaka is half [of that],
so too should this Brahman, known as the space within the heart, be understood to be full and omnipresent, not limited merely to the heart.

Although the mind is concentrated within the space of the heart, it is called *apravarti*— meaning its nature is not to move toward anything from anywhere— and it possesses the quality of being imperishable."
Just as other beings are limited and subject to destruction, so the space within the heart (hārda nabhas) is not.

He who knows Brahman as described—possessing the qualities of being full, non-moving, and of an indestructible nature—obtains prosperity, power, and the fruit of its attributes; the meaning is that even while living here, he attains that very state.
Thus ends the twelfth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, indeed, this heart has five openings for the gods.
That which is its eastern opening is the prāṇa.
That is the eye;
that is the sun.
One should worship this as radiance and as food.
He who knows thus becomes radiant and an eater of food.
With the words "Of that, indeed," etc., the text begins for the purpose of prescribing the qualities of the door-keepers and others as ancillaries to the meditation on Brahman known as Gāyatrī.
Just as in the world, door-keepers who have been brought under control through service to a king serve the purpose of attaining the king, so it is here as well.
The word "of that" (tasya) refers to the previously mentioned heart.

Immediately following this, there are five divine apertures (*devasuṣayaḥ*)—that is, five openings serving as gateways for attaining the heavenly world—which are guarded by the gods, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the sun; therefore they are called "divine apertures. Of this heart, which is the abode of the heavenly world, that eastern aperture—the opening or door situated in the east—is the *prāṇa*; [the person] is located therein by means of it.
That specific vital air (*vāyu-viśeṣa*) which moves through the gateway [of the mouth and nostrils] is called *prāṇa* because it breathes forward (*prāṅ aniti*).

The eye is connected with that very [breath] and is non-different from it; likewise, that is the Sun (*āditya*), according to the Vedic scripture: "The external *prāṇa* is indeed the Sun. Thus, by way of being the support for the eye and its form, He resides in the heart.
Regarding this, the *Vājasaneyaka* states: "In what is that Sun established? In the eye," and so forth.
For the deity is indeed the single vital breath (prāṇa), together with the eye and the sun as its support;
and the text will later state: "With the mantra 'Svāhā to Prāṇa,' one offers this entire oblation and satisfies it.
Thus, that which is called Prāṇa is Brahman, because it acts as the gatekeeper of the heavenly world.

One who desires to attain the heavenly world should meditate upon this luster as the Sun in the form of the eye, and because the Sun is the source of food, one should meditate on that luster as food. By these two qualities, he becomes radiant and an eater of food, free from disease; for one who knows thus, this is the fruit of those qualities.
The gatekeeper, being brought under control through worship, becomes the cause for attaining the heavenly world; this is the primary fruit.
Now, that which is its southern cavity is the vyāna;
it is the sense of hearing;
it is the moon.
Therefore, one should meditate upon this as "Prosperity and Glory.
He who knows thus becomes prosperous and glorious.

Now, that which is its southern cavity is a particular wind situated therein; performing vigorous action, it either separates the *prāṇa* and *apāna* or moves them in various directions—this is the *vyāna*. And the sense-organ of hearing is indeed connected to it, as is the moon, according to the Vedic scripture: "By the ear were created the quarters and the moon."

Together with their substrates, as before: this is *śrī* (prosperity) and *vibhūti* (power). Because they are the causes of knowledge through the ear and the moon, they possess the nature of *śrī*. Furthermore, for one who possesses knowledge, fame (*yaśas*)—that is, renown—arises; thus, because they are the causes of fame, they possess the nature of *yaśas*. Therefore, one should meditate upon them by means of these two qualities, and so forth, as is the same [as previously stated].
Now, that which is its western cavity is the apāna;
it is speech;
it is Agni.
One should meditate upon this as spiritual luster and food. He who knows thus becomes possessed of spiritual luster and becomes an eater of food.
Now, that which is its western cavity—the specific wind situated therein—is the *apāna*, because it moves downward, carrying away urine, feces, and so forth; and speech is likewise [the apāna].
Due to their connection, fire is also like that; this is *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster), meaning the splendor resulting from the performance of duties and the study of the Vedas.
Because it is connected with fire, the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) is [likened to fire];
because it is the cause for consuming food, the *apāna* breath possesses the quality of being "food-eating" (*annādya*).
The rest is the same.
Now, that which is its northern cavity is the Samāna; that is the mind;
that is Parjanya.
One should meditate upon this as both fame and prosperity;
he who knows thus becomes famous and prosperous.
Now, that which is its northern cavity—the cavity situated in the north—is a specific kind of vital air called *samāna*, because it carries equally what has been eaten and drunk;
the mind (*manas*), the internal organ connected to that [air], is the deity Parjanya, whose nature is rain, as are the waters caused by Parjanya, according to the Vedic scripture:
"The waters and Varuṇa were created by the mind."
This is also fame (*kīrti*). Because it is the cause of the mind’s renown,
fame is the state of being well-known by others regarding oneself.
Fame (*yaśas*) is renown, which is cognizable through one's own sensory organs. Prosperity (*vyuṣṭi*) is radiance, the charm residing in the body.
Furthermore, because it arises from glory (*kīrti*), it is also called "glory."
The rest is the same.
Now, that which is its upper cavity is the udāna;
it is wind;
it is space.
Therefore, one should worship this as both vigor and greatness.
He who knows thus becomes vigorous and great.

Now, that which is its upper opening is the *udāna* [breath]; it is called *udāna* because it moves upward (*ud-aniti*) starting from the feet and because it performs actions for the purpose of ascending and exertion. That is the wind (*vāyu*), and its support is space (*ākāśa*). Because these two—wind and space—are the cause of vigor (*ojas*), they are "vigor" (*ojas*), and because of their greatness, they are "the Great One" (*mahaḥ*).
The rest is the same.
These indeed are the five Brahman-purushas, the gatekeepers of the heavenly world.
He who knows these five Brahman-purushas as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world, in his family a hero is born;
he attains the heavenly world, he who knows these five Brahman-purushas as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world.

These aforementioned five, because of their connection with the five apertures, are the five persons of the Brahman within the heart, like royal officers stationed at the gates; they are the gatekeepers of the heavenly world within the heart.
For by these—sight, hearing, speech, mind, and breath—which are directed outward, the gates of access to the Brahman within the heart are blocked.

For this is directly evident: because the senses have not been conquered and the mind is firmly rooted in attachment to external objects—which are false—it does not abide in the Brahman within the heart.
Therefore, it has been truly said that these five persons of Brahman are the gatekeepers of heaven.
Consequently, he who knows and meditates upon these gatekeepers of the heavenly world as distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, through that meditation—

He brings them under his control, just as one might bring the gatekeepers of a king's palace under control through service; having brought them under his control, he proceeds unhindered to the heavenly world, just as one approaches a king, for the Brahman in the heart is like a king.
Furthermore, in the family of this knower, a heroic son is born, due to his devotion to heroic beings.
By the removal of that [sin], it serves as the cause for engaging in the meditation on Brahman;
and since that leads, through a traditional succession, to the attainment of the heavenly world, the attainment of the heavenly world itself is the sole fruit.

Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds that are highest and unsurpassed—that is indeed this light which is here within this person. This is its visible manifestation: that one perceives warmth by touch in this body.

This is its scriptural description: when one covers his ears and hears, as it were, a roar, as it were a tumult, as it were the crackling of a blazing fire—that is what one should meditate upon as "seen and heard. He who knows this becomes pleasing to look at and renowned; he who knows this becomes pleasing to look at and renowned.
Now, when that wise man attains the heavenly world through the service of heroic persons,
that which was stated as "three-quarters of him are the immortal in heaven" must be brought within the range of the senses of sight and hearing by means of an inferential mark (*liṅga*),
just as fire and other such things are inferred by means of smoke and other marks.
For in this way, there would be a firm conviction regarding the matter as it has been stated, namely, "this is exactly so," and a certainty through its non-difference [from that].
Therefore, he says: "that which is beyond (paraḥ) this heaven (amuṣmāt divaḥ)," where the masculine gender has been changed [to neuter] for the sake of grammatical agreement.
The light shines.
Because it is self-luminous and eternally radiant, it is said to "shine" as if it were shining,
since a luminosity characterized by flaming like that of fire and so forth is impossible [in its case].
The explanation of the phrase "on all sides in the backs" (*viśvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu*) is "on all sides in the backs" (*sarvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu*).
The meaning is "above the cycle of existence" (*saṃsāra*).
For indeed, the entire [universe] is nothing but the cycle of existence.

Because it is non-transmigratory, being one and without differentiation; and in order to eliminate the suspicion that this might be a *tatpuruṣa* compound (meaning "among the unsurpassed"), he says "in the highest worlds," meaning in Satyaloka and so forth, because the Supreme Lord, who resides within the effects such as Hiraṇyagarbha, is in close proximity there; thus it is said, "in the highest worlds."
This indeed is that very thing which is this light within this person, perceived internally by means of the eye and the ear— namely, through the mark of heat and sound;
and that which is grasped by the skin through the form of touch is grasped by the eye alone,
because the skin provides a firm conviction [of the object].
And because color and touch are invariably concomitant, how is it that the mark of that light comes to fall within the range of the sense of touch and sight? To this he says:
"When," that is, at which time.
The word "this" (*etad*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
In this body, by touching—that is, by direct contact with the hand—one perceives heat, which is the state of hot touch that coexists with visible form.
For that heat is the infallible mark (*liṅga*) of the light of the conscious Self (*caitanyātmajyotis*) which has entered the body for the purpose of manifesting name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*).
For heat does not deviate from a living self; indeed, it is known that "one who is warm shall live, while one who is cold shall die.
Furthermore, at the time of death, it is accepted that the fire [of the body] merges into the supreme deity, thereby attaining non-distinction with the Supreme.
Therefore, heat is an uncommon mark [of the self], just as smoke is of fire.
Therefore, this vision of that supreme [Light] is, as it were, a direct perception; the meaning is that it is the means for perceiving it.
Likewise, this hearing of that Light is also said to be the means for hearing it.
When—*yatra* meaning when—the person desires to hear (*śuśrūṣati*), that is, wishes to listen to the sign of the Light, then he covers his ears; *etac-chabdaḥ* is an adverbial modifier of the action.
"Having grasped and covered"—the meaning is having veiled [the ears] with the two fingers—one hears a "ninada," like the roar of a chariot;

one hears a sound like the bellowing of a bull, and just as one hears the sound of a fire blazing outside, so too one hears a sound within the body. Since this light has the characteristics of being seen and heard, one should meditate upon it as both "seen and heard."
Likewise, from meditating upon [the quality of] beauty, one becomes beautiful to behold and renowned;
for the fruit that arises from meditating on the quality of touch is realized as beauty of form,
because form and touch always coexist.
And because being beautiful to behold is desirable,
in this way the fruit of knowledge would be logically established, but not [the fruit of] possessing such qualities as softness to the touch;
he who knows these two aforementioned qualities in this manner.
But the attainment of the heavenly world is said to be the unseen fruit;
the repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"All this, indeed, is Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him"—thus, being tranquil, one should meditate upon it.
Now, truly, a person consists of volition; according to his volition in this world, so does a person become after departing from here.
He should perform a sacrificial rite.

Furthermore, desiring to enjoin the meditation upon that very Brahman—who is immortal, possessed of infinite attributes and infinite powers, and who is to be worshipped through various distinct forms—as possessing specific qualities and powers, the text says: "All this, indeed.
Here, the particle *khalu* is used for the purpose of poetic ornamentation (*vākyālaṅkāra*).
