This world, which is modified by name and form and is the object of perception and other means of knowledge, has Brahman as its cause; it is called *brahma* because it is the most preeminent (*vṛddhatama*).
To the question, "How is everything Brahman?", he says: "From that born" (*taj-jalam*).
Everything—from fire, water, and earth onwards—is born from that Brahman;
therefore, it is "born from that" (*taj-ja*).
Likewise, by that very same process of birth, in reverse order, it dissolves into that very Brahman and merges with it as its own self; thus it is "tal-laya" (dissolution into That).
Likewise, during that very time of maintenance, it breathes and moves;
thus, through its identity with Brahman, it remains undifferentiated throughout the three periods of time, because it is not perceived apart from it.
Therefore, this very world is that [Brahman]; and how it is that this is indeed one and without a second, we shall explain in detail in the sixth chapter. And because all this is Brahman, [so it is].

Therefore, being peaceful—free from defects such as passion and hatred—and self-controlled, one should worship all that is Brahman with the qualities about to be described. How should one worship? One should perform *kratu*; *kratu* is resolve, determination, or an unwavering conviction that "it is exactly thus and not otherwise. One should perform that *kratu*, which is connected by way of mediation to the word "worship" (*upāsīta*).

Furthermore, what purpose is to be accomplished by means of the *kratukaraṇa* (the instrument of sacrifice), or how is the sacrifice to be performed? And how is it that the *kratukaraṇa* is the means for achieving the intended goal? It is for the sake of explaining this point that the passage beginning with "Now, therefore" (*atha*) and so forth is presented.
Here, the word "now, therefore" (*atha khalu*) has the sense of providing a reason (*hetvartha*).
Because the person— the living soul— is composed of will, consists primarily of will, and is characterized by determination;

as is his will, as is his nature of will, as is his resolve, as is the certainty he possesses while living here in this world, even so does he become after departing from this body, that is, after dying.
The meaning is that one becomes the very nature of the fruit corresponding to one's ritual action (*kratu*).
For this is seen from the scripture:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when one abandons the body at the end," and so forth.
Since this systematic arrangement is thus seen in the scripture, one who knows it should perform the sacrifice exactly as we shall describe it.
Because a result corresponding to the sacrifice is established through the authority of the scripture in this way, that sacrifice must be performed.

Consisting of mind, having vital breath for its body, having light for its form, with true resolve, having space as its self, possessing all works, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, pervading all this, speechless, and free from longing.
How so?
"Consisting of mind" means primarily mental.
That by which one thinks is the mind; it becomes engaged with objects through its own function. One is "consisting of that" by means of that mind.
Thus, it appears as if engaged in activity, yet for the most part it appears as if withdrawn from it;

for this very reason, it has the vital breath (prāṇa) as its body. The vital breath is the subtle body (liṅgātman), a fusion of the two powers of cognition and action, according to the Vedic scripture: "That which is the vital breath is wisdom (prajñā), and that which is wisdom is the vital breath."
He whose body is that [breath] is "one whose body is breath" (*prāṇa-śarīra*).
This is because of another scriptural passage stating, "Consisting of mind, he is the leader of the body of breath. He is "of the nature of light" (*bhārūpa*).
He whose form is light—that is, whose nature is characterized by consciousness—is *bhārūpa*.
He is *satyasaṅkalpa*:
he whose volitions (*saṅkalpa*) are true, that is, non-false, is this *satyasaṅkalpa*.
The meaning is that the volition (*saṅkalpa*) of the Lord is not of uncertain fruit, as is the case with transmigrating beings.
Because the volition is obstructed by "untruth"—that is, by the cause of false results—it possesses false fruits.
As he will state later: "For they are obstructed by untruth."
Ākāśātmā:
He whose self, that is, whose essential nature (svarūpa), is like space, is Ākāśātmā.
Pervasiveness, subtlety, and the absence of form and other qualities are the points of comparison between the Lord and space.
"Performing all actions":
because the entire universe is created by that Lord, the whole world is his action;
he is "the performer of all actions," according to the Vedic revelation that he is indeed the creator of everything.
"Having all desires":
he is "one who has all desires" because all his desires are free from defects;
for it is stated in the Smṛti: "I am the desire toward living beings that is not contrary to Dharma."
Now, from the statement "I am Kāma," a *bahuvrīhi* compound must be understood here; likewise, the meaning of the *smṛti* passage "I am Kāma" should be explained. [He is] "possessing all fragrances":
he for whom all fragrances are sources of pleasure—he is this "possessor of all fragrances."
"Virtuous fragrance is in the earth," according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*).
Likewise, tastes are also to be understood in this way, because it is heard in scripture that the apprehension of non-virtuous fragrance and taste is caused by a connection with evil (*pāpman*).
Therefore, by means of that [nose], one smells both the pleasant and the foul.
For it is stated in the Śruti, "He is indeed pierced by evil in these [bodies]";
yet there can be no contact with evil for the Lord,
because defects such as ignorance (avidyā) are impossible in His case.

This entire world is *abhyāttaḥ*, meaning pervaded; the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used here in the active sense of the root *at* in the meaning of pervasion. Likewise, it is called *vāk* because by it one speaks (*vācyate*); or rather, *vāk* is simply speech itself (*vākaḥ*).
The word *vāk* is derived from the root *vac* with the suffix *ghañ*, meaning "speech" as an instrument.
One who possesses that is *vākī*; one who does not possess it is *avākī*.
Furthermore, the negation of speech (*vāk*) here is intended as an illustration [for the negation of all other faculties].
Since the Lord possesses the hearing of smells, tastes, and so forth, the sense organs such as the nose would necessarily be obtained for the purpose of perceiving odors and the like;
therefore, they are negated by the negation of speech.
This is based on the wording of the mantra: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes and hears without ears," and so forth.
Disregard is the absence of agitation.
For agitation would indeed occur for one who has not attained his desire upon attaining it;
but for the Lord, who has attained all desires and is eternally satisfied, there is no agitation whatsoever.
This Self of mine within the heart is smaller than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a mustard seed, or a grain of millet, or the kernel of a grain of millet.
This Self of mine within the heart is greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds.

This Self of mine, possessing the qualities described above, is within my heart—that is, in the interior of the lotus of the heart—and is subtler than a grain of rice or a grain of barley; this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating its extreme subtlety.

Having raised the doubt that by saying it is "subtler" than a *śyāmāka* grain or a *śyāmāka* kernel—which possess limited dimensions—it might be understood as having a minute dimension, the text begins the following [section] to negate that: "This Self of mine within the heart is greater than the earth," and so forth.
By demonstrating its greatness through comparison with that which is of greater magnitude, he shows its infinite magnitude.
He is all actions, all desires, all odors, all tastes; he has pervaded this entire universe, speechless and indifferent. This is my Self within the heart;
this is Brahman.
"Having departed from here, I shall attain that"—he who has such a conviction certainly has no doubt.
Thus said Śāṇḍilya, yes, Śāṇḍilya.

From the passage beginning with "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and ending with "greater than these worlds" (*jyāyānebhyo lokebhyaḥ*), it might be concluded that the Lord is to be meditated upon as possessing the aforementioned qualities and characteristics, but not as being qualified by those very qualities—just as when one says, "Bring the king's man," or "Bring the man with the brindled cows," one does not exert effort toward bringing the qualifying attributes themselves;
such a conclusion would follow here as well. Therefore, the repetition of the words "all works" (*sarvakarma*) and so forth is intended to preclude that [conclusion].
Therefore, the Lord alone, distinguished by qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (manomaya), is to be meditated upon.

For this very reason, unlike in the sixth and seventh [chapters], He does not here consecrate [the seeker] to self-sovereignty with the words "That thou art" or "All this is indeed the Self. Rather, based on the indicative mark—"This is my Self, this is Brahman; from here I shall attain Him"—it is understood that by the word "Self," it is not the inner individual self (pratyagātman) alone that is denoted.
Because the genitive case in "mameti" conveys the sense of a relationship (*sambandha*), and because in "etam abhisambhavitāsmi" there is a designation of both object and agent;
[one might object]: "But in the sixth [chapter], the phrase 'atha sampatsye' shows that the attainment of Being (*satsampatti*) is separated by another time. [We reply:
No, for its purpose is to show the persistence of the remainder of the commenced impressions (*saṃskāra-śeṣa*); it does not have the meaning of being separated by another time.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of contradicting the meaning of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Even though the word *ātman* has the sense of the "inner self" (*pratyagātman*), and although it is stated in the context of "All this, indeed, is Brahman" that "This is my Self within the heart; this is Brahman," nevertheless, without entirely abandoning even a slight sense of concealment, [the text speaks of] this Self from here...
It has been said: "Having departed from this body, I shall attain [that state].

For one who knows thus, there may be the thought, "I shall become the Self according to the form of my resolve (*kratu*"; "Truly, it will be so; I shall indeed be thus after departing, or I shall not be thus. There is no doubt regarding this matter, namely, the connection between the resolve and its fruit.
"The wise man attains the state of lordship in that very manner"—this is what the sage named Śāṇḍilya, it is said, declared.
The repetition [of the word] is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The treasure-chest has the intermediate space for its belly and the earth for its base; it never decays.
The quarters are its corners, and the sky is its upper opening."
This very one is the treasure-chest of wealth; upon him this entire universe is supported.
It has been stated that "a hero is born in his family.
However, the mere birth of a hero is not sufficient for the protection of the father;
for another Vedic text says, "Therefore, they say a son who is well-instructed is beneficial for the world."

Therefore, for the purpose of explaining how that long life might be possible, the commencement of the description of the "sheath" (kośa) is made. It was not mentioned immediately after [the previous section] due to the preoccupation with the more venerable consciousness; it is now commenced right here. That sheath has the intermediate space as its belly—that is, it has an internal cavity—and thus it is called "antarikṣodara. It is a "sheath" (kośa) because of its similarity to a sheath in many respects.
Furthermore, it has the earth as its base—meaning the earth is its root—and it does not decay nor perish, because it consists of the three worlds.
For he abides for the duration of a thousand yugas;

all the directions are its sides and corners. The sky is the upper opening of this casket; thus, this casket possesses the qualities described. It is a "repository of wealth" (vasudhāna), because the wealth known as the fruits of the actions of living beings is deposited within it.

Within which the entire universe—the fruits of the actions of all living beings along with their means—is contained; that is to say, this world is supported, dependent upon, and situated therein, as it is perceived through direct perception and other means of valid knowledge.
Of that [sacrificial fire], the eastern direction is named Juhū; the southern is named Sahamānā;
the western is named Rājñī.
Subhūti is the name of the northern quarter;
its calf is the wind.
He who knows this wind as the calf of the quarters does not weep for the loss of a son.
Thus, I know this wind as the calf of the quarters;
do not weep like a son’s wailing.

Of this [person], the eastern direction is the front part; it is named *juhū* because ritualists, facing east, offer oblations (*juhvati*) in this direction—thus it is called *juhū*. The southern direction is named *sahamānā*, for in this direction, in the city of Yama, living beings endure (*sahante*) the fruits of their evil deeds—thus it is called *sahamānā*. Likewise, the western direction is named *rājñī*; it is presided over by King Varuṇa, or it is so called because of its connection with the glow of twilight.
The northern direction is called Subhūtā because it is presided over by prosperous lords such as Īśvara, Kubera, and others;
its calf is the wind, because the wind is born from the directions,
as seen in such expressions as "the east wind" (*purovāta*).

Whoever, desiring the long life of a son, knows the wind—possessing the qualities described above—as the immortal calf of the quarters, he does not weep the "son's weeping," that is, he does not weep on account of a son; the meaning is that his son does not die.
Since such is this specific knowledge concerning the treasure-chest and the calf of the quarters, therefore, desiring the life of my son, I know and understand this wind as the calf of the quarters.
Therefore, do not weep the "son's cry"; do not weep on account of the death of a son.
The meaning is: let there be no weeping for a son for me.
I take refuge in the inviolable treasury with this, with this, with this;
I take refuge in the vital breath with this, with this, with this;
I take refuge in the earth with this, with this, with this.
I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ by means of this, this, and this; I take refuge in Svaḥ by means of this, this, and this.
"I take refuge in the inviolable and indestructible treasury as it has been described; I have taken refuge for the sake of my son's life.
He pronounces his son's name three times: "by this one, by that one, by this one.
Likewise: "I take refuge in the vital breath (prāṇa) by this one, by that one, by this one."

"I take refuge in Bhūḥ by means of [this person], by means of [this person], by means of [this person]; I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ by means of [this person], by means of [this person], by means of [this person]; I take refuge in Svaḥ by means of [this person], by means of [this person], by means of [this person].
In every instance, he takes the triple obeisance, saying "I take refuge," again and again.
When I said, "I take refuge in Prāṇa," Prāṇa indeed is all this being that exists here as anything whatsoever;
it was to that very thing that you then resorted.
That which I said, "I take refuge in Prāṇa," was an introductory statement for the sake of explanation.
For Prāṇa indeed is this entire being, namely this world;
as he will say later: "as the spokes in the hub of a wheel."
Therefore, by that very surrender of my life-breath, I attained—that is, I became one who has taken refuge in—all of that reality.
Now, when I said, "I enter the earth," I meant, "I enter the earth; I enter the intermediate space; I enter the sky. Thus did I speak.
Likewise, by saying "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," I have said that one takes refuge in the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
Now, when I said, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," I meant that I take refuge in Agni, I take refuge in Vāyu, and I take refuge in Āditya.
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," I meant that I take refuge in Agni and the other deities.
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in heaven," that was simply a way of saying, "I take refuge in the Rigveda, I take refuge in the Yajurveda, I take refuge in the Samaveda."
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in *svaḥ*," I meant that I take refuge in the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas.

Thereafter, one should mutter the mantras; having meditated correctly upon the previously mentioned undecaying treasury together with its calves in the form of the directions, the repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
Man, indeed, is the sacrifice.
Those twenty-four years of his constitute the morning libation (prātaḥsavana).
The Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables;
the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī;
the Vasus are connected with that part of it.
The vital breaths are indeed the Vasus,
for they cause all this to dwell.

The meditation (*upāsana*) and recitation (*japa*) for the longevity of one's sons have been explained. Now, prescribing this meditation and recitation for the sake of one’s own long life, the author says:

for only by living does one personally partake in the fruits such as [the welfare of] sons, and not otherwise; therefore, one should accomplish the sacrifice (*yajña*) as the self. "Person" (*puruṣaḥ puruṣaḥ*) refers to the aggregate of causes and effects characterized by life, as it is commonly known.
The word *eva* (or *vāva*) has the sense of restriction;
the meaning is that the person alone is the sacrifice.
For it is thus that he accomplishes the nature of a sacrifice through general analogies.
How so?
Those twenty-four years of that person's lifespan constitute the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) of the sacrifice.
By what similarity? He says: "The Gāyatrī metre consists of twenty-four syllables; the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) of the ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*) indeed possesses the Gāyatrī metre.
Therefore, a person endowed with a twenty-four-year lifespan is identical to the morning pressing. Thus, by virtue of this similarity to the ritual sacrifice, it is called a 'sacrifice' (*yajña*)."

In the same way, for the two subsequent periods of life as well, the attainment of the two *savanas* (pressings) should be stated by virtue of the commonality in the number of syllables of the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters.

Furthermore, of this *puruṣayajña* (human sacrifice), the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) has the Vasus as its presiding deities; that is to say, they follow along with it as the masters of the *savana*, just as in the case of the ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*).

Since the Vasus—the gods such as Agni and the rest—are also present in the sacrifice of the person (*puruṣayajña*) just as they are in the ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*), [the text] specifies: "The Vasus are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)," meaning speech and the other senses, as well as the winds (*vāyu*).

For it is because these [breaths and winds] cause this entire collection of living beings, beginning with man, to dwell (*vasayanti*) that they are called Vasus; for when the vital breaths abide in the body, all this dwells there, and not otherwise.
Thus, because of their dwelling (vasana) and their perfuming (vāsana), they are called Vasus.
If at this age something should afflict him, he should say:

"O Prāṇas, O Vasus, extend for me this morning pressing so as to reach the midday pressing, lest I, the sacrifice, be lost in the midst of the Prāṇas and the Vasus. Thereupon he rises up from it and becomes free from disease.

If, while this [sacrifice] has been accomplished and this stage of life— the morning pressing (*prātaḥ savana*)— has been completed, some cause for fear of death such as disease or the like should afflict him and produce suffering, then that person who has accomplished the sacrifice, regarding himself as the sacrifice, should speak— that is, he should recite— this mantra: "O Prāṇas, O Vasus, this morning pressing of mine..."
"Let my sacrifice proceed; extend it through the midday pressing"—the meaning is: "make it continuous, unified, and joined with the midday pressing and with life.
"May I, the sacrifice, not be lost among you—the Prāṇas and the Vasus who are masters of the morning pressing"—the meaning is: "may I not perish, may I not be cut off."
The word *iti* marks the completion of the mantra.
By means of that recitation and meditation, he rises up—that is, emerges—from that affliction;
having emerged and being liberated, he indeed becomes free from disease and free from affliction.
Now, those forty-four years constitute the midday pressing;
the *triṣṭubh* consists of forty-four syllables,
and the midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*.
The Rudras are dependent upon him;
the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the Rudras,
for they cause all this to weep.
Now, the passage beginning with "the forty-four years" and so forth is the same [as before].

They are called *rudra*s because they weep (*rudanti*) and cause others to weep (*rodayanti*); for these vital breaths (*prāṇa*s) are indeed cruel (*krūra*) in their middle course, and thus they are *rudra*s.
If, at this stage of life, something should afflict him, he should say:
"O Prāṇas, O Rudras, may you extend for me this midday pressing and the third pressing; let not the sacrifice be lost among you, the Prāṇas, the Rudras.
He rises from that very affliction and becomes free from disease.
Now, those forty-eight years constitute the third pressing;
the Jagatī meter consists of forty-eight syllables,
and the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī.
The Ādityas are dependent upon this [breath]. The Ādityas are indeed the vital breaths (prāṇas),
for they take up all this [universe].
If, at this stage of life, something should afflict him, he should say:

"O vital breaths, O Ādityas, extend this third pressing of mine along with my life-force, so that I, the sacrifice, may not perish in the midst of the vital breaths and the Ādityas! Thereupon he rises up from it and indeed becomes free from disease.
Likewise, the Ādityas are the vital breaths;

for they take up (ādadate) this entire collection of sound and the rest, and are therefore called Ādityas. "The third pressing is life" means that they complete—that is, they continue—the hundred and sixteen-year sacrifice until its conclusion; the rest is the same as before.
Knowing this, Mahidāsa Aitareya indeed said:
"Why do you afflict me with this, since I shall not depart because of it?
He lived for one hundred and sixteen years.
He who knows this lives for a full hundred and sixteen years.

Showing that knowledge, when certain, indeed leads to its fruit, [the text] cites this example: "The learned Mahidāsa by name—the son of Itarā, known as Aitareya—said this regarding the vision of sacrifice:
'O fever (roga), why do you thus afflict me? I, who am the sacrifice, shall not perish because of this affliction caused by you; therefore, your labor is in vain.'"
This is the meaning.
The phrase "he spoke thus" is to be connected with what precedes.
Having reached such a certainty, he lived for one hundred and sixteen years.
Any other person who is likewise certain also lives for one hundred and sixteen years; that is to say, he who knows—that is, understands—the accomplishment of the sacrifice as it has been described.
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"When he is hungry, when he is thirsty, and when he does not find pleasure—these are his initiatory rites."

The general reference to sacrifice, beginning with "when he desires to eat" and so forth, is connected to the Person (Puruṣa) by means of the preceding [passage]. "When he desires to eat" means when he wishes to eat; likewise, "he thirsts" means he wishes to drink.
When he does not find pleasure because of the non-attainment of desired objects and the like, and when he experiences such suffering, those are his initiations (*dīkṣā*),
due to the commonality of suffering with that of a ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*).
Now, what he eats, what he drinks, and what he enjoys—that he performs by means of the *upasad* rites.
Now, when one eats, drinks, and enjoys pleasure through union with desired objects and the like, that attains similarity to the *upasad* rites.

For the *upasad* rites possess a happiness characterized by the vow of subsisting on milk, and there is a sense of relief because the days of eating little are drawing near; thus, there is a commonality between eating and the other acts and the *upasad* rites.
Now, when he laughs, when he eats, and when he engages in sexual intercourse, he goes by means of the *stutis* and *śastras*.
Now, when one laughs, when one eats, when one consumes food, or when one engages in sexual intercourse, one attains equality with the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns,
because of the commonality of possessing sound.
Now, as for austerity, charity, uprightness, non-violence, and truthfulness—these are its sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
Now, as for austerity, charity, uprightness, non-violence, and truthfulness— these are its sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās),
because they share the common quality of promoting the growth of dharma.
Therefore they say, "He will procreate;
he has procreated. This is merely his rebirth; death itself is the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
And because the sacrifice is a person, therefore others say of his mother when she is about to give birth,
"She will press [the Soma]," and when she has given birth, "Pūrṇikā has pressed it. Just as in a ritual sacrifice one says,
"Devadatta will press the Soma," or "Yajñadatta has pressed the Soma."
Therefore, either because of the commonality of the word, man is the sacrifice;

for that which is called "he will procreate" and "he procreated" constitutes the very re-birth of this sacrifice named "man," just as the connection with such words exists in the case of a ritual sacrifice.
Furthermore, death itself is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of this human sacrifice, due to the commonality of being the conclusion.
Having taught this to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, Ghora Āṅgirasa said:
"He indeed became free from thirst.
At the time of his end, he should take recourse in these three [mantras]: 'Thou art the imperishable; thou art the unswerving; thou art sharpened by the vital breath.'"
In this regard, there are these two verses.

Now, this very vision of the sacrifice was told by one named Ghora Āṅgirasa (by name) and belonging to the lineage of Aṅgiras, to his disciple Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī; having said, "This is that triad," and so forth—as indicated by the intervening text—he, even after hearing this vision, remained as thirsty for other forms of knowledge as before.

Thus, this particular knowledge is distinguished in that it cuts off the thirst of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, for other sciences; in this way, the text praises the knowledge of the Person as the Sacrifice.

Ghora Āṅgirasa, having taught this knowledge to Kṛṣṇa, said: "What did he say? To that, he replied: "One who knows the sacrifice as it has been described should, at this time—at the moment of death—resort to these three mantras; that is to say, he should recite them. What is that? 'Thou art the undecaying (akṣita),' meaning undiminished or uninjured; this is one Yajus. By implication, having unified the Sun residing in the sky with the vital breath (prāṇa), he speaks thus.
Likewise, he says of that very same [breath]: 'Thou art the unfallen (acyuta),' meaning not fallen from its own nature; this is the second Yajus."

"Prāṇasaṃśitam"—prāṇa is that which is sharpened (saṃśita), and it is also "saṃśita," meaning properly refined and subtle; "tat tvam asi" is the third Yajus. In this regard, there are two Ṛk verses intended for the glorification of the knowledge, not for the purpose of recitation, because the instruction "one should attain the triad" precludes the number three [of mantras].
For in that case, there would be a number of five.
From the beginning, from the ancient seed;
we have risen up out of the darkness,
beholding the higher light.
"Beholding the higher light, we have gone to the god Sūrya among the gods, to the highest light—the highest light. Thus [it is said]. "The highest light—the highest light. Thus [it is said].
In the word *āditya*, the phonetic adjunct (*anubandha*) *t* after the letter *ā* is meaningless, as is the particle *iti*.
"Of the ancient" means of that which is long-standing or primordial.
They behold the light—the radiance—of the "seed," the causal source of the world known as *sat*.
The word "ā" (ā) has its grammatical suffix elided and is connected with the verb "paśyanti" (they see).
What light do they see? It is that light of Brahman which pervades everything, like the day after day.

The meaning is that those who know Brahman, whose eyes have turned away [from the external] and whose inner organs are purified by the means of practice such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), perceive the light on all sides.
The expression "the supreme, the highest" (*paraḥ param*) involves a change of gender because it qualifies the light (*jyotis*).
That which is kindled and shines in the sky—that which possesses radiance—abiding in that Brahman;
by which light Savitṛ is ignited and heats, the moon shines, lightning flashes, and the hosts of planets and stars gleam.
Furthermore, another seer of mantras, beholding the aforementioned light, said:
"Having risen above darkness"—the remainder of the phrase being "beyond [it]," which is characterized by ignorance;
or rather, "having seen that supreme light which removes darkness, situated in the sun, we have risen up," thus connecting with the distant verb.
That light is *svaḥ*—our own, residing in our own hearts.
And that is the one light situated in the sun;
having seen it—which is higher, more excellent, or more sublime in comparison to any other light—they say, "We have risen up. To what have we risen? He says:

To the radiant god among all the gods, to Sūrya—so called because he impels (*īraṇāt*) the juices, the rays, the vital breaths, and the world—we have gone forth; we have attained that light, the supreme light, the most excellent of all lights; "Aho!"—the meaning is that we have reached it.
This is that light which has been praised by the two *ṛc*s and illuminated by the triad of *yajus* verses.
The repetition is for the purpose of completing the arrangement of the sacrifice.
Thus ends the seventeenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman"— this is with reference to the self.
Now, with respect to the divine:
"Space is Brahman"— thus both have been taught, namely, that which pertains to the self and that which pertains to the divine.
The Lord has been described as consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and as the "ether-self" (*ākāśātman*) because He constitutes a single portion of the qualities of Brahman.

Now, the present section beginning with "Mind is Brahman" (*mano brahma*) is commenced for the purpose of enjoining the meditation upon the mind and the ether as the entire Brahman. "Mind" (*manaḥ*)—that by which one thinks—is the internal organ; one should meditate upon that as the supreme Brahman. This vision concerning the self is the "internal" (*adhyātma*) perspective.
Now, we shall speak concerning the divine—that which pertains to the deities.
One should meditate upon space as Brahman. Thus, both this internal [subject] and the divine have been taught and instructed as objects for the vision of Brahman.
Because of the subtlety of both space and the mind,
and because Brahman is perceivable by the mind, the mind is suitable for the contemplation of Brahman;
and space is also suitable because of its all-pervasiveness, subtlety, and freedom from limiting adjuncts.
This Brahman has four quarters:
speech is one quarter, breath is one quarter, the eye is one quarter, and the ear is one quarter;
thus with respect to the self.
Now, with respect to the deities:
fire is one quarter, wind is one quarter, the sun is one quarter, and the quarters of space are one quarter.
Thus, both have been taught: that which pertains to the self (adhyātma) and that which pertains to the deities (adhidaivata).
This very Brahman called "mind" (*manas*) has four quarters—that is, it has four parts.
How does the mind-Brahman have four quarters? He says: speech, breath, sight, and hearing—these are the quarters with respect to the self (*adhyātma*).
Now, with respect to the deities, for the Brahman that is space, these are fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters.
Thus, Brahman is declared to have four quarters in both ways: namely, with respect to the self and with respect to the deities.
Speech indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows with fire as its light.
He who knows this shines and glows with fame, renown, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
In this context, speech alone is the fourth foot of the mind-Brahman with respect to the other three feet;
for by means of speech, as if by a foot, one stands firm toward the objects to be expressed, such as cows and the like.
Therefore, speech is like a foot of the mind.
Likewise, the vital breath (prāṇa) is a foot, the sense of smell (ghrāṇa) is a foot;
by means of that, one moves toward the object of odor.
Similarly, the eye is a foot and the ear is a foot; thus, the mind as Brahman possesses four feet within the internal self.
Now, with respect to the deities (adhidaivata), fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters are perceived as being attached to the ether of Brahman like the feet of a cow;
therefore, fire and the others are called the "feet" of that ether.
Thus, both internally (adhyātma) and with respect to the deities, it is established as four-footed.
In this context, speech alone is the fourth quarter of the Brahman that is the mind.
It shines and blazes, it heats and produces warmth, by means of Agni as its presiding deity (adhidaivata) as its light.
Alternatively, the meaning is that speech, kindled by consuming things pertaining to fire such as oil and ghee, shines and heats—that is, it becomes energetic for the purpose of speaking.
And the fruit of the knower shines and blazes with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge, he who knows it thus as it has been described.
Prāṇa indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows with Vāyu as its light.
He who knows this shines and glows with fame, renown, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa).
The eye indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows with the sun as its light.
He who knows this shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
The ear indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows with the quarters as its light.
He who knows this shines and glows with fame, renown, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa)—he who knows this, he who knows this.
Likewise, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows for the perception of smell through the wind;
likewise, the eye [shines] through the sun for the grasping of forms, and the ear through the quarters for the grasping of sound.
The fruit of this knowledge is the same everywhere; the attainment of Brahman is the unseen fruit for one who knows thus.
The repetition is intended to mark the conclusion of the exposition.
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"The sun is Brahman"—this is the instruction. Its further explanation follows.
In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; that became existent;
that grew.
That egg came into being;
it lay for the duration of a year;
then it split open.
Those two eggshells became silver and gold.

Since it has been stated that "the Sun is a foot of Brahman," this [section] is commenced for the purpose of viewing the Sun in its entirety as Brahman. The instruction (ādeśa)—that is, the teaching—that "the Sun is Brahman" is now being further explained (upavyākhyāna) for the sake of praise.
At the beginning, prior to its production, this entire world existed in an unmanifest state where name and form were non-existent (asat), yet it was not [absolutely] non-existent (asat).

"How could one bring forth the existent from the non-existent?"—because this prohibits the doctrine that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production]. An objection might be raised: "But here, because of the injunction 'from the non-existent alone,' there would be an option.
No, for an option is impossible regarding a real entity, unlike the case of actions.
How then is it that this is "only non-existent"?
Have we not already said that because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) have not yet been manifested, it is "as if non-existent," or "non-existent"?
Is it not the case that the word "eva" (only) has the sense of restriction?
This is true;

however, it does not determine the non-existence of sentient beings. What then? It determines the non-existence of conditioned name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). For the use of the word "existent" (*sat*) is observed in reference to the sphere of conditioned name-and-form.

Furthermore, that manifestation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa*) depends for the most part upon the sun for the world; for in its absence, this [world] would be blind darkness and nothing at all could be discerned. Therefore, just as in a sentence intended for praise, one might say "this royal family exists" even while it is present, when referring to King Pūrṇavarman who is endowed with every virtue, so it is here.
Nor is it intended here to establish either the existence or non-existence of the world, because the passage "The sun is Brahman" is devoted to the instruction [of meditation];
for at the conclusion, it will summarize with the words, "One meditates on the sun as Brahman.

That which was "Being" (sat) was that which was denoted by the word "Non-being" (asat) prior to its origination—motionless and inactive, like non-being, yet facing toward the effect, with activity having just slightly arisen.
Then, having acquired momentum, that [Being] became differentiated through the manifestation of names and forms to a slight degree, like a seed that has begun to sprout.
From that, gradually becoming grosser, an egg (*aṇḍa*) was formed—that is, it came into being—from those waters.
The form *āṇḍam* is a Vedic archaism for the elongated form *āṇḍam*.
Then that egg remained for a measure—that is, a duration—of the well-known time called a year, existing as an undifferentiated essence.
Then, after that period measured by a year, it burst open, like the egg of a bird;
and of that split egg, two shells came into being: one of silver and one of gold.
That which was silver is this earth;
that which was gold is the sky;
and that which was the placenta are the mountains.
The membrane is the mist with clouds;
the veins are the rivers.
That which is the water of the dwelling is the ocean.

Of those two skull-halves, that which was the silver skull-half is this earth—meaning the lower shell of the cosmic egg characterized by the earth; that which was the golden skull-half is the sky—meaning the upper shell of the cosmic egg characterized by the celestial world.
That which was the placenta, the covering of the embryo, at the time when the gross egg split into two parts, became the mountains.
The subtle membrane that envelops the embryo, together with the fats, became the mist, the fog, and the hoarfrost; this is the meaning.
The vessels and veins in the body of the born embryo became the rivers.
The water contained in its bladder (*basti*) became the ocean.
Now, that which was born is yonder sun.
As he was being born, shouts and cries of joy arose after him, as did all beings and all desires.
Therefore, at his rising and at his setting, shouts and cries of joy arise after him, as do all beings and all desires.

Now, that which was born in the form of an embryo within that egg—He is this very Āditya. As that Āditya was being born, shouts, sounds, cries, loud noises, and wide-sounding roars arose; just as here, at the birth of the first son of a lord, all beings, both stationary and moving, and all the voices of those beings [arose].
Desires (*kāmāḥ*) are so called because they are desired; they are objects such as women, clothing, food, and so forth.

Since the arising of the desires of living beings is caused by the birth of the Sun, therefore even today, with respect to that Sun, there is "returning" (*pratyāyanam*) toward its rising and its setting—or alternatively, "returning" (*pratyāyanam*) means its repeated coming back again and again.
"Towards that" means "having made that the cause.
All beings, all desires, sounds, and roars arise in response;
for this is well known to occur at the rising of the sun.
He who, knowing it thus, venerates this Āditya as Brahman— verily,
it is near that auspicious sounds should come to him and overwhelm him, yes, they should overwhelm him.
The meaning is that whoever, knowing him as possessing the aforementioned greatness, meditates upon the sun as Brahman, attains its very nature.

Furthermore, there is a visible result: "quickly" (*abhyāśaḥ*)—meaning rapidly—is an adverbial phrase referring to what happens for one who knows this; "the virtuous" (*sādhavaḥ*) means those with excellent voices (*ghoṣāḥ*) [praise] this very knower.

The correctness (*sādhutva*) of the sounds (*ghoṣa*) and so forth consists in the absence of any connection with evil (*pāpa-anubandha*) when they are employed. "They may go forth, they may come back, they may repeat themselves, and they may repeat themselves again"—the meaning is that it is not merely a matter of their coming and going, but that they should cause delight and produce pleasure.
The double repetition is for the purpose of concluding the chapter and for the sake of showing respect.
Thus ends the nineteenth section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Brāhmaṇa of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a man of faith, a giver of much, a provider of many cooked meals,
and one who maintained dwellings on all sides, thinking, "People shall eat my food from every direction."
The superimposition of the vision of the quarters of Brahman upon air and vital breath was described previously.
Now, the subsequent section begins so that these two may be meditated upon as Brahman itself directly.
The narrative is intended for easy comprehension.

And for the purpose of demonstrating the procedure for the giving and receiving of knowledge, as well as for showing through a narrative that faith, the giving of food, lack of arrogance, and so forth, are the means for attaining knowledge:
*Jānaśruti* is the offspring of *Janashruta*;
*ha* is used in the sense of tradition (*aitihya*).
The grandson of that son was Pautrāyaṇa; he was indeed one to whom gifts were given with faith (*śraddhādeya*), meaning that what was to be given to Brāhmaṇas and others was given preceded by faith.
He was a "giver of much" (*bahudāyī*), meaning his habit was to give abundantly. He was a "one for whom much is cooked" (*bahupākya*), meaning in whose house much was to be cooked day after day.
The meaning is that for those seeking food, much food was cooked in his house.
Endowed with such qualities, this Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa lived at a certain distinguished place and time.
He, indeed, had "āvasathas"—those dwellings in which people come and stay—constructed and built throughout all directions, in villages and cities; that is the meaning.
The intention is this: "In every way, those dwelling in those dwellings shall eat—that is, they shall consume—my food."
Then, as they were flying through the night, one swan addressed another thus:
"Ho there, O Bhallākṣa, Bhallākṣa! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is spread out as far as the sky; do not touch it, lest it consume you!"
While that king was thus situated on the roof of his palace during that time of dharma, some swans descended at night.
Satisfied by the merit of the king’s gift of food, sages or deities, having assumed the form of swans, descended within the range of the king’s vision.
At that moment, as those swans were flying, one falling behind addressed the swan flying in front, saying: "Ho!"
"O Bhallākṣa! Bhallākṣa!"—addressing him thus with "Ho! Ho!", he shows respect, just as one might say, "Look! Look at this wonder!
By calling him "Bhallākṣa," he indicates his dull sight.

Alternatively, because [the other] possessed the conceit of having correctly perceived Brahman and had been repeatedly rebuked by him, being thus oppressed, he calls him "Bhallākṣa" out of indignation to indicate that very fact.

The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was equal—that is, identical—to the sky, meaning it was luminous, produced by the power born of giving food and other merits, spread out, and pervading; the sense is that it touched the celestial realm.
Or, it means his light was equal to the day.
"Do not let it cling to you"—the meaning is: do not allow yourself to become attached to, or to enter into connection with, that light.
By the implication of that, the meaning is "may that light not burn you"—that is, may it not consume you; the change in verbal person (*puruṣavyatyaya*) is used so as to say "may it not burn."

The other replied to him: "Who indeed is this Raikva whom you call 'the one with the yoked mule' while he is actually such [an ordinary person]? [Nārada asked: "But how is it that Raikva is 'the one with the yoked mule'?"
To him who had spoken thus, the other, the leader, replied: "O sir, this king is base and wretched;

why do you revile him—who being such, and endowed with what greatness—by speaking of him with such great respect, as if he were Raikva? Raikva is called 'Sayugvān' because he is accompanied by a *yugvan*, that is, a cart (*gantrī*)."
He said this to him: "It is as if you were Raikva; it is improper and unfitting to speak of such a person in his presence"—this is the intended meaning.
And the other said, "How is it that you speak of Sayugvā Raikva? To him who had spoken thus, Bhallākṣa replied, "Listen to how that Raikva was."
Just as when one has won at dice, the lower stakes are gathered together [into the winning throw], even so all that good which creatures perform converges upon him who knows what he knows—
namely, that "he who knows this has been told this by me."

Just as in the world, when the *kṛta*— known as *kṛta*, famous in the context of gambling, and marked with four points— wins for those engaged in a game of dice, then for that victorious one, the others— the lower *ayas* (dice) marked with three, two, and one point, named *tretā*, *dvāpara*, and *kali* respectively— converge, meet, and become subsumed within it.
The meaning is that because the marks of three, two, and one exist within the "made-die" (kṛtāya), they are included within it.

Just as in this illustration, so too everything—including Raikva, who stands in the place of the "made-die," and those who stand in the places of the "three-die" (tretā) and so forth—is subsumed within Raikva.
What is that? Whatever good, auspicious, and righteous acts all creatures in the world perform, all of that is included within the merit of Raikva.
And the meaning is that within its fruit, the fruit of all living beings' dharmas is included.
Likewise, there is another who knows that which is to be known; what is it that he knows? It is that which Raikva knows.

The phrase "he attains that" carries over [from the previous context]: whoever else knows that which is to be known—that entire collection of qualities belonging to all living beings and their fruit—he likewise attains it, just like Raikva.
The intention is this: a learned man who is thus constituted and addressed by me in this manner becomes, like Raikva, one who occupies the position of the *kṛtāya* throw in dice.
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa overheard this.
As he was rising, he said to his charioteer, "My dear man, you speak of Raikva as if he were Sayugvā.
But how indeed is Raikva Sayugvā?"
Just as when one has won at dice, all the lower stakes gather around him, even so everything that people do that is good gathers toward him;
he who knows what he [the teacher] knows—that is what has been declared by me.

Then, while staying on the roof of his palace, King Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa heard this very speech of the swans, which was of the nature of a censure of himself and of the nature of a praise for another wise man such as Raikva.
Remembering that speech of the swans, he passed the remainder of the night over and over again.

Then, being awakened by the bards with words full of praise, the king, while still rising from his bed and even as he was casting off sleep, said to the steward (Kṣattṛ): "O dear one, do you speak of me as if I were Raikva with the cart?
It is he alone who is worthy of praise, not I"—this is the intended meaning.
"Or rather, I wish to see him; go and tell me about that Raikva who possesses the cart.
Here, the word *eva* (even/only) is either for the sake of emphasis or may be considered redundant.
Then the attendant, desiring to bring Raikva and knowing the king's intention, replied: "How indeed is it that Raikva possesses the cart?"
When the king had spoken thus, wishing to know that sign in order to bring him [Raikva], he asked, "How indeed is this Raikva with the cart?
And he (Raikva) spoke only the words of Bhallākṣa.
The steward, having searched for him, returned saying, "I did not find him.
He said to him, "O fellow, go where a Brahmin is sought; there you shall find him."
Remembering that, the steward went to a city or a village, searched for Raikva, and returned, saying, "I did not find him; I did not know where he was.

The king said to him: "O steward, go to that very place where one searches for and tracks down a Brāhmaṇa who knows Brahman—in a secluded spot such as a forest, on a riverbank, or in some solitary place—and there seek out this Raikva."
The meaning is: "Perform a search."
He sat down near a man who was scratching an itch beneath a cart.
He addressed him, saying, "Are you, O venerable one, Raikva with the cart?
"Indeed, I am," he replied, "for I am the spokes."
The steward returned, saying, "I have found him."

Thus addressed, the steward (Kṣattṛ), having searched for him and seen him in a secluded place beneath a cart— a *gantrī*— scratching and rubbing his scabies, thought, "This must surely be Raikva with the Cart," and sat down near him, approaching with humility.
And he addressed that Raikva, saying:
"O Venerable One, you are indeed Raikva with the cart.
Thus questioned, he acknowledged it without respect, replying: "I am indeed [Raikva] with the spokes."
Having realized that, he returned, thinking, "I have known what was not known"; the meaning is that he came back.
Thus ends the first section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules,
approached him and spoke to him.
Having understood there the sage’s inclination toward the life of a householder and his desire for wealth,

Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa took six hundred cows, a gold necklace for the neck, and a chariot yoked with two mules— a chariot drawn by two mules— and having taken that wealth, he approached Raikva; that is, he went toward him.
And having gone to him, he spoke to him, addressing him thus.
"Here are six hundred cows, this gold necklace, and this chariot drawn by mules;
O venerable sir, instruct me in that deity upon which you meditate."
"O Raikva, here are these six hundred cows brought for you by me; here is this gold necklace and this chariot drawn by mules—accept this wealth, O Blessed One, and instruct me.
The meaning is: instruct me by teaching that deity which you worship."
The other replied to him: "Alas, O Śūdra! Let it remain yours alone, along with the cows.
Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking a thousand cows, a gold necklace, a chariot drawn by mules, and his daughter, went back to him.
To the king who had spoken thus, the other, Raikva, replied:
"Ah. This particle *aha* is used elsewhere for the purpose of restraint (*vinigraha*), but here it is meaningless, because of the separate use of the word *eva*.

"Having taken it away, having joined it with a necklace—this cart, having taken it along with the cows, let it remain yours alone; it shall not be mine, for I have no need for this which is insufficient for my purpose"—such is the intended meaning of the address "O Śūdra.
But surely he was a king, since it was stated that he spoke to the charioteer because of his connection to the *kṣattṛ*;
and since a Śūdra lacks the qualification for approaching a Brāhmaṇa to acquire knowledge, how can Raikva speak this inconsistent word, "O Śūdra"?

Regarding this, the teachers say: "Upon hearing the words of the swan, grief entered him; because of that grief, having heard of the greatness of Raikva, he ran toward him. Thus the seer spoke the word "Śūdra" to demonstrate his own indirect knowledge [of the man's identity].
Or rather, he approached him for the sake of acquiring knowledge with wealth alone, like a Śūdra, and not with service.
"But he was not a Śūdra by birth. Others, however, say that he addressed him as "Śūdra" out of anger because only a small amount of wealth had been brought;
for it is a sign that the term is applied when a large quantity of wealth is being taken.
Having learned of that thought of Raikva, Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa once again took an additional thousand cows, his wife—the Ṛṣi’s beloved daughter—and himself, and went back to him. He said to him:
"Raikva, here are a thousand cows, this necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, this wife, and this village in which you dwell; O Venerable One, instruct me further."
Lifting up her face, he said to her, "Bring these [gifts]; you shall converse with me through this very mouth of a Śūdra.
These are the Raikvaparṇas by name, among the Mahāvṛṣas, where he dwelt with him;
to him he then spoke.

"Here is a thousand cows, this necklace, this chariot with mules, and this daughter of mine brought here for the sake of a wife; and this village in which you dwell—I have prepared all this for your sake. Accepting all of this, please instruct me, O Venerable One. When he had spoken thus, the king’s daughter, who had been brought there for the sake of a wife, indeed became his very mouth—the gateway.
"Regarding the giving of knowledge, one who receives it at a sacred place (tīrtha) means one who knows [the proper way].
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), a giver of wealth, one who is intelligent, a learned scholar (śrotriya), and a beloved— through knowledge,
knowledge itself declares these six to be my sacred places."
Thus the statement of Vidyā is understood.
Knowing this and accepting it, he spoke—that is, he said—and brought forth;
that is, he fetched. "Whatever these cows are, and whatever other wealth there is, that is well," is the completion of the sentence.

The word "śūdrā" is merely an imitation of what was said before, and not because of any other cause, as in the previous case. By this very means—that is, by way of receiving knowledge—he caused me to speak; "ālāpayiṣyathāḥ" means "you made me speak. These are those villages known as Raikvaparṇa, famous among the Mahāvṛṣa regions, where Raikva had lived; those villages the king gave to that Raikva.
To that king who had given him wealth, it is said, Raikva spoke this knowledge.
Thus ends the second section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Air, indeed, is the absorber.
For when fire goes out, it enters into air alone."
When the sun sets, it enters into the wind;
when the moon sets, it enters into the wind.

Air, indeed, is the absorber (*saṃvarga*). The word "indeed" (*vāva*) serves to emphasize that it is air alone. It is called the "absorber" because of its absorbing, its gathering together, or its swallowing up.
It is the absorber because it brings the deities to be mentioned hereafter—fire and the others—into its own nature.
The quality known as "absorption" (saṃvarga) is to be meditated upon as being like the wind, based on the examples found from the beginning of the section on the Kṛta age up to its end.
He asks: how is it that the wind possesses the nature of absorption? [He answers:]...

When, at whatever time, the fire goes out—that is, reaches extinction and subsides—then that fire enters into the air alone; it attains the very nature of the air. Likewise, when the sun sets, it enters into the air alone; when the moon sets, it enters into the air alone.
But how can the sun and the moon, while remaining in their own essential forms, go into the wind?
This is not a fault, because at the time of setting, their non-perception is caused by the wind.
For the sun is indeed led to its setting by the wind, since movement is the effect of the wind;
or else, at the time of dissolution, when the forms of the sun and moon perish, their essence as light would merge back into the wind alone.
When the waters dry up, they merge into the wind alone;
for the wind indeed gathers them all together.
Thus with respect to the deities.
Likewise, when the waters dry up—that is, reach a state of desiccation—they merge into air alone.
For it is because air gathers together these very powerful elements, such as fire and the rest;
therefore, the meaning is that air, possessing the quality of being the "absorber" (saṃvarga), is to be meditated upon.
Thus has been described the contemplation of the "appropriator" (saṃvarga) with respect to the deities.
Now, with respect to the self: breath indeed is the absorber. When one sleeps, speech goes into breath.
The eye is breath;
the ear is breath;
the mind is breath.
For the vital breath indeed gathers all these together.
Immediately following this, the vision of the absorber (*saṃvarga*) within the self is stated:
"The principal breath (*prāṇa*), indeed, is the absorber.

When that person sleeps—at whatever time—he absorbs speech into breath, just as fire [absorbs] into air; he absorbs sight into breath, hearing into breath, and mind into breath; for it is breath that absorbs all these, beginning with speech."
Thus [it is said].
These two, indeed, are the two absorbers:
Vāyu among the gods, and Prāṇa among the vital breaths.

These two, indeed, are the two absorbers (saṃvargau). Vāyu alone is the absorber among the gods, and the principal vital breath (prāṇa) is the absorber among the vital breaths, such as speech and the rest.
Now, while Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni were being served food, a religious student begged from them;
they both refused to give him anything.

Now, this narrative is commenced for the purpose of praising these two. The particle *ha* indicates tradition (*aitihya*). Śaunaka is the descendant of Śunaka; Kāpeya belongs to the lineage of Kapi; and Abhipratārin by name is the descendant of Kakṣasena.
While Kākṣaseni and Upaveśi were seated for their meal and being served by the cooks, a celibate student (brahmacārī) who was a knower of Brahman (brahmavid) begged for alms.
Recognizing the pride of that brahmacārī as a knower of Brahman, and desiring to test him, the two did not give him alms, thinking, "What will he say?"
He said:
"The one God has swallowed the four great ones. Who is he, the guardian of the world?
O Kāpeya, mortals do not perceive him, though he dwells in many forms, O Abhipratārin."
"Because this food was not given to him for whom it was intended."

The religious student said: "Four of the Great Self"—this is the accusative plural. "One god" refers to Agni and the others; "the wind" refers to speech and the others; "the vital breath" refers to Prāṇa.
Who is that Prajāpati who swallowed them, who has consumed them?

"Who is it that swallows?"—thus some ask. "The world" (*bhuvana*) means that in which all beings (*bhūtāni*) exist; it refers to the entire realm beginning with the earth. Its "guardian" (*gopā*) means its protector, its preserver, its keeper—the meaning is "protector.

O Kāpeya, mortals—those subject to death or lacking discrimination—do not perceive, do not know, that Prajāpati. O Abhipratārin, he dwells in manifold ways through the modes of the internal self (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaivata*), and the elemental (*adhibhūta*).
For to that Prajāpati for whose daily eating this food is brought and prepared, this food has not been given.
Then Śaunaka Kāpeya, reflecting upon this, returned [to his position]:
"He is the Self of the gods, the progenitor of creatures, with golden tusks, the devourer, the wise one.
They speak of His greatness as vast, since He, though Himself not being eaten, eats that which is uneatable."
"O student, we do not worship this; give him alms," they said.
Then Śaunaka Kāpeya, reflecting upon and mentally pondering those words of the students, went back to the student and approached him.
Having arrived, he said: "You said, 'Mortals do not see [Him],' but we see Him.
How so? He is the Self of everything, both the stationary and the moving."
Furthermore, having withdrawn and swallowed the gods, such as Agni and the rest, into himself, he is their progenitor again in the form of Vāyu as the presiding deity (adhidaivata),

and in the form of Prāṇa within the self (adhyātma), he is the generator of speech and the other senses, as well as of all creatures. Alternatively, the Self (Ātman) is the progenitor of the gods— Agni, speech, and so forth— and of all creatures, both stationary and moving.

"Hiraṇyadaṃṣṭra" means one whose fangs are unbroken. "Babhasa" means one whose nature is to devour. "Anasūri": a *sūri* is a wise man; one who is not a *sūri* is an *asūri*. The negation of that is *anasūri*, which means he is indeed a *sūri*.
The knowers of Brahman declare that the greatness—the majesty and manifestation—of this Prajāpati is great, exceeding all measure and immeasurable;
for he himself, not being eaten or consumed by others, eats—that is, consumes—the "non-food" which consists of the forms of the deities such as fire and speech.
The particle *vā* is meaningless (used here as a filler).
"O student, we— 'ā'— worship this very Brahman characterized as previously described; 'we' connects with the distant word 'ā'."
"Others do not worship this; rather, they describe it thus: 'We worship the Supreme Brahman itself.
He said to his servants, "Give alms to him."
They indeed gave it to him.
These five and those other five, being ten, constitute the *kṛta* throw.
Therefore, in all directions, food itself is the *daśakṛta*.
This very Virāj is the eater of food;
by her all this is seen.
All this becomes seen by him, he becomes an eater of food—whoever knows thus, whoever knows thus.
Therefore, they indeed gave it to him;

for they are those who are swallowed— Agni and the others— and he who is their swallower, Vāyu, as well as the other five beginning with speech, and likewise the other five within the self (adhyātma) beginning with speech and Prāṇa.

All those ten together constitute that [total]; four units for one [place], thus four; three units for another, thus three; two units for another, thus two; and one unit for another, thus one—in this way, being ten, they constitute that total.

Since this is so, therefore, in all ten directions, the ten [elements] beginning with fire and the ten beginning with speech are indeed food, because of the commonality of the number ten; for the Śruti says, "The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food. Thus, they are food precisely because of the number ten.
For that very reason, we have stated that the "Kṛta" [die] is ten, because it is included within the "Kṛta" as a fourfold unit.
This very Virāj is the number ten; she is both food and the eater of food. By virtue of being the Kṛta-number (four), she is food; by virtue of the Kṛta-number (ten), she is the eater.
Through her, as the food and the eater, this entire world situated in the ten directions is seen—that is, perceived as having become the Kṛta-number.
For one who knows this, everything connected with the ten directions becomes seen and perceived as having become the Kṛta-number.
Furthermore, he who knows thus—meaning one who perceives as described—becomes an eater of food.
The repetition is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the meditation.
Thus ends the third section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Satyakāma Jābāla addressed his mother Jabālā: "Mother, I wish to live the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). Of what lineage (gotra) am I?"

Having unified the entire world—consisting of speech and so forth, as well as fire and so forth—which is praised in terms of the relationship between food and the eater of food, and having divided it into sixteen parts, the instruction is begun that the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*) is to be established therein.
The narrative is intended to demonstrate that faith (*śraddhā*) and austerity (*tapas*) are auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) of the meditation on Brahman.
Satyakāma by name—the particle *ha* indicates tradition—and Jābāla, the offspring of Jabālā (thus named because he was born of Jabālā), addressed his own mother. He called out to her.
"Brahmacarya is for the purpose of grasping the Veda; O venerable sir, I shall dwell in the teacher's family.
Of what lineage am I? What is my lineage? Who indeed am I? Thus [he asks].
She said to him:
"I do not know this, dear father—what your lineage is.
Wandering much as a maidservant in my youth, I obtained you."
I do not know this, to what lineage you belong;
I am Jabālā by name,
and you are Satyakāma by name.
"You should say that you are Satyakāma Jābāla."
Thus questioned, Jabālā said to her son: "I do not know this gotra of yours, my dear, as to what gotra you belong.

When asked, "Why do you not know? she replied: "In my husband's house, I was a maidservant performing much service for guests, visitors, and others; being constantly occupied with such service, my mind was so intent on attending to them that it did not occur to me to remember my gotra and such things."
And at that time, in my youth, I obtained you;
at that very moment, your father passed away.
Thus, being without a protector, I do not know what your lineage is.
"I am Jābālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name; therefore, if asked by your teacher, you should say, 'I am Satyakāma Jābāla'—this is the intended meaning."
He went to Hāridrumata Gautama and said,
"I shall live the life of a religious student under your lordship;
let me approach your lordship as a pupil."
He said to him, "Of what lineage are you, my dear? He replied,
"I do not know this, sir, of what lineage I am."
I questioned my mother, and she replied to me: "In my youth, while wandering about as a servant, I obtained you;
therefore, I do not know to what lineage you belong."
"I am indeed named Jabālā;
you are named Satyakāma.
"Therefore, sir, I am Satyakāma Jābāla."
Satyakāma went to Gautama Hāridrumata—the descendant of Haridruma, belonging to the Gautama lineage—and having approached him, said:
"O Venerable One, I shall live as a student of sacred knowledge under you; therefore, I would enter upon the life of a disciple before you. To him who had spoken thus, Gautama said:
"Of what lineage are you, O gentle one?"—having been asked this, for it is required that a disciple whose family and lineage are known be initiated, Satyakāma replied:
"I do not know this, sir, of what lineage I am;
however, I did ask my mother."
When she was questioned by me, my mother replied to me as before, saying, "I wander much," and so forth.
I remember her words; thus, O sir, I am Jābāla Satyakāma.
He said to him:
"This is not fit for one who is not a Brahmin to explain.
Fetch some fuel, my dear."
"I will lead you away; I have not departed from the truth.
Having led him away, he set aside four hundred cows that were emaciated and weak, and said, "O Somya, follow these.
As he was driving them forward, he spoke.
"I shall not return until I have completed a thousand [years]," he said; he then lived abroad for a multitude of years,
and when those years had reached a thousand.
Gautama said to him: "A non-Brahmin is not especially entitled to speak such words as these, which are endowed with sincerity and truth;
for by nature, only Brahmins are straightforward, and no others.
Since you have not departed from the truth, which is the duty of the Brahmin caste."
"Therefore, O gentle one, I shall initiate you as a Brahmin; therefore, bring fuel for the sake of the purificatory rite and for the oblation," he said.

Having initiated him, he drove out from the herd of emaciated and weak cattle those that were set aside, and having separated four hundred cows, he said to him: "O gentle one, follow after these cows."
Having been addressed thus, he said to them as he was setting out toward the forest: "I shall not return, nor shall I come back, until the thousand [cows] are complete.

Having spoken thus, he led the cows into the forest—which abounded in grass and water and was free from the pairs of opposites—and dwelt there for a long period of years. When those cows, having been properly tended, reached the number of a thousand, they were then fully accomplished.
Thus ends the fourth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then a bull addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma!
He replied, "Revered sir."
"We have reached a thousand, my dear;
please lead us to the teacher's house."

The deity Vāyu, who presides over the quarters, being pleased by his faith and austerity, entered into the bull and, having assumed the form of the bull, spoke to him for the sake of bestowing grace, addressing him as "Satyakāma. Satyakāma responded to him, saying, "Yes, venerable sir."
"We have reached [the number], my dear; our thousand is complete according to your promise. Please lead us to the teacher's family."
"And I shall declare to you a quarter of Brahman.
"Let the Blessed One speak it to me," [he replied].
He said to him:
The eastern direction is a fraction; the western direction is a fraction;
the southern direction is a fraction.
The northern direction is one part.
This, my dear, is the four-part foot of Brahman named "The Radiant."
"Moreover, I shall tell you, the Supreme Brahman, one quarter of It.
Thus addressed, he replied, "Let the Blessed One tell it to me.
Being thus addressed, Ṛṣabha spoke to that Satyakāma.

The eastern direction is a quarter (kalā) of Brahman’s foot; likewise, the western direction, the southern direction, and the northern direction are each a quarter. O Saineya, this indeed is a foot of Brahman consisting of four quarters—that is, it has four parts (kalās)—and this foot of Brahman is named "The Radiant" (Prakāśavān). It is thus called "The Radiant."
That which has this as its name;
likewise, the three subsequent quarters of Brahmā also consist of four kalās each.
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Radiant," becomes radiant in this world;
he wins radiant worlds—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Radiant."

Whoever, knowing this four-part foot of Brahman as described above, meditates upon it as characterized by the quality of "being luminous," for him there is this fruit: he becomes luminous in this world, meaning he becomes renowned.
Likewise, as an unseen result, having died, he conquers—that is, attains—the luminous worlds associated with the gods and other celestial realms.
He who, knowing this very thing, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Radiant," [attains that state].
Thus ends the fifth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. "Agni shall tell you a quarter," [said Śāṇḍilya]. On the following day, he drove the cows toward [the teacher's house].
When it became evening, he kindled the fire there, penned the cows, added fuel, and sat down behind the fire facing east.
"He will tell you the foot of Agni," said Ṛṣabha, and then he ceased speaking.
Satyakāma, having performed his daily obligatory rites on the following day, set out with the cows toward the teacher's house.
As they proceeded slowly toward the teacher's house, at the time and place when they gathered together in one spot for the evening, they came to rest.
There, having kindled the fire, penned the cows, and placed a fuel-stick upon it, he sat down behind the fire facing east, meditating on the words of the bull.
Agni spoke to him, saying, "Satyakāma!
He replied, "Revered sir."
Agni addressed him, calling out, "Satyakāma!
and Satyakāma replied to him, saying, "Yes, venerable sir."
"Dear boy, let me tell you one quarter of Brahman.
"Let my lord tell it to me.
He spoke to him.
The earth is a part; the intermediate space is a part;
the sky is a part.
The ocean is one sixteenth part.
This, my dear, is the four-sixteenth part of Brahman, named the Endless.

"Dear boy, let me tell you one quarter of Brahman. "Let the venerable sir tell it to me. He said to him: "The earth is one part, the intermediate space is one part, the sky is one part, and the ocean is one part"—thus did Agni declare this vision which has the self as its object.
"This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman named the Endless."
He who, knowing this thus, worships this four-part foot of Brahman as "the infinite," becomes infinite in this world;
he wins infinite worlds—he who, knowing this thus, worships this four-part foot of Brahman as "the infinite."
Whoever meditates upon the aforementioned quarter as having the quality of being infinite becomes possessed of that very quality in this world;
and after death, he conquers the worlds of the infinite, "he who knows it thus," and so forth, as before.
Thus ends the sixth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

"A swan, you shall tell me one quarter," [said Śāṇḍilya]. On the following day, he drove the cows toward home. When they had gathered in the evening, he kindled a fire there, penned the cows, added fuel to the fire, and sat down behind the fire, facing the east.
The swan flew down toward him and called out, "Satyakāma! "Revered sir," he replied.
"That fire, the *haṃsa*, will tell you one quarter"; having said this, he ceased speaking.
The *haṃsa* is the sun, because of its whiteness and its commonality with flying.
"When the next day had dawned," and so forth, is the same as before.
"Dear boy, let me tell you one quarter of Brahman.
"Let the Blessed One tell it to me.
He said to him:
Agni is a digit; Sūrya is a digit;
Candra is a digit.
Lightning is a part.
This, my dear, is the four-part foot of Brahman named "The Luminous."
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Luminous," becomes luminous in this world;
he wins luminous worlds—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Luminous."

"Agni is a portion, the sun is a portion, the moon is a portion, and lightning is a portion—this indeed is Soma," thus he spoke, and the vision [of the Self] is indeed restricted to the realm of light; from this, the solar nature of the Haṃsa is understood.
The fruit for the knower is that he becomes radiant and endowed with splendor in this world, and after death, he conquers the worlds of those luminaries such as the moon and the sun.
The subsequent [portion] is the same.
"Thus, in the seventh section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: 'I will tell you a quarter [of Brahman] tomorrow.
On the next day, he drove the cows toward [his teacher's house]."
When it became evening, he kindled the fire at that place, penned the cows, added fuel to the fire, and sat down behind the fire facing the east.

The swan also ceased, saying, "The water-fowl will speak to you regarding the foot. The water-fowl is a bird that dwells in water; because of its connection with the waters, it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Then, on the following day, and so forth, as before.
A water-crow, flying down toward him, called out, "Satyakāma!
He replied, "Venerable sir."
"Dear boy, let me tell you one quarter of Brahman.
"Let the venerable sir tell it to me," [he replied].
He said to him:
Breath is a part;
the eye is a part;
the ear is a part.
The mind is a sixteenth part.
This, my dear, is the four-part foot of Brahman called "Possessing a Support."
And that water-bird, Prāṇa, spoke of his own domain, namely vision, saying "Prāṇa is Kālā," and so forth, ending with "he who possesses an abode" (āyatanavān).
An "abode" (āyatana) is the mind, because it is in that foot where the enjoyments brought by all the sense organs reside; thus, the foot is named "possessing an abode."
He who, knowing this thus, venerates this four-part foot of Brahman as "possessing an abode," becomes possessed of an abode in this world;
he wins worlds that possess an abode—he who, knowing this thus, venerates this four-part foot of Brahman as "possessing an abode."
He who worships that quarter in this manner becomes possessed of a dwelling and a refuge in this world;
likewise, after death, he conquers worlds that are spacious and well-provided with dwellings.
"He who knows it thus," and so forth, as before.
Thus ends the eighth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
He arrived at the teacher’s family home.
The teacher addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma!"
"Yes, Blessed One," he replied.
Being thus a knower of Brahman, he reached the family of his teacher.
The teacher addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma!
He replied, "Revered sir."
"My dear, you truly shine like one who knows Brahman. Who has instructed you?
"Others than human beings," he replied.
But let the Blessed One himself explain this to me regarding sensual pleasures.
"O Somya, you truly shine like one who knows Brahman.
One who knows Brahman has serene senses, a smiling countenance, and is free from anxiety, having accomplished his purpose;
therefore, the teacher says, 'You shine like one who knows Brahman.'"
Reflecting, "Who indeed? he said, "Who has instructed you?
And he replied, "Satyakāma [instructed me], and others besides humans;
the deities have instructed me."
The intention is: "What other human being, being merely a man, would dare to instruct me, a disciple of the Blessed One?
Therefore, he made this declaration: "I have declared that [instruction] comes from none other than humans. The intention is:
"Only the Blessed One himself may speak to my desire—that is, according to my wish; what is the use of what others say? I do not take that into account."
"For I have indeed heard from those like your venerable self that knowledge learned from a teacher reaches its most perfect realization.
Therefore, he said this very thing to him:
'In this matter, nothing whatsoever is omitted—nothing whatsoever is omitted.'"
