Furthermore, for it has been heard by me from seers equal to the Blessed One that regarding this matter,

knowledge indeed reaches its most excellent state— its highest degree of perfection— only when learned directly from a teacher; therefore, [thinking] "the Blessed One alone should speak," the teacher, being thus addressed, spoke to him that very same knowledge which had been declared by the gods.
In this regard, not even a single portion, not even a mere fragment, of the knowledge of the sixteen parts has departed—that is, it has not vanished.
The repetition [of the phrase] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the knowledge.
Thus ends the ninth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a religious student with Satyakāma Jābāla.
He tended his sacred fires for twelve years.
He used to dismiss his other pupils upon their completion of studies, but he never dismissed him.
Thinking, "I shall again declare the knowledge of Brahman in another manner," [the text] begins by describing the path for those who know it and the knowledge of the fires.

The narrative is as before, intended to demonstrate that faith and austerity are the means for the knowledge of Brahman: "Upakosala by name, the son of Kamala (Kāmalāyana), [studied] with Satyakāma Jābāla"—here, *ha* has the sense of traditional report (*aitihya*).
For twelve years he attended upon the fires of that teacher; he performed the service of the fires.
That teacher, having caused the other students to master their sacred study and have them perform the ceremonial bath (*samāvartana*), did not cause Upakosala alone to perform it.
His wife said to him: "The student has performed his penance and has served the fires well;
let not the fires speak against you.
Speak to them for us."
Without having told him that, he indeed went away on a journey.
The teacher’s wife said to him: "This student has been a disciplined celibate; he has properly tended the fires and has indeed performed his service.
Yet the venerable one does not allow him to return home from the fires.
Therefore, knowing that he does not allow our devotee to return, let the fires not speak ill of you, and let them not bring reproach upon you."
"Therefore, explain to Upakosala the knowledge he desires. Although he was thus addressed by his wife, he did not say anything at all; without speaking, he simply went away on a journey.
He, however, resolved to fast due to illness. His teacher’s wife said to him: "O student, eat! Why indeed do you not eat?"
He said, "There are many desires here in this person, each with its own course. I am filled with diseases;
I shall not eat."

That Upakośala, afflicted by mental disease and suffering, resolved—that is, fixed his mind—to fast, to practice *anaśana*. While he was staying silently in the fire-sanctuary, the teacher’s wife said to him: "O student (*brahmacārin*), eat; why indeed, for what reason do you not eat?
He replied: "In this person who has not accomplished his purpose—the common, ordinary man—there are many, numerous desires regarding what ought to be done."
"Various perils" (*nānātyaya*) refers to those diseases and anxieties regarding what ought to be done; the meaning is that these are mental sufferings caused by the attainment of duties.
I am filled with them.
Therefore, I shall not eat.
Then the fires deliberated among themselves:
"The student has performed his penance; he has served us well.
Come, let us teach him. And they said to him:
"Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman."

When the religious student had spoken and become silent, then the three Fires—having been won over by his service, filled with compassion, and being well-disposed—spoke together; they said collectively:
"Come now, let us all instruct this religious student—who is devoted to us, distressed, ascetic, and full of faith—in the knowledge of Brahman.
Having thus deliberated, they said to him: "Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman."
He said:
"I know that breath is Brahman;
but I do not know *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*."
They said:
"That which is indeed *kaṃ* is the same as *kha*;
that which is *kha* is the same as *kaṃ*."
And they told him about the vital breath and the ether.

The religious student said: "I understand what you have said—that *prāṇa* is Brahman—because its meaning is well-established. Since life exists when it is present and ceases when it departs, and since that term is conventionally used in the world for a particular kind of air (*vāyu*), its status as Brahman is logical.
Therefore, because its meaning is well-established, I understand that *prāṇa* is Brahman."
"But as for *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*, I do not know them. [The teacher asks: "Is it not the case that even the words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ* have well-known referents, namely pleasure (*sukha*) and space (*ākāśa*);
why, then, does the religious student lack knowledge of them?"

He thinks: "Surely, how can that which is denoted by the word 'ka', namely pleasure, be Brahman, given its momentary perishability; and how can that which is denoted by the word 'kha', namely the insentient ether (ākāśa), be Brahman?
Furthermore, how could your statement not be authoritative?
Therefore, he says, "I do not understand."

To the religious student who had spoken thus, those fires said: "That which we called 'ka' is indeed 'kha', that is, space (ākāśa). Thus, being qualified by 'kha', 'ka' would be distinguished from the pleasure born of the contact between the sense organs and their objects, just as a blue lotus, when qualified [by its color], is distinguished from red and other colors.
Know that what we have called "kha," meaning space, is indeed "ka," meaning happiness.
Thus, when space is qualified by happiness, it is distinguished from the material, insentient space, just as a blue lotus is distinguished [from other lotuses].
This happiness resides in the [supreme] space, not in any other worldly kind.
The meaning is that space (*ākāśa*) is the locus of happiness, and not the other [element] consisting of the physical elements.
Now, if space is intended to be qualified by happiness, let there be only one of the two as the qualifier— either "that which is *kaṃ* is indeed *kha*" (where the latter is the surplus),
or "that which is *kha* is indeed *kaṃ*" (where the former is the surplus).
[Objection: But have we not already stated that the exclusion of both bliss and space from worldly bliss and space is intended?
If it is argued that when space is qualified by bliss, the exclusion of both follows as a matter of course, [we reply: that is indeed true;
however, what is enjoined as the object of meditation is space alone as qualified by bliss, and not the bliss which is merely the qualifying attribute of space.
The state of being an object of meditation would be established;
for the employment of a qualifier is exhausted precisely by its function of restricting the qualified.
Therefore, bliss (*sukha*) is also qualified by "by itself" (*svena*) for the sake of being an object of meditation.
And from what is this determined?
That "kaṃ" is Brahman because of its connection with the word "brahman" in the phrase "kaṃ brahma.
For if the intention had been to teach that the ether (kha) qualified by the attribute of pleasure (kaṃ) is the object of meditation, the fires would have first said, "kaṃ khaṃ brahma."
They did not speak in this manner;
rather, they said, "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman.

Therefore, for the purpose of removing the student's delusion, it is indeed appropriate to indicate the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the words *ka* and *kha*, beginning with the passage, "That which is Ka, etc."
The Śruti declares this very meaning of the statement spoken by the fires for our understanding: "And [He gave] breath to that religious student (brahmacārin);
its space is 'tadākāśaḥ'.
The meaning is that the space within the heart (hārda ākāśa) is the space related to breath as its locus.

Because of the description of possessing the quality of bliss, both that ether— which is characterized by the quality of bliss as Brahman— and the vital breath (prāṇa) residing therein, which is also Brahman solely through its contact with Brahman, the fires spoke of both the prāṇa and the ether collectively as "Brahman."

Thus ends the tenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him: "The earth, fire, food, and the sun—this person who is seen in the sun, that am I; he indeed am I."
The fires, having come together, spoke the Brahman to the religious student;
immediately thereafter, they each began to declare their own respective domains of knowledge.
Among them, first of all, the Gārhapatya fire instructed this religious student.
"Earth, fire, food, and the sun—these are my four bodies.
Among them, that person who is seen in the sun, he am I; and the Gārhapatya fire, he is indeed I; and that which is the Gārhapatya fire, it is I, the person in the sun.
This statement, "He indeed am I," is made by way of returning [to the original point].
The relationship between the earth and food, characterized by their state as objects of consumption, does not exist between the Gārhapatya fire and the sun.
Since the attributes of being the eater, the cooker, and the illuminator are indistinguishable, the absolute identity of these two is established;
however, the earth and food are related to these two by virtue of being the objects of consumption.
He who, knowing it thus, venerates it, destroys his evil deeds and becomes a possessor of the world.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
his descendants do not perish.
We enjoy that [fruit] both in this world and in the other,
who, knowing it thus, meditates upon it.

Whoever thus meditates upon the Gārhapatya fire as divided fourfold according to the aforementioned manner— as food and the eater of food— destroys and eliminates evil deeds, that is, sinful action. He becomes a possessor of worlds, endowed with a world such as ours, namely the world of Agni, even as we are here in this world.
He attains a full lifespan of a hundred years; he lives long and brilliantly, not remaining unknown—this is the meaning. And his descendants—that is, the persons born in his lineage—do not perish;
the meaning is that there is no interruption of his lineage.
Furthermore, what is it that we enjoy and protect while living in this world and in the next world?
The meaning is: for one who, knowing this as it has been described, meditates upon it, this is the fruit.
Thus ends the eleventh section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then the Anvāhāryapacana fire instructed him: "The waters, the quarters, the stars, and the moon—this person who is seen in the moon, that am I; he indeed am I."
He who, knowing it thus, venerates it, destroys his evil deeds and becomes a possessor of the world.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
his descendants do not perish.
We enjoy that [bliss] both in this world and in the next,
who, knowing it thus, meditates upon it.

Then the Anvāhāryapacana fire, the southern fire, instructed him: "The waters, the quarters, the stars, and the moon—these are my four bodies. Having divided myself fourfold, I abide as the Anvāhāryapacana fire.
Therein, that person who is seen in the moon is I; he indeed is I," as before.

The identity of the Anvāhāryapacana fire and the moon is established through their connection with food and their commonality as luminous bodies (*jyotiṣṭva*), as well as through their connection with the southward direction.
The waters and the stars are likewise connected by way of being food, as previously described.
This is because the moon is well known to be the object of enjoyment for the stars.
Dakṣiṇāgni is "food" (anna) because it produces food, just as Gārhapatya is food like the earth.
The rest is the same.
Thus ends the twelfth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him: "Breath, space, heaven, lightning.
"That person who is seen in the lightning—that am I; he indeed am I."
He who, knowing it thus, venerates it, destroys evil-doing and becomes a possessor of the world.
He attains a full lifespan; he lives long;
his descendants do not perish.
We enjoy that [bliss] both in this world and in the next,
who, knowing it thus, meditates upon it.
Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him: "Breath, space, heaven, and lightning—these are my four bodies.
That person who is seen in the lightning, I am he," and so forth, as before, on account of their common characteristics.
However, because heaven and space are the substrates, their connection with lightning and the Āhavanīya fire is solely by way of being objects of enjoyment.
The rest is the same.
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
They said:
"O Upakosala, my dear, this is our knowledge and the knowledge of the Self."
"But your teacher will tell you the way.
Then his teacher arrived;
the teacher addressed him by name, "Upakosala!"

Then they, having come together, said: "O gentle Uddālaka Āruṇi, this is your knowledge of us—the meaning being your knowledge of fire (agni-vidyā)—as well as the previously mentioned knowledge of the Self (ātma-vidyā), namely, 'Breath is Brahman,' 'Bliss is Brahman,' and 'Space is Brahman.
But the Teacher will tell you the way [to the goal] for the attainment of the fruit of knowledge. Having said this, the fires ceased speaking.
In the course of time, the teacher arrived; and the teacher addressed that disciple, saying, "Upakosala!"
"Yes, Blessed One," he replied.
"My dear, your face shines like that of one who knows Brahman. Who, indeed, has instructed you?"
"Who, indeed, would teach me, sir? he asked, as if concealing himself.
"These [fires] here are surely such [as you say], but they are different," he said, pointing toward the fires.
"What, my dear, did they actually tell you? he asked.
"Indeed," he replied, "they have told you, my dear, only about the worlds.
But I shall tell you that [which you seek]: just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this."
"Let the Blessed One speak to me.
He said to him:
"Venerable sir," he replied. "My dear boy, your face shines clear like that of one who knows Brahman. Who, indeed, has instructed you? Being thus addressed, he replied:

"Who, indeed, would instruct me—that is, who could provide such instruction, O venerable sir, while you were away? Here, he seems to deny it; the phrase "he seems to deny" (apanihnuta iva) connects with the distant word "seems" (iva). He does not actually deny it, nor is it exactly as the fires had described.
The intention is that he said:

"How is it that these fires, whom I have served, have spoken? Surely, because they saw you, they appear as if trembling, whereas previously they were otherwise. Thus, pointing toward the fires with a questioning tone (*kākvā*), he addressed them, asking: "What, my dear, did the fires indeed say to you? Being thus questioned, he acknowledged, saying, "They spoke thus"—but he stated only a mere hint (*pratīkamātram*), something small, and not everything exactly as it was spoken by the fires.
For the Teacher said: "O Somya, those [predecessors] of yours indeed spoke of the worlds—earth and the others—but not of Brahman in its entirety.
However, I shall tell you that Brahman which you desire to hear;
listen to the greatness of the knowledge of that Brahman as it is being spoken by me, just as [water does not cling] to a lotus leaf."
"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so also, as I shall explain, evil action does not cling to, nor does it adhere to, one who knows Brahman in this way.
When he had spoken thus, the teacher said, "Let Upakosala tell me [more], sir. To him the teacher spoke.
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"That person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self," he said.
"This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
Therefore, even if one pours clarified butter or water upon it, it flows away along the very eyelashes.

This person who is seen in the eye by those whose vision has turned inward—by those who are peaceful, discerning, and endowed with the means such as celibacy—is the seer of sight and the eye of the eye, according to other scriptural passages such as "He is the seer of sight.

Now, it might be argued that what was said by the Fires is false, because they stated, "But the teacher shall tell you the path," implying he would speak only of the path; thus, the Fires were ignorant of the future subject matter.
This is not a fault.

Because it is stated that "this very blissful space is seen in the eye," and because it is referred to as the seer with the words, "This is the Self of living beings"—thus he spoke—this which we have declared to be the reality of the Self is indeed immortal, characterized by non-death and indestructible; it is fearless, for fear arises only where there is the apprehension of destruction, and since that is absent, it is fearless. Therefore, this is Brahman, the Great, the Infinite.

Furthermore, what is the majesty of this Brahman, the Person in the eye? It is this: even if one pours a drop of water or sap upon that place, the eye, it goes only to the eyelashes or the eyelids; it does not adhere to the eye, just as water does not adhere to a lotus leaf.
This is the majesty of the location itself; how much more, then, must the stainlessness of the Person in the eye—the occupant of that location—be described? Such is the intended meaning.
They call this "the gathering of all that is desirable" (saṃyadvāma), for all desirable things gather toward it. All desirable things gather toward him who knows this.
They call this person, as described above, "the one in whom all things lovely meet" (*saṃyadvāma*).
Why?
Because all "lovely" (*vāma*) things—that is, desirable, worshipful, and beautiful things—meet together and converge upon him; therefore, he is "the one in whom all things lovely meet."
In this very way, all blessings come together for one who knows this thus.
He indeed is Vāmanī;
for he leads all things that are desirable (vāmāni). He who knows thus leads all things that are desirable.

He is indeed the "Bringer of All Desirable Things" (Vāmanī), for he leads, brings, and carries all desirable things—the fruits of meritorious deeds—to living beings in accordance with their merit; and for the knower, he leads all desirable things as his own inherent nature.
He who knows this leads all desirable things.
He indeed is the illuminator,
for he shines in all worlds;
he who knows this shines in all worlds.
This very one is indeed the "Light-conductor" (bhāmanī), for he shines—that is, blazes—in all worlds through forms such as the sun, the moon, and fire.
According to the Vedic scripture, "By his light all this is illumined," he is therefore called the "Light-conductor" because he leads (nayati) the lights (bhāmāni).
One who knows this likewise shines in all worlds.
Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for this person or not, they all pass into the light;
from the light, into the day;
from the day, into the waxing fortnight.
From the waxing fortnight, he goes to those six months during which the sun moves northward; from the months, to the year;
from the year, to the sun.
From the sun to the moon;
from the moon to the lightning. There, a person who is non-human—
He leads them to Brahman.
This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman. Those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool; they do not return.
Now, the destination of the knower of Brahman as described is being stated:

whether or not the officiating priests perform the funeral rites (*śavya*) for one who has died and is such a knower, in every case, that knower is not obstructed by those unperformed funeral rites and reaches the world of Brahman.
Nor does he acquire any superior world by performing the funeral rites for the dead;
for another Vedic text states, "He increases neither by action nor does he become less.
By showing disregard for the funeral rites, the text praises knowledge; it does not, however, mean that one who knows this should not perform the funeral rites at all.
For it is inferred elsewhere that when the funeral rites (*śavakarma*) are not performed, there is some obstruction to the commencement of the fruit of an action;

therefore, by showing that for one who possesses knowledge (*vidyāvat*), the commencement of the fruit occurs without obstruction— whether the funeral rites are performed at the time of the commencement of the fruit of knowledge or not—

it indicates that those who meditate on the blissful space situated in the eye, which has such qualities as being "the center of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*), "leading downward" (*vāmanī*), and "leading upward" (*bhāmanī*), [attain this result] through the knowledge of the fires (*agnividyā*) together with the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

And let there be another karma for them, or let there not; in every case, they "attain the light"—the meaning is that they attain and reach the deity who presides over the light. From the light, [they go] to the deity who presides over the day; from the day, to the deity who presides over the waxing fortnight (the bright half of the month); from the waxing fortnight, to those six months during which the sun moves northward.
The sun goes toward those months, which have the northern solstice as their deity; from those months, to the year, whose deity is the year;

from that year, to Āditya; from Āditya, to the moon; from the moon, to lightning. There, a certain person—non-human (amānava), meaning one who does not belong to the human creation—comes from the world of Brahman to those [beings] situated there.
Brahman leads them to the world of truth (satyaloka), because of the designations of "the goer," "the goal to be reached," and "the leader";
for these would be untenable if the attainment were merely of Brahman as pure Being (sanmātra).
Indeed, it is logical to say in that case: "Being Brahman itself, he attains Brahman."
He will explain the realization of pure Being (sanmātra) through the elimination of all distinctions;
for a path that has not been seen does not present itself for travel, as another Vedic scripture states: "That which is unknown does not benefit one."

This is the "path of the gods" (*devapatha*); it is called the path of the gods because it is characterized by the gods, such as those beginning with *arciḥ*, who are appointed as its guides. It is also called the "path of Brahman" (*brahmapatha*) because it is characterized by Brahman, which is the goal to be reached.
Those proceeding by this path—those going toward Brahman—do not return to this human whirlpool, which pertains to Manu and is characterized by the creation of Manu.

They do not turn back; mounted upon the wheel of the continuous cycle of birth and death, they revolve again and again like a water-wheel. Thus, "they do not turn back" means they do not attain that [state]. The repetition—"they do not turn back, they do not turn back"—is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the fruitful knowledge.
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
This indeed is the sacrifice that purifies; this, as it blows, purifies all this.
Because he purifies all this as he goes,
therefore he alone is the sacrifice;
his mind and speech are the two tracks.

In this section on the secret doctrine, it is introduced here because of the context and the commonality of being "forest-related" (*āraṇyaka*): when an injury occurs during a sacrifice, the *vyāhṛtis* must be prescribed as an expiation, and silence must be maintained by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who is the Brahman; therefore, this is begun: "This indeed is that very Vāyu who blows here; he is the sacrifice."
The particles *ha* and *vā* are indeclinables (*nipāta*) that indicate a well-known fact;
for it is well known in the Vedas (*śruti*) that sacrifice is established in wind:
"Svāhā! You are placed in the wind."
This is indeed the sacrifice, according to such scriptural passages as, "He who blows here is the sacrifice.
For it is wind alone that is the substratum of action, owing to its nature of being mobile;
and because of the Vedic revelation: "Wind alone is the initiator of the sacrifice; wind is its foundation."
Indeed, this very one, as he moves and goes, purifies, cleanses, and purges this entire world;
for there is no purification for one who does not move.
Indeed, the removal of defects is seen in one who moves, not in one who is stationary.
And because this [sacrifice] purifies all this [universe], therefore it is indeed sacrifice (*yajña*), since it purifies (*punāti*).
Of this very distinguished sacrifice, speech is occupied with the utterance of mantras,
and the mind is occupied with the knowledge of things as they truly are.
These two, speech and mind, are the two paths (vartanī), the two ways by which the sacrifice being performed proceeds; they are the two paths.
For another Vedic text states: "The sacrifice is the successive progression of speech and thought, which possess the movement of inhalation and exhalation.
Therefore, since the sacrifice proceeds by means of speech and mind, speech and mind are called the two paths of the sacrifice.
Of these two, the Brahman prepares one with his mind,

while the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ prepare the other with their speech. When, after the Prātaranuvāka has been commenced but before the concluding verse (paridhānīyā), the Brahman speaks out [interfering], [the sacrifice is flawed].
He prepares only one of the two tracks;
the other falls away. Just as a wagon traveling on one foot or a chariot moving on one wheel comes to ruin, even so his sacrifice comes to ruin.
If the sacrifice is damaged, the sacrificer suffers accordingly; having performed such a sacrifice, he becomes worse off.
Of those two paths, one path he prepares with his mind through discriminative knowledge;
the three priests— the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ— prepare the other path, characterized by speech, by means of speech alone, with the Brahman priest acting as the officiant.
In that case, speech and mind are the two paths to be purified in the sacrifice.

Now, when the *prātaranuvāka* recitation has been commenced— that is, at the time it has begun— if that Brahman priest should speak, abandoning his silence, before the final concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) [is reached], then he [incurs a fault] regarding one or the other [path].

While being consecrated by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), he prepares the path of speech; however, the path of the mind falls away, perishes, and becomes riven. That sacrifice, being unable to proceed by means of either one—the path of speech—comes to ruin.
He asks: "In what manner? [He replies: "Just as a cart with only one wheel."

Just as a one-legged man, walking along a path, comes to grief, or as a chariot, moving while turning on only one wheel, comes to grief, even so does the sacrifice of this sacrificer come to grief— that is, it perishes— when performed by a bad Brahmin.
When the sacrifice comes to grief, the sacrificer comes to grief.
For the sacrificer has the sacrifice as his life-breath;
therefore, when the sacrifice is injured, his injury is incurred.
Having performed such a sacrifice, he becomes worse—more sinful.
Now, when the Prātaranuvāka has been introduced and the Brahman priest does not speak out before the concluding verse (paridhānīyā), they prepare both paths;
neither one is lost.

Just as a two-legged man walking or a chariot moving on both wheels comes to rest, even so does his sacrifice come to rest; as the sacrifice comes to rest, the sacrificer follows it in coming to rest.
Having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.

Furthermore, when the learned Brahman priest, having adopted silence, remains without uttering speech until he speaks the *paridhānīyā* verse, in that very manner all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) prepare both paths; neither one of them is neglected.
To the question "In what way?", he says:
there are two examples which are the reverse of those previously mentioned.
Thus, the sacrifice of this sacrificer, proceeding by its own two paths, becomes firmly established; the meaning is that it proceeds without perishing, by means of its own self.

As the sacrifice becomes firmly established, the sacrificer follows it and becomes firmly established. That sacrificer, having performed the sacrifice thus endowed with the knowledge of silence and Brahman, becomes superior; that is to say, he becomes the best.
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Prajāpati brooded over the worlds.
As they were being heated, he extracted their essences:
fire from the earth and wind from the intermediate space.
The Āditya from the sky.

In this context, silence is prescribed for the Brahman priest; therefore, when that [silence] is violated during his duties as Brahman or during other duties such as those of the Hotṛ priests, the oblation with the *vyāhṛtis* is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). To that end, he states that the *vyāhṛtis* must be enjoined: "Prajāpati performed austerity directed toward the worlds"—that is, aiming at the worlds, he practiced austerity characterized by meditation with the desire to extract their essence.
As those worlds were being heated, he drew out—that is, extracted and took—their essences in the form of their refined substance.
Which ones?
The essence of fire from the earth.
Vāyu from the intermediate space;
Āditya from heaven.
He brooded over these three deities;
from them, as they were being brooded upon, he extracted their essences:
from Agni, the Ṛg-verses.
The Yajus formulas come from Vāyu; the Sāmans from Āditya.
Again, in this very manner, he meditated upon these three deities beginning with Fire;
from them as well, he extracted the essence, the sap, which is the triple knowledge (trayī-vidyā).
He brooded over this threefold knowledge;
from it, as it was being brooded upon, he drew out its essences:
"Bhūḥ" from the Ṛg-verses.
"Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajus formulas;
"Svaḥ" from the Sāmans.
If, therefore, it should be damaged on account of the Ṛgveda, one should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire with the words "bhūḥ svāhā.
By means of the essence of the Ṛcs, by the vigor of the Ṛcs, one thereby mends the damage of the sacrifice caused to the Ṛcs.
He again brooded over this triple knowledge.
From it, as it was being brooded upon, he drew forth its essence:
the Vyāhṛti "Bhūḥ" from the Ṛg-verses, and the Vyāhṛti "Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajus-formulas.
The *svāhā* is the *vyāhṛti* for the Sāmans;
from these [three] alone come the worlds, the gods, the Vedas, and the *rasas* of the great *vyāhṛtis*.

Therefore, if in that sacrifice anything should be damaged (*riṣyet*) on account of a *ṛc*—that is, due to a connection with a *ṛc* or because of a *ṛc*—the sacrifice would incur injury (*kṣatam*); one should then offer an oblation into the Gārhapatya fire with "Bhūr Svāhā."
That is the expiation there.
How so? "Of the *ṛcs* alone" is an adverbial phrase;

by means of the essence (*rasa*) of the *ṛcs*, by means of the vigor (*vīrya*) and vital power (*ojas*) of the *ṛcs*, he joins together—that is, he repairs—the broken, severed, or wounded part that has arisen in the sacrifice associated with the *ṛcs*.
Now, if it should be damaged on account of the Yajus formulas, one should offer an oblation in the Dakṣiṇāgni with "Bhuvaḥ svāhā!
By means of the essence of the Yajus formulas, by the vigor of the Yajus formulas, he thereby mends whatever in the sacrifice has been injured through the Yajus formulas.
Now, if it should be damaged during the Sāman, he should offer an oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Svaḥ svāhā!
By means of the essence of the Sāmans, by the vigor of the Sāmans, he thereby mends the injury of the sacrifice caused by the Sāmans.

Now, if it should be damaged on account of the Yajus—that is, due to a cause related to the Yajus—one should offer an oblation into the Dakṣiṇāgni with the words, "Bhuvaḥ svāhā. Likewise, if there is damage on account of the Sāman, one should offer an oblation into the Āhavanīya with the words, "Svaḥ svāhā.
In this way, as before, one restores the sacrifice.
But if there is a flaw caused by a Brahmin, one should offer oblations in the three fires with the three *vyāhṛtis*;
for that flaw belongs to the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*).
Now, as for the question "By what [qualification] does one attain the office of Brahman?", it is by this very triple knowledge (*trayi-vidyā*), according to the Śruti;
or else, another logical ground must be sought for the cause of the office of Brahman in the event of a flaw.
It is as follows: one might join gold with salt;
silver with gold; tin with silver; lead with tin; iron with lead; wood with iron; and wood with leather.
Thus, by means of the power of these worlds, of these deities, and of this threefold knowledge, he heals whatever is injured in the sacrifice.
Indeed, that sacrifice becomes one for which healing has been performed where there is a Brahman priest who knows thus.
For example, one might join gold with salt;
or with alkali such as borax and the like for a hard [substance], for that makes it soft.
One might join silver with gold which cannot otherwise be joined;
likewise, tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, wood with iron, and wood with leather by means of a leather binding.

In this same way, through the power of these worlds, of these deities, and of this Ātreyī knowledge—by its vigor known as "sap" (rasa) and its vital energy—one joins together whatever in the sacrifice has been shattered.
This sacrifice is indeed like one prepared by a physician;
it becomes like a man afflicted by disease who has been treated by a well-trained doctor.
What is that [sacrifice]?
The meaning is: in whatever sacrifice there is such a Brahman priest—one who knows the expiatory rite consisting of the oblations of the aforementioned *vyāhṛtis*—that is [the true] sacrifice.
This sacrifice indeed slopes toward the north where there is a Brahman priest who knows thus.
Regarding such a knowing Brahman, there is this verse:
"Whithersoever it turns back, thither it goes."
Furthermore, this sacrifice indeed becomes inclined toward the north, sloping northward, and elevated toward the south;
that is to say, it becomes a cause for attaining the northern path.
Wherever there is such a Brahman priest, regarding such a knowing Brahman priest as an officiating minister (ṛtvij), there is this following verse intended as a praise of the Brahman.

From whatever part of the sacrificial ground the ritual action of the officiating priests turns back and the sacrifice becomes impaired, the Brahman priest, by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), mends that very injury of the sacrifice and proceeds, thereby protecting it. Just as a single human king protects his subjects, so indeed does the Brahman who knows this protect the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests. Therefore, one should appoint only such a person as the Brahman, and not one who does not know this—not one who does not know this.
The human being is but one; the Brahman alone, as the officiating priest, protects the Kurus and the horses.
Indeed, one who knows this protects the sacrifice, the patron, and all the officiating priests.
Therefore, one should appoint only such a person as this to be the Brahman priest, and not one who does not know thus, not one who does not know thus.
The Brahman priest is so called because he practices silence (*mauna*), or because of his reflection (*manana*), or because of his knowledge;

therefore, like a mare (*vaḍavā*) protects horses mounted for battle, even so does the learned Brahman protect the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) by removing the defects committed by them.

Since the Brahman is thus distinguished and learned, one should therefore appoint as Brahman only such a person who knows the aforementioned *vyāhṛtis* and other rites, and never one who does not know this.
The repetition is for the purpose of marking the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the seventeenth section of the fourth chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the preceptor of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Verily, he who knows the eldest and the best becomes indeed the eldest and the best.
Breath, indeed, is the eldest and the best.
The northern path for the knower of Brahman with attributes has been described.

Now, in this fifth chapter, having reiterated that same path for the householder who knows the five fires as well as for those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) who are endowed with faith and devoted to other forms of knowledge, [the text describes] another path connected with the southern direction, characterized by smoke and so forth, which pertains to those who perform mere ritual works and results in rebirth.
And now, beginning with the statement that the third course of transmigration is even more difficult than the previous ones and must be described for the sake of generating dispassion,

[the text] addresses how the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was repeatedly mentioned in the preceding section in such passages as "The vital breath is superior to speech and the others" and "The vital breath, indeed, is the absorber.
How is it superior among speech and the rest, given that there is no difference in their all acting through collective effort?

And how is he to be worshipped? Because of his preeminence and other qualities, the following is commenced immediately thereafter: "Whoever knows the eldest and the best"—the eldest indeed by age, for Prāṇa is the eldest among speech and the other organs;
for while the person is still in the womb, the activity of Prāṇa attains its own nature prior to that of speech and the others, by which the embryo [survives].

The eye and other organs increase once the constituent parts of their locations have been produced; subsequently, speech and the others acquire their functional activity. Thus, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the eldest in terms of age.
Its superiority, however, will be demonstrated through the illustration beginning with "like a fine horse" and so forth.
Therefore, in this aggregate of causes and effects, the vital breath alone is both the eldest and the best.
Verily, he who knows the most excellent becomes the most excellent among his own people. Speech, indeed, is the most excellent.

Whoever knows him who is truly the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*)—the best at clothing, the best at covering, or the wealthiest—he indeed becomes the most excellent among his own kinsmen. But who, then, is the most excellent? He says: Speech (*vāk*) is indeed the most excellent; for eloquent men live superior to others and become the wealthiest; therefore, speech is the most excellent.
He who knows the foundation indeed stands firm in this world and in that world;
the eye, verily, is the foundation.
He who knows the foundation indeed finds firm footing both in this world and in that other world beyond.
What, then, is the foundation? It is said: the eye, verily, is the foundation.
For by seeing with the eye, one finds firm footing on even ground and on difficult terrain; therefore, the eye is the foundation.
Verily, he who knows attainment—for him desires, both divine and human, are attained.
The ear, indeed, is attainment.
Verily, to him who knows attainment, both divine and human desires are attained. What, then, is attainment? It is said: the ear is indeed attainment.

Because by means of the ear the Vedas are grasped, and through them the knowledge of their meaning arises, and from that rituals are performed, and from those comes the attainment of desires—thus, because it is the cause of the attainment of desires, the ear is indeed attainment.
Verily, he who knows the abode becomes the abode for his own people;
the mind, indeed, is the abode.
Whoever indeed knows the abode (āyatana) becomes the abode of his own people; that is to say, he becomes their support. What is that abode? I say: the mind (manas) is indeed the abode.
The mind is the abode—the support—for the objects presented by the senses, which serve as the objects of experience and exist in the form of mental impressions (pratyaya).
Therefore, it has been said that the mind, indeed, is the abode.
Then, indeed, the vital breaths disputed with one another regarding who was superior, each saying, "I am superior!
I am superior!"

Then, indeed, the vital breaths (prāṇas), possessing the qualities as previously described, disputed—that is, they spoke variously and contradictorily—with respect to this purpose: "I am superior," "I am superior," "I am superior."
Those vital breaths (prāṇas) went to their father Prajāpati and said, "Venerable sir, who among us is the best?
He said to them, "He among you,
upon whose departure the body appears most wretched, he is the best of you."

Indeed, they, thus disputing among themselves, went to Prajāpati, their father and progenitor, in order to ascertain which among them was the best; having approached him, they said, "O Blessed One, who among us is the best, superior in qualities?"— in this manner they questioned him.

Their father said to them: "Among you, he by whose departure this body appears most wretched—worse even than when alive—and after the vital breaths have departed, appears even more wretched still, like a corpse, untouchable and impure, he shall be the best of you. He spoke thus with a questioning tone, wishing to avoid that particular suffering.
Thereupon, Speech departed.
Having been away for a year, she returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied,
"Just as those who do not speak live by means of speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind— so [did we live]."
Speech indeed entered.
The eye departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said:
"How were you able to live without me?"
"Just as the blind, though not seeing, breathe with the breath, speak with speech, hear with the ear, and think with the mind—so it is.
Then the eye entered.
The ear departed.
Having been away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me? They replied:
"Just as the deaf live—without hearing, yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and thinking with the mind—so did we."
It entered the ear.
The mind departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said:
"How were you able to live without me?"
"Just as children, though breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and hearing with the ear, are without mind"—thus [it was said].
Then the mind entered.
When the vital breaths had been thus addressed by the father, that speech indeed departed;
having departed and stayed away for a full year, it returned and spoke to those other vital breaths:
"In what way, by what means, were you able—without me—to live and maintain yourselves?"
They said, "Just as the senseless," and so forth.
"Senseless" means like those who are mute; they live in the world without speaking with speech.
How? By breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and reflecting with the mind—meaning they perform all the activities of the sensory organs in this manner.
The meaning is: "In this way we lived.
Having realized its own inferiority compared to the vital breaths (prāṇas), speech indeed entered back [into the body]; that is to say, it became engaged once more in its own function.
The rest is the same: "The eye indeed departed; the ear indeed departed; the mind indeed departed," and so forth.
"Just as children" means those who lack mental composure, that is, whose minds have not yet matured.
Then, as the vital breath (prāṇa) was about to depart, just as a fine horse might tear up the pegs of its foot-tethers, so did it tear up the other vital breaths.
They gathered around it and said,
"Venerable sir, please remain!"
"You are the best among us; do not depart."

When speech and the others had been thus examined, immediately thereafter it is told what that principal vital breath (*mukhya prāṇa*) did when it desired to depart— that is, wished to go out. Just as in the world a fine horse— a beautiful steed— when struck by a whip by its rider for the sake of testing, might tear up, dig out, and root out the tethering pegs— the spikes used for binding its feet— so did it root out and pull up the other vital breaths, speech and the rest.

Those vital breaths, being thus agitated and unable to remain in their own places, came together and said to that chief vital breath: "O Venerable One, come, be our lord; for you are the best among us, and do not depart from this body."
Then Speech said to him:
"Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent.
Then the Eye said to him:
"That which I am established in, you are established in that."
Then the sense of hearing said to him:
"As I am the attainment, so are you that attainment.
Then the mind said to him:
"That which is my sphere of experience, that is your sphere of experience."

Then Speech and the others, establishing the preeminence of the Breath through their own functions, spoke to him—just as subjects bring tribute to a king. How so? First, Speech said: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*). The word *yat* is an adverbial modifier; the meaning is, "insofar as I possess the quality of being the most excellent."
"You are that Vasiṣṭha"—by this, I meant that you possess the quality of being Vasiṣṭha, which I had mistakenly attributed to myself due to ignorance;
the same should be applied to the subsequent cases regarding the eye, the ear, and the mind.
Indeed, they do not call them "speeches," nor "eyes," nor "ears," nor "minds";
they call them simply "breaths" (prāṇas),
for the breath indeed becomes all these.
This statement from the Śruti is appropriate; for this reason, speech and the other organs addressed the principal breath (mukhya prāṇa),
since neither common people nor those learned in the scriptures refer to speech and the other instruments as "speeches," "eyes," "ears," or "minds."

What then? They call them, they speak of them, as "the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*). Since the vital breath indeed constitutes all these collections of instruments beginning with speech, the statement made by speech and the others is entirely appropriate to the principal vital breath; thus [the text] seeks to conclude the meaning of the section.
Now, one might ask: how is this logical—that they should vie with one another and contend for their own superiority, like conscious persons?

For it is not possible for the eye and the other senses to speak individually without setting aside speech; likewise, their departure from the body, re-entry, going to Brahman, or the praise of the vital breaths would not be tenable [if they were insentient]. In this regard, the sentience of speech and the other organs is established by scripture through their being presided over by conscious deities such as Agni and others. If it is argued that this contradicts the tenets of the logicians regarding the presence of multiple sentient beings in a single body: [we reply that] this is not so.
No;
for it is accepted that Īśvara is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Those logicians who indeed accept Īśvara maintain that the internal effects and instruments, such as the mind, and external things, such as the earth and so forth, proceed with necessity only when presided over by Īśvara.
It is like a chariot and so forth.
Furthermore, we do not admit that deities such as Fire (Agni) and others, even if they possess consciousness, are the enjoyers within the self;
rather, what then?

For it is accepted that the Lord is the superintendent merely by his presence over those [powers] which possess instruments and effects, which have the vital breath as their sole deity, and which involve millions of variations through the distinctions of the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva);
he is indeed without instruments.
And the followers of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad recite: "He who first generated Hiraṇyagarbha," and so forth.
We shall explain later that the *jīva*—the enjoyer who is connected with the fruits of action—is distinct from the body.

Furthermore, this dialogue among speech and the other organs is imagined here for the purpose of determining the preeminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

It is just as in the world when men, disputing among themselves as to who is superior, ask someone who is an expert in their particular qualities: "Who among us is the best by virtue of our qualities?"

He said to them, "Strive each one of you to accomplish this task; he by whom this task is accomplished shall be the best among you. Having been told this, they strove accordingly and determined who was the best, whether for themselves or another.
It is with reference to this worldly transaction that the Śruti has attributed [the roles] to speech and the other organs.

How indeed could a wise person understand the preeminence of the vital breath (prāṇa), seeing that life is observed even in the absence of each of the others—speech and so forth—but not in the absence of the vital breath?

And thus says the Śruti of the Kauṣītakins: "One lives deprived of speech, for we see the mute; one lives deprived of sight, for we see the blind; one lives deprived of hearing, for we see the deaf; one lives deprived of mind, for we see infants."
"One whose arms are severed lives; one whose thighs are severed lives," and so forth.
Thus ends the first section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
He said, "What shall be my food?
They replied, "Whatever there is here, down to the dogs and down to the birds."
This, indeed, is the food of the cart;
"cart" (ana) is its manifest name.
For one who knows this, there is indeed nothing that is not food.

The principal vital breath (mukhya prāṇa) said: "What shall be my food? The Śruti, conceiving the principal vital breath as the questioner and speech and the others as the respondents, says: "Whatever is known in this world as the various kinds of food, including that of dogs and down to that of birds—for all living beings."
"Whatever food there is, that is your food," so said Speech and the others.

Having turned away from the form of the invented narrative intended for the realization that "the Prāṇa's food is everything; the Prāṇa is the eater of all food," the Śruti speaks in its own direct form: "Now, whatever food is eaten here in the world by living beings, it is [the food] of this Prāṇa."
The meaning is that this food is eaten by means of the *prāṇa* alone. The word "ana" is the direct name of *prāṇa*, intended to demonstrate its quality of pervading all types of activity;
for if it were preceded by the prefix *pra*, there would be only a specific, limited sense.
And thus, the mention of the name of the eater of all foods is this direct designation of the eater of all foods as "the Nameless" (An-ama).
Indeed, for one who knows thus— for one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) as described, thinking "I am the vital breath, abiding in all beings, the eater of all foods"—
there is indeed nothing whatsoever among all things to be eaten by living beings that is not food for him.
The meaning is that everything indeed becomes food for him;

this is because the knower has become the vital breath (prāṇa). For another scriptural passage, beginning with "From the vital breath indeed he rises, into the vital breath he sets," concludes: "For one who knows thus, the sun indeed rises; for one who knows thus, the sun sets. Thus it is from the source of another Śruti.
He said, "What shall be my garment?
They replied, "Water.
Therefore, those who are about to eat wrap themselves with water both before and after.
He indeed becomes one who gains clothing;
he indeed becomes one who is not naked.
Then Prāṇa spoke again;
the conceptualization is exactly as before.
"What shall be my garment? he asked. "Water," said Vāk and the others.
Since water is the dwelling-place of the vital breath (prāṇa), therefore learned Brāhmaṇas, both before eating and after having eaten, perform this rite.
What is it?

With water, which serves as the place of clothing, they wrap themselves—performing the act of dressing—both before the meal and after the meal, being intent on obtaining and sustaining the primary vital breath.
"He becomes possessed of clothing";
the meaning is that he indeed obtains clothing.
"He becomes unclothed" [is the opposite].
Since nakedness is already precluded by the fact of having obtained a garment, the statement "he becomes not naked" means that he possesses an upper garment (*uttarīya*).

Regarding the sipping of water (*ācamana*) for the sake of purification, which is known to be performed by one about to eat and by one who has eaten, what is prescribed here is merely the contemplation that "this is the garment of the vital breath.
The phrase "they clothe him with waters" does not refer to another act of sipping water.

Just as the view that food being eaten by worldly living beings belongs to the *prāṇa* is a mere matter of perception, so too is it with the questions and answers such as "What is my food? and "What is my clothing?"; for they are identical in nature. If the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) were performed as a new injunction for that specific purpose, then even the food of worms and the like would have to be prescribed as edible for the *prāṇa*. Since both the question and the answer are equal in their intent toward knowledge, and since the context concerns knowledge, it is not proper to apply the "half-old-woman" logic (*ardhajaratīya-nyāya*) here.

As for the objection that the well-known sipping of water (ācamana) does not serve the purpose of purification (*prāyatya*) nor the purpose of providing clothing for the breath (*prāṇa*), we do not say that the sipping of water serves both purposes in that way.
Rather, we say that what is enjoined here is the contemplation (*darśana*) that the water used as a means for the purificatory sipping constitutes the clothing of the breath.
In that case, the charge of the fault of implying that the sipping of water serves both purposes is untenable.
If it is argued that the mention of clothing in the context of sipping water (ācamana) is intended for the purpose of obtaining clothing, we say no.

For there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) in a sentence whose purpose is to convey knowledge of clothing, if it were to enjoin a previously unestablished sipping for the sake of clothing, and simultaneously enjoin a visualization (dṛṣṭi) of that act as being for the sake of non-nakedness; this is because there is no evidence for the sipping to serve both those purposes.
Having taught this to Gośruti Vaiyāghrapadya, Satyakāma Jābāla said:
"Even if one were to say this to a withered stump, branches would surely grow upon it and leaves would sprout."
This very vision of the vital breath (prāṇa) is now being praised.
How so?
Satyakāma Jābāla, having taught this very vision of the vital breath to one named Gośruti Vaiyāghrapadya—the son of Vyāghrapad—he said to him: "There is something else as well."

The words to be spoken next: what did he say? He says: "Even if one who knows the vital breaths were to say this to a withered stump—'Let them be born,' 'let them arise,' 'let branches grow on this stump,' and 'let leaves and foliage sprout'—how much more would it be so for a living person?"

Now, if he should desire to go to the Great [Heaven], having been initiated on the new moon day, on the night of the full moon he should churn a mash of all herbs with curds and honey; then, having offered a portion of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "Svāhā to the Eldest, to the Best," he should pour the residue into the mash.
Immediately thereafter, if one should desire to go to, or wish to attain, great greatness— that is, if one should so desire—
this rite is prescribed for him;
for when greatness exists, prosperity approaches.

For one who desires greatness, this ritual action is undertaken with the following purpose in mind: that from the illustrious [state] wealth will be obtained, from that the performance of rites, and from that one will attain either the path of the gods or the path of the fathers; it is not for one who merely desires the enjoyment of sense-objects.

The following rule regarding time and other factors for this [rite] is stated: having been initiated on the new moon day—meaning that, like one who has undergone initiation, he observes the rules such as sleeping on the ground and becomes endowed with virtues such as austerity, truthfulness, celibacy, and so forth—he does not, however, undertake the entire collection of ritual acts belonging to the Dīkṣā itself;
for the rite called Mantha is not a modification (vikāra) of those [Dīkṣā rites].
Based on another scriptural passage stating "one who observes the Upasad vow," he undertakes an austerity consisting of consuming only milk, which serves as a means of purification.

On the night of the full moon, he begins the ritual; having taken a very small amount of every herb—both cultivated and wild—as much as he is able, and having husked them, he grinds that raw flour and places it in a vessel made of Udumbara wood, shaped like a *kaṃsa* or a *camasa*, along with curds and honey.

Having poured it from another vessel and stirred it, he should place it before him; then, having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the *āvasathya* fire at the place of pouring with the mantra, "To the eldest, to the best, svāhā!", he should pour the residue clinging to the *sruva* ladle into the stirred mixture, letting the remainder fall down.
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To Vasiṣṭha, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To Pratiṣṭhā, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To Saṃpat, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash.
Having offered a portion of clarified butter into the fire with the formula, "To the abode, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash.

The rest is the same. Having offered [the oblations] with the formulas, "To Vasiṣṭha, to stability, to prosperity, to the abode, svāhā!"—one for each—he should likewise pour the remnants together after the offering.
Then, having stepped back and placed the stirred offering in his joined palms, he mutters:
"Thou art named 'Amā'; for all this belongs to thee as 'Amā'."
For he is the eldest, the most excellent, the king, and the sovereign; may he lead me to seniority, excellence, kingship, and sovereignty, [thinking],
"May I alone be all this."
Then, having stepped back slightly from the fire and moved away a little further, he places the churned mixture in his joined palms and mutters this mantra:
"Ama by name art thou, for Ama is indeed thine. *Ama* is the name of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

For it is by means of food that the vital breath (prāṇa) breathes within the body; therefore, because the substance for churning is the food of the vital breath, it is praised as being the vital breath itself with the words, "Thou art Amas. Why? Because "amas" means together (saha), since this entire whole world belongs to thee who hast become the vital breath.
For this *mantha* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the eldest and the best;
and for that very reason, it is the king, the radiant one, the sovereign who, presiding over all, is the protector.
May this *mantha*, my own vital breath, lead me to the multitude of qualities such as seniority and excellence, so that I myself may become this entire world, just like the vital breath.
The word "iti" serves to indicate the conclusion of the mantra.
Then, indeed, he sips water line by line with this Ṛg-verse:
he sips with "We choose that of Savitṛ," and he sips with "The nourishment of the god."
Reciting "The best, the supporter of all," he sips [the water]; reciting "We meditate on the swift power of Bhaga," he drinks it all.
Having rinsed the bronze vessel or the wooden cup, he lies down behind the fire.
Whether on a skin or on the bare ground, he remains silent and self-controlled;
if he should see a woman, he should know that his rite has been successful.
Immediately thereafter, he sips and consumes with this verse that is about to be recited, doing so foot by foot;
that is, he consumes each morsel with each individual quarter-verse of the mantra.
That food belongs to Savitṛ, the impeller of all.
Having unified the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the sun (*āditya*), it is said:
"We choose"—that is, we pray for—the form of the sun as *mantha*.
The intention is: "By means of that food belonging to Savitṛ, by consuming which sustenance, may we become possessed of the very nature of Savitṛ."
The phrase "of the god Savitṛ" is to be connected with what precedes.

"Most excellent" means most praiseworthy; "most nourishing" means the best sustainer of the entire world, or that which provides it in an extraordinary degree. In every respect, this is an epithet of the food.
*Turam*, *tvaram*, *tūrṇam*, and *śīghram* mean "quickly.
The word "of the divine Savitṛ" (*bhagasya devasya savituḥ*) is understood as referring to his own nature (*svarūpam*).
"We meditate upon" (*dhīmahi*) means we should contemplate; the intention is that we do so being pure in soul, having been refined by excellent nourishment.

Alternatively, [the sacrificer] thinks, "We have performed the ritual action that is the cause of fortune and the attainment of greatness; may we reflect upon that sacrifice," and then he drinks all the remnants of the churning, having rinsed and washed the *kaṃsa*— the vessel shaped like a *kaṃsa*— or the *camasa*—
the vessel shaped like a *camasa*— which is made of Udumbara wood.

Having drunk [the water] and sipped it (ācamya), he lies down behind the fire with his head toward the east, either on a skin of a sacrificial horse (vājina), or on a bare mound of earth (sthaṇḍila), or simply on the ground.

"Restraining his speech" (vācaṃyama) means being one whose speech is controlled. "Unassailable" (aprasāhaḥ) means not being overcome or overpowered by undesirable dreams such as those involving women and so forth; the meaning is that he remains with a fully restrained mind.
If one who has become thus should see a woman in dreams, then he should know: "This rite of mine will be successful."
Regarding this, there is this verse:

"When, in dreams, one sees a woman during rites performed for the sake of desired objects, one should know that there will be success in that matter; in that vision of a dream, in that vision of a dream."
Regarding this matter, there is also this verse, which is a mantra:

"When one sees a woman in dreams—meaning in dream-vision or at the time of dreaming—during rites performed for desired ends, for the sake of fulfilling desires, one should know that there will be success therein;
the meaning is that one should know that the accomplishment of the fruits of those rites will come to pass."
The intention is that this occurs when there is the vision of such auspicious dreams as women and so forth.
The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the ritual action.
Thus ends the second section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Śvetaketu, the grandson of Aruṇa, went to the assembly of the Pañcālas.
Pravāhaṇa Jaibali spoke to him.
"The prince has instructed you, father.
"Indeed he has, O venerable one," [he replied].

The various states of transmigratory existence, beginning from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, must be described for the sake of detachment in those desiring liberation; therefore, the following narrative is commenced. "Śvetaketu, by name" (the particle *ha* indicates tradition);
the son of Aruṇa is Āruṇeya; he went to the assembly, that is, the council, of the Pañcālas.
When he had arrived, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali—the son of Jīvala by name—said to him:
"O boy, did your father instruct you?
What did your father instruct you? is the meaning.
Thus addressed, he said, "Yes, indeed, I have been instructed, O Blessed One," speaking thus to indicate his understanding.
"Do you know where creatures go from here?
"No, venerable sir.
"Do you know how they return?"
"No, Blessed One.
"Do you know the point where the two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the fathers—diverge?
"No, Blessed One."
He said to him: "If you have been instructed, do you know that which is above this world—where living beings go when they depart? Do you know that? The meaning is: "Do you know that?
He replied, "No, venerable sir," meaning, "I do not know that which you ask.
[The teacher continued: "In that case, do you know, by what manner or process they return?"
"No, Venerable Sir," he replied.
"Do you know the point of divergence—the place of mutual separation—of the two paths, the ways of travel, namely the path of the gods and the path of the fathers, for those who go together?
"No, Venerable Sir," he replied.
"Do you know how that world is not filled?
"No, Blessed One.
"Do you know how, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'?"
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
"Do you know how that world connected with the ancestors is, which they reach and from which they return again, and by what means it is not filled even though many are departing?
"I do not know that, O Venerable One," he replied.
"Do you know how, by what sequence, when the fifth oblation—numbered as five—is offered, [the person] is produced from the oblation?"

The waters, which are the means for the oblations, become "possessing human speech"— meaning that when they are offered in succession as the sixth oblation, they come to have the designation "puruṣa," that is, they receive the name of "puruṣa. This is the meaning.
Thus addressed, he replied, "No indeed, Blessed One.
The meaning is: "I do not know anything at all in this matter."
"Then, having been instructed, what did you say? For how could one who does not know these things claim to have been instructed?
He, dejected, went to his father's side.
He said to him: "The venerable sir indeed told me that he had instructed me, even though he had not actually instructed me."
Then, being thus ignorant, why did you say, "I have been instructed"?
For how could one who does not know these groups of matters asked by me—does not understand them—say among the learned, "I have been instructed"?
Thus, having been pressed and wearied by the king, Śvetaketu went to his father's presence and approached him.

And he said to his father: "O Venerable One, at the time of my formal return, you indeed told me, 'I have not instructed you; I have not given you instruction. You spoke thus even without having provided me with the necessary guidance."

"A kinsman of royalty has asked me five questions, and I was not able to explain even one of them. He said, "Since you spoke to me about these in such a way, it is clear that I do not know even one of them myself."
"If I had known these, why would I not have told them to you?"
Gautama went to the king's court. When he had arrived, the king offered him the honors due to him. In the morning, having participated in the assembly, he departed.
He said to him:
"O venerable Gautama, choose a boon from among human wealth.
He replied:
"O King, human wealth belongs to you alone;
speak to me that very word which you spoke in the presence of the boy.
He became distressed.

Since a certain *rājanyabandhu*—one whose kinsmen are royal, meaning one who is himself of bad conduct—asked five questions, numbering five, he was unable to answer even one of them; that is, he was not able to explain them specifically according to their meaning. His father said to him: "My child, know me to be just as you were when you first came to me and spoke these questions, saying, 'I am unable to answer even one of them.'"
The meaning is: "By the sign of your ignorance, know that I too possess ignorance regarding that subject.
How so? Just as I do not know—not even one—of these questions, so too, my dear friend, you yourself do not know these questions; thus, the meaning is that I also do not know them.
Therefore, you should not harbor a mistaken notion regarding me.

"How can this be so? For I do not know whether I would have known these questions had I known them; why then, at the time of my return, did I not speak them to you, my dear son? Having said this, he went to the presence of King Jaivali Gautama.
When Gautama had arrived, he performed for him the hospitality due to one worthy of such honors.

And that Gautama, having been offered hospitality and having stayed there, departed on the following day at the time of dawn. "Sabhāga" means sharing in a portion, honor, service, or attendance; thus, being "sabhāga"—being honored by others—Gautama himself went forth to meet the king.
The king said to Gautama: "O venerable Gautama, choose—pray for—as a boon whatever human wealth, such as villages and the like, belongs to a man.
Gautama replied: "O King, let that human wealth remain with you alone.
Tell me, speak to me, that very speech which you uttered in the presence of my son—the youth—consisting of the five questions. Thus was he addressed by Gautama.
The king indeed became distressed and sorrowful, wondering, "How can this be?"
He commanded him, "Dwell with me for a long time.
He said to him,
"As you have addressed me, Gautama..."
"So that this knowledge, which previously had not gone to the Brahmins before you, [remains so];
therefore, indeed, in all the worlds, the governance belongs to the Kṣatriya alone.
He then spoke to him.

Having become distressed and considering that the Brahmin was not to be refused, and thinking that knowledge must be imparted according to the proper rule, he commanded Gautama, saying, "Dwell [here] for a long time. Regarding the fact that the king had previously rejected the knowledge and later commanded him to dwell for a long time, the king—being possessed of all knowledge—apologizes to the Brahmin by stating the underlying reason, and said to him: "O Brahmin..."
"O Gautama, you have spoken to me in such a manner; therefore, out of ignorance, understand that you must speak to me that very speech characterized by knowledge.
In this regard, it must be explained how and in what manner this knowledge has not gone, nor has it ever gone, from the Brāhmaṇas before you."
Furthermore, the Brāhmaṇas did not govern by means of this knowledge;

rather, it is well known in the world that, for that reason, in all the worlds of old—in former times—the governance, that is, the state of being a ruler, of the Kṣatra alone, of the Kṣatriya caste itself, by means of this knowledge, existed among those to be instructed.
This knowledge has come down through the lineage of the Kṣatriyas until this present time.
"Nevertheless, I shall tell this to you; after giving it to you, it will go to the Brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, you should forgive what I have said," having spoken thus, the king imparted the knowledge to him.
Thus ends the third section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire;
the sun is its fuel."
The rays are the smoke;
the day is the flame;
the moon is the embers.
The stars are its sparks.
This question regarding "water in the fifth oblation" is answered first,
because answering it would be conducive to answering the others.
That commencement of the effect of the two Agnihotra oblations has been described in the Vājasaneyaka.
Regarding that, there are questions concerning the departure, the movement of the two oblations, their support, their satisfaction, their return, and how they rise up toward the world.
The resolution of these has been stated in that very same place: "When these two oblations are offered, they depart; they enter the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*);
they make the intermediate space itself the *āhavanīya* fire, the wind the fuel, and the rays the bright oblation; they [enter] the intermediate space."
"Having gratified you, they then ascend," and so on, just as before; having gratified them, they then return from heaven.
Having entered this earth and gratified [the beings], they enter the person.
Then, having entered woman, he arises again toward the world. Thus it is said.
In that context, it was stated that the mere commencement of the effect of the two *agnihotra* oblations occurs in such a manner.

Here, however, desiring to prescribe the meditation upon that commencement of the effect—characterized by the transformation of the *agnihotra*-unseen-force (*apūrva*)—as being the Fire itself, which serves as the means for attaining the Northern Path, he says:
"That world indeed, O Gautama, is the fire," and so forth.

In this world, when the two oblations of the Agnihotra have been offered in the morning and evening, using milk and other materials, preceded by faith—oblations which, having been transformed through the states of smoke, flame, embers, and sparks in the Āhavanīya fire, and through the states of the causal factors such as the agent and so forth, ascend by way of the intermediate space and enter the heavenly world—they become two subtle elements. Because they are essentially composed of water, they are designated by the word "water" (ap); and because they have faith as their cause, they are designated by the word "faith" (śraddhā). The fire that is their substratum, and everything else [associated with them], is also included therein.
The connection with that is expressed by the words "the fuel and so forth.
And that meditation (*bhāvanā*) upon fire and the rest which pertains to the two oblations is likewise indicated in that same manner:
"That world indeed, O Gautama, is the fire—just as the *āhavanīya* fire is here the locus for the *agnihotra*."
Of that fire called the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), the sun itself is the fuel; for by it being kindled, that world shines.
Because of this kindling, the sun is the fuel-stick (samit).
The rays are the smoke, because they rise from it.
For from the fuel, smoke arises;
the day is the flame due to the commonality of luminosity and because it is the effect of the sun; and the moon is the embers.
Because they become manifest upon the subsiding of the day; for when the flame subsides, the embers become manifest.
The stars are like sparks of the moon, due to the commonality of being scattered fragments.
Into this very fire, the gods offer faith as an oblation;
from that offering, King Soma comes into being.

In this very fire characterized as previously described, the gods—the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the sacrificer appearing in the form of Agni and the other deities from the perspective of the higher divinity (*adhidaivata*)—offer faith (*śraddhā*).

These "faiths" are the subtle waters, permeated by faith, which take the form of the state resulting from the transformation of the *agnihotra* oblation. This is because, in the inquiry concerning the oblations, it is heard in the scripture that "in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called man" (*pañcamyām āhutāv āpaḥ puruṣavacaso bhavanti*), thus establishing water as the substance to be offered.
It is known from scripture that "the waters are indeed faith; having begun with faith and having led it forth, one performs the ritual.
One offers that faith in the form of water.
From that oblation, King Soma arises as the transformation of the waters—which are denoted by the word "faith"—when they have been offered into the fire of the heavenly world.

Just as it was stated that the essences of the flowers of the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas, brought by the bees of the *Ṛk* and so forth, initiate in the sun an effect characterized by glory and the like, such as the red color; in the same way, these subtle waters denoted by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*), which are inherent in the *agnihotra* oblations, enter the heavenly world and initiate the lunar effect, which is the fruit of the two *agnihotra* oblations.

The sacrificers, who are the performers of that rite, consist of oblations; they are permeated by the contemplation of oblations and, drawn by the ritual act in the form of an oblation, enter the heavenly world (dyuloka) accompanied by faith and water.
For it was for that purpose that the Agnihotra was offered by them.

However, in this context, it is primarily the transformation of the oblation itself—through the sequence of its connection with the five fires—that is intended for the sake of meditation, and not the destination of the sacrificers.
He will later describe that [path] for the ignorant by way of smoke and so forth, and the higher path for the wise, which is produced by knowledge.
Thus ends the fourth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Parjanya, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire;
its fuel is the wind.
The cloud is the smoke;
lightning is the flame;
the thunderbolt is the embers.
The thunderclaps are the sparks.
He speaks for the sake of the second stage of the oblation: "Parjanya indeed—Parjanya himself, O Gautama—is the fire. Parjanya is a specific deity presiding over the instruments of rain.
Of him, the wind alone is the fuel;
for by the wind, Parjanya as fire is kindled.
Because rain is observed when there is the intensity of preceding winds and so forth;
the cloud is smoke, because it is the effect of smoke and because it is perceived in the same manner as smoke;
and lightning is flame.
Because of their commonality of luminosity;
[the phrase] "thunderbolts and embers" is used because of their hardness, or because of their connection with lightning.
The *hrādunayaḥ* are sparks; the *hrādunayaḥ* are the sounds of thundering,
because of their commonality with the scattered nature of clouds.
Into this very fire, the gods offer King Soma;
from that oblation, rain comes into being.
Into this very fire, as before, the gods offer King Soma.
From that oblation, rain comes into being.
The waters called Śraddhā, having transformed into the form of Soma, reach the fire of Parjanya in the second stage and transform into rain.
Thus ends the fifth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The earth, O Gautama, is indeed the fire;
its fuel is the year."
Space is the smoke;
night is the flame;
the quarters are the embers.
The intermediate directions are the sparks.
"Earth, O Gautama, is indeed the fire," and so forth, as before.
Of that fire called earth, the year alone is the fuel;
for it is by means of the time of a year that the earth is kindled for the production of rice and other crops.
Space is smoke;
space is seen as if rising from the earth,
just like smoke from fire.
Night is the radiance of the earth, for night is appropriate to the earth which is non-luminous by nature; because it consists of darkness,
it is like the radiance appropriate to fire.
The quarters are the embers, due to the commonality of being extinguished;
