likewise, the intermediate quarters are the sparks, due to the commonality of being minute.
Into this very fire the gods offer rain;
from that oblation, food comes into being.
The passage beginning with "In that" and so forth is the same [as before].
From that oblation, food—rice, barley, and so forth—is produced.
Thus ends the sixth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"Man, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. His speech is the fuel."
The breath is the smoke;
the tongue is the flame;
the eye is the embers.
The ear is the sparks.
Man, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. His speech is the fuel,
for by speech— through the mouth— a man is kindled, not one who is mute.
The vital breath is the smoke, because it issues from the mouth like smoke;
the tongue is the flame, because of its redness;
the eyes are the embers, because they are the locus of light.
The ear is the sparks,
because of their similarity in being scattered.
Into this very fire the gods offer food;
from that oblation, semen comes into being.
The rest is the same.
They offer food prepared from rice and other grains;
from that oblation, semen comes into being.
Thus ends the seventh section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"Woman, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; her lap is the fuel."
That which he invites is the smoke;
the womb is the flame;
that which he performs within are the embers.
Delights are sparks.
A woman, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire.
Her lap is the fuel,
for by it she is kindled for the production of sons and the like.
That which he whispers is smoke,
because whispering arises from woman;
the womb is flame, because of its redness.
That which one performs within [the body] are the embers because of their connection with fire;
the delights are the fragments of pleasure, being sparks due to their insignificance.
Into this very fire, the gods offer semen;
from that oblation, the embryo comes into being.
In this very fire, the gods offer semen as an oblation;
from that oblation, the embryo comes into being.
Thus, through the sequence of the offerings of faith, soma, rain, food, and semen, it is the waters themselves that become the embryo.

In that context, because water is present in the aggregate of the oblations, there is an intention to emphasize its predominance in the statement, "In the fifth oblation, waters come to be called 'man'.
However, it is not the case that waters alone initiate the effects such as soma and the rest;
nor do waters exist here in their non-tripartite (untrifunctionalized) state.

Even though they are composed of the threefold [elements], the acquisition of specific designations is observed—such as "this is earth," "these are waters," or "this is fire"—based on the predominance of one or another.

Therefore, it is the elements in their combined state alone that, due to the predominance of water and being associated with action, are called "waters" when they initiate effects such as Soma and so forth.
And the predominance of liquidity is indeed seen in Soma, rain, food, semen, and bodies.
And although the body consists largely of fluid and is composed of earth,
when the fifth oblation has been offered there, the waters take the form of semen and become the embryo.
Thus ends the eighth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"But it is at the fifth oblation that the waters come to be called 'man'.
Enveloped by the fetal membrane, the embryo lies within for ten or nine months, or for some other duration, and then it is born.
Thus, the first question—namely, that "in this way, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'"—has been explained.

As for what was stated in the *Vājasaneyaka* regarding how the two oblations, having returned from the heavenly world and so forth, enter the earth, the man, and the woman in succession, and then rise up again toward the world—that is mentioned here as a relevant digression.
And here, in the first question, it was asked: "Do you know where creatures go from here?"
And this is its commencement:
that embryo is the fifth specific transformation of the waters— those which are associated with the act of offering and designated by the word *śraddhā* (faith)— which,
enveloped by the *ulba* (the inner membrane) and covered by the *jarāyu* (the outer membrane), having lain within the mother’s womb for ten or nine months, or for as long as it may be.
In whatever time—whether less or more—it is born immediately thereafter;

this is stated for the purpose of inducing detachment, beginning with the words "covered by the womb" and so forth, for the embryo is smeared with that [womb] and covered by the impure cloth of the *ulba* within the mother’s belly, which is filled with urine, feces, wind, bile, phlegm, and the like. It is indeed a miserable state.

It instills detachment by showing that the embryo— whose seed is impure blood, which grows through the entry of the mother’s consumed food and drink, and whose power, strength, vigor, splendor, wisdom, and movement are suppressed— must lie within [the womb]; and then, its emergence through the birth canal while being tormented is a most painful birth,
having lain inside for a very long time, whether nine or ten months, unbearable even for a single moment.
Once born, he lives for as long as his lifespan lasts.
When he has departed, they carry that deceased man from here back to the very fires from which he came and from which he was produced.

Having been born thus, he performs karma for the sake of going and coming again and again like a water-wheel, or for the sake of revolving horizontally like a potter’s wheel, throughout his entire lifespan until such time as the life-span acquired by karma is exhausted; he lives for that long.

When his life-span is spent, he becomes a departed one (preta), dead, deceased, and destined by karma toward the next world. If, while living, he was authorized in Vedic ritual or knowledge, then when he has died, they carry him from this village for the sake of Agni—that is, for the purpose of the fire—to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
The sons carry [the body] for the sake of the final rite;

they bring it back to that very fire from which it came—by way of the sequence of oblations beginning with faith—from the presence of Agni, and from which it was produced and born from the five fires; the meaning is that they cause it to reach its own source, Agni.
Thus ends the ninth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
those who know this thus,
and those who in the forest worship with faith, [saying] "Austerity is Brahman"— they pass on by the path of light.
They attain the flame;
from the flame, the day;
from the day, the waxing fortnight.
From the waxing fortnight, those six months during which he moves northward—those he should observe.
From the months [he goes] to the year;
from the year to the sun;
from the sun to the moon.
From the moon, to lightning;
there a person who is not human leads them to Brahman.
"This is the path of the gods."
"Do you know where people go from here?"—this question has arisen and must be answered.

In that regard, among those householders who are authorized and have risen for the sake of the world, those who know—that is, understand—in this very way, as previously stated, the vision of the five fires:
"We have been born in succession from the fires beginning with the heavenly world; we are of the nature of fire, having the five fires as our self. Thus they should know.
How is it understood that those described as "knowing thus" (*itthaṃ-viduḥ*) are specifically householders and no others?
For the author will later state that those householders who do not know thus, being devoted solely to sacrifices, public works, and almsgiving, go to the moon by way of smoke and so forth;
and that those characterized as forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasa*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) who worship with faith and austerity [go] together with those who know thus.

He will later describe their departure by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*); and because of the remaining possibility (*pāriśeṣya*) and the connection with the *agnihotra* oblation, only householders are understood here by the phrase "those who know thus" (*itthaṃ viduḥ*).
But surely, since celibate students (*brahmacārin*) are also not included—being mentioned separately by the words "village" and "forest"—how can the remaining possibility be established?
This is not a fault.

On account of the authority of the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis, for those of "upward-directed semen"—that is, lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins)—the northern path is intended; thus, they do not require a specific instruction [regarding the means]. Now, if it is accepted that the state of having upward-directed semen is the cause for attaining the northern path based on the authority of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, then the knowledge of "being thus" (itthaṃvit) would become purposeless. No, for it is purposeful with respect to householders.

For those householders who do not know "thus" (the qualified Brahman), the southern path consisting of smoke and so forth is well known by their very nature; whereas for those who know "thus"—that is, those who know the qualified Brahman or the other [unqualified] Brahman—it is said:
"Now, whether they perform funeral rites for him or not, they go by the northern path," as indicated by the scriptural mark (*liṅga*).

[Objection: Is it not improper to claim that while the state of being an *āśrama* is common to both celibates (*ūrdhvaretas*) and householders, only the celibates travel by the northern path and not the householders? [Response: No, because of the abundance of Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra* and others [performed by householders].
And even though this is so, there is no fault;
for they are indeed impure.
For them, passion and hatred arise from the causes of association with enemies and friends;
likewise, merit and demerit arise from the causes of harming and favoring others.
Furthermore, many causes of impurity, such as violence, falsehood, deceit, and unchastity, are unavoidable for them.
Therefore, they are unpurified;
because of their lack of purification, there is no proceeding by the northern path.

On the other hand, others—whose selves are pure due to the avoidance of violence, falsehood, deceit, unchastity, and so forth, and who are free from passion (rajas) due to the avoidance of enmity, friendship, attachment, hatred, and the like—for them, the northern path is appropriate.

And thus the authors of the Purāṇas say: "Those who desired offspring, being undiscerning, have resorted to the cremation grounds; those who did not desire offspring, being discerning, have indeed attained immortality."

Since those householders who possess such knowledge and those forest-dwellers follow the same path and attain the same fruit of immortality, it would follow that knowledge is useless for the forest-dwellers;
and thus there would be a contradiction with the Śruti:
"Neither do the sacrificial fees go there, nor do the ignorant ascetics."
And it is contradictory [to say] that "it does not benefit one who does not know it. No;
for what is intended is immortality as abiding until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*).
Regarding this very point, it has been stated by the authors of the Purāṇas: "Indeed, abiding until the dissolution of all beings is declared to be immortality."
And with respect to that absolute immortality, there is no contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "The sacrificial gifts do not go there," and "Not being known, he does not save him.
Nor is there a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "They do not return," and "They do not return to this human whirlpool.
This is because of the qualification "this human [whirlpool]" and because of the statement, "For them, there is no return here."
For if they were not to return in an absolute sense, the qualification "to this human world here" would be meaningless.
If it is argued that "this here" refers merely to the generic form (ākṛti), we say no;
since the meaning of eternal non-return is already understood from the word "non-return" itself, the postulation of a generic form is useless.
Therefore, for the sake of making the qualification "here" meaningful, it must be understood that there is no movement elsewhere;

nor is there movement via the path beginning with light through the *mūrdhan* (cranial) artery for those who possess the realization that "Being is one alone, without a second. Such a person, being Brahman already, attains Brahman.
Therefore, it became all that;
its vital breaths do not depart, but are absorbed right here— so it is known from hundreds of scriptural passages such as these.

If it is argued that the meaning intended is that when the living self (jīva) desires to depart from the body, the vital breaths (prāṇas) do not depart separately but go along with it; we say no, because the qualification "they are merged right here" would then be redundant. Furthermore, since the departure with the vital breaths is already established by the statement, "all the vital breaths follow after it departs."
Therefore, the doubt that they "depart" is entirely unfounded.

Even when it is said that they "do not depart" because liberation is distinct from the course of transmigratory existence and there might be a suspicion that the vital breaths (prāṇas) accompany the individual soul (jīva), even then the qualification "they are merged right here" would be purposeless.
Furthermore, for one who is separated from the vital breaths (prāṇas), neither movement nor the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) is possible.

Because the Self (ātman) is omnipresent and partless, the mere connection with the vital breaths—like sparks from a fire—is indeed the cause of the distinction of being a living soul. Therefore, upon separation from that [connection], it is impossible to conceive of either the state of being a living soul or movement, provided that the Śruti scriptures are the authoritative means of knowledge.
It cannot be imagined that a real, subtle part called the *jīva* departs, splitting away and leaving a hole in the nature of reality (*sadrūpa*).

Therefore, from the statement, "Going upwards by that [path], he attains immortality," it is understood that for one who meditates on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahma*), there is a journey through the artery together with the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and that this immortality is merely relative, not liberation (*mokṣa*) itself.
This is clear from the specific qualification following the description of "that unconquered city" and "the lake Airammadīya": "This is the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) belonging to them alone."

Therefore, those householders who know the five fires, and these forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājakas*) in the wilderness, together with perpetual students (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins*), worship [the path] through faith and austerity— meaning they are faithful and ascetic;
the word "worship" (*upāsate*) here signifies intent or devotion,
as in the expression "they worship [the path of] sacrifice, public works, and charity."

Furthermore, those who, according to another scriptural passage, meditate upon Brahman as the Truth known as Hiraṇyagarbha—all of them reach and attain the *arciḥ*, the deity presiding over the light.
The rest is the same as explained in the fourth [chapter] regarding the path.
This path of the gods has been described as terminating at Satyaloka, not extending beyond the cosmic egg.
This is because of the Vedic mantra-text: "That which lies between the father and the mother."
Now, those in this world who worship with the thought, "Sacrifice and charity, what has been given," they pass into smoke;
from smoke, into night.
From the night [of the new moon] they go to the second half of the month;
from the second half of the month, those six months toward which the sun moves southward—
these do not reach the year.
The word "atha" (now) serves the purpose of introducing a different subject. These are the householders who are in the village.
The term "village" is a specific qualification of householders intended to distinguish them from those who dwell in the forest (*araṇya*).
Just as the term "forest" is a qualification for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) intended to distinguish them from householders, so it is here.
They worship such things as *iṣṭāpūrta*: *iṣṭa* refers to Vedic ritual acts such as the *agnihotra*; *pūrta* refers to the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, gardens, and so forth;
and *datta* refers to the distribution of wealth to worthy recipients outside the sacrificial altar according to one's ability.
They thus attend to these through service, protection, and other such means.
Because the word *iti* has the sense of indicating a manner, they—being devoid of [right] vision—attain, that is, reach, smoke, which is the deity presiding over smoke.

Carried by her, they go from smoke to night, the deity of night; from the deity of night to the deity of the latter fortnight, namely the deity presiding over the dark fortnight; and from the latter fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves southward. Thus it goes to the southern path.
Savitṛ:
the meaning is that they enter those months, which are deities presiding over the six months of the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
For since the deities of the six months move in groups, the plural form "months" (*māsān*) is used; these performers of ritual action do not [enter] them.

The years under discussion are indeed the two solstices—the southern and northern—which constitute parts of a single year; in that context, for those who have set out on the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), it was stated that there is an attainment of the whole year from the months of the northern solstice.
Therefore, here too, having heard of the attainment of the months of the southern solstice which are its constituent parts, [there follows] the attainment of the year as their whole.
Since it has been stated previously that "attainment is reaching," the attainment of that [year] is here prohibited by saying, "these do not reach the year."
From the months, [he goes] to the world of the fathers;
from the world of the fathers, to space;
from space, to the moon.
This is King Soma;
that is the food of the gods;
the gods consume it.
From the months they go to the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka); from the world of the ancestors to space; and from space to the moon.
Who is this moon that is reached by them? It is this King Soma who is seen in the atmosphere, the food of the Brahmins, and the food of the gods.
That moon, as their food, is consumed by the gods, Indra and the others.
Therefore, having traveled by means of smoke and so forth and having become the moon, those performers of ritual acts are consumed by the gods.
[Objection: But surely the performance of sacrifices and other rites would lead to misfortune if, having become food, they were to be consumed by the gods.
[Reply: This is not a fault.
This is because "food" (*anna*) is intended here in the sense of mere requisites;
for they are not consumed by the gods by being taken up as mouthfuls.
Rather, they serve as mere requisites for the gods, like wives, cattle, servants, and so forth.
Furthermore, the word *anna* (food) is seen used for objects of enjoyment, as in: "Women are food; cattle are food; the subjects are food for kings," and so forth.
And yet, although these women and others are objects of enjoyment for men, their own experience of enjoyment is not absent.
Therefore, even while being objects of enjoyment for the gods, the performers of ritual actions (karmiṇaḥ) are happy and sport with the gods.
And for them, a body suitable for the enjoyment of pleasure begins to form from the watery substance of the lunar orb.
This was stated previously: "The waters, signified by the word 'faith,' when offered into the fire of the heavenly world, become King Soma.

Those waters, conjoined with karma and accompanied by the other elements, reach the heavenly world and attain the state of the moon; they then become the originators of the bodies and so forth for those who worship the sacrifices and other such rites.

And when the final oblation of the body has been offered into the fire and the body is being consumed by that fire, the waters arising from it, together with the smoke, envelop the sacrificer from above, reach the lunar orb, and become the external body— standing in the place of *kuśa* grass and clay. And they remain there, experiencing the fruits of sacrifices and other rites, by means of the body thus begun.
Having dwelt there for the duration of the flight of a barleycorn, they then return again by this very same path: to the ether;
from the ether, to the air.
Having become wind, he becomes smoke;
having become smoke, he becomes mist.

"Until the exhaustion of that karma which is the cause for its enjoyment"—the word *sampāta* means "falling together," referring to the exhaustion of karma; thus, *yāvat-sampātam* means "until the exhaustion of karma.
Having dwelt in that lunar orb for that long, immediately thereafter they return again along this very path (*adhvan*) which is about to be described.
From the use of the term "returning again" (*punar-nivartante*), it is understood that they have previously gone to and returned from the lunar orb more than once.
Therefore, having accumulated karma such as sacrifices and other rites in this world, they go to the moon;
and upon the exhaustion of that [karma], they return.
It is not possible for them to remain there even for a single moment.
It is due to the exhaustion of the karma that serves as the cause for its duration,
just as a lamp goes out due to the exhaustion of its oil.
In this regard, does one descend from there upon the total exhaustion of all that karma by which one ascended to the lunar disk, or rather with some remainder?
What follows from that?
If there is the exhaustion of all karma, then liberation would occur for one residing in the lunar orb itself.
Let it be for now whether or not liberation should actually take place right there.
Consequently, for one who has arrived here [in this world], the enjoyment of a body and so forth would not be possible;
furthermore, there would be a contradiction with such Smṛti texts as "by the remainder" (śeṣeṇa). [Objection:
But surely, even apart from *iṣṭāpūrta* and *datta*, many other karmas exist that serve as the cause for the enjoyment of a body in the world of men.
Furthermore, those [limbs] are not consumed by the lunar disk;
therefore, they remain undiminished.
There is no contradiction in this, for it is precisely those [limbs] for the sake of which he ascended the lunar disk that have been exhausted.
Furthermore, the word "remainder" (śeṣa) is not contradictory because all [karmas] share the commonality of being objects of experience (*karman*).
For this very reason, there is no fault in the claim that liberation occurs precisely therein,
since it is possible for each individual sentient being to initiate even those karmas whose fruits consist of experiences in various conflicting wombs.
Furthermore, it is not possible for all karmas to be exhausted in a single birth;

for it is recorded in tradition that each individual karma, such as the killing of a Brahmin, initiates multiple births, and because it is impossible for those who have reached the state of stationary beings (plants, etc. and are utterly deluded to initiate karma that would cause upward progression.
Furthermore, for those who have become embryos and are falling away [from the womb], since action is impossible, transmigration would not occur.
Therefore, the experience of all actions does not take place within a single lifetime.
As for what some say—that at the time of death, through the destruction of the abundance of all actions, actions initiate a new birth—[that is incorrect].
In that regard, it is not tenable to say that some karmas remain merely uncommenced while others initiate a birth;
for death is the manifestor of all karmas, just as a lamp is the manifestor of its own range of objects.
That [objection] is incorrect.
Because it is accepted that everything has everything as its essence,

for if everything were to have everything as its essence, then— due to being restricted by place, time, and causal conditions— it would be impossible for anything to be suppressed in its entirety anywhere, nor could there be the manifestation of anything in its entirety.
The same would apply to actions as well, since they possess a substratum.

And just as the various contradictory latent impressions (*vāsanā*) formed by previous births as humans, peacocks, monkeys, and so forth, are not destroyed when a birth as a monkey begins due to the karma that brings about that monkey-birth, so too it is logical that the karmas which serve as the causes for attaining other births are likewise not destroyed.

For if all the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the experiences of previous births were completely obliterated, then when a monkey birth is initiated by karma having a monkey as its cause, a newborn monkey would not possess the skill of clinging to its mother’s belly while she moves from one branch to another;
this is because such behavior has not been practiced in this present life.
Nor can it be said that he was a monkey in his immediately preceding past birth, because of the Vedic scripture:
"Knowledge and action take hold of him, as does his prior wisdom.
Therefore, since there is no destruction of all karma accompanied by its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is the possibility of residual karma remaining.
Since this is so, there is no contradiction in the fact that transmigration arises from the remainder of the karma that has been experienced.
As for the question, "What is this path toward which they return?", it is said:
they return "by the same way," that is, by the very way they came.

But surely, the sequence of going was stated as "from the months to the world of the fathers, from the world of the fathers to space, and from space to the moon," yet the return is not described in that same way;
rather, it is stated as "from space to air," and so forth. How then can it be said to be "in the same manner as they went"?
This is not a fault.

Since the attainment of space and the attainment of earth are equal, there is no restrictive rule here that "they return exactly by the same way they came. Rather, the rule is that they return even in a manner other than that; thus, the phrase "by the same way they came" is intended as a mere illustration.
Therefore, they first attain elemental space.
Those waters which had constituted their bodies in the lunar sphere dissolve upon the exhaustion of those karmas that were the cause of their enjoyment there,
just as the solid form of ghee dissolves upon contact with fire.
Having dissolved, they become subtle, as if having become space while situated in the intermediate region; from that intermediate region they become air.
Established in air and having become air, being carried hither and thither, the one whose karma is exhausted becomes air together with them.
Having become air, together with them he indeed becomes smoke.
Having become smoke, it becomes a cloud, which consists merely of the form of a mass of water.
Having become mist, it becomes a cloud;
having become a cloud, it rains.
These are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans. From this state, indeed, it is most difficult to escape.
For whoever eats the food and whoever sheds the semen, that very thing comes into being again.
Having become a cloud, it then becomes a rain-cloud capable of pouring forth; having become a cloud, it then rains down upon elevated regions.
The meaning is that, in the form of rain-showers, it falls with its residual karma.
These are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, beans, and so forth.
The plural designation is used because those whose karma has been exhausted are many;
the singular designation is used for the preceding [elements] such as clouds, because they possess a single form.
This is because thousands of configurations—such as mountain slopes, fortresses, rivers, oceans, forests, and desert regions—are formed by the falling streams of rain.
Therefore, for that very reason, it is indeed *durniṣprapataram*—difficult to emerge from, difficult to depart from, and difficult to escape from.

For once they have been carried by the current of water from the mountain slope and reach the rivers, from there they reach the ocean, and then they are devoured by creatures beginning with the letter *m* (such as fish); and those, in turn, are devoured by another.

And right there in the ocean, they dissolve along with the crocodile and are drawn away by the waters of the sea; then, carried by the clouds, they fall again through showers of rain upon a desert or an inaccessible rocky slope, where they remain until perhaps they are swallowed or eaten by snakes, predatory beasts, or others.
These too are eaten by yet others; in such ways do they undergo successive transformations.
Sometimes those born among inedible stationary beings might wither away right there.

Even for those born among edible stationary beings, the connection with the body of a seed-discharging being is indeed difficult to obtain because of the vast number of stationary beings; therefore, it is difficult to escape from that state.
Alternatively, it is even more difficult to emerge—that is, more difficult to depart—from this state of being rice, barley, and so forth.
Regarding the word *durniṣprapataram*, one *t* should be understood as elided.
The state of being rice, barley, and so forth is difficult to escape from; even more difficult to escape than that is the connection with the body of the one who emits semen (*retaḥsig*).
This is because those who have been eaten—whether they be children whose semen has not yet flowed upward, or men devoid of virility, or the elderly—perish in the interval.

Because there are many eaters of food, it may happen by some chance that they are eaten by those who emit semen; when that occurs, for those who have attained the state of being semen-emitters, their karma gains its functional manifestation.
How so?
For whoever, being joined with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), emits semen that has consumed food into a woman during her fertile period, he becomes again and again of that very form.

This "becoming more" (*bhūyaḥ*) refers to the predominance of the form of those constituent parts. The latent disposition, having entered within the womb of the woman in the form of semen, assumes the form of the semen-discharger because the semen is permeated by the form of the semen-discharger.
For from another scriptural passage it is known that "light is produced from all the limbs";
therefore, the meaning is that [the intermediate being] takes on the very form of the one who emits the seed.
Thus it is said:
From a man a man is born, and from a cow only one with the form of a cow—not one with the form of another species; therefore, it is logical that "he becomes that very thing again.

However, for those others who, unlike those possessing latent tendencies (*anuśayin*), do not ascend to the lunar orb but instead, due to their terrible evil deeds, attain the state of rice, barley, and so forth right here, and subsequently the state of humans and the like, the crossing back out is not as difficult or impossible as it is for those with latent tendencies.
Why is this?

Because by means of their karma, they have acquired bodies such as rice and barley; thus, when the cause for that enjoyment is exhausted and the bodies of rice-stalks and so forth perish, they—possessing consciousness—migrate to other new bodies according to what has been earned by their karma, just like a leech. They do not migrate without consciousness.
This is because of another scriptural passage stating, "He enters [the new body] endowed with consciousness.

Even though they depart for another body with their sense organs withdrawn, nevertheless, like those in a dream, they go to the other body precisely as endowed with consciousness, by means of the knowledge and latent impressions (vāsanā) manifested by the karma that causes the attainment of that other body.
This is because of the authority of scripture (*śruti*).
Likewise, the journey by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*) and the path beginning with smoke (*dhūma*) occurs through an emergent consciousness (*udbhūta-vijñāna*), as if in a dream,
since the journey has its cause in karma that has attained its functional manifestation (*labdhavṛtti-karma-nimitta*).

In the same way, it is not possible for those who possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and have been born as rice and so forth to enter into a connection with the body of a woman and a seed-discharger while still possessing consciousness.
For there is no persistence of consciousness during the cutting, threshing, and grinding of rice and other grains.
[Objection: But surely, since the transition to another body is the same for those descending from the lunar orb, it is logical that they possess consciousness, just like a leech.

If that were the case, then for those who perform sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*), there would result a terrible experience in hell, starting from the lunar sphere and continuing until birth as a Brāhmaṇa or other [high caste].
And such being the case, the practice of sacrifices and works of public utility prescribed by scripture would lead only to misfortune.
Furthermore, the authority of the Śruti would be undermined, because Vedic rituals would be followed by undesirable consequences.
No, for there is a distinction [between the two cases], like climbing a tree and falling from it.

For one who intends to transition from one body to another, it is logical that he possesses consciousness (*savijñānatva*) through a consciousness manifested by karma, since the karma has already acquired its functional activity;
this is just as one climbing to the top of a tree does so while desiring to grasp the fruit.
Thus, those traveling by way of the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) would possess consciousness,
as would those ascending to the lunar orb by way of smoke (dhūma-ādi);
but it is not so for those descending from the lunar orb, who lack consciousness like men falling from the top of a tree.
And just as it is observed that those struck by a mallet or similar instrument— who, due to the sensation caused by that blow, have their faculties rendered unconscious and obstructed—
are devoid of consciousness while being carried from one place to another by their own bodies; in the same way, those who desire to descend from the lunar orb to another body such as that of a human,
whose watery bodies have been dissolved due to the exhaustion of the karma that was the cause of their heavenly enjoyment, have their faculties obstructed.

Therefore, not having abandoned the waters that constitute the seed of the body, as if in a state of swoon, they descend through this world via the sequence beginning with space; they then become joined to stationary bodies according to their birth caused by karma, their cognitive faculties being obstructed so that their consciousness remains unmanifest.
Likewise, during the stages of reaping, threshing, grinding, processing, eating, the transformation into rasa and other constituents, and the emission of semen, they remain as if in a state of swoon.

Because the karma that initiates another body has not yet attained its fruition, [the subtle bodies] persist in all states without relinquishing their connection with the water that serves as the seed of the body; thus, their possession of consciousness is not contradicted, just as in the case of a leech. However, the lack of awareness in the intermediate state is like that of one who is in a swoon, so there is no fault.
Nor can it be inferred that Vedic rituals possess a dual nature (as both causes) simply because they involve violence;
for such violence is enjoined by the scriptures.

According to the Vedic revelation, "One should not harm any living beings, except at the sacred sites (*tīrtha*)," it is accepted that violence enjoined by the scriptures does not constitute a cause of unrighteousness (*adharma*).

Even if it were admitted that [Vedic rites] are causes of demerit, their removal would be possible through mantras—just as poison and the like are removed—so that it is not logical for Vedic actions to initiate the effect of suffering, any more than the consumption of poison can be undone by a mantra.

Regarding this, it is said: "Those here whose conduct has been pleasant will, in all likelihood, attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya.
But those here whose conduct has been foul will, in all likelihood, attain a foul womb—the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla."

In that regard, among those who possess latent tendencies (*anuśayin*), those whose conduct and moral discipline (*śīla*) in this world are delightful and beautiful are called "those of delightful conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇa*). Those for whom the latent tendency is beautiful— characterized by delightful conduct— and whose karma is meritorious,
are designated as "those of delightful conduct."
For it is indeed possible to perceive the existence of virtuous latent tendencies (*śubhānuśaya*) in those who are free from cruelty, falsehood, and deceit.

By virtue of that merit resulting from such latent tendencies, and by the remainder of the karma to be experienced in the lunar sphere, they very soon—indeed, almost immediately—attain, reach, or enter a pleasant womb free from cruelty and the like; that is to say, according to their own past actions, they attain a Brahmin womb, a Kshatriya womb, or a Vaishya womb. (Note: *Yat* is used here as an adverbial particle [kriyāviśeṣaṇa] meaning "so that" or "in such a way that.")
Furthermore, those who are the opposite of that— whose actions are characterized by foul conduct, who possess impure latent tendencies—
it is likely that they will attain a foul womb according to their karma; indeed, being devoid of connection to dharma, they will attain a loathsome and foul womb,
such as the womb of a dog or the womb of a pig, precisely in accordance with their own past deeds.

But those twice-born ones whose conduct has been pleasant, who remain steadfast in their own duties and perform sacrifices and other rites, go by way of smoke and so forth; they go and return again and again like a water-wheel.
If, however, they should attain knowledge, then they go by way of the flame and so forth.
Now, those who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small creatures that return again and again, saying, "Be born and die.
This is the third station.
Because of this, that world is not filled up.
Therefore, one should feel revulsion toward it.
On this point, there is this verse:

But when they neither practice knowledge nor perform rites such as the *iṣṭāpūrta*, then they go by neither of these two aforementioned paths— characterized by the arcirādi and dhūmādi routes— and those beings become small creatures such as gadflies, mosquitoes, and insects, which return repeatedly.
Therefore, the meaning is that, having fallen away from both paths, they are indeed born and die again and again.
This is said to be a description of the succession of their births and deaths:
"Be born, die"—this is called activity caused by Īśvara. By means of the very characteristics of birth and death, there is merely the passing of time.
The meaning is that there is no time for ritual actions or enjoyments [there].
This is the third station characterized by small creatures for those wandering in *saṃsāra*, in comparison with the two paths mentioned previously.
Because of this, even those who go by the southern path return again; for those not qualified for knowledge and action, there is simply no going by the southern path.
Therefore, that world is not filled.

As for the fifth question, it has been explained by means of the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*). The first [question] is resolved by means of the southern and northern paths; for although the casting of the dead into the fire is common to both the southern and northern paths, those who turn away from these two paths proceed by different ways—some by the path beginning with light (*arcis*) and others by another.
By means of smoke and so forth, they again reach the six months of the northern and southern solstices; having united, they turn back once more.
Others [reach] the world of the ancestors after a year, and others after the months; thus it has been explained.
Furthermore, the return of those whose latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have been exhausted is described as proceeding from the lunar disk through space and so forth.
That this world is not filled has been stated by its own specific term: "therefore that world is not filled.
Since the course of *saṃsāra* is thus so painful, one should feel revulsion toward it.

And because small creatures, whose moments are consumed by the experience of sensations born of birth and death, are cast into a terrible, impassable darkness like a bottomless ocean without a boat, and are without hope of crossing over; therefore, one should feel disgust for such a course of saṃsāra, one should feel loathing, one should become filled with aversion, thinking: "May I never fall into such a terrible great ocean of saṃsāra."
Regarding this matter, there is this verse for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the five fires.
The thief of gold, the drinker of liquor,
the violator of the teacher’s bed, and the killer of a Brahmin— these four fall, as does the fifth who associates with them.
A thief of gold—that is, a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold;
a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor;
and one who dwells upon the bed of his guru—that is, his wife.
The killer of a Brahmin, the slayer of a Brahmin—these four fall;
and the fifth is he who associates with them.
Now, indeed, he who knows these five fires in this way is not tainted by evil even while associating with them;
he becomes pure, cleansed, and possesses a world of merit—he who knows thus, he who knows thus.
Now, moreover, he who knows the five fires as they have been described—even if he associates with those who commit great sins—he is not tainted by evil; he remains pure.

Purified by that vision of the five fires, he becomes one whose world is meritorious—that is, his world, such as that of Prajāpati, becomes meritorious. This applies to whoever knows thus, knowing the entire collection of matters asked in the five questions as they have been explained.
The repetition is for the purpose of demonstrating the resolution of all the questions.
Thus ends the tenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, Jana Śārkarākṣya, and Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi— these great householders and great Vedic scholars, having come together, engaged in a philosophical discussion.
"What is the self? What is Brahman?"
For one traveling by the southern path, there is the fear of a lack of food, thinking, "That is the food of the gods; the gods consume it.
Furthermore, the miserable course of transmigratory existence characterized by minute creatures has been described.
Desiring to eliminate both these defects, the subsequent section of the text is commenced for the purpose of attaining the state of being the consumer of Vaiśvānara.
This is known from such indicative marks as, "You shall eat food; you shall see what is dear.

The narrative, however, is for the sake of easy comprehension and for the purpose of demonstrating the proper method for the transmission of knowledge. *Prācīnaśāla* is his name; he is the descendant of Upamanyu, thus *Aupamanyava*.
*Satyayajña* is his name; he is the descendant of Pulūṣa, thus *Pauluṣi*.
Likewise, Indradyumna by name was the descendant of Bhallavi, thus Bhāllavi; his descendant was Bhāllaveya.
Jana by name was the descendant of Śarkarākṣa, thus Śārkarākṣya.
Buḍila by name was the descendant of Aśvatarāśva, thus Āśvatarāśvi.
All five of these were great householders (*mahāśāla*), meaning they were endowed with extensive halls;
they were great Vedic scholars (*mahāśrotriya*), meaning they were perfected in sacred learning, study, and conduct.
Being such as these, they came together and assembled, and in a certain place they engaged in *mīmāṃsā*, that is, they conducted an inquiry.
How so?
"Who is our Self (ātman)? What is Brahman?"—thus the words *ātman* and *brahman* function as mutual qualifiers and qualified.

The term *brahman* excludes the *ātman* as limited to the internal self (*adhyātma*), while the term *ātman* excludes the worshipability of a *brahman* such as Āditya that is distinct from the *ātman*.

Through non-differentiation, it is established that the Self alone is Brahman and Brahman alone is the Self; thus, Vaiśvānara, who is the Self of all, is Brahman and He is the Self—this is proven by such indicative marks as, "Your head would have fallen off," and "You would have become blind."
They made an agreement:
"Venerable sirs, this Uddālaka Āruṇi is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self;
let us go to him."
They indeed approached him.
Even though they deliberated, they did not reach a certainty; therefore, they made an effort to find an instructor for themselves.
[They thought: "Uddālaka Āruṇi—well-known by name, venerable (bhagavat), and the son of Aruṇa—is currently studying this very Vaiśvānara Self as we intend it.
Having thus resolved, "Come now, let us go to him," they went to that Āruṇi.
He reflected:
"These great householders and great Vedic scholars will question me;
I shall not be able to answer them all."
"Come, let me instruct another."
Upon seeing them, he understood the purpose of their arrival and prepared himself accordingly.
How so?
"These great householders and great Vedic scholars will indeed question me about Vaiśvānara; I shall not be able to provide a complete answer to everything they ask, nor do I venture to speak."
Therefore, thinking, "I shall now instruct another one of them; I will speak as their teacher," [he approached].
He said to them:
"Venerable sirs, this Aśvapati Kaikeya is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self.
Come, let us go to him."
They indeed approached him.
Having thus prepared them, he said to them:
"Venerable sirs, this man named Aśvapati, the son of Kekaya—a Kaikeya—is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self correctly," and so on, as before.
When they had arrived, he caused separate honors to be prepared for each of them.
Rising in the morning, he said:
"In my kingdom there is no thief, no miser, and no drunkard."
"I am neither one who has not maintained the sacred fires, nor am I ignorant, nor am I self-willed; how much less so my wife?
Indeed, venerable sirs, I am about to perform a sacrifice.
Whatever wealth I shall give to each individual officiating priest, that same amount I shall give to you, venerable sirs."
"May the Blessed Ones dwell here."
They said:
"Whatever purpose a person may pursue, that indeed one should speak of;
you are currently studying this very Self, Vaiśvānara."
"Tell us that very thing."
He said to them,
"I shall answer you in the morning.
With fuel in their hands, they returned in the forenoon.
Having brought them near, he spoke this to them.
When they had arrived, the king had the royal priests and servants provide them individually with the honors and offerings due to them.
On another day, as the king was rising in the morning, he approached them with humility and said, "Accept this wealth from me.
When he was refused by them, he thought, "They surely see some fault in me, since they do not accept wealth from me," and wishing to demonstrate his own virtuous conduct, he spoke as follows:
In my kingdom, there is no thief who steals the property of others;
no miser who fails to give despite possessing wealth; and no one who drinks liquor, even if he be a preeminent brahmin.
One who has not maintained the sacred fires is not a hundredfold [in merit];
nor is one who is ignorant [of his duty] according to his qualification;
nor is one who acts willfully, going to the wives of others.
For this very reason, the meaning is that how could a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) not be one of wicked conduct?
And when they said, "We do not seek wealth," he [the king] said: "Thinking it to be small, these [women] do not accept the wealth.
O venerable sirs, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice in a few days."
"For that purpose, I have prepared wealth such that I shall give to each venerable one as much wealth as is prescribed for each individual officiating priest (ṛtvij).
May the venerable ones dwell here and witness my sacrifice. Having been thus addressed, they said:
"Whatever purpose or need a man has for which he would approach someone, he should indeed state that very purpose."
"This alone is the purpose of our coming"—this is the principle of the virtuous.
We are seekers of the knowledge of Vaiśvānara;
you indeed now teach us this very Self as Vaiśvānara; you know it perfectly.
"Therefore, tell that very thing to us. Being thus addressed, he said to them:

"In the morning, I shall speak to you; I shall give you my reply. Having been told this, they—knowing the king's intention and with fuel in their hands, carrying loads of sacrificial wood—approached the king on the following day in the forenoon.

Since it was thus that these great *mahāśāla* Brāhmaṇas, who were great *śrotriya*s, having abandoned the pride of being *mahāśāla*s, approached the king— who was inferior by birth— with humility and with fuel-bundles in their hands for the sake of knowledge, so too should others who desire to acquire knowledge act.
And he imparted knowledge to them even without performing the initiation (*upanayana*), that is, without having performed the ritual of initiation for them.
The meaning of the narrative is that, just as [Prajāpati] bestowed knowledge upon those who were worthy, so too should knowledge be given by another;
this connects with what is to be said later: "He spoke this very knowledge of Vaiśvānara."
Thus ends the eleventh section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"Aupamanyava, upon which Self do you meditate?
"On the sky itself, O Venerable King," he replied.
This indeed is the Self of Good Brilliance, Vaiśvānara, whom you venerate as the Self; therefore, pressed Soma, extra-pressed Soma, and poured Soma are seen in your lineage.
He states how he spoke: "O Aupamanyava, whom do you worship as the Self, as Vaiśvānara? Thus he questioned him.
Now, one might object: "Is this not improper—that a teacher should question his disciple?
This is not a fault.
"Come to me with what you already know; then I shall tell you what is beyond that," according to the principle seen in the *Nyāya-darśana*.

Furthermore, in other instances as well, a question is observed to be asked by a teacher for the purpose of generating insight in a student who lacks it—such as Ajātaśatru’s question: "Where was this [person] then? Whence did he come? [To this, Śvetaketu replied:
"I meditate upon Vaiśvānara as heaven itself, O venerable King," he said.

This indeed is Vaiśvānara known as "Sutejas" (the One of Excellent Splendor), for his splendor is excellent; he is the Self because he constitutes a limb of the Self. Since you meditate upon him as the Self—that is, as a portion of the Self—therefore, through the meditation on Sutejas Vaiśvānara, your soma will be *suta* (pressed) in ritual action, *prasuta* (well-pressed), and *āsuta* (thoroughly pressed) in the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) and other rites.
The meaning is that in your family, those born of your lineage are seen to be exceedingly devoted to ritual action.
"You eat food and see what is dear;
he who eats food and sees what is dear, and in whose family there is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), is one who meditates thus upon this Vaiśvānara Self.
But, he said, 'this is only the head of the Self.'"
"Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me."
Being one whose digestive fire is kindled, you eat food and behold what is dear and desired—sons, grandsons, and so forth.
Another also eats food and beholds what is dear; he possesses the status of an agent, such as "his son has been born," "he has procreated," or "he has performed the *āsuta* sacrifice.
And there is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family for whoever thus meditates upon this Vaiśvānara exactly as described.
This is indeed the head of Vaiśvānara as the Self; it is not the entire Vaiśvānara.
Therefore, by worshipping Vaiśvānara with the notion that he is the whole, your head—your "mūrdhā"—would have fallen off, meaning it would have been shattered, because you grasped him erroneously.
This would have happened had you not come to me. Had you not come, it would not have occurred.
The intention is: "It was well that you have come to me."
Thus ends the twelfth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi:
"O Prācīnayogya, upon which Self do you meditate?"
"O venerable King," he said, "it is indeed Āditya.
This is the all-formed Self, Vaiśvānara, as the Self which you worship.
Therefore, many all-formed things are seen in your lineage."

Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi, "O Prācīnayogya, upon which Self do you meditate? He replied, "Sir, O King, I meditate upon Āditya (the Sun) alone. [This is so] because Āditya possesses the nature of the "All-form" (*viśvarūpa*) due to having white, blue, and other colors, or because he is the form of all things. For all forms indeed belong to Tvaṣṭṛ; therefore, Āditya is the All-form. From meditating upon him, much that is multiform—both for this world and for the sake of the next—is seen as an instrument of utility within your family.
A chariot drawn by mules comes to him, female slaves, and gold neck-ornaments.
He eats food and sees what is dear.
He who thus meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises in his family the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
"This, however, belongs to the Self through the eye," he said.
"You would have become blind if you had not come to me."
Furthermore, following you shall come a chariot yoked with two mules—a "mule-chariot"—and a necklace for female slaves—a "slave-necklace," meaning a golden chain accompanied by female slaves.
"You shall eat food," and so forth, is the same as before.
Savitṛ, however, is the eye of Vaiśvānara.
"Because you did not come to me, you would have become blind—deprived of sight—due to worshipping him with a collective intellect," as stated previously.
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya:
"O Vaiyāghrapadya, upon which Self do you meditate?"
"O venerable King," he said, "it is indeed Vāyu.
This Vaiśvānara Self, whom you worship as the Self, is the one whose paths are manifold.
Therefore, offerings come to you from various directions, and rows of chariots follow you from various directions."
Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: "O Vaiyāghrapadya, upon what Self do you meditate? and so forth, as before.

He whose paths are separate—meaning Vāyu, who exists through various divisions such as the *āvaha* (the wind that brings), the *udvaha* (the wind that carries upward), and so on—is this Vāyu, the "separate-pathed" one (*pṛthagvartmā*).

From meditating upon this Vaiśvānara, whose Self consists of separate paths, offerings (*balayaḥ*) characterized by garments, food, and the like, come to you from various directions; that is, they arrive from many different quarters.
Rows of separate chariots, even lines of chariots, follow after you.
"You shall eat food and see what is dear;
he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
But this is only the breath of the self," he said.
"Your vital breath would have departed had you not come to me."
"You would have eaten food," and so forth, is the same as before.
He said, "This breath of yours has indeed been lost; your breath would have departed—that is, it would have gone out—if you had not come to me."
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he said to Jana Śārkarākṣya:
"Śārkarākṣya, which Self do you meditate upon?"
"Space alone, O venerable King," he said.
"This Vaiśvānara Self which you meditate upon is indeed the 'Abundant' (Bahula) Self.
Therefore, you are abundant in offspring and wealth."
Then he said, "Janam," and so forth, which is the same as before.
This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self, the manifold (*bahula*). Its manifoldness is due to the all-pervasiveness of space (*ākāśa*).
And because of your worship of many virtues, you are "bahula," abundant, in terms of progeny characterized by sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as in wealth such as gold and the like.
"You shall eat food; you shall see what is dear.
"He who venerates this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
"But," he said, "this is only the trunk of the Self."
Your doubt that you would not come to me has been shattered.
"But this doubt is indeed a doubt; it is the middle body of Vaiśvānara.

Since the root *dih* means 'to increase,' the body is abundant with flesh, blood, bones, and so forth; that is your 'sandeha. Your body would have perished—it would have been shattered—had you not come to me."
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi:
"O Vaiyāghrapadya, upon which Self do you meditate?"
"Water indeed, O venerable King," he said.
"This is indeed the Vaiśvānara Self, the wealth, which you venerate as the Self.
Therefore, you are wealthy and prosperous."
Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, and so forth, as before:
"This indeed is *rayi*, the Vaiśvānara Self; it is of the nature of wealth.
From water comes food, and from that, wealth."
Therefore, you are possessed of wealth, you are wealthy, and you are endowed with nourishment in your body; for nourishment has food as its cause.
"You eat food; you see what is dear.
He who venerates this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
But this, he said, is only the bladder of the Self."
"Your bladder would have burst had you not come to me."

"This bladder, indeed, is the bladder of my own Vaiśvānara—the bladder being the place where urine is collected; that bladder of yours would have burst, it would have been torn asunder, had you not come to me."
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he said to Uddālaka Āruṇi:
"Gautama, as whom do you worship the Self?"
"O venerable King," he said, "it is the earth itself.
This Vaiśvānara Self, which you venerate as the Self, is indeed the foundation.
Therefore, you are firmly established through offspring and cattle."
"You eat food; you see what is dear.
He who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
But these, he said, are only the feet of the Self."
"Your feet would have withered away had you not come to me."
Then he said to Uddālaka, and so forth, as before.
"The earth alone, O venerable King," he replied.
"This indeed is the foundation; it is the feet of Vaiśvānara."
"Your feet would have withered away; they would have become faded and limp had you not come to me."
Thus ends the seventeenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
He said to them:
"Indeed, you have been eating food while knowing this Vaiśvānara Self as if it were separate."
But he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self as of the measure of a span, as the all-measuring,
eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.
He said this to those who possessed the aforementioned vision of Vaiśvānara:
"Indeed, you all..."—the two particles *vai* and *khalu* here are merely expletives.

[The meaning is: "Though this single Vaiśvānara Self is non-different, you, perceiving it as if it were different, eat food with the notion of a limited self; you are like those born blind [who do not see] an elephant."

But he who [meditates on] this [Self] as a single entity thus distinguished by the aforementioned members, beginning with the sky as the head and ending with the earth as the feet— it is "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*) because it is measured (*mīyate*) and known within the body (*adhyātma*) by means of the "spans" (*prādeśaiḥ*), namely the members beginning with the sky as the head and ending with the earth as the feet;
or, it is "measured by a span" because it is measured as the eater (*attṛtvena*) within the organs such as the mouth.
Alternatively, "measuring a span" (prādeśamātra) refers to having the dimensions of the space from the heavenly world down to the earth.
They are called "spans" (prādeśāḥ) because they are specifically pointed out (pradiśyante) by the scripture; thus, it means having such a dimension, namely the heavenly world and so forth.
In another Vedic recension, however, they conceive of it as being "measuring a span" by imagining it to extend from the head down to the chin.
But here, it is not intended in that sense;

for [the text] concludes with "Of this very Self," and so forth. It is called *abhivimāna* because it is measured out (*mīyate*) as the innermost Self (*pratyagātmatayā*), known as "I"; this very Self is Vaiśvānara.

He leads all men to a destination corresponding to their merit and demerit; this Lord Vaiśvānara is the Self of all. Or, he is Vaiśvānara because he is the "all" (viśva) and the "man" (nara), since he is the Self of all.
Or, he is Vaiśvānara because he is led by all men as their innermost Self (pratyagātman). One should meditate upon him in this way.

He who, being the eater of food, eats food in all worlds— beginning with the heavenly world— in all beings, both moving and stationary, and in all selves— that is, in bodies, senses, minds, and intellects (for it is in these that the designation "self" is applied)— eats food as one who knows Vaiśvānara, being the Self of all.
The meaning is not that he eats like an ignorant person who identifies with the mere physical body alone.

Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is *sutejas* (the brilliantly shining), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartman* (of diverse paths), the trunk is *bahula* (abundant), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), the feet are the earth itself; the chest is the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), the body hair is the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the heart is the *gārhapatya* fire, the mind is the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and the mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire.
Why is it so?

Because of this: of that very self, Vaiśvānara, which has been under discussion, the head indeed is *sutejas* (of excellent luster), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartman* (having various paths), the trunk is *bahula* (abundant), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), and the feet are the earth itself.

Alternatively, this statement is for the purpose of an injunction, meaning "one should meditate thus. Now, desiring to identify the Agnihotra sacrifice with the eating of one who knows Vaiśvānara, he says: Of this eater, Vaiśvānara, the chest itself is the altar, because of its similar shape.
The hairs on the chest are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), for they are seen spread out upon the chest just as grass is spread upon an altar.
The heart is the Gārhapatya fire, for from the heart the mind is, as it were, brought forth and remains immediately adjacent to it; therefore, the Anvāhāryapacana fire is the mind.
The mouth is the Āhavanīya fire, for food is offered into it, just as oblations are offered into the Āhavanīya.
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Therefore, whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as an oblation.
Whatever first oblation he may offer, let him offer it with the words: "Svāhā to Prāṇa!"
The vital breath is satisfied.
This being the case, whatever food may come at the time of eating for the purpose of a meal, that should be offered as an oblation.
Since what is intended here is merely the completion of the *agnihotra*, the detailed procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) of the *agnihotra* do not apply here.

As for the first oblation that the eater should offer, he says how one should offer it: with the mantra "To Prāṇa, Svāhā!"—the meaning is that by this mantra, one should cast into the fire a portion of food measured according to the standard of a sacrificial cutting (*avadāna*), as indicated by the word "oblation" (*āhuti*).
By that, the vital breath is satisfied.
When the vital breath is satisfied, the eye is satisfied;
when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied;
when the sun is satisfied, the sky is satisfied.
When the heaven is satisfied, whatever the heaven and the sun preside over is satisfied;
following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.

When the vital breath (prāṇa) is satisfied, the eye, the sun, and the sky, and so forth, are satisfied; and whatever else the sky and the sun preside over as their domain, that too is satisfied. Following its satisfaction, one who eats himself is likewise satisfied—this is directly perceived.
Moreover, [he is satisfied] through his offspring and other such things.
*Tejas* is the radiance, brilliance, or boldness residing in the body;
*brahmavarcasa* is the splendor resulting from virtuous conduct and the study of the Vedas.
Thus ends the nineteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, the second oblation he should offer, he should offer with the words: "Svāhā to Vyāna! Thereby Vyāna is satisfied.
When the vyāna breath is satisfied, the ear is satisfied;
when the ear is satisfied, the moon is satisfied;
when the moon is satisfied, the quarters of space are satisfied.
When the quarters are satisfied, whatever the quarters and the moon preside over is satisfied;
following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Then, as for the second, fourth, and fifth [days], it is the same.
Thus ends the twentieth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which he should offer as the third oblation, let him offer it with the words: "Svāhā to Apāna!
Thereby the apāna is satisfied.
When the apāna is satisfied, speech is satisfied;
when speech is satisfied, Agni is satisfied;
when Agni is satisfied, the earth is satisfied.
When the earth is satisfied, whatever the earth and fire preside over is satisfied.
Following their satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Thus ends the twenty-first section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which he should offer as the fourth oblation, he should offer with the words: "To Samāna, svāhā!
Samāna becomes satisfied.
When the breath is satisfied, the mind is satisfied;
when the mind is satisfied, Parjanya is satisfied;
when Parjanya is satisfied, lightning is satisfied.
When the lightning is satisfied, whatever the lightning and the rain-god preside over is satisfied.
Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Thus ends the twenty-second section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which he should offer as the fifth oblation, let him offer it with the words: "Svāhā to Udāna!
Thereby Udāna becomes satisfied.
When the udāna breath is satisfied, the skin is satisfied; when the skin is satisfied, the air is satisfied;
when the air is satisfied, space is satisfied;
when space is satisfied, whatever the air and space preside over is satisfied.
Following his satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Thus ends the twenty-third section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
He who, not knowing this, performs the Agnihotra sacrifice—just as if one were to remove the live coals and pour the offering into the ashes, so would that [sacrifice] be.
Whoever, being ignorant of this aforementioned vision of Vaiśvānara, performs the well-known Agnihotra sacrifice—

that act of his offering in the Agnihotra would be equivalent to casting oblations into ashes instead of embers fit for the offering, having set them aside; such is his Agnihotra when compared with the Agnihotra of one who knows Vaiśvānara— thus [the text] censures the conventional Agnihotra by means of this comparison.
The Agnihotra sacrifice is praised for those who know Vaiśvānara.
Now, for one who, knowing this thus, performs the Agnihotra sacrifice, his offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.
And for this reason, this Agnihotra is distinguished.
How so?

"Now, he who, knowing it thus, performs the Agnihotra"—that is, for one possessing the aforementioned knowledge of Vaiśvānara—[the results accrue] "in all worlds," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
Because "one who eats the offered food" and [the other term] have the same meaning.
Just as a tuft of reed-grass thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so are all his evils consumed when one who knows this thus offers the Agnihotra.

Furthermore, just as the tip of a tuft of *iṣīkā* grass, when cast into or placed upon a fire, would be consumed and burnt away instantly, even so all the evils— known as merit and demerit— accumulated over many births, as well as those existing prior to the arising of knowledge and those coexisting with knowledge, are entirely consumed without remainder for this wise one who has become the Self of all and is the eater of all food.

They would be burnt away, with the exception of the evil karma that initiated the present body; because its fruit has already begun to take effect—like an arrow aimed at a target—there is no burning of it.
He who, knowing this thus, performs the Agnihotra sacrifice and eats [the remnants].
Therefore, indeed, if one who knows this should give even the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla,
it would be as if he had offered it into the Vaiśvānara Self within himself.
Regarding this, there is this verse:

Even if he were to give leavings—that is, offer what remains of his food—to a Caṇḍāla, who is unworthy of receiving leavings, even if he were to perform that which is forbidden, namely the giving of leavings, it would be as if he had offered it into the Vaiśvānara fire residing within his own self; it would not be a cause for demerit. Thus, he praises knowledge itself. Regarding this matter of praise, there is also this verse, a mantra: [The verse follows.]
Just as hungry children here wait upon their mother,
so do all beings wait upon the Agnihotra sacrifice.

Just as in this world hungry children wait upon their mother, thinking, "When will our mother give us food?", even so all beings who subsist on food wait upon the Agnihotra meal of one who knows this, thinking, "When indeed will he eat?"
The meaning is that the entire world becomes satiated by the meal of the wise.
The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi, once lived.
His father said to him: "Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student.
For truly, my dear, no one of our lineage becomes like a mere kinsman of Brahmins without having studied the Vedas."

The connection of this chapter begins with the words, "Now there was Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi. It has been stated that "All this is indeed Brahman, for it originates from it, dissolves into it, and breathes in it" (*tajjalān*). How this world is born from that [Brahman], dissolves into that very same [Brahman], and breathes by means of that very same [Brahman]—this must now be explained.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that when one wise person eats, the entire world becomes satisfied; this is possible only if the Self, which dwells in all beings, is one, and not if there were a plurality of selves.
And as to how that oneness [is to be understood], this sixth chapter is commenced for that purpose.
The story of the father and son is intended to demonstrate the supreme excellence of this knowledge.
Śvetaketu by name—*ha* is used in the sense of tradition—he was the grandson of Āruṇi (Āruṇeya). He existed [as such].

Considering that son to be a worthy vessel for knowledge, and seeing that the time for his initiation (upanayana) was passing by, his father Āruṇi said: "O Śvetaketu, go to a teacher suitable for our family and dwell there in studenthood (brahmacarya).

It is not fitting, O gentle one, that one born of our lineage should become like a mere Brahmin by name (brahmabandhu)—one who merely designates Brāhmaṇas as his kinsmen, yet does not himself possess the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa. Thus he spoke because [Śvetaketu] had not studied the Vedas after being initiated.
Having approached [his teacher] at the age of twelve, he returned at twenty-four, having studied all the Vedas; being high-minded, considering himself a learned scholar, and arrogant, he came home.
His father said to him:
From this, the father’s absence is inferred,

since he himself, though possessed of merit, did not initiate his son. That Śvetaketu, having been told by his father, approached a teacher when he was twelve years old and remained with him until he was twenty-four.

Having studied all four Vedas and understood their meaning, he was "high-minded"— one whose mind is great and profound, and who considers himself unequaled by others; being such a high-minded person, he was "conceited about his learning," having the character of one who thinks himself a learned scholar (*anūcāna*), and being "stiff" or "unyielding" by nature, he returned home.

Seeing his son in such a state—arrogant, conceited, and stiff, with a character unbecoming of himself—the father spoke out of a desire to lead him into the True Dharma: "Śvetaketu, since you are so high-minded, considering yourself well-versed in the Vedas, and yet remain so stiff, what excellence have you attained from your teacher? Or have you asked your teacher about that *ādeśa*? By *ādeśa* is meant that which is to be understood solely through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher—that by which the Supreme Brahman is pointed out; you have not asked your teacher about that.
"Śvetaketu, my dear, since you are now so high-minded, considering yourself well-versed in the Vedas, and so arrogant—

have you perhaps asked for that instruction by which what is unheard becomes heard, what is unthought becomes thought, and what is unknown becomes known? How, venerable sir, does that instruction come about?"

He specifies that instruction by means of which, when heard, even what has not been heard becomes heard; what has not been thought becomes thought; what has not been reasoned out becomes reasoned out; and what has not been known becomes known—namely, the uncertain becomes certain.

It is understood from the narrative that even after having mastered all the Vedas and attained all other objects of knowledge, one remains truly unfulfilled as long as one does not know the reality of the Self.

Having heard this wonder, he thought, "How indeed can that which is unknown be known through the knowledge of something else? and so, considering it thus, he asks: "In what way, O Venerable One, does that instruction come about?"
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, everything made of clay would be known—
the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'— so it is."
Listen, my dear, to how that instruction is given:
just as in the world, when one clod of clay—which serves as the cause—is known, all other things made of clay—the entire collection of modifications consisting of clay—would thereby be known.
How is it that when the cause, the clod of clay, is known, the effect, which is something else, becomes known?
This is not a fault,
because the effect is non-different from its cause.
As for what you think— that when one thing is known, another is not known— [that is not so].
This would indeed be so, if the effect were something other than the cause; however, the effect is not something other than the cause.
How then does this world designate "this is the cause" and "this is its transformation"?
Listen.
"A mere beginning in speech" means a commencement by speech, or that which has speech as its support.
What is this modification? It is a name; "nāmadheya" means simply a name, the suffix *-dheya* being used in the sense of the base itself.

Name is merely an object of speech, being only a designation; in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a modification. On the contrary, it is only the clay that exists as the real entity—clay alone is the true reality.
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single ingot of gold, everything made of gold would be known—
the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'gold' alone is the reality."
Just as, my dear, by means of a single piece of gold in the form of a metal gem, all other products such as bracelets, crowns, and armlets would be known;
the phrase "a mere modification of speech" and so forth is the same [as before].
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of iron might be known—
the modification being a mere verbal handle, a mere name, while 'iron' alone is the truth—
so, my dear, is that instruction."
"Surely those venerable ones did not know this;
for if they had known it, why would they not have told me?
Let the venerable one himself tell it to me."
"So be it," he said, "yes."
Just as, my dear, by means of a single piece of black iron— meaning, by means of a nail-cutter characterized by it—
all that which is made of black iron, the entire collection of objects fashioned from black iron, would be known; the rest is the same.
The employment of numerous examples is for the purpose of following the distinction between the illustration and the subject illustrated, and for the sake of firm conviction.

When the father had said, "My dear, that instruction which I have spoken is thus," the other replied: "Surely those venerable, worshipful gurus of mine did not know, they did not understand, this very matter which you have spoken."
"For if they had indeed known this matter, how could they not have told it to me—who am virtuous, devoted, and a follower? Therefore, I think they did not know it.
[The son] spoke thus even though he was describing the inferiority of his teacher, out of fear of being sent back to the teacher's house.
