Then the Blessed One said, "Tell me that very thing by which, once known, I may attain omniscience. Being thus addressed, the father replied, "So be it, my dear."
Thus ends the first section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second.
Regarding this, some say: 'In the beginning, this was Non-being alone, one only, without a second.'"
Therefore, being is born from non-being.

"That which is real" means existence alone; it is a subtle reality, devoid of distinctions, all-pervading, one, stainless, partless, and consciousness—this is what is understood from all the Vedāntas.
The word "eva" (only) is for the purpose of restriction.
To the question, "What is it that is being restricted?", he says:
This world, which is perceived as modified by name, form, and action, was indeed that very Being (*sat*); thus it is connected with the word "was" (*āsīt*).
When it is asked, "When was this indeed Being? it is said: "In the beginning," that is, prior to the origin of the world.
Is it not the case that this [entity] is now qualified by the statement "that which was at the beginning"?
No; how then is it qualified?
Even now this is indeed existent, but because it possesses the qualifications of name and form, it becomes the object of the word and the cognition "this," and thus it is "this."
However, prior to origination, this [world] was accessible only through the mere word and cognition of "Being" (sat); thus it is determined that "In the beginning, this was Being alone.
For prior to origination, it is not possible to apprehend this entity as being possessed of name and form, just as in the state of deep sleep.
The intention is that, just as one who has arisen from deep sleep perceives only existence, understanding that in deep sleep the reality was merely Being alone, so too was it prior to origination.

Just as it is said in the world: when a potter, desiring to create a jar or the like in the forenoon, has observed a lump of clay spread out and has gone to another village, and having returned in the afternoon, observes there the effect divided into many varieties such as jars, bowls, and so forth, he says, "This very jar, bowl, and the rest existed only as clay in the forenoon"; in the same way, it is said here as well: "In the beginning, this was Being alone."
"Only one" means that there is nothing else apart from what has fallen into its own causal function; thus it is said to be "only one.
"Without a second" means:

Just as, apart from clay, another instrumental cause such as a potter is observed who transforms the clay into the form of a jar and so forth, so too, the existence of a second distinct entity as a cooperative cause for Being (sat) would follow [from the logic of the example]; this is what is negated by the term "without a second" (advitīya).
It is called "without a second" because no second distinct entity exists for it.

But surely, even in the Vaiśeṣika position, the co-referentiality with "existent" (sat) is established for everything, because the word and the cognition of "existent" recur with respect to substances, qualities, and so forth; for we observe such instances as "existent substance," "existent quality," and "existent action."

This may indeed be true now; however, prior to its production, it is not accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas that this effect was already existent, because they maintain that the effect was non-existent before its production.
Nor do they admit that the Existent (Sat) alone, without a second, existed prior to production.
Therefore, this "Existent" is said to be a cause other than the "Existent" imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, as evidenced by the analogies of clay and so forth.

In this regard, concerning the determination of the reality prior to its origination, certain Nihilists (vaināśika), while determining that reality, say: "Prior to its origination, this world was one alone, without a second; it was merely the absence of Being.
For the Buddhists postulate that the reality prior to origination is merely the absence of Being (*sad-abhāva-mātra*);
they do not, however, accept any other entity that is the opposite of Being.
The Naiyāyikas maintain that reality (*tattva*) consists in the fact that what is apprehended as "existent" or "non-existent" is, when grasped as it truly is, the opposite of that [apprehension].

Now, if the nihilists (*vaināśika*) intend that prior to origination there was merely the absence of existence, how can they speak of a connection with time—saying "this existed prior to origination"—as well as a connection with number, and the state of being "without a second"? How can these things be predicated of them?
"Certainly, it is not tenable for those who accept only the existence and non-existence [of things].
Even the acceptance of mere non-existence is untenable, because an accepter cannot logically exist without an act of accepting.
If you argue that the accepter is accepted only now and did not exist prior to the production [of the object], we say no."

Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the non-existence of that which exists prior to its production, the conceptualization that "prior to production it was simply non-existent" is untenable. [Objection: But how, if the form of a thing (*vastvākṛti*) is the meaning of a word, can the meanings of the words and the sentence in the statement "In the beginning, this was non-existent, one only, without a second" be established? And if those are not established, would this sentence not result in being invalid (*apramāṇa*)? [Response: This is not so. For the word *asan* ("non-existent") denotes the absence of the manifestation of the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) of an entity; it does not denote absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: "Prior to creation, this world existed in a state of equilibrium (*sāmyāvasthā*), devoid of distinctions such as name and form (*nāmarūpa-vibhāga*). Thus, the meaning of the words and the sentence is perfectly consistent. Furthermore, since the term *asan* is used here in the sense of "unmanifested" (*avyakta*), it does not follow that the sentence is invalid. Just as the term *san* ("existent") is applied to a jar when it is manifested through its specific characteristics, yet is not applied when it is unmanifested, so too the term *asan* is applied to the world when it is unmanifested, but not when it is manifested. Consequently, the objection that the sentence would be invalid is refuted. Moreover, because the term *asan* is used in the sense of "unmanifested," the subsequent statement—"From that, through the exercise of *tapas*, the *sat* was produced"—is also logically consistent. For if the world were absolutely non-existent, it could never be produced from that [source], just as a rabbit's horn cannot be produced. Therefore, the objection regarding the lack of validity is likewise refuted. Furthermore, the term *asan* is used in the sense of "unmanifested" even in the case of things like a jar, which are indeed existent; thus, the statement "prior to production it was non-existent" is not contradictory. Indeed, the term *asan* is applied to a jar when it is unmanifested, but not when it is manifested. Therefore, the objection that the sentence would be invalid is refuted. Finally, because the term *asan* is used in the sense of "unmanifested," the subsequent statement—"From that, through the exercise of *tapas*, the *sat* was produced"—is also logically consistent. For if the world were absolutely non-existent, it could never be
This is not a fault,
because the sentence is intended to exclude the apprehension of existence (*sat*).
To begin with, this word "existent" (*sat*) denotes the universal form (*ākṛti*) of existence.

The two phrases "one only, without a second" (*ekamevādvitīyam*) and "this was" (*idamāsīt*) are in grammatical apposition with the word *sat* (Being). Likewise, the negative particle (*nañ*) employed in the sentence concerning *sat* depends entirely upon that very sentence concerning *sat*, producing a cognition whose object is the meaning of the sentence concerning *sat*, characterized as: "This Being was one only, without a second."
Therefore, it turns [the mind] away from the meaning of the existent, just as one mounted on a horse, while holding onto the horse, turns the horse away from objects directed toward it;
it does not, however, assert the non-existence of the existent itself.
Consequently, this statement beginning with "it is indeed non-existent" is employed for the purpose of removing the person's erroneous apprehension.

For once the erroneous apprehension has been shown, it can then be turned away; thus, because the sentence beginning with "non-existent" (asat) possesses purposefulness, its status as revealed scripture (*śrautatva*) and its authority (*prāmāṇya*) are established, and so there is no fault.
Therefore, from the non-existent—which is of the nature of the total absence of everything—the existent (*sat*), which is real, was born, i.e., it arose.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
"But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? he said. "How could being be born from non-being? Verily, my dear, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second."
Having shown this contrary apprehension as the position of the great nihilists (mahāvaināśika), [the text] refutes it:

"But from what source of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), my dear, could it be so—that 'being is born from non-being'? How could it be? The meaning is that it is not possible from any source of valid knowledge whatsoever."
As for their claim that a sprout is seen to arise from the very non-existence of the seed upon its destruction, that too contradicts their own tenets.
How so?
For those very parts of the seed that are characterized by the seed’s specific configuration persist even in the sprout; it is not through the destruction of those parts that the sprout is produced.

Furthermore, that which is the seed's shape and configuration is not accepted by the Nihilists (*vaināśika*) as being a real entity existing apart from the parts of the seed, such that it would be destroyed upon the arising of the sprout.
If, on the other hand, it exists as a real entity distinct from its parts, then there is a contradiction with their own tenets.
If it is argued that the form of the seed's configuration, accepted [only] conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), is what is destroyed; [then...]
What is this so-called "conventional reality" (saṃvṛti)? Is it a non-entity (abhāva) or an entity (bhāva)?
If it is a non-entity, there is no example [to support it].
If it is an entity, even so, the sprout does not arise from a non-entity; for the sprout arises from the parts of the seed.
If it is argued that the parts are also destroyed, we say no;
for the same [objection] applies to their parts.
Just as for the Nihilists (vaināśika) there is no whole (avayavin) consisting of the form and configuration of a seed, so too there are no parts; thus, for them as well, destruction is untenable.

Since the seeds themselves have subtle parts, and those parts have other even subtler parts, this regressus ad infinitum would never cease; thus, the destruction of everything would be impossible. Furthermore, because the cognition of existence persists, existence itself does not cease. Therefore, for those who maintain that existence [is real], the production of existence from existence alone will be established. However, for those who maintain non-existence, there is no example for the production of existence from non-existence.
The production of a jar from a lump of clay is observed by proponents of existence (*sadvādins*), because [the jar] exists when that [clay] exists and does not exist when it is absent.
If the jar were produced from non-existence alone, one seeking a jar would not take up a lump of clay;
furthermore, the application of the word and the cognition "non-existence" would follow [illogically] in relation to the jar and so forth.
But this is not the case; therefore, there is no arising of existence from non-existence.

As for what they say—that the cognition of clay is the cause of the cognition of a jar, and thus the cognition of clay is called the cause of the cognition of a jar, but that in ultimate reality neither clay nor jar exists—this too [is untenable], because the existing cognition of clay [would have to produce] an existing [cognition].
If it is argued that "the cause of the cognition of a jar" does not imply the arising of existence from non-existence—

because there is merely a sequence of cause and effect (nimitta-naimittika) between the cognition of clay and the cognition of a jar, rather than a relationship of material cause and product (kārya-kāraṇatva)— we say no;
for when a mere succession of cognitions is perceived, the nihilists (vaināśikas) lack any external example [to support their position].
"Therefore, my dear, how indeed could it be so? he said. "How?—in what manner could existence (sat) be born from non-existence (asat)?

The intention is that there is no example whatsoever for the production of existence from non-existence. Having thus refuted the position of the proponent of non-existence, he concludes by establishing his own position: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed existence alone."

But surely, even for the proponent of existence (*sadvādin*), there is no example whatsoever for the claim that "from the existent, the existent arises," since one does not observe the production of another jar from [the material of] a jar.
True; it is indeed so that from the existent another existent is not produced. Rather, the existent itself persists in a different configuration.
Just as a snake becomes coiled,
and just as clay undergoes various transformations such as powder, a lump, a jar, or shards—
if that is so, since everything exists in every state, how can it be said that "this was not" prior to its origination?
It is said:

"But have you not heard that the restriction 'only Being' (sadeva) applies to that which is denoted by the word 'this' (idam), namely the effect? In that case, it follows that prior to its origination, that which is denoted by the word 'this' was simply non-existent (asat), and that now this has come into being. No.
This is because only "Being" (sat) persists as the object of the word and cognition "this," just as clay alone persists as the object of the words and cognitions "lump," "jar," and so forth.

Now, an objection may be raised: just as the substance clay exists, so too do the lump, the jar, and the like; therefore, since the cognition of the effect is an object of a cognition distinct from the cognition of "Being," the collection of effects must be a different entity from "Being," just as a cow is a different entity from a horse.
[We reply: No, because although the lump, the jar, and so forth mutually exclude one another, they do not deviate from their nature as clay.
Although a jar deviates from a lump, and a lump likewise deviates from a jar, they do not deviate from the nature of clay; therefore, both the lump and the jar are merely clay.
(A cow deviates from a horse, or a horse deviates from a cow.
Therefore, jars and the like are merely the particular configurations of clay and other substances.
Thus, it is logical that prior to its production, all this is merely the configuration of the existent;
for it is "only the existent," since the mere configuration of the modification is a matter of verbal designation.

[Objection: But how can a modification or structural arrangement be possible for that which is partless, given such scriptural passages as: "Being is without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless; for the divine Person is formless, both within and without, and unborn"?
[Reply: This is not a fault.

Because modifications in the form of effects arise from the real parts—just as the forms of snakes and the like are conceptually constructed from the constituent parts of a rope—and because of the scriptural teaching:
"The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth; so too, Being alone is the truth.
Thus, this [world] is indeed one without a second in the ultimate sense, even at the time when it is perceived as "this" (the world).
It thought: "May I be many; may I procreate.
It emitted heat.
That heat (tejas) thought:
"May I become many; may I procreate.
It emitted the waters (āpas).
Therefore, whenever a person grieves or perspires, from that very heat water is produced.
That [Being] "saw," that is, performed the act of seeing or perceiving. And for this reason, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by the Sāṃkhyas is not the cause of the world;
for it is admitted that the *pradhāna* is insentient.
But this [Brahman] possesses consciousness because it is a seer. To explain how it "saw," he says: "May I become many, may I be abundant, may I be born forth, may I be produced in abundance.
This is just as clay becomes a jar or similar forms, or as a rope appears in the form of a snake through mental construction.
"In that case, everything that is perceived is indeed non-existent, like a rope perceived in the form of a snake and so forth through mental construction.
[Objection: Then everything that is perceived is indeed non-existent, like a rope perceived in the form of a snake and so forth. [Reply: No;
because it is precisely the existent that is perceived otherwise through the distinction of duality, we say that nothing whatsoever is non-existent anywhere."

Just as logicians, having imagined another distinct entity apart from what exists, then assert its non-existence prior to its arising and after its destruction, we never at any time or in any place imagine any other designation or designated object apart from what exists.
Indeed, everything that is designated and everything that is designated as something else is [ultimately] Being alone.

Just as a rope is designated as a "snake" by one who perceives it through the cognition of a snake, or as a lump, a jar, and so forth are designated by the words "lump," "jar," and so on in the world through the cognition of things other than clay; and just as for those who perceive the distinction from the rope, the designation and cognition of a "snake" cease, and for those who perceive the distinction from clay, the words and cognitions of "jar" and so forth cease—in the same way, for those who perceive the distinction from Being, the words and cognitions of other modifications cease.
They turn back;
for from that [Brahman] words turn back,
together with the mind, having failed to reach it— according to such scriptural passages as, "It is unexpressed, it is without abode," and so forth.
Having reflected thus, it emitted fire; having created fire.

Now, an objection is raised: since another Vedic text states, "From this very Self, space was produced," and from space came air, and from that thirdly came fire—how is it that here fire is said to be created first from that [Self], and yet space is also said to arise from that same source? This appears contradictory.
This is not a fault; for it is logical to conceive that after the creation of space and air, that Being created fire.

Alternatively, the sequence of creation is not intended here; rather, what is intended is that all this is an effect pre-existent in its cause (satkārya), and therefore Being alone is one and without a second.
This is because of the examples of clay and so forth;
or else, since the threefold compounding (trivṛtkaraṇa) is intended to be explained, [the text] describes the creation of fire, water, and food alone.
"Fire" is well-known in the world as that which burns, cooks, illuminates, and is red.
That Being, having emitted that fire which was established in the form of fire, gazed upon it—the meaning is that the Being, who is Sat, gazed.
"May I become many; may I procreate," as before.
It emitted water.
Water is well known in the world as being liquid, cohesive, flowing, and white.

Since water is an effect produced from fire (*tejas*), therefore, wherever and at whatever time a person feels cold, suffers from heat, perspires, or breaks into sweat, from that very fire water is then produced.

Those waters reflected: "May we become many; may we propagate. They created food (*anna*). Therefore, wherever it rains, there food becomes most abundant; from water alone, indeed, does that edible food arise.
is born.
Those waters, as before, looked; the meaning is that the *sadas* (the sacrificial hall), existing in the form of water, looked.
"May we become many, may we become abundant, may we be born, may we come into being"—thus they thought. They created food, characterized by the earth.
Since food is made from water, therefore, in whatever region it rains, in that very place food becomes most abundant and plentiful. Thus, that edible food is produced from water alone.
Although "they created food" was previously said of the Earth, here, however, because of the qualification "food that is edible," rice, barley, and so forth are meant.
Food is heavy, stable, retentive, and black by nature—this is well known.

But surely, the act of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) is not perceived in fire and the other elements, since there is no prohibition against them killing and so forth, nor is any effect such as fear observed in them; how then can it be said that "that fire saw," and so on?
This is not a fault.

Because fire and the other elements are transformations of the causal Seer, and because they produce effects characterized by a fixed sequence as if belonging to that existent Seer, the element is said to "see," as if it were seeing fire and the rest.
[Objection: But even for the Existent (Sat), the status of being a Seer is merely figurative. [Reply: No;
since the seeing of the Existent is cognizable solely through the word [of scripture], it is not possible to assume it is figurative.
In the case of fire and the other [elements], however, it is logical to assume that the primary act of seeing is absent; therefore, it is proper to postulate that the term is used figuratively.
But could it not be inferred that even though it exists, the Pradhāna is insentient because it is a cause like clay?

Therefore, since the insentient Pradhāna exists for the sake of a sentient being and produces effects characterized by a fixed temporal sequence, one might infer that it "saw," as if it possessed sight, and thus the act of seeing is merely figurative.

Furthermore, in the world, metaphorical treatment as if something were conscious is observed even for that which is insentient, such as when one says, "The bank wishes to fall. It might be the same in the case of the *sat*. No;
for it is taught that the Self (*ātman*) is that very *sat*, since the instruction regarding the Self is given with respect to that [which is *sat*].

If it is argued that the designation of a self (*ātma-upadeśa*) is also figurative—just as in the expression "Bhadrasena is my self," where the term "self" is applied figuratively to one who is not the self because he performs all the purposes of the self—that is not so;
for there is the teaching of liberation: "For one whose resolve is fixed upon the Real and the True, thinking 'I am Being' (*sad-asmi*), the delay is only for so long.
If it is argued that even this [teaching] is figurative, [we reply: no.
For one who identifies with the *pradhāna* as the self, the proximity to liberation exists; thus, even the teaching of liberation is merely figurative.

It is just as in the world when someone set out to go to a village might say, "I have reached the village," out of consideration for his haste. This is not so, because the discourse begins with the statement: "By knowing which, that which was unknown becomes known."
When this [Brahman] is known, everything becomes known, because everything is non-different from it and because of the scriptural statement that it is "without a second.

There remains nothing else to be known—whether taught by the Śruti, or to be inferred through a logical mark (liṅga)—by which the instruction on liberation could be considered figurative. Furthermore, if one were to assume that the entire meaning of this chapter is figurative, the effort of the one who so assumes would be in vain; for the knowledge that accomplishes the human goal has already been attained through reasoning alone.
Therefore, because of the authority of the Veda, there is no abandonment of the meaning heard [in scripture];
thus, it is established that the world has an intelligent cause.
Thus ends the second section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"Of these beings, there are indeed only three origins: the egg-born, the living-born, and the soil-born."
Regarding these beings such as birds and so forth, which are indeed possessed by individual souls (*jīva*), the use of the demonstrative pronoun "these" (*eṣām*) indicates direct perception;

it does not refer to fire and the other elements, because their tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is yet to be described, and without that tripartition, a reference through direct perception would be untenable.
Furthermore, the term "divinities" (*devatā*) is applied to fire and the others in the passage: "These three divinities."
Therefore, for those beings—birds, animals, plants, and so forth—there are exactly three seeds as their causes, and no more.
What are they? It is said:
"The egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*) is that which is born from an egg; the egg-born is indeed the egg-born, such as birds and the like.
For birds, snakes, and so forth are seen to be born from birds, snakes, and so forth;
therefore, the meaning is that a bird is the seed of birds, a snake the seed of snakes, and likewise anything else born from an egg is the seed of its own kind.
Now, one might object: "That which is born from an egg is called 'egg-born' (*aṇḍaja*); therefore, it is logical that the egg itself is the seed. How can the egg-born being be called the seed?"

This would indeed be true if the Vedic revelation were dependent upon your will; however, the revelation is independent of you, since it declares that "only those born from eggs and so forth are the seeds, not the eggs and so forth.

Furthermore, it is observed that in the absence of those born from eggs and so forth, there is an absence of their respective lineages, whereas this is not the case in the absence of the eggs and so forth.
Therefore, only those born from eggs and so forth are the seeds of those born from eggs and so forth.

Likewise, "born from a living being" (*jīvaja*) means that which is born from a living being, namely the *jarāyuja* (viviparous), such as humans, cattle, and so forth. "Born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*) refers to that which sprouts; the *udbhit* is the stationary (*sthāvara*) [being], and what is born from that is *udbhijja*. Alternatively, the seed (*dhānā*) is the *udbhit*, for it is born from that; thus *udbhijja* refers to the seed of stationary beings, meaning the seed of stationary things. As for those born from sweat (*svedaja*) and born from decay (*saṃśokaja*), they are included within the categories of the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) and the sprout-born (*udbhijja*) respectively, according to their possibility.
In this way, the restriction that there are only three seeds becomes logically established.
That deity thought:
"Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate names and forms."
This very Nature, designated as *Sat* (Being), the source of fire, water, and food, was declared to be the Deity; she reflected (*aikṣata*) just as before, thinking, "May I become many.
That purpose of becoming many has not yet been accomplished; therefore, having once again undertaken that same purpose of becoming many, she reflected further.
How?
Now, [the text says]: "Come, let me enter these three deities—fire and the others—as previously described, with this living self (jīva).

By saying "with this living self," she recalls her own self as the sustainer of the vital breaths (prāṇa), which was experienced during the previous creation and is now present within her own intellect. Thus she says: "With this living self, the ātman."
By the statement "by the Self that sustains the vital breaths," it is shown that [the Self] is not distinct from one's own self, being characterized by the nature of consciousness.
Having entered [into the body],
and having acquired specific cognition through contact with the subtle elements consisting of fire, water, and earth—
"Name and form"—the meaning is: "I shall manifest name and form; I shall make them clear; I shall distinguish them such that 'this one has this name' and 'this one has this form.

Now, one might object: is it not improper for the omniscient Deity, who is beyond the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), to intentionally resolve, "I shall enter a body that is the locus of hundreds of thousands of evils and experience suffering," and then actually enter it, given her independence?
It is true that this would not be logical if she had intended, "I shall enter by my own unmodified form and experience suffering," for it was not so.
How then?
Because of the scriptural statement: "Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman)."
Indeed, what is called the *jīva* is merely a reflection of the Deity.

It is produced by the contact with the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, as well as the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), like the reflection of a person entering a mirror, or like that of the sun and other luminaries in water and similar surfaces.

This appearance of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*) arising from the connection of the Deity—who possesses inconceivable and infinite power—with the intellect and the rest, is caused by the failure to grasp the distinction from the true nature of the Deity; it is the cause of various conceptual cognitions such as "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded."
Because the deity has entered [the body] merely as a reflection in the form of the individual soul (jīva), it is not itself connected with the physical experiences of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Just as a person, the sun, and others, when reflected merely as images in a mirror, water, and so on, are not affected by the defects of the mirror, the water, or the like, so too is the deity.
As the sun, though the eye of the entire world, is not tainted by external ocular defects.
So too, the one inner self of all beings, being external [to them], is not tainted by the suffering of the world.
And in the Vājasaneyaka it is said: "He is omnipresent and eternal like space.

But [one might object]: if the individual soul (jīva) were merely a shadow, it would follow that it is entirely false, and consequently, its existence in the next world, this world, and so forth, would also be false.
This is not a fault.
Because it is admitted that [the world] is real by virtue of having Being (sat) as its essence;
and the entire collection of modifications, such as name and form, is real only through that essence of Being, while in itself it is indeed unreal, since it has been stated:
"The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."

The same applies to the individual soul (jīva) as well; for it is a well-established principle that "the offering corresponds to the spirit. Therefore, since all worldly transactions and all modifications are real in their nature as Being (sat), yet unreal insofar as they are other than Being, no fault can be raised here by the logicians.
Thus, it can be said that the various dualistic doctrines, which are mutually contradictory, are merely the conceptual constructions of one's own intellect and do not abide in reality.
"Let me make each of these threefold.
This very deity, having entered these three deities by means of this very living self (jīva-ātman), differentiated names and forms.

Having thus entered into these three deities, and having perceived, "I shall manifest name and form, which exist as seeds within my own self in an undifferentiated state," [He thought], "And I shall make each one of these three deities threefold.

In making each one threefold, there is a predominance of each one individually, while the other two remain subordinate; for otherwise, there would be only a single threefold-making, like that of a rope, rather than a distinct threefold-making for each of the three.
For in this way, fire, water, and food would each obtain their own distinct names and designations, such as "this is fire," "these are waters," and "this is food.
And when distinct names and designations are obtained, the purpose is the successful accomplishment of the correct practical usage regarding these deities.
Having observed this, that very deity entered into these three deities by means of this very living self (jīva), as if into the interior of the solar orb.

Having entered the Vairāja body and having entered the bodies of the gods and others first, he manifested names and forms according to his own resolve, thinking: "This one has such a name, and this one has such a form."
Of these, he made each one threefold.
"Now, my dear, learn from me how each one of these three divinities becomes threefold."

And of those deities, the deity made each one threefold by way of their qualities and primary substances. Let alone the fact that these aggregates of deities, once differentiated by name and form, consist of the three elements of fire, water, and food;
rather, listen as I explain how each of these three deities becomes threefold in relation to these aggregates—understand this from my words and grasp it through examples.
Thus ends the third section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat;
that which is white is the form of water."
That which is black is of the food.
The "fire-ness" of fire has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. "The three forms"—this alone is the truth.

An illustration of that very tripartition of the deities which was previously mentioned is now stated; for an "illustration" (udāharaṇa) is so called because it is cited for the purpose of establishing [the principle] in a single instance. This is what is said: "That which [is] of Agni, consisting of the threefold [deities]..."
Know that whatever is black is the very form of that fire, and it is the form of food and of the earth when they have not yet been differentiated into the three forms.
This being so, that notion of "fire" which you held regarding this [earth] as distinct from the three forms— that fire-nature of the fire has now departed,
meaning that the cognition of fire and the word "fire" which existed prior to the discernment of the three forms have both vanished.

Just as a crystal, when perceived in conjunction with a visible red substrate, becomes the cause for the word and the cognition "this is a ruby," yet those words and cognitions of a "ruby" cease once there is a discerning knowledge of the distinction between the substrate and the crystal for one who knows that distinction— so it is in this case.

Now, one might object: "What is achieved here by this conceptualization of intellect and words? It is more reasonable to say that before the distinction of the three forms was made, there was only fire, and that the 'fire-ness' of that fire departed upon the distinction of its red and other forms—just as a cloth ceases to exist when the threads are pulled away.
This is not so; for fire is merely intellect and word, since it says: 'Fire is a modification originating in speech, a mere name'; the meaning is that it is name-only."
Therefore, even the cognition of fire is merely false.
What, then, is true therein? It is precisely these three forms that are true; the point of the determination is that there is not even an atom's worth of truth existing apart from these three forms.
That which is the red form of the sun is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The nature of the sun has departed from the sun;
it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone are real.
That which is the red form of the moon is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The moonhood of the moon has departed;
it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.
That which is the red form of lightning is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The lightning-nature of lightning has departed;
it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.

Likewise, the passage beginning "Whatever of the sun, whatever of the moon, whatever of lightning" and so forth is the same [as before]. Now, one might object: after saying, "My dear, understand how each of these three deities becomes threefold," the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) was shown by means of four examples—fire and the others—all of which concern fire alone (*tejas*), and no example was given for food (*anna*) and water (*ap*).
This was shown in the section on triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).
This is not a fault;
for the Śruti considers that even the examples concerning water and food are to be understood in exactly this same way.

The example of fire (*tejas*) is for the purpose of illustration; it is suitable because it possesses color-form (*rūpavattva*) and its meaning is clear. Smell (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*) are not cited as examples because they cannot exist in all three [of the elements].
For smell and taste do not exist in fire.
Touch and sound are not cited as examples because they cannot be shown separately.

If the entire world has been made tripartite, then—just as in the case of fire and so forth—the three forms alone are real; thus, just as the "fire-ness" of fire has departed, the "world-ness" of the world has departed.

Likewise, since food is a shoot of water, "water" alone is the truth, and food is merely a modification based on speech; similarly, since water is a shoot of fire, its status as a mere modification based on speech applies, and "fire" alone is the truth;
and since fire is a shoot of Being, its status as a mere modification based on speech applies, and "Being" alone is the truth—this is the meaning intended to be expressed.
But surely, air and space remain unaccounted for among fire and the other elements because they are not included therein;

likewise, smell, taste, sound, and touch also remain unaccounted for. Thus, how can everything else become known by knowing the "Being" (sat), or else some other method must be stated for its knowledge?
This is not a fault.
Because everything is perceived within a substance possessing form:

first, since both sound and touch are apprehended in luminous matter (tejas) which possesses form, the existence of wind (vāyu) and space (antarikṣa)—which possess the qualities of touch and sound respectively—is inferred therein.
Likewise, taste and smell are included within water and earth, which possess form.

By demonstrating the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of the three material elements—fire, water, and food—the Śruti considers everything that is included within them to be known as possessing the three forms, because it is a modification (*vikāra*) thereof.
For there is no apprehension of air or ether, nor of their qualities of smell or taste, apart from a material substance that possesses form.
Alternatively, the Śruti intends the tripartition even of those things that possess form merely for the sake of illustration.

Just as it is true that when the tripartite [elements] are formed there are only three forms, so too is the same principle applicable to the fivefold division (pañcīkaraṇa). Therefore, because everything is a modification of Being (sat), by knowing Being, all this becomes known; thus it is established that Being alone is the one, non-dual reality.
Thus, it is well said that when that one thing exists and is known, all this becomes known.
Knowing this, indeed, those of old—the great householders and great Vedic scholars—used to say:
"Nowadays, no one will be able to cite anything to us that has not been heard, not thought, or not understood.
For they had gained such knowledge from these [teachers].
Knowing this, the ancient great householders (mahāśāla) and great śroṇiyas who have passed away said: "Indeed, they say.

What did they say? [The text] says: "In our family, today as now, no one at all—among those possessing the aforementioned knowledge—will utter anything unheard, unthought, or unknown; no one will so utter it.
The intention is that because those born in our family possess true knowledge, everything is indeed known to them.

Furthermore, as to how they came to know everything, he says: because they understood that from these three forms—red and the others—which had been made tripartite and were thus known, all else that remained was exactly like this, they became all-knowing; the meaning is that by virtue of that knowledge, they were indeed omniscient.
Or rather, "they understood from these" means that once Agni and the other examples were understood, they understood everything else.
"That which appeared as if red—that they recognized as the form of fire (tejas).
That which appeared as if white—that they recognized as the form of water (āpas). That which appeared as if black—that they recognized as the form of food (anna)."
Or rather, they understood that what had seemed as if unknown was actually the combination of these very deities.
"Now, my dear, learn from me how each one of these three deities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold."
How so?

When that which was being doubted as having another form—such as the form of a pigeon—was perceived by those former knowers of Brahman as if it were red, they understood that to be the form of fire (*tejas*); likewise, that which was perceived as if white, they understood that to be the form of water (*āpas*).

They understood that whatever form was perceived as if black belonged to food; likewise, they understood that even that which was extremely difficult to discern, which was as if unknown and not specifically grasped, was simply the combination, the aggregate, of these same three deities.

Thus, first of all, the external object has been understood, like fire and the others; now, my dear, listen as I explain how these three aforementioned deities, having reached the person—the aggregate of causes and effects characterized by the head, feet, and so forth—and being utilized by that person, each become threefold within the person.
Having said this, he spoke:
Thus ends the fourth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts.
Its coarsest constituent becomes feces.
That which is the middle is the flesh;
that which is the subtlest is the mind.
Food that is eaten and consumed is divided into three parts by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) as it is being cooked.

How so? Of that food which is thus divided into three parts, the coarsest element—the most substantial portion of the divided substance—becomes feces. That which is the middle portion of the food's constituent elements, having been transformed through the sequence of chyle (*rasa*) and so forth, becomes flesh. That which is the subtlest... [text ends]

That most subtle element (anu-tamaḥ), having reached the heart and entered the subtle channels known as hitā, brings about the stability of the aggregate of instruments such as speech; transforming into the form of the mind, it effects the accumulation of the mind.
Consequently, because the mind is accumulated from food, it is understood to be merely material (bhautika) and not eternal or partless, as defined in the Vaiśeṣika system.

Furthermore, as for what will be stated—that "the mind is its divine eye"—that too is not with reference to eternality; rather, it is with reference to its pervasiveness over the objects of all the senses, such as those that are subtle, concealed, or distant. And we shall explain that even the eternality [of the mind] relative to the objects of the other senses is merely relative, in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "Being, one, without a second."
The water that is drunk becomes divided into three parts:
its grossest constituent becomes urine;
its middle constituent becomes blood.
That which is the smallest is the vital breath (prāṇa).

Likewise, the water that is drunk is divided into three parts: its coarsest constituent becomes urine; its middle constituent becomes blood; and its subtlest constituent becomes the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
For it will be said: "The vital breath consists of water; it will not be cut off for one who drinks."
The consumed fire is divided into three parts:
its grossest constituent becomes bone;
its middling constituent becomes marrow.
That which is most minute is speech.
Likewise, the fire [element] that consumes and digests the oil, ghee, and so forth eaten [by one] is divided threefold: its coarsest constituent becomes bone;
its middle constituent is the marrow, the oily substance within the bone;
and its subtlest constituent is speech.
For it is well known in the world that by consuming oil, clarified butter, and other such substances, one's speech becomes clear and capable of expression.
"For, my dear, the mind consists of food;
the vital breath consists of water;
and speech consists of fire."
"May the Blessed One inform me further," [he said].
"So be it, Soma," he replied.
Since this is so—verily, my dear, the mind consists of food, the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire—one might object:

"But surely mice and other creatures that eat only food possess both speech and vital breath; likewise, sea creatures such as fish and crocodiles that consume only water possess both intelligence and speech; and even those that drink only oil possess vital breath."
And if that [subtle body] were to be inferred, how could it be said, "For, my dear, the mind consists of food," and so forth?
This is not a fault,
because everything has been made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta), and thus everything is possible everywhere.

"For no one eats food that has not been made tripartite, nor are waters drunk that have not been made tripartite, nor does anyone eat fire that has not been made tripartite"—thus, the eloquence and possession of breath by food-eaters such as mice and others is not contradictory. Having been thus instructed, Śvetaketu said: "Venerable sir, please explain to me further once more—by means of an illustration—how 'my dear, the mind consists of food,' and so forth; for even now, this matter is not yet fully understood by me."
A correct certainty has arisen:

since food, water, and oil, when consumed, augment the mind, vital breath, and speech within a single body—which is indistinguishable in its nature as consisting of fire and water—by way of their subtlest constituent elements (*aṇiṣṭhadhātu*) without overstepping their own respective natures, this is difficult to discern; it is with this intention that he says, "Therefore, even more," and so forth.
To him who had spoken thus, the father said, "So be it; yes, Soma. Listen here to an illustration regarding this matter which you ask about, so that it may be understood."
Thus ends the fifth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"My dear, when curd is being churned, that subtle essence which rises upward becomes ghee."

O dear one, that subtle essence, the atomic portion, of the curd being churned rises upward; having gathered together, it goes upward in the form of fresh butter, and that becomes clarified butter (ghṛta).
In the very same way, my dear, when food is eaten, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward;
it becomes the mind.

Just as in this illustration, my dear, so indeed it is with food—rice and the like—when it is being eaten and consumed, and is churned by the digestive fire in the stomach together with the vital air (vāyu) as if by a churning-stick; that subtle essence which rises upward becomes the mind (*manas*).
This means that, having come together with the constituents of the mind, it accumulates the mind.
My dear, when water is being drunk, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward;
it becomes breath.
"In the same way, my dear, when water is being drunk, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward and becomes the vital breath."
Of the fire, my dear, when it is being consumed, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward;
that becomes speech.
In the same way, my dear, when fire is consumed, its subtlest essence rises upward and becomes speech.
"For, my dear, the mind consists of food;
breath consists of water;
and speech consists of fire."
"May the Blessed One inform me further," [he said].
"So be it, Soma," he replied.
"The mind, my dear, consists of food; breath consists of water; and speech consists of fire"—the intention [of the teacher] is that what I have said is indeed correct.
Therefore, let all this be so regarding water and fire;

however, as for the statement that "the mind consists of food," I have not yet attained absolute certainty. Therefore, may the venerable sir please explain further to me, by means of an illustration, how the mind consists of food.
"So be it, my dear," the father said.
Thus ends the sixth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"O gentle son, a person consists of sixteen parts.
Do not eat for fifteen days."
"Drink water at will;
for the vital breath consists of water, and it will not fail one who drinks."

Of the food that has been eaten, that which is the subtlest constituent (dhātu) deposited its power in the mind; this power of the mind, nourished by food, is intended to be designated as the "parts" (kalās) of the person after being divided sixteenfold.
Endowed with that power of the mind—nourished by food and divided sixteenfold—the aggregate characterized as the body and the instruments [of action] becomes possessed of it.

The body qualified by the living soul (jīva) is called the "Person" (puruṣa) consisting of sixteen parts; for when this [food] exists, the person becomes a seer, a hearer, a thinker, a knower, an agent, and a cognizer, capable of all actions, whereas when it diminishes, there is a loss of capacity.
And he will say later: "Then one is a seer of food," and so forth.
The efficacy of every instrument of action is produced by the mind alone;
for in the world, those endowed with mental power are seen to be strong,
and some even subsist on meditation because food is the very essence of all things.

Therefore, the mental vigor produced by food constitutes sixteen parts for this person; he is this "sixteen-part person" (*ṣoḍaśakalaḥ puruṣaḥ*). If you wish to perceive this directly, do not eat for fifteen days—do not perform the act of eating.

However, drink water according to your desire, because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of one who does not drink water will be severed, will undergo destruction, since we have already stated that the vital breath consists of water and is a transformation of water.
For an effect is not able to remain without falling away without the support of its own cause.
He did not appear for fifteen days; then he approached him and said, "Sir, what shall I recite? [The father replied:
"The Ṛg-verses, my dear, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants."
He said, "Sir, they do not indeed occur to me."

Having heard this, desiring to perceive for himself that the mind consists of food, he did not eat for fifteen days. Then, on the sixteenth day, he approached his father; having approached him, he said, "Sir, what shall I recite? The other replied, "O gentle son, recite the Ṛg verses, the Yajus formulas, and the Sāman chants."
Thus addressed by his father, he said: "No, indeed; it is not that deer and other such animals do not appear to me in my mind; rather, the meaning is this, O venerable sir."

He said to him: "Just as, my dear, if of a large fire kindled there were only a single ember the size of a firefly remaining, it would not burn much from that; even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts, only one part remains."
"Therefore, you do not experience the Vedas at present; eat,
and then you will understand them from me."
When he had spoken thus, his father said: "Listen to the reason why those [Vedas], the Ṛg and the others, do not manifest to you. (He said to him:

"Just as in the world, my dear, of a great fire—that is, one of vast dimension that has been kindled and built up with fuel—if a single ember, the size of a firefly, should remain or be left over once it has been extinguished, then from that ember, even slightly more than that dimension..."

"It would not burn much; even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts nourished by food, only one part remains, a single fragment left over. It would not burn much; even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts nourished by food, only one part remains. With that—now, at this time, like a spark no larger than a firefly—you do not experience the Vedas, you do not comprehend them."
And having heard my words in their entirety, you shall understand; for now, eat and rest.
He smiled;
then he approached him,
and whatever he asked him, he understood it all.
He indeed ate in that very manner; thereafter, desiring to serve his father, he approached him.

When the son had arrived, the father questioned him regarding whatever there was in the Rigveda and other branches—whether it were the textual form or the collection of meanings—and Śvetaketu understood all of that, both in terms of the meaning and the text of the Rigveda and so forth.
He said to him:
"Just as, my dear, if from a large blazing fire only a single ember the size of a firefly were left, and one were to kindle it by adding grass, it would burn much more than before."

His father said to him again: "Just as, my dear, from a great fire that has been kindled," and so on, the rest is the same: suppose a single ember, no larger than a firefly, were left over from an extinguished fire; if one were to kindle and increase it by adding grass and powder, then by means of that blazing ember, one would burn much more even than before, from its previous size.
"In this way, my dear, of your sixteen parts, one part remained.
It was replenished by food and kindled;
with it, you now experience the Vedas."
"For, my dear, the mind consists of food;
the vital breath consists of water;
and speech consists of fire."
He understood it from him—yes, he understood it.
Thus, my dear, of those sixteen parts of food which were of the nature of vital power, one part remained; it was left over when you had not eaten for fifteen days.

Just as the moon wanes during the dark fortnight, one by one, each part diminished day by day; that remaining part, however, was replenished, increased, and nourished by the food you ate, and it blazed forth.
The lengthening [of the vowel] is Vedic; "prājvalīt" means "increased.
By the food you have eaten, the *kalā* (digit) has been supplied, increased, and accumulated; it has flared up.
The lengthening is Vedic; "prājvalīt" means "flared up" or "increased."
"Prājvālīt" is an alternative reading; in that case, the meaning is that, having been kindled by him, she herself burst into flames.
By her being thus increased, you now—this very day—experience and perceive the Vedas.

Thus, through both its cessation and its persistence, the fact that the mind consists of food (*annamaya*) is established; he concludes with the words, "For the mind, my dear, consists of food," and so forth.

The intention is that just as this quality of the mind being composed of food (*annamaya*) is established for you, so too are these other points—namely, that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is composed of water (*apomaya*) and speech (*vāk*) is composed of fire (*tejomayī*)—already established.
Śvetaketu understood (*vijajñau*) this which had been told by his father, namely that the mind and the others consist of food and the rest.
The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is intended to mark the end of the section concerning the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).
Thus ends the seventh section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Uddālaka Āruṇi said to his son Śvetaketu: "My dear, learn from me the state of deep sleep.
When a person here is said to be 'sleeping,' then, my dear, he has become united with Being."
He has gone to his own;
therefore they say of him, "he sleeps," for he has gone to his own.

In that mind, the supreme deity has entered by means of the living self (*jīva-ātman*), just as a person [is seen] in a mirror, or as the sun and other luminaries [are seen] in reflections within water and the like.
That mind, consisting of food (*annamaya*), is joined with and attained through speech and breath, which consist of fire and water respectively.

Composed of that [mind] and situated in it, the living self is enabled to perform the worldly activities of thinking, seeing, hearing, and so forth; and upon the cessation of those [activities], it returns to its own nature as the deity itself.

This has been stated in another Śruti passage: "He meditates, as it were; he moves, as it were; becoming a dream with his intellect, he transcends this world"; "This very Self is Brahman, consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind," and so forth; "By means of dream, [he transcends] the bodily [self]," and so forth;
and "When breathing, he becomes what is called breath," and so forth.

Desiring to explain to his son that state of abiding in that supreme deity— who is present within one's own self— of this very person whose mind has become known as "mind," who has withdrawn from the objects of the senses by means of the pacification of the mind, Uddālaka Āruṇi indeed spoke thus to his son Śvetaketu.
"End of dream" (*svapnānta*) means the middle of a dream; it is called "dream" because of the occurrence of seeing, and its "end" (*anta*) is deep sleep (*suṣupta*).

Alternatively, "end of dream" means the true nature (*satattva*) of the dream; even in that case, by implication, it refers to deep sleep alone, according to the statement: "He has gone to his own self."

For the knowers of Brahman do not maintain that the merging of the individual soul (jīva) occurs anywhere other than in deep sleep. For just as when a mirror is removed, the reflection of a person existing in the mirror merges back into its own source— the person— so too, upon the cessation of the mind and other organs, the individual soul, which is of the nature of a reflection of consciousness, enters into the mind as the Self for the purpose of the manifestation of names and forms.
That supreme deity attains its own true self, having abandoned the state of being a living soul (jīva) known as the mind.
Therefore, it is understood that the state of deep sleep alone is what is denoted by the term "the end of dream" (svapnānta).
However, where one who is asleep sees dreams, that dream-vision is associated with pleasure and pain; for it is well known that merit and demerit are the originators of pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, it is only through the support of ignorance (*avidyā*) and desire (*kāma*) that merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*apuṇya*) can initiate their effects—namely, pleasure, pain, and the perception thereof—and not otherwise. Thus, while in the dream state, one is indeed joined with ignorance, desire, and karma—the causes of transmigratory existence—and therefore does not "merge even into its own self.

This is known from such scriptural passages as: "Unaffected by merit, unaffected by evil; for at that time he has crossed beyond all the sorrows of the heart"; and "This, verily, is his state free from desire; this is the supreme bliss," and so forth.
He says, "I shall show you your own form as a deity, entirely free from the state of being a living soul (jīvatva)," while you are in deep sleep itself.
"O gentle one (somya), understand what I am telling you regarding the end of dream (svapnānta)"—the meaning is that you should grasp it clearly and with firm attention.
It is now stated when this "end of dream" occurs.
At whatever time this name occurs for a person who is about to sleep—
it being well-known in the world that "he sleeps"—
he states that this name is figurative (*gauṇa*).

When it is said that "a person sleeps," at that time he becomes united with *sat*—the deity denoted by the word *sat*, which is the subject under discussion; he becomes joined with it, becoming one with it.

Having entered into the mind, he abandons the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) produced by contact with the mind and other faculties, and has gone back to his own true nature (*sad-rūpa*), which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, for this reason, worldly people call him "he sleeps."
For he has indeed gone back into his own self;
consequently, there occurs a cessation of the activities of the organs—which have become exhausted due to their various functions—from their respective operations.
And from scripture we learn: "Speech indeed becomes weary, the eye becomes weary," and so forth.
And thus, when speech is withdrawn, the ear is withdrawn, the mind is withdrawn—these and other instruments are swallowed up by the vital breath (prāṇa).
When the single, unwearied prāṇa awakens within the nest of the body, then the individual soul (jīva), in order to dispel its fatigue, attains its own self in the form of its deity.
It is logical that there can be no removal of fatigue except through abiding in one's own true nature; hence the well-known worldly expression: "He has gone to his own."

For it is observed in the world that those afflicted by diseases such as fever find rest when they are freed from them and established in their own self; thus, it is logical that the same should be the case here as well.
This is also supported by scriptural passages such as, "Just as a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary... and so forth.
"Just as a bird tied by a string, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down upon its very bond;
even so, my dear, that mind, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down upon the vital breath (prāṇa).
For the mind, my dear, has the vital breath as its bond."

In this regard, there is this illustration for the meaning as it has been stated: just as a bird, bound by a string held in the hand of a bird-catcher, being tethered and seeking release from its bonds, flies in every direction but, failing to find or reach any other abode or refuge for rest apart from its bonds, resorts back to the very bond itself.

In this very way, O Śaubhya, just as in this illustration, that mind—which is composed of sixteen parts, nourished by food, and determined to be the primary subject—is designated as the "mind" because the *jīva* has entered it, resides within it, and is characterized by it, just as one might refer to the occupants of a bed by the name of the bed itself (*mañcākrośana*).

This *jīva*, which has the mind as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), having fallen and gone in various directions—directions indicated by ignorance, desire, and karma, characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth—in the states of waking and dreaming, experiences them; such is the meaning.

Except for its own Self, which is called "Being" (Sat), having found no abode— that is, no place of rest— the Supreme Deity, who is called "Being," is designated as "Prāṇa," being characterized by Prāṇa, which is the support of all activities and instruments.
This is according to such scriptural passages as, "The Prāṇa of Prāṇa," and "He whose body is Prāṇa, whose form is light."

Therefore, one resorts to that deity, Prāṇa—indeed, the one called Prāṇa. For, my dear, the mind has Prāṇa as its bond; that is to say, the mind has the deity characterized by Prāṇa as its support, and the individual soul (jīva) is that which is characterized by the mind.
"Understand from me, my dear, hunger and thirst.
When a person is said to be 'hungry,' it is the waters themselves that lead away what has been eaten.
Just as one says 'cow-leader,' 'horse-leader,' or 'man-leader,' so they call water 'the leader of food' (aśanāya)."
In this regard, my dear, understand that this sprout which has sprung up cannot be without a root.

Having thus shown to his son that the true nature of the individual soul (jīva)—which is the root of the world—is established by means of the well-known term "sleeping" (svapiti), [the text] now says this, desiring to show that Being (sat) is also the root of the world through the succession of causes and effects such as food and so forth:
"Hunger and thirst. Hunger is the desire to eat; [the form] is derived by the elision of the letter *yā*.
The desire to drink is thirst; these two are hunger and thirst. Understand the true nature of hunger and thirst:
at what time does a person receive this name? What is it? It is when one desires to eat—that is, "he wishes to eat" (*aśiśiṣati*).
He explains for what reason that person receives a name at that time:
when the solid food eaten by the person is led away by the water he has drunk and, having been liquefied, is transformed into the state of chyle and so forth, then the consumed food is digested;
and thus, his name "he who desires to eat" (*aśiśiṣati*) occurs as a figurative designation.
For every living being desires to eat when the food has been digested; thus,
in this sense, it is well known that the name *aśanāyā* (hunger) is derived from its being the leader (*netṛ*) of what is eaten (*aśita*),
just as a cowherd is called *gonāya* because he leads (*nayati*) the cows (*go*).
Likewise, one who leads horses is called *aśvanāya*, meaning a horse-herder;
one who leads men is called *puruṣanāya*, such as a king or a general.
In this same way, worldly people refer to those waters as *aśanāya*, by means of the elision of the visarga.

In this regard, since it is so, understand this: this body, produced by food that has been eaten and transformed into the states of the seven fluids (*rasa*) and so forth, has emerged and arisen as a sprout (*śuṅga*), like a shoot from the seed-pod of a banyan tree; O Śaubhya, recognize this effect called the body as having arisen just like a sprout from a banyan or similar tree.

"What is to be understood in this regard? It is said: "Listen; since this thing called the body has a cause, like a sprout, it will not be rootless—that is, devoid of a root. When this was said, Śvetaketu spoke.
"Where could its root be, if not in food? In this very way, my dear, seek water as the root by means of food as the sprout; seek fire as the root by means of water as the sprout."
"O gentle one, seek the root of Being by means of the sprout that is fire.
O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support."
"If this body, together with its root, is like the sprout of a banyan tree and so forth, where might its root be?"—being thus questioned, the father said:
"Where might its root be? Nowhere other than food; food is its root"—this is the intended meaning. How so?
For food that has been eaten is liquefied by water and, being cooked by the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), is transformed into the state of nutrient-essence (rasa).
From the essence comes blood; from blood, flesh; from flesh, fat; from fat, bones; from bones, marrow; and from marrow, semen.
Likewise, food consumed by a woman is transformed through the same sequence of essence and so forth, becoming menstrual blood (lohita).

The meaning is that this sprout of the body, rooted in food, has been fully developed— growing day by day like a wall built up with lumps of clay— as it was joined with those two, semen and blood, which are products of food, and as it was being filled by the very food consumed daily. And just as the sprout of the body is thus rooted in food, O dear one, so too, by means of this sprout of food which is its effect, you must seek out and realize the root of that sprout of food, which is water.
Since water, too, possesses the nature of arising and perishing, it is indeed a sprout; therefore, my dear, by means of water as a sprout—its effect—seek its cause, fire, as the root.

Since fire, too, possesses the nature of arising and perishing, it is a sprout; therefore, my dear, by means of fire as a sprout, seek that which has Being (*sat*) as its root—the one, non-dual, ultimate reality, in which all this world is superposed through ignorance, being a mere verbal handle, a modification, a name, and thus unreal, like the collection of illusory constructs such as a snake [superposed] upon a rope.

Therefore, this is the root of this world; thus, O gentle one, all these creatures characterized as stationary and moving have "Being" (sat) as their root—that is, Being as their cause—and not only are they rooted in Being, even now, at the time of their continued existence, they have Being as their abode, meaning they have Being as their very support.
For indeed, there is no existence or stability for a jar or similar objects without depending upon clay.
Therefore, because they have Being as their subtle essence, those beings for whom Being is the abode are "beings with Being as their abode" (sadāyatanāḥ prajāḥ).

And at the end, those for whom Being is the support—that is, the resting place, the dissolution, the completion, the conclusion, and the remainder—are "those with Being as their support" (satpratiṣṭhāḥ).
Now, when a person is said to be thirsty, it is the fire itself that leads away what has been drunk.
Just as one says "ox-leader," "horse-leader," or "man-leader," so does one call that fire "water-leader" (*udanyeti*).
In this regard, my dear, recognize this very thing as the sprout that has emerged.
"This shall not be without foundation."
Now, he says that the investigation of the root of Being must be carried out by way of the door of thirst:
"When—at which time—a person has this name 'thirsts,' meaning he desires to drink. Like the expression "he wishes to eat," this too is merely a figurative name.

The waters that carry the food which has been liquefied and eaten moisten the body—the "shoot" of food—and would cause it to become flaccid due to the abundance of water, were they not dried up by heat. Furthermore, when those waters are thoroughly dried by heat and undergo transformation into the state of the body, a desire to drink arises in the person; at that time, the person is said to "thirst. This is what is being stated:
the heat itself then dries up the water and other elements that have been drunk, and leads them—that is, transforms them—into the state of blood and vital breath (prāṇa) residing within the body.
Just as [the word] "gonāya" and so forth are explained in the same way, so too does the world describe that heat as "udanya," meaning it "leads water" (*udakaṃ nayati*), hence "udanya.
The form "udanyeti" is Vedic; in that case as well, it is to be understood as before.
This very sprout called the body belongs to the waters as well, and nothing else; the rest is the same as previously stated.
"Where could its root be, if not in water? My dear, seek the root of heat by means of water as the sprout;
my dear, seek the root of Being by means of heat as the sprout."
"O gentle one, all these creatures have Being (sat) as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support.
Now, O gentle one, it has already been explained how each of these three divinities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold, threefold.

When this person departs, O gentle one, speech merges into the mind; the mind merges into the vital breath (prāṇa); the vital breath merges into heat (tejas); and heat merges into the highest divinity."
By implication, this very thing called the body is also a sprout of fire;
therefore, through the body as a sprout of water, water is understood as the root,
and through water as a sprout, fire is understood as the root.
By means of the sprout of fire, one reaches the root that is Being, as before. Thus,

having led his son to seek the root that is Being— which is the ultimate reality, free from fear, free from terror, and effortless— of this sprout of the body composed of fire, water, and food, which is a mere modification of speech, [the father] says, "I am hungry" and "I am thirsty."

By way of the well-known names, he points back to what was previously stated: that which remains to be explained here in this section—namely, how fire, water, and food, when consumed by the person, bring about the growth of the body-sprout, which is the aggregate of causes and effects, without confusion of their respective natures—that should be understood as having already been stated here.
Thus, he refers to what was said before.

Indeed, in whatever manner these three deities called fire, water, and food, having reached the person, each become threefold— that has already been stated previously in the passage beginning with, "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts," and so forth.
In that very context, it was also stated that those middle constituents (*dhātu*) of the consumed food and other elements nourish the body composed of seven constituents (*sāptadhātuka*).

It becomes flesh, it becomes blood, it becomes marrow, it becomes bone; and it has been said that those subtlest elements which build up the mind, the vital breath, speech, and the aggregate of the internal organs of the body— that becomes the mind, that becomes the vital breath,
and that becomes speech.

Now, as for this aggregate of vital breaths and organs which, when the body has fallen apart, departs from the previous body and proceeds toward another body presided over by the living self—the sequence in which it goes, he explains: "When this person, my dear, is departing—that is, dying—his speech merges into the mind; it is withdrawn into the mind.
Then his relatives say, 'He does not speak.'"
For the activity of speech is preceded by the mind, according to the Vedic scripture: "Whatever one conceives with the mind, that one speaks with speech.
When speech is withdrawn, the mind functions in the mind alone through the mere activity of thinking.

When the mind is also withdrawn, then the mind becomes merged in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as at the time of deep sleep; then those standing nearby say, "He does not know. And the vital breath, breathing upward with its external organs withdrawn into itself—as seen in the Saṃvarga-vidyā—stirring the hands and feet, cutting through the vital spots (*marman*), and emitting the breath like a fire being extinguished, is gradually withdrawn and becomes merged in heat (*tejas*).

Then his kinsmen say, "He does not move," and being in doubt as to whether he is dead or not, they touch the body; perceiving warmth in the body, they say, "The body is warm, he lives. But when even that heat, which is the sign of life, is withdrawn, then that heat subsides into the supreme deity.

Thus, when the mind has been withdrawn in this sequence and has reached its own root, the individual soul (jīva) residing therein is also withdrawn along with the withdrawal of its causal conditions, as in the state of deep sleep.
If it is withdrawn preceded by a true resolve (*satyābhisandhi*), it attains Being alone and does not rise again for the sake of another body, as one does from deep sleep and the like.

Just as in the world one who dwells in a place of fear somehow reaches a place free from fear, so it is with this [knower]. But the other, who does not know the Self, rises from that very root—as if from deep sleep—and having died, enters again into the web of bodies.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Venerable sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.

Since that which is called "Being" (sat), having arisen from the root, enters the body as the individual soul (jīva)—and this has been described as being of atomic nature (aṇimāṇubhāva)—it is the root of the world. "This is its self-nature" (aitadātmyam): that whose self (ātman) is this Being is "this-selfed"; the state of being that is "this-selfedness. By means of this self called "Being," this entire world is possessed of a self.
There is no other transmigrating self for this [world] than that;
"there is no hearer other than this" and so forth, according to another scriptural passage.
And that very Self by which all this world is possessed of a self—that cause called "Being" (sat) is the Truth, the ultimate reality.
Therefore, that very Self is the world’s direct form, its true essence, and its reality.
This is because the word "Self" (ātman), when used without a prefix, is conventionally established in the sense of the inner Self (pratyagātman), just like the word "cow" (go) and others.
Thus, having been instructed by the words, "That Being art thou, O Śvetaketu," the son said: "Venerable Sir, please explain this to me further."

What you have said is doubtful to me; namely, that every day all creatures, upon deep sleep, become merged in Being (sat), yet having become so merged, they do not know, "We have become merged in Being.
Therefore, the meaning is: please convince me by means of an illustration.
Thus addressed, the father said, "So be it, my son."
Thus ends the eighth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"Just as, my dear, bees prepare honey, bringing together the juices of trees of various kinds and reducing those juices to a single state."
Regarding what you ask—why those who have attained the *Sat* day after day do not realize, "We have become the *Sat*"—listen to an illustration on this point.

Just as in the world, my dear, honey-makers—those who make honey, namely the honey-bees—produce honey, they being intent upon it; how so? Having gathered together the juices from trees of various species, various locations, and various directions, they bring those juices to a state of unity, a single condition, by means of their honey-nature; that is, they cause them to attain the state of honey.

Just as those juices there do not obtain distinction, thinking, "I am the juice of this tree; I am the juice of that tree," even so, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know, "We are merging into Being."
Just as those juices, having attained oneness through their state as honey, do not find distinction therein— [thinking],
"I am the juice of this mango tree or of that jackfruit tree"—
for just as in the world, when many conscious beings have come together, there is an attainment of distinction [such as], "I am the son of so-and-so" or "I am the grandson of so-and-so."

And having attained that state of distinction (*viveka*), they do not become merged; for in this world, even though the juices of many kinds of trees—such as sweet, sour, bitter, and pungent—have attained oneness through their nature as honey, no distinction between their states of being sweet and so forth is perceived.
This is the intended meaning.

Just as in this illustration, in exactly the same way, my dear, all these creatures, day after day, having attained Being (*sat*) at the time of deep sleep, as well as at death and cosmic dissolution, do not know, they do not discern, [that they have attained] Being.
"We have attained [it]," or "We have attained [it]."
