Whatever they become here—whether a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, an insect, a moth, a gadfly, or a mosquito—they become that very thing.
And because they thus attain Being even while remaining ignorant of the true nature of the Self as Being,

therefore, whatever species— such as that of a tiger or the like— they have entered in this world due to the cause of their past actions, thinking "I am a tiger," "I am a lion," and so forth, they remain marked by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those actions and cognitions; and thus, even though they have entered into Being, they continue to exist in that very state.

They come into existence again and again; having returned to being, they become a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, an insect, a moth, a gadfly, or a mosquito—whatever they were previously in this world, that is what they become again. The meaning is that even for a transmigrating creature separated by millions of billions of ages, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) previously cultivated do not perish.
For it is stated in another scriptural passage: "The births [of beings] correspond to their respective wisdom."
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.
Those creatures which, having entered into that [state], manifest again;

whereas others than these, who are intent upon the True Reality (sat-satya-ātman) and enter the subtle state of the True Self (sad-ātmānaṃ), do not return—this "subtle one" (aṇiman) and so forth has already been explained.
Just as in the world, a person who has slept in his own house, having risen and gone to another village, knows, "I have come from my own house," even so...
When [Nārada] said, "Please explain further to me why the consciousness of living beings does not arise as 'I have come from Being,'" his father replied, "So be it, my dear."
Thus ends the ninth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"My dear, these rivers flow eastward from the front and westward from the back;
they go from the ocean into the very ocean."
He becomes just like the ocean;
just as those [rivers] do not know there, "I am this one," or "I am that one."
Listen to an illustration in this regard: my dear, just as these rivers such as the Gaṅgā flow toward the eastern direction, being directed eastward;

and those such as the Sindhu flow toward the western direction, going westward—these, having been drawn up from the ocean, the reservoir of waters, by clouds and fallen again in the form of rain, take on the form of rivers like the Gaṅgā and once more enter the very same ocean, the reservoir of waters. So it is.

They become just like the ocean; just as those rivers, having attained oneness with the nature of the ocean in that ocean, do not know, they do not perceive: "I am the Gaṅgā," "I am the Yamunā," or "I am the Mahī."
In just this way, my dear, all these creatures, having come from Being, do not know that they are coming from Being.
Whatever they may be here—a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito—that they become, so they return.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.

In this very way, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know [their origin]; therefore, having come from Being, they do not know, "We are coming from Being," or "We have come.
Their case here is the same as that of the tiger and so forth [in the previous illustration].
It is seen in the world that waves, ripples, foam, bubbles, and the like, having arisen in water, vanish again, returning to that very state.

"But as for the living beings, even though they daily go toward that causal state of atomic subtlety during deep sleep, death, and cosmic dissolution, they do not perish—please, revered sir, explain this further to me by means of an illustration.
"So be it, my son," said the father.
Thus ends the tenth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

"My dear, if one were to strike this great tree at its root, it would continue to exude sap while living; if one were to strike it in the middle, it would continue to exude sap while living; if one were to strike it at the top, it would continue to exude sap while living.
Pervaded throughout by this living self (ātman), it stands drinking deeply and rejoicing."
"Listen to an illustration of this, my dear," [the father said], pointing to a tree standing before him—a large tree possessed of many branches—and continued:
"If someone were to strike it at its root with an axe or similar weapon, it would not wither from that single blow alone; rather, while still living, its sap would flow.
Likewise, if one were to strike it in the middle, it would flow while living; likewise, if one were to strike it at the top, it would flow while living. This is that [tree]."
Now this tree, pervaded and permeated by the living self, stands drinking deeply— drinking excessively water and drawing up terrestrial juices through its roots— rejoicing and attaining delight.
When the living soul leaves one branch of this tree, that branch withers; when it leaves a second, that branch withers;
when it leaves a third, that branch withers.
Everyone abandons everything; everyone withers away.
When the living self (*jīva*) abandons— meaning it withdraws its own portion that had spread into— one of its branches that is seized by disease or struck down,
then that branch withers;
for the living self has entered the collection of the organs of speech, mind, breath, and action, and thus, upon their withdrawal, it is withdrawn.

Furthermore, that which is eaten and drunk by the living being endowed with vital breath (*jīva*) becomes sap, and by nourishing the tree-like living body in the form of sap, it serves as a sign of the existence of the *jīva*.
For the *jīva* remains in the body through what is eaten and drunk, and those things eaten and drunk follow the karma of the *jīva*.
When karma arises that causes the impairment of one limb, then the *jīva* abandons one branch; it withdraws its self from that branch.
Then, at that time, that branch withers.
The sap, which is the cause for the maintenance of life and is impelled by the karma of the living being, does not remain once the living being has withdrawn.
And upon the departure of the sap, the branch undergoes desiccation.
Likewise, when this [living being] abandons the entire tree, then the whole tree withers;

because of signs such as the tree’s exuding sap and its drying up, and because of scriptural citations regarding the analogy, it is shown that the doctrine of the Buddhists and the followers of Kaṇāda— that immobile beings are insentient— is baseless, since immobile beings possess consciousness.
"Know it to be even so, my dear," he said. "Verily, this [body] dies when abandoned by the living self (jīva); the living self does not die.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self."
That is the Truth;
that is the Self;
"That thou art, Śvetaketu."
"May the Blessed One inform me further," [he said].
"So be it, Soma," he replied.

"Just as in this illustration of the tree it was shown that the tree joined with the living soul (jīva) is said to live—being unwithered and endowed with the drinking of sap and so forth—and when deprived of it, it is said to die; even so, my dear, know this," he said. "Indeed, this body alone dies when deprived of the living soul, but the living soul does not die. And regarding the remainder of a task, one who has risen from sleep thinks, "This remaining task of mine is not yet completed."
Because one observes the attainment of meditative absorption through recollection,

and because one observes the desire for breast milk and so forth in beings as soon as they are born, it is understood that there is a recollection of the experience of drinking milk and the suffering [of not getting it] experienced in a past previous birth.
Furthermore, because Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra* are purposeful, the living self does not die.
"That which is this subtle essence," and so forth, is the same [as before].

But how can this extremely gross world, consisting of name and form such as earth and the rest, be born from that Being which is extremely subtle, whose nature is pure existence, and which is devoid of name and form? Explain this further to me by means of an illustration.
"So be it, my son," the father said.
Thus ends the eleventh section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

His father said to him, "What do you see here? Being thus addressed, he replied, "I see these very small, almost minute seeds, O Venerable One. [The father said,] "My dear child, break one of these seeds. Being thus addressed, he replied, "It is broken, O Venerable One."
"If that grain is split, what do you see when it has been split? Having been asked this, he said, "I see nothing at all, O Blessed One."
He said to him: "O Somya, that subtle essence which you do not perceive—indeed, O Somya, from this very subtle essence stands forth this great banyan tree.
Have faith, O Somya!"
He said to that son: "O gentle one, when this banyan seed-cup has been split open, you do not perceive—that is, you do not see—the minute particle of the banyan seed.

Nevertheless, O gentle one, from this very subtle, invisible seed-particle, this great banyan tree exists as its effect; having come into being, it stands tall, or rather, it rises up—this is what the word 'ud' (in *ucchabda*) signifies."
Therefore, you must supply [the ellipsis] and believe, my dear, that from the subtle Being alone this gross world— consisting of name, form, and so forth— has arisen as its effect.

Desiring to perceive for himself the matter spoken by his father, he did exactly so. His father said to him: "Tomorrow morning, my dear child, bring that salt which you placed in the water last night. Being thus addressed, wishing to retrieve that salt, he felt about in the water but did not find it; that is, he did not perceive where that salt was.
That which exists as a reality alone was merged and closely joined within the waters, though it had not yet come into being.
"Just as it has melted away.
'One should sip water from the edge of his body.
How so?"
"Salt.
"Sip water from the middle.
"How?"
"Salt," he says.
"One should sip water from the edge," he says.
"How so? he asks.
"Salt," he said. "Having thrown this away, then come back to me.
He did exactly so.
And that [process] revolves eternally.
He said to him: "In this very place, my dear, you do not indeed perceive that; it is indeed right here."

"Just as you do not perceive salt that has dissolved, yet even though that salt in its solid form is no longer grasped by the eye or by touch, it certainly exists in the water and is perceived through another means"—desiring to convince his son of this, he said, "My dear, having taken some of this water from the surface, taste it.
When the son had done so, he asked, "How is it? and the other replied, "The salt is there by its taste."

"Likewise, having taken [some] from the middle of the water, sip it; how is it? "Salty. "Likewise, having taken [some] from the bottom part, sip it; how is it? "Salty. "If it is thus, then having spat this water out and discarded it, and having sipped [fresh water], come back to me. He did exactly that; the meaning is that he came into the presence of his father after discarding the salt.
While he was saying this, [the father said: "That salt which I threw into this very water at night continues to exist eternally and perpetually; it remains present and truly persists.
To him who had spoken thus, the father said:

"Just as this salt was previously perceived through sight and touch, and though it is no longer apprehended by those two senses after dissolving in the water, it certainly still exists because it is perceived by another means, namely, the tongue."
In the very same way, right here in this very sprout— the body composed of fire, water, food, and so forth— indeed (vāva),
as indicated by the teacher's instruction and traditional recollection,
you do not perceive with your senses, nor do you behold, that which exists already as the subtle cause of the sprouts of fire, water, food, and so on, just like the minute seed of a banyan tree.
Just as in this very water, salt that was not perceived through seeing or touching was indeed found by means of the tongue;
even so, it is said, you shall perceive the root of this existing world right here by another means, like a minute grain of salt—this is the completion of the sentence.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please explain this to me further," he said.
"So be it, my dear," he replied.
The passage beginning with "He who... is the same [as before].

If this is so, then even though the root of the world cannot be perceived by the senses—just like a grain of salt—it can nevertheless be perceived through another means; and through its perception, I would have my purpose fulfilled, whereas through its non-perception, I would remain unfulfilled. Therefore, I shall strive for the perception of that very [root].
"What is the means?"—"Please, venerable sir, explain this to me further by means of an illustration."—"So be it," he said.
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"My dear, suppose a man were brought from the region of Gandhāra with his eyes bound, and he were then to be released in a place where there are no people.
Just as he might there cry out, facing east, north, south, or west—having been brought with his eyes bound and released with his eyes bound."

Just as in the world, my dear, suppose a thief who has stolen goods were to bring some man from the Gandhāra country with his eyes bound— his sight obstructed— and leave him in a forest, and then even further away in a place where people have passed by, where people no longer go, and which is utterly devoid of people; there, he would be bewildered regarding the directions.
"Eastward" means facing east, or looking toward the east;
likewise, "northward," "southward," or "westward" means one should blow, make a sound, or cry out [in that direction].
"With my eyes bound, I was brought here from Gandhāra by a thief, and with my eyes still bound, I have been released."
Just as one might untie his blindfold and tell him, "The Gandhāras are in this direction;
go in that direction," he, being learned and wise, by asking the way from village to village, would eventually reach the Gandhāras;
even so does a person who has a teacher know it here.
For him, there will be delay only so long as he is not liberated; then he shall attain [it].

While he was thus crying out, some compassionate person, having loosened and released him from his blindfold and his bonds, might say to him, "The Gandhāras are in this direction; go in that northern direction. Thus released from his bonds by the compassionate one, that wise man—being instructed and intelligent, and capable of ascertaining the path for entering the village as taught by another—would inquire from village to village.
Only one who possesses discrimination would reach Gandhāra itself, and not another of dull intellect who thirsts merely for the sight of other lands—
just as this example has been described: a man from his own country, Gandhāra, whose eyes were bound by thieves,

being undiscriminating and confused about the directions, and afflicted by hunger, thirst, and so forth, [entered] a forest filled with a multitude of various fears and calamities such as tigers and robbers.

Having been cast into [prison], afflicted by suffering and crying out, desiring liberation from his bonds, he somehow remained there until he was released by some compassionate person; having reached his own country, Gandhāra, he became peaceful and happy.

In exactly the same way, this world—which consists of fire, water, food, and so forth, and is like a forest of bodies filled with wind, bile, phlegm, blood, fat, flesh, bone, marrow, semen, worms, urine, and excrement, and which possesses many pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, and pleasure and pain—is [separated] from its true nature as the Self of the existent (Sat).

With eyes bound by the cloth of delusion, fettered by the snares of craving for numerous objects—seen and unseen—such as wife, son, friends, cattle, and kinsmen, and cast in by the thieves of merit, demerit, and the like, one thinks: "I am the son of such-and-such; these are my relatives; I am happy, I am miserable, I am foolish, I am wise, I am righteous, I have many kinsmen; I am born, I am dead, I am aged; I am a sinner; my son is dead; my wealth is lost."

"Alas! I am ruined! How shall I live? What is my refuge? What is my protection?"—thus crying out, possessed by a web of many hundreds of thousands of calamities, he somehow, through a preponderance of merit, encounters a certain person who knows the Self as the True Brahman, who is supremely compassionate, liberated from bonds, and most devoted to Brahman.
By that knower of Brahman, he is shown the path for perceiving the defects of the objects of worldly existence out of compassion, and thus becomes dispassionate.

You are not a transmigrating being separated from the objects of saṃsāra, nor do you possess attributes such as being the son of so-and-so; rather, having been released from the binding of the cloth of delusion caused by ignorance—just like the man from Gandhāra—and having attained your own true Self which is Being (*sat*), you shall become happy and at peace. It is this very meaning that the scripture expresses when it says, "The man who has a teacher knows. For such a person who possesses a teacher and whose binding of ignorance has been released, the delay is only for that long—that much time alone.
The ellipsis of the sentence is "the delay [is due to] the non-attainment of the nature of the eternal Self.
As for how long that time lasts, it is said: "until I am released"—that is, "until I shall be released," expressed here with a change of person (from first to third) by virtue of the context.

The body was originated by a certain karma; its experience [is what follows], and thus the word "atha" (then) signifies immediate succession. Now, one might object: just as the fall of the body and the attainment of Being do not occur immediately after consciousness because of the force of residual karma (*karma-śeṣa*), so too there exist karmas accumulated in previous lives whose fruits have already begun to manifest (*pravṛtta-phala*). Therefore, when the body falls for the sake of experiencing the fruits of those [karmas]...
Another body must be initiated in this [life];

and once knowledge has arisen, one continues to perform actions—whether enjoined or prohibited—for as long as one lives; therefore, for the sake of experiencing their fruits, another body must necessarily be initiated, and from that [come] further actions, and from those, yet another body; thus, knowledge would be rendered purposeless.

Because actions possess fruits, if actions were to be destroyed by knowledge, then liberation would occur at the very moment knowledge is attained; for since knowledge is the cause of attaining Being (sat), the body would fall away immediately.

Consequently, there would be an absence of a teacher, contradicting the scriptural statement, "A person who has a teacher knows [the truth]," and thus the possession of a teacher would be rendered impossible, leading to the undesirable conclusion that liberation does not result from knowledge.

Nor is it the case that knowledge has an uncertain result, like the knowledge of the means for reaching another country; for there is a logical distinction between actions whose results have already begun to manifest and those whose results have not yet begun. As for the claim that because actions whose results have not yet begun possess a certain fruit, another body must necessarily be initiated for the knower of Brahman after the fall of the current body in order to experience the fruits of those unmanifested actions—that is incorrect.
This is because of the authority of the Vedic scripture stating, "For the wise man, the delay is only so long. [Objection:
But surely the authority of other scriptural passages such as, "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action," and so forth, is also established. [Reply:
That is indeed so.
Nevertheless, there is a distinction between actions whose results have already begun to manifest (*pravṛttaphala*) and those whose results have not yet begun to manifest (*apravṛttaphala*).
How so?
Those actions whose results have already begun to manifest—by which the body of the wise person was initiated—are exhausted only through their experience.

Just as an arrow or a missile released toward a target comes to rest only when its momentum is exhausted, and not because there is no purpose for it at the very moment it pierces the target, so it is here.

However, other actions whose fruits have not yet begun—whether performed before the arising of knowledge or after it, whether currently being done or done in past lives—are burnt away by knowledge; they perish just as they do through expiatory rites, as stated in the *Atharvaṇa*: "His actions are destroyed."

Therefore, even though the knower of Brahman lacks any purpose such as living on, there must necessarily be the experience of the fruits of those actions whose momentum has already been set in motion; thus, it is rightly said that "for him, the delay is only so long [as he is not liberated]," and the objection regarding the aforementioned defect is untenable.
Furthermore, we have already stated that after the arising of knowledge, there is an absence of karma for the knower of Brahman in the passage: "He who is established in Brahman attains immortality."
And you ought to remember that.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.
The meaning of "He who," and so forth, has already been explained. [Nārada said:
"By what sequence the wise man, possessed of a teacher, attains union with Being (sat), please let the Blessed One explain that sequence once more by means of an illustration.
[Sanatkumāra replied: "So be it, Soma," he said.
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"My dear, when relatives gather around a man who is suffering from illness and say, 'Do you know me?
Do you know me?', he still knows them as long as his speech has not merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity."

O gentle one, when a person is afflicted by illness—possessing afflictions such as fever—his kinsmen and relatives surround him and wait upon him, asking, "Do you know me? Am I your father, son, or brother? This continues until the speech of that dying man merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity; this has already been explained.
Then, when his speech is merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the highest deity, then he no longer knows.

The very process of death that belongs to the transmigrating being is itself this process of the knower’s attainment of Being; this is what he says: when one has attained union with the supreme deity, with *tejas*, "then he does not know.
But the ignorant person, having risen from Being, enters again into the state previously cultivated—whether as a tiger and so forth, or as a god, a human, and so on.

The knower, however, having entered into Being-Brahman-Atman, which is illuminated by the lamp of knowledge produced by the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, does not return; such is this process of attainment of Being.

Others, however, say that [the soul] departs through the artery at the crown of the head and goes to Being (sat) by way of the sun and other gates; but that is incorrect, because movement is observed only when there is an intention directed toward place, time, means, and results.
For one who perceives the oneness of the Self with Being and whose intention is fixed on Truth, an intention toward untruth—such as place, time, means, and results—is not possible.
Because of contradiction;
and since ignorance, desire, and action—which are the causes for going—are consumed by the fire of true knowledge, going is simply impossible.
As it is said in the Atharva Veda: "For one whose desires are fulfilled and who has realized the Self, all desires vanish right here. Etc.
And because of the scriptural teaching of the analogy of the river and the ocean.
That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth;
that is the Self.
"That thou art, Śvetaketu.
"Venerable sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.
The passage beginning with "He who... and so forth is the same [as before].

If the attainment of Being (*satsampatti*) is equal for one who is dying and for one who desires liberation, then regarding the reason why the wise person, having attained Being, does not return while the ignorant person does return—let the venerable sir explain this further by means of an illustration.
"So be it," he said, "Yes."
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "O Soma, they bring a man here, seized by the hand, saying:
'He has stolen; he has committed theft. Heat the axe for him!'"
If he is the doer of that act, then by that very fact he makes himself false.
Having formed a false intention and having concealed himself with falsehood, he takes up the heated axe;
he is burned.
Then he is killed.

Listen, my dear, to this: suppose men of the king’s court bring before them for arrest or examination a man suspected of the crime of theft, having seized him by the hand with his hands bound, asking, "What has this man done? They reply, "He has stolen this person's wealth.
They then ask, "Does he deserve imprisonment merely for the act of stealing?"
"Otherwise, even if the money were returned, there would be the risk of imprisonment," they said; then they spoke again, saying, "He committed theft; he seized the wealth by means of music.
While they were speaking thus, the other denied it, saying, "I did not do that.
(They then said, "You have committed a doubtful theft regarding this wealth.")
Regarding that denial, they say, "Heat the axe for him," meaning, "Let him purify himself.

If he is the doer of that theft and yet denies it outwardly, being such a person, he thereby makes himself false—being one thing, he represents himself as otherwise. Thus, with his mind fixed on falsehood, having concealed himself within by means of untruth, he remains hidden.
Having forged a hatchet while it was red-hot, he accepts it out of delusion; he is then burned and executed by the king's men due to the fault of his own deception through falsehood.
Now, if he is not the doer of that [crime],
then by that very truth he makes himself true.
Being committed to the truth, having concealed himself with truth, he takes up the heated axe.
He is not burned; then he is liberated.
Now, if he is not the doer of that deed, then by that very truth he makes himself true;
having concealed himself within by means of that truth—the fact of his not being the thief—he takes up the heated axe.
Being one whose resolve is fixed on truth, he is not burned because of the intervention of truth, and he is released from those who falsely accused him.

Even though the contact with the surface of the hand and the heated axe is equal for both the thief and the non-thief, the one who harbors a false intention is burned, but not the one who harbors a true intention.
Just as he would not be burned there, so it is with this:
"All this has that as its self; that is the truth."
"That is the Self;
that art thou, Śvetaketu. Then he understood it from him—yes, he understood it.

Just as one who is devoted to truth (*satyābhisandha*) would not be burned or scorched when grasping a heated axe because his palm is shielded by truth, so too, although the merging into Being (*satsampatti*) at the time of the body's fall is equal for both the knower who is devoted to the Truth that is Brahman and others, the wise man, having merged into Being, does not return again to assume the bodies of tigers, gods, or other beings.

But the ignorant person, through attachment to the unreal modifications [of nature], attains again the state of a tiger or the like, or the state of a deity and so forth, according to his karma and according to his learning.

That which is the cause of liberation and bondage—whether produced by attachment to the Self or by non-attachment; that which is the root of the world, that which is the abode, and upon which all creatures are established;
that of which everything consists; and that which is unborn, immortal, fearless, auspicious, and non-dual—that is the Truth.
"That is the Self; you are that, O Śvetaketu"—this sentence, whose meaning has already been stated, is repeated more than once.

But who is this Śvetaketu, the referent of the word "you"? He is one who, having heard the instruction regarding the Self, having reflected upon it, and having understood it, [realizes] that which was unheard, unthought, and unknown.

Desiring to understand his father, he asked: "How indeed, O Venerable One, does that instruction come to pass? This very person—the hearer, the thinker, and the knower—is the Supreme Deity itself that has entered into this aggregate of causes and effects composed of fire, water, and food; for the purpose of manifesting its own name and form, it was awakened by its father through illustrations and reasons such as "That thou art," like a man reflected in a mirror, or like the sun in water and other media.
Indeed, it has been said that he "knew," meaning he realized, "I am indeed Being.
The repetition of the verb is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter.
Furthermore, what is the fruit produced here in this sixth [chapter] by means of the authority of the statement?

The result of this is the cessation of the cognition that one is authorized for agency and enjoyership with respect to the self—that which we have called the meaning denoted by the word "Thou," for the purpose of hearing and understanding it, and for the sake of the fruit of knowing what was previously unknown.
Prior to this knowledge, one thinks: "I alone shall perform such actions as the Agnihotra; I am authorized here;
and I shall enjoy the fruit of these actions both in this world and the next, or, once the actions are performed, I shall have fulfilled my duty. It is thus.

The cognition that arose within him— "I am the one authorized for agency and enjoyment"— is removed by the statement "That which is the single, non-dual root of this existent world, That Thou Art," because of their mutual contradiction.

For when this Self—non-dual and one—is known as "I am this," the cognition of duality, such as "this other thing is mine," "this must be done by me," or "having done this, I shall enjoy its fruit," is no longer tenable.
Therefore, it is logical that when the knowledge of the existent, true, non-dual Self arises, the knowledge of the individual soul (jīvātman) as a modification and as unreal ceases.

But [an objection may be raised]: in the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the notion of Being (*sat*) is intended to be superimposed upon the referent denoted by the word "thou" (*tvam*), just as the notion of Brahmā and others is superimposed upon the sun, the mind, and so forth.

And just as in the world one has the notion of Viṣṇu and others in images and so forth, it is not so that Śvetaketu is [already] the Existent itself; for if Śvetaketu were already the Existent, how could he not know himself, such that the instruction "That thou art" would be given to him? No, because this differs from the passages concerning the sun and other deities.

In passages such as "The sun is Brahman," the direct nature of Brahman is not understood because of the intervention of the word "iti" (thus). Furthermore, because the sun and so forth possess form and other qualities, and because space and the mind [are mentioned] with the intervention of the word "iti," they are not Brahman here. However, in this case, having shown the entry of Being itself into this world, the text teaches the identity of the Self with Being through the unrestricted statement, "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). [Objection: But would it not be like saying, "You are a lion," where one who possesses qualities such as prowess is addressed? [Reply: No.
Because of the teaching that "Being alone is real, one, and without a second," just like clay and so forth;
furthermore, the attainment of Being would not be taught by means of a figurative cognition with the words "for him there is delay only so long," since a figurative cognition is false.
It is not a praise, because Śvetaketu is not an object of worship— as in the case of "Thou art Indra, thou art Yama"—
nor would he be praised by being taught that he is the True (Sat).

For a king would not be worthy of praise by being called "you are a slave," nor is the partial restriction of one who exists as the Self of all appropriate— such as saying "you are a village overseer" to a ruler of a country— as in the case of "That thou art.
Furthermore, no other alternative is possible here besides the instruction that [the individual] has Being as its Self.
If it is argued that here it is merely the cognition "I am Being" that is enjoined as something to be performed, and not the unknown fact "I am Being" that is being made known, [we reply]:
even on this view, such statements as "the unheard becomes heard" would be untenable.
No; for the injunction of the cognition "I am Being" is intended as a glorification (stuti).
No, for there is the scriptural instruction: "The man who has a teacher knows; for him, the delay is only so long.

For if it were merely the thought "I am Being" that was enjoined as something to be performed, and not the fact that the referent of the word "thou" (tvam) is indeed of the nature of Being, then the instruction regarding the means of knowledge—"the man who has a teacher knows"—would have to be stated [as a requirement], just as in injunctions such as "one should perform the Agnihotra," where having a teacher is already implied by the purpose [of the rite]. But this is not the case here.
Furthermore, the introduction of a delay by saying "his delay lasts only so long" would be improper;
for even if the reality of the Self were not known, it would follow that liberation occurs simply by forming the cognition once.
Nor can it be said that when "That thou art" is spoken, the cognition produced by the authoritative statement—"I am not [this body]"—can be set aside or claimed not to have arisen.

Because all the statements of the Upaniṣads culminate solely in that [realization], just as it is impossible to say that the cognitions of the duty to perform the Agnihotra and other rites—produced by the injunctions for the Agnihotra and so forth—are either false or non-existent, so it is here.
As for what was said: "How could the Self, being existent, not know itself? [the answer follows].
This is not a fault.

Since living beings naturally perceive themselves as "I am the individual soul (jīva), the agent, and the enjoyer," distinct from the aggregate of the body and its organs, how could they possibly possess the knowledge of the True Self?
And yet, even while such a cognition of distinction exists, their cognition of agency and so forth occurs and is indeed observed.
Similarly, because one possesses the notion of a self with respect to the body and so forth, the realization of the true Self would not occur.

Therefore, it is established that this statement, "That thou art" (tattvamasi), serves solely to sublate the cognition of the individual soul (jīvātman) which is subject to modification and unreality.
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
thus ends the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
"Nārada approached Sanatkumāra, saying, 'Teach me, O Blessed One!
He said to him, 'Approach me with what you already know;
thereafter I shall tell you what lies beyond that.'"
He said:

The sixth chapter, which is primarily devoted to the instruction on the reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-tattva*), is employed solely for the purpose of determining the eternal identity of the Self (*sad-ātma-ekatva*). Since the principles (*tattva*) characterized as modifications prior to Being (*sat*) have not yet been pointed out, [the author] intends to point them out in sequence—beginning with Name (*nāman*) and ending with Breath (*prāṇa*)—and by means of them, to point out the unsurpassed reality called the Plenum (*bhūman*), just as one points out the moon by means of a branch. Thus, this [chapter]...
He begins the seventh chapter.

For, since the principles lower than Being (sat) have not yet been specified, while Being alone has been specified, someone might harbor the doubt that there is something else unknown; to prevent this, he desires to specify them.

Alternatively, like ascending a staircase, having first made known the gross and then the subtle—the objects of the intellect—he desires to specify Name and the rest so as to consecrate [the seeker] in the sovereignty (svārājya) that transcends those.

Alternatively, since the principles (tattvas) beginning with Name and so forth are progressively more distinguished, and the principle called the Infinite (bhūman) is the most excellent among them, they are presented in sequence for the purpose of praising that [Infinite].
The narrative (ākhyāyikā), however, is for the purpose of praising the higher knowledge (paravidyā).
How so?

Even Nārada, the celestial sage, though he had accomplished all that was to be done and possessed all knowledge, still grieved because he did not know the Self; how much more, then, must it be said of any other being of little learning who has not performed superior meritorious deeds and has not achieved his purpose? Alternatively, this narrative of Sanatkumāra and Nārada is commenced to demonstrate that there is no means for attaining unsurpassed bliss other than the knowledge of the Self—by means of which even Nārada, the celestial sage, despite being endowed with the power to accomplish all forms of knowledge, did not attain the highest good, and by means of which [the goal is reached] through the excellence of noble lineage, learning, conduct, and the power of spiritual means.

Having abandoned pride, he approached Sanatkumāra like an ordinary person for the sake of attaining the means to the highest good; thus, it is made known that the knowledge of the Self is the means for attaining the unsurpassed.
He indeed approached him, saying, "Teach me, O Blessed One, teach me! (adhihi adhiṣva).
"Teach me, O Venerable One"—this is the mantra.
Nārada approached Sanatkumāra, the lord of yogis and most devoted to Brahman.
To him who had approached according to the proper rule, he said: "If you know anything regarding the Self, by means of that—by proclaiming it—you should approach me; this is what I [desire]."
When he had said, "I know it; therefore, because of my knowledge of you, I shall speak further to you," Nārada replied.

"Venerable Sir, I have studied the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvana as the fourth, the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas, the Veda of the Vedas, the rites for the ancestors, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, etymology, the science of the single path, the science of the gods,

the science of sacred knowledge, the science of elemental spirits, the science of government, the science of the stars, and the science of serpents and celestial beings— this, O Venerable Sir, [I have studied]."
I meditate upon it.
"O Venerable One, I study and remember the *Ṛgveda*—that is, I am aware of it. This is because he is questioned regarding his knowledge (*vijñāna*).

Likewise, [he mentions] the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvaṇa* as the fourth *Veda* (since the word "Veda" was the subject under discussion), and the *Itihāsa-Purāṇa* as the fifth *Veda* (of the Vedas, with the *Mahābhārata* as the fifth).
For it is through grammar that the *Ṛgveda* and the others are understood by way of the division of words and so forth.
The ancestral rites according to the *Śrāddhakalpa*,
the calculation of *Kāśī*,
and the divine knowledge of portents.
*Nidhi* refers to the treatises on treasures such as those concerning Mahākāla;
*vākovākya* refers to the science of logic (*tarkaśāstra*);
and *ekāyana* refers to the science of ethics (*nītiśāstra*).
The science of the gods (*devavidyā*) is etymology (*nirukta*).

The science of Brahman—namely, that which is designated as *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma*—is the "science of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*), consisting of phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual procedure (*kalpa*), and metrics (*chandaḥ*).
The science of beings (*bhūtavidyā*) is the treatise on spirits (*bhūtatantra*).
The science of the Kṣatriyas is the Dhanurveda (the science of archery).
The science of the stars is Jyotiṣa (astronomy and astrology).

The science of the serpents and the divine beings consists of the science of serpents (Gāruḍa) and the science of divine beings, which includes knowledge of the preparation of perfumes, dancing, singing, instrumental music, the arts, and so forth.
"Venerable sir, I have studied all this."
Therefore, O Blessed One, I am indeed a knower of mantras, but not a knower of the Self.
For I have heard from those like your reverence that "the knower of the Self overcomes sorrow.
Thus, O Blessed One, I am in sorrow.
"May the Blessed One ferry me across to the further shore of sorrow.
He said to him: "Whatever you have studied here, that is indeed nothing but name."
Therefore, O Blessed One, although I know all this, I am merely a knower of mantras; the meaning is that I am one who possesses only the knowledge of the literal meaning of words.
For every word is a mere designation, and every designation is included within the mantras.
"I am merely a knower of mantras" means that I am a knower of mantras and a knower of ritual actions.
For it will be stated that "rites [are accomplished] by means of mantras. One who knows the mantras does not know the Self;
for does not the Self also manifest through the mantras? If so, how can one who knows the mantras not be a knower of the Self? No;
because the distinction between the designator and the designated is a product of transformation (vikāra).
And transformation is not accepted as being the Self.
But surely the Self is also denoted by the word "Self"? [For it is said:
"From whence words turn back."
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "where one sees nothing else," and so forth.
[Objection: How then do words such as "the Self alone is below" and "that is the Self" convey the Self?
[Response: This is not a fault.

When a word is employed with reference to the inner self (pratyagātman) as embodied, which is the locus of difference, and after the body and other such things have been rejected as being the self, that which remains—though inexpressible—is nevertheless communicated.

Just as when an army is seen together with its king, even though the king is not visible because he is concealed by umbrellas, banners, flags, and so forth, the verbal usage "the king is seen here" occurs; and when one seeks to determine the specific identity of that king, asking "Who is this king? [the answer is given].
Just as when another king who is not currently visible is excluded from view, the cognition of "king" still arises [regarding him], so it is here.

Therefore, [the ignorant person thinks]: "I am a knower of mantras and a knower of rituals; I am indeed one who knows all ritual actions and their effects, which are modifications. Thus, he is a knower of modifications (*vikāra*), meaning he is not a knower of the Self (*ātman*), nor a knower of the true nature of the Self's primordial essence (*prakṛti*). For this very reason it is said: "The person who has a teacher knows."
And because of such scriptural passages as, "From which words turn back," and so forth;

for since there certainly exists in me that heard knowledge derived from scripture (*āgama-jñāna*), by which one who knows the Self transcends—overcomes—sorrow, mental anguish, and the state of feeling one has failed to achieve one's purpose; therefore, O Blessed One, because I do not know the Self, I grieve and am constantly tormented by the conviction that I have failed to achieve my purpose—[please instruct] me, such as I am.

"May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore—the end—of this ocean of grief; may he bring about the fulfillment of my intellect through the raft of self-knowledge; may he lead me to fearlessness"—this is the meaning.

To him who had spoken thus, [the teacher] said: "Whatever indeed you have studied here—that is, whatever you have learned—the knowledge of its meaning is indicated by the act of study; that is to say, you have known it. This is merely a name."
For the Śruti declares: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."

Namely: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaṇa as the fourth; the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth among the Vedas; the Veda of Vedas; the Pitrya, Rāśi, Daiva, Nidhi, Vākovākya, Ekāyana; and the knowledge of the gods, the knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of beings, the knowledge of the Kṣatra, the knowledge of the stars, and the knowledge of serpents and divine beings.
"This is merely Name;
meditate upon Name."
Whether it be called the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, and so forth, this is merely a name;
meditate upon the name as Brahman with the thought that it is Brahman,
just as one worships an image with the thought that it is Viṣṇu.
He who meditates on "Name" as Brahman—
so far as Name extends, so far he has unlimited freedom, provided he meditates on "Name" as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than Name?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than name.
May the Blessed One explain that to me."

Now, hear what the fruit is that belongs to him who meditates upon "Name" as Brahman: as far as Name extends, as far as the range of Name reaches— in that domain of Name, he has freedom of movement at will, like a king in his own territory.
"He who meditates on name as Brahman"—this is the concluding summary.
The intention is: "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than name, something else worthy of being viewed as Brahman?
Sanatkumāra said, "Indeed, there is something greater than name. When this was said, [Nārada] replied, "If there is such a thing, may the Venerable One tell it to me."
Thus ends the first section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Speech, indeed, is greater than name.
For speech makes known the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth, and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa.

The fifth [Veda] among the Vedas, the ancestral rites, the science of numbers, the science of portents, the science of treasures, the science of argumentation, the science of etymology, the science of the gods, the science of sacred formulation (*brahman*), the science of elemental spirits, the science of royal power, the science of the lunar mansions, the science of serpents and celestial beings;
and heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire, gods and humans, cattle and birds.

And [speech makes known] grasses and trees, beasts of prey, down to insects, moths, and ants; it makes known dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Verily, if speech had not existed, neither dharma nor adharma would have been made known, neither truth nor falsehood, neither the good nor the bad, neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant.
"Speech alone makes all this known; meditate upon speech."
Speech indeed—
speech is the sense organ situated in the eight locations, such as the tongue and the roots of the teeth, which manifests phonemes;
and since phonemes constitute names, speech is said to be greater than name.
In the world, it is observed that the cause is greater than the effect, just as a father is greater than his son;
in the same way, how is speech greater than name? He says: "Speech indeed makes the Ṛgveda known, [informing us] 'This is the Ṛgveda';
likewise for the Yajurveda," and so on, the rest being the same.
"Knowing the heart" means being dear to the heart;
the opposite of that is "not knowing the heart.

If speech did not exist, then dharma and so forth would not have been made known. In the absence of speech, there would be an absence of study; in the absence of study, there would be an absence of hearing its meaning; and in the absence of hearing it, dharma and so forth would not have been made known.
The meaning is that it would have been known.
Therefore, speech alone makes all this known through the utterance of words; thus, speech is greater than name. For this reason, meditate upon speech as Brahman.
He who venerates speech as Brahman—
so far as speech extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who venerates speech as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than speech?"
"Verily, there is something greater than speech. May the Blessed One explain that to me."
The rest is the same.
Thus ends the second section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Mind, indeed, is greater than speech.
Just as one’s fist encompasses two *vāmalaka* fruits, or two *kola* fruits, or two *akṣa* fruits, even so does the mind encompass both speech and name.
When he intends with his mind, "I shall study the mantras," then he studies;
when he intends, "I shall perform rituals," then he performs them;
and when he desires, "May I have sons and cattle," then he desires them.
If one desires, "May I obtain this world and that world," it is because the mind is indeed the self;
for the mind is indeed the world.
"The mind, indeed, is Brahman;
meditate upon the mind."
The mind (*manas*), which is the internal organ characterized by the function of mental reflection (*manasyana*), is greater than speech.
For it is the mind, possessing the activity of reflection, that impels speech toward what is to be spoken;
therefore, speech is contained within the mind.
And whatever is included within something else is more extensive than that [container], because it pervades it.
Just as in the world, a fist encompasses two *āmalaka* fruits, or two *kola* (badara) fruits, or two *akṣa* (vibhītaka) fruits; the fist pervades those fruits, for they are contained within the fist.
In this way, speech and name experience the mind, just as the *āmalaka* fruit [experiences] its own color and so on.
When, at whatever time, a person reflects with the mind—that is, the internal organ—what is this reflection? It is the desire to speak (*vivakṣā-buddhi*). How so?

Having formed the desire to speak, thinking, "I shall study and recite the mantras," he then studies them; likewise, having formed the desire to act (*cikīrṣā-buddhi*), thinking, "I shall perform ritual acts."
The meaning is: having first formed the desire, "I wish for sons and cattle," one then desires them—that is, one obtains sons and so forth—by performing the means for their attainment.
Likewise, having formed the desire, "I wish for this world and that world," one then desires them—that is, one obtains them—by performing the means for their attainment.

For the mind is indeed the self; since agency and enjoyership belong to the self only when the mind exists and not otherwise, it is said that "the mind is indeed the self. For the mind is indeed the world; for the world exists only when the mind exists, as does the performance of the means for attaining it. Since the mind is indeed the world, therefore the mind is Brahman.
Because this is so, therefore, meditate upon the mind.
He who meditates on the mind as Brahman—
so far as the reach of the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on the mind as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than the mind?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than the mind.
May the Blessed One explain that to me."
"That which... and so forth is the same as before.
Thus ends the third section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Intention (*saṃkalpa*) is indeed greater than the mind (*manas*).
For when one intends, then one thinks.
Then he utters speech;
he leads that speech into the name.
In the name, the mantras become one.
Ritual actions are performed with mantras.
Volition (*saṃkalpa*) is indeed greater than the mind.

Volition is a function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), consisting of mental reflection (*manasyana*) that establishes through a distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done.
For once the object has been established through such a distinction, the desire to act (*cikīrṣābuddhi*) arises immediately following mental reflection.

How so? When one indeed forms a volition (*saṃkalpayate*), distinguishing objects such as what ought to be done— thinking, "it is proper to do this"— then one intends (*manasyati*) such things as, "I shall study the mantras," and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, one utters speech for the purpose of pronouncing mantras and the like. And one utters that speech by first forming the intention (*vivakṣā*) to utter a name; that is, within the name—meaning within the general category of names—the specific words that are the mantras become one, that is, they are subsumed.
For it is within the general that the particular is subsumed.
Ritual acts are one with the mantras;
ritual acts are performed as revealed by the mantras, for there is no ritual act that exists without a mantra.
Indeed, it is that very ritual act which has acquired its existence through the revelation of the mantra that is enjoined as "this must be performed by the Brāhmaṇa for this specific result."
Even that origin of ritual acts which is observed among the Brāhmaṇas is merely the clarification of those very acts whose efficacy has already been established in the Mantras;
for no ritual act not revealed by the Mantras is ever seen to have originated in a Brāhmaṇa.
It is well known in the world that ritual action is prescribed by the Trayī (the three Vedas).
The term *trayī* (the triad) is a designation for the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* [Vedas].
Furthermore, in the *Atharvaveda*, it is stated: "The sages beheld ritual actions within the mantras.
Therefore, it is appropriate that ritual actions are contained within the mantras.

Indeed, these have volition as their sole point of convergence, they consist of volition, and they are established in volition. Heaven and earth were willed into being; wind and space were willed into being.
Heat and radiance were formed together;
through their formation, rain was formed;
through the formation of rain, food was formed.
For the purpose of the determination of food, the vital breaths are determined; for the purpose of the determination of the vital breaths, the mantras are determined;
for the purpose of the determination of the mantras, the ritual acts are determined.
Through the volition of actions, the world is willed;
through the volition of the world, everything is willed.
This is that very volition.
"Meditate upon volition."

Indeed, these [elements] beginning with the mind have volition as their single point of convergence; "saṃkalpaikāyanāni" means those whose single path (ayana)—that is, their course or dissolution—is volition. They are composed of volition at their origin and established in volition during their persistence.
For heaven and earth—Heaven and Earth—are perceived as motionless, as if they had performed a volitional act (*samakḷpatām*).
Likewise, Vāyu and Ākāśa also "resolved" (samakalpetām), as if they too had formed a resolution; similarly, Āpas and Tejas were seen to be motionless in their own forms.
Because of the resolution for those [elements] such as Heaven and Earth, rain resolves itself as the cause of that resolution.
For the vital breaths (prāṇas) consist of food and are supported by food.
For the Vedic revelation says, "Food is indeed a gift.
The mantras are intended for their [the ancestors'] purposeful intention;
for one who possesses vital breath studies the mantras, not one who is weak.

For rites such as the Agnihotra are intended for the purpose of the determination (*saṃkalpti*) of mantras; when these rites, revealed by mantras, are performed, they become capable of yielding their fruit.
Therefore, the world determines its fruit—that is to say, it becomes capable through its inherence in the agent of the action.
For the sake of the world’s determination, the entire universe determines itself, so that its own nature may remain unimpaired.
For all this entire world, which culminates in its fruits, has its root in volition (saṃkalpa).
Therefore, this volition is preeminent.
Having thus said, "Worship volition," he states the fruit for one who worships it.

He who meditates upon volition as Brahman attains worlds that are fashioned, eternal, firmly established, unshakable, and free from distress— provided he himself is firm, firmly established, and unshakable.
As far as the reach of volition extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon volition as Brahman.
"Venerable sir, is there anything greater than volition?
"There is indeed something greater than volition.
"May the venerable sir explain that to me."

He who meditates upon *saṃkalpa* (volition) as Brahman, with the understanding that it is Brahman—for him, these worlds are "prepared" (*kḷpta*) by the Creator; that is, they are prepared, established, and willed for him. That wise man [obtains] them as firm and eternal, in comparison to the extreme non-eternity of other things, and he himself becomes firm. For if the inhabitant of the worlds were non-firm, the preparation of the worlds as firm would be purposeless; thus, being firm, he obtains them as well-established, meaning endowed with all necessary implements.

Because it is seen that one becomes firmly established through cattle, sons, and so forth, and because he himself is established—being endowed with his own necessary means and free from distress—that is, devoid of fear of enemies and the like—he, being undistressed, attains and reaches [his goal]; this is the meaning.

"As far as the reach of his will extends"—that is, within the scope of his will—it is there that he has freedom of action according to his desire; however, this refers to the will of the individual self (ātman), and not to the will of all beings, for that would contradict the description of the subsequent results.
"He who meditates on volition as Brahman," and so forth, as before.
Thus ends the fourth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Mind, indeed, is greater than volition.
For when one perceives, then one wills.
Then he forms a thought;
then he utters speech;
and that [speech] he impels by means of a name.
In the name, the mantras become one;
in the mantras, the ritual acts.
Mind, indeed, is greater than volition.

Mind is the state of being a thinker, the possession of awareness appropriate to the time at hand, and the capacity for determining the purpose and objects of both the past and the future; it is greater even than that volition.
How so?

When one indeed perceives, "It has been obtained," then one intends either for giving or for discarding; then one forms a resolve, then one reflects in the mind, and so forth, as previously described.
These, indeed, have thought as their single path, thought as their essence, and are established in thought.
Therefore, even if one who knows much becomes devoid of thought, they say of him, "This man does not exist.
For what he knows, or what he has known as a learned man, would not be so if he were devoid of thought.
Now, if one possesses a mind that is not narrow-minded, people desire to listen to him alone;
for the mind is indeed their single path,
the mind is their self.
"The mind is the foundation;
meditate upon the mind."

Those factors beginning with volition (*saṃkalpa*) and ending with the fruit of action (*karmaphala*) have the mind as their single path, the mind as their self, arise from the mind, and are established in and abide within the mind, as explained previously.
Furthermore, what is the majesty of the mind?
Since the mind is the root of volition and the rest, therefore, even if one possesses extensive knowledge of many sciences and treatises, if one lacks the [proper] mind—

He becomes devoid of the capacity for volition and so forth; the wise say of him, "Though this man exists, he is as good as non-existent. Furthermore, whatever he knows or has heard from the scriptures and so on, they declare that even that is in vain for him.
Why?
The meaning is that they say: "If this person were truly wise, he would not have such a mind; therefore, even though he has heard it, it is as if he had not heard it at all.

On the other hand, even if one has little knowledge, if he possesses the right mental disposition (*cittavān*), people desire to listen—that is, they wish to hear—from him for the very purpose of grasping the meaning of what was said.
And therefore, the mind alone is the single point of convergence for these—volition and so forth—as explained previously.

He who meditates on Brahman as the mind (citta) indeed attains worlds that are steadfast, being himself steadfast; established, being himself established; and unshakable, being himself unshakable. As far as the reach of the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on Brahman as the mind.
"Is there, Blessed One, anything greater than the mind?
"There is indeed something greater than the mind.
"May the Blessed One tell me that."

That devotee of the mind, through the qualities of an intelligent person, does not accumulate [karmic] impressions in the mind; this, along with "the permanent," "the impermanent," and so forth, has its meaning already explained.
Thus ends the fifth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Meditation, indeed, is greater than thought.
The earth, as it were, meditates.
The intermediate space, as it were, meditates; the sky, as it were, meditates; the waters, as it were, meditate.
The mountains seem as if they were meditating;
gods and humans seem as if they were meditating.
Therefore, those among humans here who attain greatness become, as it were, participants in the attainment of meditation.
Now, those who are few, quarrelsome, slanderous, and backbiting—they are such. But those who are eminent, they become as if parts of the attainment of meditation.
"Meditate upon meditation," [he said].
He who worships meditation as Brahman—
so far as meditation extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who worships meditation as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than meditation?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than meditation;
may the Blessed One explain that to me."
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is indeed greater than the mind.

What is called meditative concentration is a continuous stream of cognition that is unwavering with respect to objects such as deities taught in the scriptures and is uninterrupted by heterogeneous elements;
this is what they call "one-pointedness."
And the greatness of meditation is seen through its fruit.
How so?
Just as a yogi becomes motionless while meditating upon attaining the fruit of meditation.
Thus, the earth appears as if meditating, motionless;
"the intermediate space appears as if meditating," and so forth—the rest is the same.

"Gods and humans" (devamanuṣyāḥ) means either gods and humans, or simply humans who are like gods; that is to say, humans endowed with qualities such as tranquility (*śama*) who do not abandon their divine nature.

Since meditation (*dhyāna*) is thus distinguished, therefore those among men in this world who attain greatness (*mahattvam*)—that is, the state of being great—either through wealth, knowledge, or virtues; the meaning is that they obtain the cause for such greatness in wealth and so forth. They are like those possessing a certain portion (*aṃśa*), a part (*avayava*), or a fraction (*kalā*) of the attainment of meditation; "attainment" (*āpāda*) means the reaching toward meditation, which is the acquisition of its fruit. The meaning is: as if they possessed some small measure of the fruit of meditation.
They appear as if motionless and not like petty people.
On the other hand, those who are few and petty, having attained not even a small portion of greatness such as wealth and so forth, are the opposite of those previously described:

they are quarrelsome, having a habit of fighting; they are slanderers, exposing the faults of others; and they are revilers, [speaking] of the faults of others as if they were right before their eyes.
Those who have the habit of speaking ill of women become slanderers;

furthermore, those who have attained greatness through wealth and such means exercise power over others—thus, powerful figures such as learned teachers, kings, and lords are like partial attainments of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). This is the meaning of what was stated previously.
Therefore, the greatness of meditative absorption is seen in its results; since it is even greater than the mind itself, one should practice it. This is the meaning of what was stated previously.
Thus ends the sixth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Knowledge, indeed, is greater than meditation.
By means of knowledge, one knows the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth, and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa.

The fifth [Veda] among the Vedas: the ancestral rites, mathematics, portents, treasures, dialogues, monistic discipline, the science of gods, the science of Brahman, the science of spirits, the science of weaponry, the science of the stars, the science of serpents and celestial beings;
and heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire, gods and humans, cattle and birds.

And he discerns by means of consciousness alone the grasses and trees, wild beasts, down to worms, moths, and ants; dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant, food and flavor, and this world and the next—
“Venerate consciousness,” he said.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is indeed greater than meditation (*dhyāna*).
Consciousness is the knowledge whose object is the meaning of the scriptures; because it is the cause of meditation, it is greater than meditation.

And how is it greater? He says: "By means of consciousness, one knows the *Ṛgveda*, [thinking] 'This is the *Ṛgveda*'; for its knowledge of the meaning serves as the authority that is the cause of meditation."
Likewise, [the text mentions] the Yajurveda and so forth.
Furthermore, sacrificial animals and the like, as well as dharma and adharma, are established by the scriptures;
while the good and the bad are established by worldly convention.
Or rather, the meaning is that one understands everything pertaining to the domain of the Smṛti, whether visible or invisible, by means of consciousness alone.
Therefore, it is appropriate that knowledge through meditation and so forth is more abundant; hence, "meditate upon consciousness."
He who meditates on consciousness as Brahman attains worlds that possess consciousness and knowledge.
As far as the reach of consciousness extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on consciousness as Brahman.
"Is there, O Blessed One, anything greater than consciousness?
"There is indeed something greater than consciousness.
"May the Blessed One explain that to me."

Listen to the fruit of worship for one possessed of discernment (*vijñāna*): he attains and reaches those worlds belonging to those who possess discernment as well as those who possess knowledge (*jñāna*). Discernment is the knowledge whose object is the meaning of the scriptures; knowledge is proficiency regarding other objects. The meaning is that he does not fail to reach the worlds inhabited by those endowed with such qualities. The phrase "as far as discernment" and so forth is as explained previously.
Thus ends the seventh section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Power, indeed, is greater than knowledge;
for even a single powerful man can shake a hundred men possessed of knowledge.
When he becomes strong, then he becomes one who rises;
rising, he becomes one who serves; serving, he becomes one who attends upon [the teacher].
Approaching [it], one becomes a seer, one becomes a hearer, one becomes a thinker, one becomes a knower, one becomes an agent, and one becomes a cognizer.

By strength indeed the earth stands; by strength the intermediate space, by strength the sky, by strength the mountains; by strength gods and humans, by strength beasts and birds, grasses and trees, wild animals, down to insects, moths, and ants.
"The world stands by power;
venerate power."
He who worships strength—
so far as strength extends, he has freedom of movement there— he who worships strength as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than strength?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than strength;
may the Blessed One explain that to me."
Power, indeed, is greater than consciousness.
"Power" refers to the capacity of the mind for intuitive insight regarding objects of knowledge, generated by the consumption of food;
as the Śruti states: "Because of fasting, the Ṛg-veda and the others do not indeed manifest to me, O sir."

Even in the body, that same capacity for rising and so forth exists, because even a single strong living being can cause a hundred conscious beings to tremble, just as a single rutting elephant can do to a hundred men gathered together;

since strength is thus caused by the consumption of food and other such things, when that person becomes strong— that is, possessed of strength— he then becomes one who rises, meaning an agent of rising, and while rising,
he becomes one who serves his elders and his teacher, meaning an agent of service and attendance.
The meaning is that by serving them, one becomes an attendant who stays near them and is intimate with them.
And by approaching—that is, by going into their presence—one becomes, through single-mindedness, a beholder of the teacher or another instructor, the guru;
thereafter, one becomes a listener to what has been spoken by him.
Then, thinking "this is established by these [reasons] in this way," one becomes a thinker through logical justification; and being a thinker, one becomes a knower, [realizing] "this is exactly so.
Having thus ascertained it, one becomes the doer—the performer—of the meaning expressed by that [knowledge], and one becomes the experiencer of the fruit of that performance; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, the greatness of power is for the purpose of [reciting] the Upanishadic passage beginning with, "By power indeed the earth stands," and so forth.
Thus ends the eighth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Food, indeed, is more than strength;
therefore, even if one were not to eat for ten nights, [one's strength would eventually fail].
If, however, he should live, then he becomes a seer, a hearer, a thinker, an understander,
a doer, and a knower; but for the sake of food, he becomes a seer, he becomes a hearer, he becomes a thinker, he becomes an understander, he becomes a doer, and he becomes a knower.
"Venerate food."
Food indeed is greater than strength, because it is the cause of strength.
How is it that food is the cause of strength? This is explained as follows:

Since food is the cause of strength, therefore even if someone were not to eat for ten nights, he would die due to the loss of that strength which has food as its cause; or, if he does not die, even if he should live, he becomes one who does not see, and likewise one who does not hear from his teacher, and so forth— all things become the opposite of what they were before.
Now, when one who has not eaten for many days becomes incapable of activities such as seeing and the like, he seeks food;
*āya* means the coming (*āgamana*) of food—that is, the acquisition of food. He who possesses this [desire] is "one who seeks food" (*annasyā’yī*).
The word *āya* is [derived] through the transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyayena*).
Alternatively, there is also a reading *annasyā'yā*, which has the same meaning,
because of the scriptural mention of effects such as "the seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) and so forth.
For it is observed that the capacity for seeing and other such functions exists when food is consumed, and not when it is not obtained; therefore, "partake of food."
He who meditates on food as Brahman attains worlds rich in food and rich in drink.
As far as the reach of food extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on food as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than food?
"There is indeed something greater than food.
"May the Venerable One tell that to me."

And as a result, he attains worlds that possess abundant food for one who offers food, and worlds that possess abundant water for one who offers drink; because food and drink are eternally connected, he succeeds in reaching those worlds.
The rest is the same.
Thus ends the ninth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Water, indeed, is greater than food.
Therefore, when there is no good rain, living beings suffer, thinking, "Food will become scarce."

Now, when there is good rain, the vital breaths become joyful, thinking, "There will be abundant food. These very waters have taken form as this earth, as the intermediate space, as the sky, as the mountains, as gods and humans, as domestic animals and birds, as grasses, trees, and wild beasts, down to worms, moths, and ants;
these indeed are the waters that have taken form.
"Water, meditate upon it."
Water, indeed, is greater than food, because it is the cause of food.

Since this is so, therefore, when at a certain time there is no good rain—that is, no auspicious rain beneficial for the crops—then people fall ill and their vital breaths become distressed. For what reason? He says: "In this year, our food will become less—that is, more scanty."
Furthermore, when there is good rain, living beings become joyful, happy, and delighted, thinking, "There will be an end [to scarcity]; there will be much, there will be plenty.

Since material food originates from water, these waters themselves have transformed into the forms of the differentiated categories of the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta). That which is this earth, that which is the intermediate space, and so forth—these are the formed waters; therefore, one should meditate upon the waters.
He who meditates on water as Brahman attains all desires and becomes satisfied. As far as the reach of water extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on water as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than water?
"There is indeed something greater than water.
"May the Venerable One tell me that."
He who meditates upon water as Brahman obtains all desires—that is to say, all desirable objects that possess form.
Furthermore, because satisfaction arises from water, by meditating on water one becomes possessed of satisfaction.
The rest is the same [as before].
Thus ends the tenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Fire, indeed, is greater than water.
Seizing the air, it heats up space; then people say, "It is burning hot, it is scorching; it will rain."
Having first manifested heat itself, it then creates the waters.
Therefore, when there are flashes of lightning—both upward and across—and peals of thunder roll, people say, "It lightens; it thunders; it will rain.
Having first manifested heat itself, it then creates the waters.
"Venerate fire."
Fire, indeed, is greater than water,
because fire is not the cause of water.
To explain how it is not the cause of water, he says:

Since fire is not born from anything else, therefore that very fire, having seized and held fast the air—having made it motionless by its own nature—heats the ether, and as he heats it, pervading the ether, people in the world say: "It is scorching, it is burning; it is heating the world in general and the bodies; therefore it will rain."

For it is well known in the world that one who has seen the cause exerted [toward an effect] possesses the cognition that "the effect will come to be. That fire first manifests itself and then immediately creates water; therefore, because it is the creator of water, fire is other than water. Furthermore, this very same fire becomes the cause of rain in the form of thunder.
How so?
Together with upward-moving lightning flashes and crosswise-moving ones, as well as those moving horizontally, thunders—sounds of rumbling—proceed.
Therefore, from seeing that, worldly people say, "It lightens," "it thunders," or "it will rain," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
"Therefore, worship the fire as the light."
He who meditates upon Brahman as splendor indeed becomes splendid;
he attains splendid, radiant worlds from which darkness has been dispelled.
As far as splendor extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon Brahman as splendor.
"Is there, O Blessed One, something greater than fire? "There is indeed something greater than fire.
"May the Blessed One tell that to me."
The fruit of the worship of that *tejas* (splendor) is that he indeed becomes resplendent;

and from being resplendent, he attains worlds that are luminous, radiant, full of light, and with darkness dispelled—that is, with the darkness of external and internal ignorance and so forth removed.
The rest has its meaning plain.
Thus ends the eleventh section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
Space, indeed, is greater than fire;
for in space both the sun and the moon exist, as do lightning, the stars, and fire.
He calls out through space;
he hears through space;
he responds through space.
He delights in space;
he does not delight in space;
he is born in space.
Space is born;
meditate upon space.
Space, indeed, is greater than fire.
Because space is the cause of fire together with air, air—having been included by the phrase "having grasped air"—was mentioned along with fire; it is not mentioned here separately from fire.
For in the world, a cause is seen to be greater than its effect.
Just as clay is greater than jars and other such objects, so too is space greater than fire together with air, because it is the cause of that [fire].
How so?
Indeed, both the sun and the moon, which are forms of light, as well as lightning, the stars, and fire—all these forms of light—are within space.
Furthermore, that which is contained within something else is small, while the other is greater.
