Moreover, one person calls out to another through space, and being called, the other hears through space; one hears the sound spoken by another and another responds;
they delight and sport with one another in space, yet no one delights in space when separated from their wife and so forth.
Space is not produced where it is obstructed by a material form;
likewise, sprouts and the like grow directed toward space, not against it.
Therefore, take recourse in space.
He who meditates on space as Brahman attains worlds that possess space,
that possess light, that are unconfined, and that are wide-extending.
As far as the reach of space extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on space as Brahman.
"Is there, O Blessed One, anything greater than space?
"There is indeed something greater than space.
"May the Blessed One explain that to me."
Listen to the fruit: that wise man attains worlds that possess light and are endowed with vastness.

Because light and space are eternally connected, he attains worlds possessed of light, which are unconfined; for "confined" (saṃbādha) means a crowding together, a mutual oppression—those worlds are "unconfined" (asaṃbādha), being free from such oppression. He attains worlds possessed of wide-reaching movement, having extensive paths and extensive scope.
The phrase "as far as space" and so forth has its meaning already explained.
Thus ends the twelfth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: Memory, indeed, is greater than space.
Therefore, even if many were to sit together, if they were without memory, they would not hear anything at all, nor would they think, nor would they understand.
"When they indeed remember you, then they will hear; then they will reflect; then they will understand.
By memory one recognizes one's sons; by memory one recognizes one's cattle.
Meditate upon memory!"
He who meditates on memory as Brahman—
so far as memory extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on memory as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than memory?"
"Is there indeed something greater than memory?
May the Blessed One tell me that."
Memory (smara) indeed is greater than space.
Memory is the act of remembering, which is a quality of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

It should be understood that it is greater than space, despite the change in grammatical gender; for when the rememberer possesses memory, everything beginning with space becomes purposeful, since it serves as an object of enjoyment for one who possesses memory.
But when there is no recollection, even that which exists is as if non-existent, because its function as a sentient being is absent.
Furthermore, in the absence of recollection, it is impossible to perceive the existence of space and so forth; therefore, recollection is more vast than space.

For it is observed in the world that memory is often deficient; therefore, even if many people were to sit together in one place, if they do not remember what was said by one another while sitting there, they would not hear any sound at all, nor would they reflect upon it.
If they were to reflect upon what is to be reflected upon, then they would reflect; but due to the absence of memory, they would not reflect, and likewise, they would not understand.
"When they indeed remember what is to be reflected upon, what is to be understood, and what is to be heard, then they hear; then they reflect; then they understand.
Thus, by means of memory one recognizes, 'These are my sons,' and by means of memory one recognizes one's cattle.
Because it is greater than these, meditate upon memory."
The rest has already been explained.
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Hope, indeed, is greater than memory.
For kindled by hope, memory studies the sacred hymns, performs rituals, desires sons and cattle, and desires both this world and the world beyond.
"Worship hope."
Hope is indeed greater than memory.
Hope is the longing for an object not yet attained; it is what they call by synonyms such as thirst and desire. And that is greater than memory.
How so?
For by means of the internal organ (āśaya), one remembers that which is to be remembered.
Remembering the form of the object of desire, he becomes Smara (the God of Love); therefore, kindled by desire and increased by the internal organ, he has become Smara.
Remembering the Ṛg and other mantras, he studies them; having studied them, he hears their meaning and the injunctions from the Brāhmaṇas and performs rituals with the desire for their fruits.

He desires sons as the fruits of those rituals, longing for them with that very intention; he practices the means to achieve them with that same intention. And desiring this world alone, he seeks it through the causes for the maintenance of the world, while remaining mindful [of his duties].

And having kindled this world with hope, one desires it through the performance of the means for its attainment; therefore, the entire world—from the mind (smara) down to the name (nāman)—is bound by the tethering of hope and revolves like a wheel within every living being.
In this regard, since hope is even greater than the mind, you should worship hope.
He who meditates on hope as Brahman—
his every desire is fulfilled through hope,
and his prayers become unfailing.
As far as hope extends, so far he has freedom of movement who meditates upon hope as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than hope? "There is something greater than hope."
May the Blessed One explain that to me."
Listen to the fruit for him who meditates upon you as hope:
by constantly meditating with hope, all desires of this meditator flourish and attain fulfillment.
Indeed, all his blessings and prayers become unfailing; the meaning is that whatever he has prayed for, all that necessarily comes to pass.
"As far as the reach of hope extends," and so forth, as previously stated.
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"Breath, indeed, is greater than hope.
Just as spokes are fixed in the hub, so everything is fixed in this breath."
The breath moves by means of the breath;
the breath gives the breath;
he gives for the sake of the breath.
The vital breath is indeed the father;
the vital breath is the mother;
the vital breath is the brother.
The vital breath is the sister;
the vital breath is the teacher;
the vital breath is the brahmin.
All this—from name as its beginning to the very end of hope—exists in a state of increasing magnitude through the relationship of cause and effect and the relationship of instrument and consequence;
it is bound on all sides by the snares and cords of hope, which serve as the basis for memory, and is entirely fastened upon that Prāṇa like a lotus stalk by its fibers.
Furthermore, by that all-pervading [Prāṇa], which extends both within and without, everything is strung together and held fast, like a multitude of gems upon a thread.
This very vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed greater than hope.
To explain how it is greater, he provides an illustration to establish that greatness:
"Just as in the world the spokes of a chariot wheel are fixed, joined, and inserted into the hub of the chariot. This is what is meant.

Thus, within this vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of an aggregate of the subtle body (*liṅga-saṃghāta*), is the primary life-force within the embodied self (*dehika-prajñātman*). It is in this that the Supreme Deity is established by means of the individual soul (*jīva-ātman*) for the purpose of manifesting names and forms—like a reflection in a mirror—and who, like a great king, is the sovereign lord with authority over all. For the scripture states: "In whom, when departing, shall I depart? And in whom, when established, shall I be established? He created the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Furthermore, it is he who follows the Lord like a shadow.

Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon the spokes and the spokes are fixed upon the hub, even so these elements (bhūtamātrā) are fixed upon the elements of intelligence (prajñāmātrā), and the elements of intelligence are fixed upon the vital breath (prāṇa).
"This very vital breath is the self consisting of intelligence," so says the Kauṣītakins.
Therefore, everything mentioned above is thus supported within this vital breath.

Therefore, this very vital breath (*prāṇa*) is independent; it moves by its own power alone through the vital breath. The meaning is that its capacity for actions such as going and so forth is not produced by anything else.

The purport of the entire section is that the whole collection of distinctions consisting of actions, instruments, and results is the vital breath itself, and nothing exists outside of the vital breath.
When the vital breath gives the vital breath, that which it gives is indeed its own self.
That to whom one gives is also for the sake of the vital breath alone;
therefore, even that which is called "father" and so forth is indeed the vital breath.
If he should speak harshly to his father, or mother, or brother, or sister, or teacher, or a Brahmin, they say to him: "Fie on you! You are indeed a slayer of your father;

you are indeed a slayer of your mother; you are indeed a slayer of your brother; you are indeed a slayer of your sister; you are indeed a slayer of your teacher; you are indeed a slayer of a Brahmin."
How is it that words such as "father" and so forth, by abandoning their well-known meanings, come to have the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as their referent?
It is said: because the words "father" and so forth are applied to fathers and others only when the vital breath is present, and because they are not so applied when it has departed.
How is that so? He says:

If anyone should reply to one of his elders, such as his father, with some harsh or inappropriate speech, including the use of the term "thou" (tvaṅkāra) and so forth, then those discerning people standing nearby say to him:
"Fie on you! Fie upon you!
You are indeed a slayer of your father—a killer of your father," and so on.

Now, even if one were to burn these [deceased] whose vital breaths have departed with a poker all at once, they would certainly not say of him: "You are a patricide," nor "You are a matricide," nor "You are a fratricide," nor "You are a sororicide," nor "You are a murderer of a teacher," nor "You are a murderer of a Brahmin."

Now, even if one were to take these very persons whose vital breaths have departed and who have abandoned their bodies, and were to burn them by arranging them together in a heap with a stake, or by burning them individually in a reversed manner— even while performing such an exceedingly cruel act characterized by burning,
which is connected solely to those bodies, people would still not say of him, "He is a parricide," and so forth.
Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance, it is understood that even those named "Father" and so forth are indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) indeed becomes all these things.
He who sees thus, thinks thus, and understands thus, becomes a transcendent speaker (*ativādī*).
If they should say to him, "Are you a transcendent speaker? [he should answer: "I am a transcendent speaker."
He should say, "I am an over-speaker," and he should not deny it.

Therefore, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) indeed becomes all these things— the fathers and so forth— both moving and stationary. He who knows the vital breath, seeing in this manner as described, experiencing it through its results, reflecting upon it thus with logical arguments, and understanding it thus by joining it with those arguments— meaning, he forms the firm conviction that "it is exactly so."
For it is through both reflection (*manana*) and discerning consciousness (*vijñāna*) that the meaning of the teaching becomes determined and seen.

Therefore, seeing in this way, one becomes an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādī*); the meaning is that one possesses the habit of speaking by transcending names and so forth, as well as hope and fear. If they should say to him: "If you are such an exceeding speaker, always functioning by transcending names and so forth, as well as hope and fear, through all words..."

If they should say to Prāṇa— who speaks thus, who sees thus, who is habituated to superior speech, and who declares, "I am the Self of the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass"— "Are you one who speaks with superiority? he should say, "Indeed, I am one who speaks with superiority," and he should not deny it.
For why would he deny it, when he has approached the vital breath— the Lord of all— as his very self, thinking, "I am this"?
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of truth.
Therefore, O Venerable Sir, may I speak transcendentally by means of truth."
"But truth indeed must be sought to be known.
"I wish to know truth, venerable sir."
Having heard that this very Prāṇa is his own self, which transcends all, the self of all, and that there is nothing beyond it, Nārada desisted;
he did not ask as before, "Venerable Sir, is there anything greater than Prāṇa?

For [the Teacher] spoke thus to that worthy disciple—who was satisfied with the knowledge of Brahman as a mere modification and as unreal, who considered himself one who had attained his goal while being a speaker of the highest truth, yet who was actually far from it—in order to dislodge him from that particular false grasp.
The Blessed One Sanatkumāra said:
"But he indeed is a superior speaker (ativādin) whom I shall describe; one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) is not a superior speaker in the ultimate sense.
His status as a superior speaker, however, is dependent upon [the knowledge of] names and so forth."

But he who knows the reality called the Plenum (bhūman), which transcends all and is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), is an "exceeding speaker" (ativādī); therefore, it is said: "But he indeed is an exceeding speaker who speaks by means of the Truth. The intention is this: "I, being one who speaks by means of the knowledge of the ultimate truth, have sought refuge in you, O Blessed One; may the Blessed One so instruct me that I may speak by means of the Truth. When it was thus stated—"If you desire to speak by means of the Truth, then the Truth itself must first be known"—Nārada replied.
"So be it; O Venerable One, let it be so. I wish to know the truth in detail; I desire to understand it from you."
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"When one truly understands, then one speaks the truth;
one who does not understand does not speak the truth."
"Only one who knows speaks the truth;
therefore, knowledge itself is what must be sought to be understood.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand knowledge."

When one truly understands reality from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), thinking "this is the ultimate truth," then, having abandoned the unreal—the entire collection of transformations which are merely the starting point of speech—one speaks only that which is the one, true *sat* (Being) existing in all states of transformation; for whatever one speaks, it is indeed that alone.
But is it not the case that even the modification (*vikāra*) is real?
When name-and-form exist, by them this vital breath (prāṇa) is concealed.

For it is stated in another Vedic text: "The vital breaths are indeed the real; of these, this [breath] is the real. Thus, the reality mentioned in the other Vedic text regarding modification is not stated with reference to the ultimate truth (paramārtha); rather, it is stated with reference to being an object of the senses.
It has been stated that "satya" and "tyat" mean "truth," and it is intended here that the realization of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) occurs through that medium.
It has also been said, "The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) are indeed truth; of them, this [Self] is the truth. That very same point is intended here as well.

In this context, however, the specific intended meaning is as follows: having raised Nārada from his conceit regarding the knowledge of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) concerning the syllable *praṇava*, [the Teacher] intends to make known that which is truly existent (*sat*) and ultimately real—the "Fullness" (*bhūman*)—saying, "I shall make you understand that.

One who does not know the truth does not speak the truth; rather, he who speaks while not knowing it does so by imagining fire and other such things to be ultimately real through words like "fire," yet they do not exist as ultimate reality apart from the three forms [of the *praṇava*].
Just as those [other] forms do not exist at all from the perspective of reality (*sat*), one does not speak the truth without knowing this; rather,
it is only by knowing this that one speaks the truth.
And that knowledge of truth is not known without being sought after or inquired about; therefore, he says, "But knowledge itself is what must be inquired about. [The student asks:
"If that is so, venerable sir, I wish to inquire about knowledge.
In this way, one should explain that among the successive stages beginning with truth and ending with action, each preceding element serves as the cause for each subsequent one.
Thus ends the seventeenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "When one indeed thinks, then one understands;
one does not understand without thinking."
"Only by means of thought (mati) does one discern; therefore, thought itself is what one must desire to understand.
"Venerable Sir, I desire to understand thought."
"When one indeed thinks" (yadā vai manute): "thought" (mati) is reflection (manana), reasoning (tarka), and attention directed toward the object of thought.
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"When one has faith, then one reflects;
one who lacks faith does not reflect."
"Only by having faith does one reflect; faith indeed is what must be sought to be understood.
"Venerable sir, I wish to understand faith."
Faith is the conviction that there is such a thing as spiritual reality.
Thus ends the nineteenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"When one is established in practice, then one has faith;
one who is not established in practice does not have faith."
"One has faith only when one has reached a firm conclusion; therefore, a firm conclusion itself must be sought to be understood.
'Venerable sir, I wish to understand what a firm conclusion is.'"
Perfection consists in devotion to such things as service to the teacher, directed toward the realization of Brahman.
Thus ends the twentieth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"When one acts, then one attains completion; one does not attain completion without having acted."
"Having performed [action], one indeed rests;
but action itself is what must be sought to be understood.
"Venerable sir, I wish to understand action."
When one indeed performs [the practice],
"performance" consists of restraint of the senses and the attainment of one-pointedness of mind;
for when that exists, the aforementioned stages beginning with "completion" and ending with "higher knowledge" come to pass.
Thus ends the twenty-first section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"When one indeed attains happiness, then one acts; having not attained happiness, one does not act."
"Having obtained only happiness, one acts;
indeed, happiness alone is that which one should desire to understand.
"I desire to understand happiness, O Blessed One."
The meaning is that even that action occurs only when it attains pleasure— that is, when one thinks, "I must attain the unsurpassed pleasure to be described"—
just as an action performed for the sake of visible results does not occur here without having attained pleasure.
Even regarding a future result, it is said that one acts "having attained" it.

Since it is logical that activity proceeds with that [Truth] as its objective, one might now argue that when the subsequent stages such as "what is to be done" (kṛtya) and so forth are present, Truth manifests of its own accord; thus, it would follow that no separate effort need be made for the cognition of it. To this, the following is said:
"But happiness alone is what ought to be sought to be known," and so forth.
To her who had thus become intent on learning, he said: "O Blessed One, you desire to know happiness."
Thus ends the twenty-second section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"That which is the Infinite (bhūman) is bliss;
in the finite there is no bliss."
"The fullness itself is happiness; indeed, the fullness alone is what one should desire to understand.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand the fullness."

That which is indeed the "plenum" (bhūman)—synonyms for which are "great," "limitless," and "abundant"—that is happiness. What is inferior to that, being subject to limitation, is "small. Therefore, in that which is small, there is no happiness.
Because a small amount is the cause of excessive craving,
and craving is the seed of suffering;
for in the world, the seed of suffering is never seen to be happiness, as in the case of fever and the like.

Therefore, it is logical that there is no happiness in what is limited; hence, bliss belongs only to the Infinite (bhūman), because in the Infinite the seeds of suffering such as craving cannot exist.
Thus ends the twenty-third section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman).
But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (alpa)."
"That which is the Plenum is indeed the immortal;
but that which is the limited is mortal.
Venerable sir, upon what is that Plenum established?"
Whether in its own greatness or not in its greatness.

"What is the characteristic of that state? He says: in that "plenum" (*bhūman*), which is the reality (*tattva*), the seer does not see anything else by means of another instrument as something distinct from the object seen;
likewise, he does not hear anything else.

Since all distinctions of objects are included within name and form (*nāmarūpa*), only seeing and hearing—the perceivers of those [objects]—are mentioned here, while the others are intended as mere illustrations.
And "thinking" (manana) mentioned here should be understood as nothing other than "he thinks";
for knowledge generally has thinking as its precursor.
Likewise, he does not cognize anything else.
That which has such characteristics is the Bhūman.

In this context, is it being stated that the absence of the perception of anything else is the Bhūman by means of the passage "he does not see anything else" and so forth, or is it rather that he does not see anything else [but] sees the Self?
What follows from this?

If it is said that [the state of] "Bhūman" is merely the absence of the perception of anything else and so forth, then it is stated that Bhūman is distinct from the conventional dealings of duality (*dvaita-saṃvyavahāra*).

On the other hand, if it is said that one perceives the Self by means of the negation of specific perceptions of other things, then a distinction between action, agent, and result would have to be admitted within that very same [Self].
If this were so, what fault would there be?
Is it not precisely this that is the fault: the non-cessation of saṃsāra?
For saṃsāra is indeed the distinction between action, agent, and fruit.

If it is argued that even in the state of the absolute oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*), there exists a distinction between action, agent, and fruit which is distinct from the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), we say no.

For if one accepts the absolute oneness of the Self as devoid of distinctions, the acceptance of a distinction between the action of seeing and so forth, along with its agent and fruit, would be a mere matter of words.

If it is further argued that even in the position where the absence of other seeing and so forth is stated, the two qualifiers "where" (*yatra*) and "he does not see anything else" (*anyat na paśyati*) would be meaningless—[we reply: they are not.

If it is argued that this is just as seen in the world, where when it is said of an empty house, "one sees nothing else," it is understood that one does not fail to see the pillars and so forth, nor oneself;
[we reply: no, because in this case too, due to the instruction of identity in the words "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), a distinction between the locus and the subject is untenable.

If it is argued that the qualification "wherein" (yatra) would be redundant—since it has been determined in the sixth [chapter] that "Being alone is real, one without a second"—and because of such scriptural passages as, "In the invisible, bodiless, manifest [Brahman], its form stands," and "By what, O amiable one, should one know the knower?"; and thus perception and so forth are impossible with respect to one's own self; we reply: No.
This is because it depends on distinctions created by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Just as, depending on the contextually present notion of unity and non-duality, "Being" (*sat*) is said to be "one, indeed, without a second"— even though it is unfit for such numerical designations—
likewise, in the case of the "Fullness" (*bhūman*), there is the qualification "in which alone."

Furthermore, because in the state of ignorance there is a reference to the perception of "other," and because it is intended to characterize the abundance [of Brahman] as being devoid of that [perception of other], the qualification "he sees nothing else" is employed.
Therefore, the collective meaning is that the empirical transaction of saṃsāra does not exist in the Abundance.
Now, where—in the sphere of ignorance—another sees another as something else, that is "the small," meaning it exists only during the time of ignorance.

Just as an object seen in a dream exists only at that time prior to awakening, so too is that [world] mortal and perishable, exactly like a dream-object. That which is its opposite, the Plenum (bhūman), is immortal;
the word "that" (tat) refers to immortality.
To Nārada, who had asked, "O Venerable One, in what is that *bhūman* (the Infinite), characterized in such a way, established? Sanatkumāra replied:
"In its own greatness. This means the *bhūman* is established in its own greatness—that is, in its majesty and manifestation.
Whether you desire to know its support in some [external] place, or whether you are asking about the ultimate reality itself, we say that it is not even established in its own greatness.
The meaning is that he is non-abiding and non-dependent, not established anywhere at all.
"Cows and horses, they call 'greatness' here; elephants, gold, slaves, wives, fields, and dwellings.
"I do not speak thus," he said. "I do speak thus," he replied.
For one is indeed established in the other.
If the Infinite (bhūman) is established in its own majesty, how then is it said to be "without foundation"?
Listen:
in this world, cows, horses, and so forth are called "majesty" (mahiman).
"Cows and horses" (*go'śvam*) is a *dvandva* compound in the singular form.
Everywhere, the term "greatness" (*mahiman*) is well known as referring to [a collection] such as cows and horses; Caitra is dependent upon that and established therein.

Just as I am not thus dependent on some other greatness of my own, I say that the Infinite (*bhūman*) is not like Caitra; here, the connection with the distant phrase "for one is established in another" serves as the reason.
"But I speak thus," he said, "it is indeed so," and so forth.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"He is below, He is above; He is behind, He is in front; He is to the south, He is to the north;
He alone is all this."
Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the "I-maker" (ahaṃkāra) alone:
"I am indeed below, I am above, I am behind, I am in front, I am to the south, I am to the north—I am all this."
Why, then, is it said that he is not established anywhere?
Because that very plenitude (*bhūman*) itself is below; there exists nothing other than it in which he might be established.
The same applies to what is above, and so forth.
If there were something else greater than the Infinite (bhūman), then the Infinite would indeed be established in that; but such a thing does not exist.
He alone is everything.
Therefore, for that reason, He is not established anywhere.

Lest someone should have the doubt that the "Plenum" (bhūman) might be something other than the seeing individual soul (jīva)—given the instruction regarding the locus and the subject of the instruction in the passage "where one sees nothing else," and given the indirect reference in "that itself is below"—there follows immediately after this the "Instruction by means of the Ego" (ahaṅkārādeśa). It is called the "Instruction by means of the Ego" because it is taught through the ego-sense.
For the purpose of showing that the Plenum is not other than the seer, the Plenum itself is pointed out by means of the ego-sense in such passages as "I myself am below," and so forth.
Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the Self alone:
"The Self alone is below; the Self is above; the Self is behind; the Self is in front; the Self is to the south; the Self is to the north; the Self indeed is all this.
He who sees thus, who thinks thus, and who understands thus, finds delight in the Self, sports with the Self, has union with the Self, and rejoices in the Self; he becomes a self-ruler.
He has freedom of movement at will in all worlds.
But those who know otherwise than this are subject to other rulers; their worlds are perishable, and they have no freedom of movement at will in any world.

Since even the aggregate of the body and so forth is designated by the ignorant through the notion of "I," let there be no such doubt; therefore, immediately after that, the instruction regarding the Self is given: it is taught as the Self alone, in its pure and truly existent nature.

Seeing the Self alone as everything—everywhere, one, unborn, all-pervading like space, and devoid of anything else—that wise person, through reflection and higher knowledge, finds delight in the Self alone; his delight, his pleasure, is in the Self.

He who has this is one whose delight is in the Self (*ātmarati*), as well as one whose play is in the Self (*ātmakrīḍa*). Delight (*rati*) has the body alone as its means, whereas play (*krīḍā*) has external means.

The meaning is this: it is observed that in the world one plays with riches and friends; however, for the knower, it is not so. Rather, both [riches and friends] come to be solely by means of the realization of the Self.
Furthermore, the pleasure born of pairs—that is, the pleasure produced by duality—is independent of pairs for that knower.

Likewise, while the bliss of the Self for the ignorant is a bliss caused by sound and other sense-objects, it is not so for this knower. Rather, for him, everything is at all times and in every way caused by the Self alone, being independent of external objects such as the body, life, and enjoyments.
This is the meaning.
A wise person characterized in this way, being consecrated to self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) even while living, becomes indeed self-ruling (*svarāṭ*) even when the body has fallen away.
Because he becomes thus, for that very reason, he possesses the freedom to move at will (*kāmacāra*) in all worlds.

In the case of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other elements belonging to the preceding stages, it was stated that "his" [the knower's] sovereignty consists in having his own will restricted only to those [limited domains]. Since this lack of sovereignty follows logically from the fact that [those powers] are subject to gradation, the cessation of that very state—attained as self-sovereignty (*svarājya*) and freedom of will—is here described by the passage beginning with "He is self-ruling" (*sa svarāṭ*). Furthermore, those who otherwise—that is, contrary to the aforementioned vision, or even if they know exactly what was said but not correctly—become "ruled by another" (*anyarājānaḥ*); that is, they have another, a superior, as their ruler and master.
These are the "minor kings.
Furthermore, those for whom the world is subject to destruction are called "those whose world is perishable.
We have already stated that because the vision of duality has a limited scope, it is "limited" and "mortal."
Therefore, those who perceive duality possess worlds that are subject to decay, exactly in accordance with their own perception; for this very reason, they lack freedom of movement in all the worlds.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
For one who sees thus, who reflects thus, and who understands thus—verily, from the Self comes breath;
from the Self comes hope; from the Self comes memory; from the Self comes space; from the Self comes fire; from the Self comes water; from the Self come appearance and disappearance.
"Food is from the Self, strength is from the Self, discernment is from the Self, meditation is from the Self, thought is from the Self, volition is from the Self,
mind is from the Self, speech is from the Self, name is from the Self, sacred formulas are from the Self, actions are from the Self— indeed, all this is from the Self alone."
The phrase "of him, indeed, of this very one," and so forth, refers to the aforementioned knower who has attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).

Prior to the realization of the Self as Being (*sadātman*), there occurred the origination and dissolution of everything from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) down to names, all of which were perceived as other than one's own Self; however, once the realization of the Self as Being is present, these two processes now occur solely from one's own Self, and the same applies to all other worldly transactions.
For the wise person, [it arises] from the self alone.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering.
The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every way."
Thus it is said:
"He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold, five-fold, seven-fold, nine-fold, and again he is remembered as eleven-fold."
One hundred and ten, one, and twenty thousand;
through purity of food comes purity of being;
through purity of being, mindfulness becomes firm.
Upon attaining mindfulness, there is the complete liberation from all knots.
To him whose impurities have been rubbed away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra shows the further shore of darkness;
they call him Skanda.
Moreover, regarding this matter, there is also this verse as a mantra: "The seer does not see. The meaning is that the "seer" is the wise one who perceives as previously described;
he does not see death—that is, dying—nor disease, such as fever, nor even the state of suffering, which is the nature of pain.

The seer sees everything indeed as everything; he sees the Self alone as everything. From that, he attains everything in every way, by all means. Furthermore, that wise one, prior to the differentiation of creation, exists as a single unity, and at the time of creation, he becomes possessed of infinite diverse modes through the distinctions of the *saṃsṛj* and other categories. Again, at the time of dissolution, he returns to his own fundamental, ultimate state of oneness, remaining entirely independent. Thus, the text praises knowledge by describing its fruit in order to inspire interest in it.

Now, the means for the purification of the aforementioned knowledge—which serves as the cause for its correct manifestation, just as the purity of a mirror is the cause for the manifestation of the face—is taught: "In the purity of food" (*āhāra-śuddhau*). That which is brought forth is "food" (*āhāra*); it refers to the cognition of objects such as sound, which is brought forth for the enjoyment of the enjoyer. The means for its purification is taught: "In the purity of food. That which is brought forth is "food";

it is the cognition of objects such as sound, brought forth for the enjoyment of the enjoyer. The purity of that cognition, characterized by the perception of objects, is "purity of food"—that is, being untainted by the defects of passion, hatred, and delusion.
The meaning is "cognition of objects. When that impurity of food exists, there occurs purification—that is, clarity—of the *sattva* (the internal organ) which possesses it.
And when the *sattva* is purified, there arises a firm and uninterrupted mindfulness, which is non-forgetfulness, regarding the Self as the Bhūman as it has been understood.

And when that attainment of mindfulness is gained, there occurs a complete release— that is, a specific liberation or destruction— of all those knots of the heart which consist of the snares of misfortune created by ignorance, which have been hardened by the impressions of experiences throughout many other births, and which reside within the heart. Since this successive [attainment] has its root in the aforementioned purity of food, the meaning is that it must therefore be practiced.

Having stated the entire meaning of the teaching without remainder, the Śruti concludes the narrative: "To him whose impurities were washed away"— for Nārada, whose impurity (kaṣāya), consisting of defects such as passion and hatred, was like the resin of a tree because it has the nature of staining the mind, had been washed away, rubbed off, and destroyed by the alkaline solution of the practice of knowledge and dispassion— to that worthy one whose impurities were washed away, [he spoke of] the further shore of darkness, characterized by ignorance.
It shows, or has shown, the reality of the ultimate truth; this is the meaning.

Who is he? The Blessed One (Bhagavān), who knows the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going, and who knows both knowledge and ignorance—he is to be called the Blessed One.
Such is the nature of Sanatkumāra.
Those who know him speak of and call that very god Sanatkumāra by the name Skanda.
The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad-Brahmaṇa.
Now begins the eighth chapter. Om.
Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped dwelling; within it is a small space.
That which is inside that [space] is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand.

Although it has been understood in the sixth and seventh chapters that Brahman is devoid of distinctions of direction, space, time, and so forth, and is indeed one, real, non-dual, and that "all this is the Self alone," nevertheless, the intellect of those of dull understanding— which has been habituated to the notion that objects possess distinctions of direction, space, and so on— cannot be suddenly turned toward the ultimate reality. Furthermore, since the human goal is not accomplished without the realization of Brahman, [the following is taught] for the sake of that realization.
The region of the heart-lotus (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*) must be taught.

Although Brahman is the sole object of the correct cognition of "Being" (*sat*), and the fulfillment of the human goal is not achieved without realizing it, the region of the heart-lotus must nevertheless be taught for the sake of that realization. Furthermore, although the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and is the sole object of the correct cognition of "Being," nevertheless, because those of dull intellect desire it to possess qualities, its possession of qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāma*) and so forth must also be stated.

Likewise, although for those who know Brahman there occurs a spontaneous cessation from objects such as women and the like, nevertheless, the thirst directed toward sense-objects—which has been produced by the habit of indulging in such objects over many lifetimes—cannot be turned back all at once; therefore, specific means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must be prescribed.

Similarly, although for those who know the oneness of the Self there is an absence of a goer, a going, and a destination due to the destruction of the cause for the persistence of the particular ignorance, [the means must still be prescribed].
Just as lightning vanishes into the sky, as wind ceases within itself, or as fire subsides when its fuel is consumed, so too does [the soul] find rest within its own self; nevertheless,

for those whose intellects are conditioned by the notions of a traveler and a journey, and who meditate on Brahman as characterized by qualities located in the region of the heart, the departure via the artery at the crown of the head must be explained— thus the eighth chapter begins.

For the non-dual Brahman, which is the ultimate reality, is devoid of distinctions such as direction, place, quality, state of existence, or fruit; yet it appears as if non-existent to those of dull intellect.
The Śruti thinks: "Let them first abide on the path of the existent (the conventional truth), and then I shall gradually cause them to grasp that which is the ultimate reality.
Immediately thereafter, there is this small, lotus-like *puṇḍarīka*, which is like a dwelling (*veśma*) because it possesses gatekeepers and other such features.

In this city of Brahman—that is, the city of the Supreme Brahman—just as a king’s city is provided with many constituent elements such as subjects and so forth, so too is this [city] endowed with the various sense organs, mind, and intellect, which act for the sake of their Master; thus it is called the "city of Brahman.
And just as there is a palace within a king's city, so too within that city of Brahman, the body, there is a small dwelling (dahara-veśma), meaning the locus for the perception of Brahman;
just as Śālagrāma is the locus for Viṣṇu.
For it has been stated that Brahman, which is called "Being" (sat), entered this body— which is like its own modification— as the individual soul (jīva) for the purpose of manifesting name and form.

Therefore, within this house of the heart-lotus, by those who have withdrawn their senses, who are detached from external objects, and who are especially endowed with the means of celibacy and truth while meditating upon the Brahman possessing the qualities to be described, Brahman is perceived.
Such is the meaning of the section.
"Dahara" means smaller; because this dwelling (veśman) is small, that which exists within it is even smaller.
The "interior space" (antarākāśa) is Brahman, known as Ākāśa.
For it will indeed say, "It is called space (ākāśa)";
because it is bodiless, and because of its commonalities of subtlety and omnipresence, it is like space.
That which is within—that is, in the middle of—that which is called space, is what must be sought.

The meaning is that this very same [Reality] must indeed be specifically desired to be known; having sought it out through means such as relying on a guru and listening to the teachings, it must be directly realized.
If they should say to him: "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space. What is there that is to be sought, or what is to be understood?
he should reply.

If the disciples should challenge the teacher who has spoken thus, they might ask: "How is it that within this limited city of Brahman, inside the small lotus-palace, there is even less space than that?"
"What might there be in a house as large as a lotus?
What could there be in a space even smaller than that? they asked. "In this small space within, what exists? Nothing at all exists," such is the intended meaning.

"If there were indeed something [in the heart] even the size of a jujube fruit, what would be the use of searching for it or desiring to know it? What benefit would accrue to the seeker?"—to one who has spoken thus, saying that there is no purpose in that which is to be searched for or desired to be known, the Teacher would say; such is the statement of the Śruti.
As vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart.
Both heaven and earth are contained within it;
both fire and wind, both sun and moon, as well as lightning and the stars.
And whatever he has here and whatever he does not have—all that is contained within this.
Listen!
Regarding that which you say— that because the interior of the white lotus is small, what resides within it must be even smaller—
that is incorrect.
For I did not say, "The small space within this [lotus]," thinking that the space had entered the lotus-heart and was smaller than the lotus-petal.

What then? The lotus is small; the internal organ (antahkarana) situated within it conforms to its shape and is delimited by the space of the lotus. When that [space] is purified, for yogis who have withdrawn their senses, it appears like a reflection in clear water or in a mirror.

And when [the mind] is pure, the light of consciousness, which is its own essential nature and transparent, is perceived as being of that very measure; thus we said, "In this small space within," with reference to the limiting adjunct of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
But by its own nature, this space within the heart—in which one must seek and desire to understand—is as large in extent as this well-known elemental space. This is what we have stated.
Nor is it said that [Brahman] is "that great" with the intention of implying a magnitude equal to space.
What then? It is because there is no other illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) that corresponds to Brahman.
But how, then, is it understood that Brahman is not actually equal to space?

"By which the sky, heaven, and earth are pervaded"—from such scriptural passages as, "From this very Self, indeed, space was produced," and "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, is space," and so forth. Furthermore, both heaven and earth are contained within this space of Brahman, which is qualified by the adjunct of the intellect (*buddhi*); they are properly situated and established therein, just as it has been said: "as the spokes are in the hub."
Likewise, both fire and wind, and so forth, are the same;
and whatever belongs to this embodied self as its own property exists here in this world,
as well as that which does not exist as its own property.
That which has perished and that which is yet to come are said to be "non-existent," but they are not absolutely non-existent;
for it would be impossible to concentrate the mind upon what is utterly non-existent.
If they should say to him: "If everything is contained within this city of Brahman—namely, all beings and all desires—and if it is overtaken by old age or perishes, what remains of it?"

If the students should say this again to him after he has spoken thus: "In this [space]—meaning the inner space characterized by the city of Brahman—all this is contained, as well as all beings and all desires. [Objection:
How is it that the students speak of "all desires" when they were not mentioned by the teacher?
This is not a fault, for the Teacher has already stated that "whatever belongs to him here and whatever does not belong to him" refers precisely to desires;
moreover, all desires are indeed included by the word "all.

When—at which time—this body, called the city of Brahman, undergoes decay characterized by wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth, or is cut down by weapons and the like, it perishes, falls apart, and is destroyed.
What else remains beyond that?

The intention is this: just as milk, curd, oil, and so forth, which reside in a jar, perish when the jar perishes, so too, upon the destruction of the body, that which resides in the body perishes successively because of the destruction of each preceding [substratum].
When such destruction has thus occurred, what else remains beyond what has been described? Nothing remains; that is the intended meaning.
He should say:
"This does not decay through his decay; it is not slain by his being slain.
This is the true city of Brahman; within it, all desires are contained."
This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true.
For just as subjects here enter upon their lives according to instruction—
whatever end they desire, whatever region or whatever portion of land— it is precisely that upon which they subsist.
Thus urged by his pupils, that teacher should speak in order to dispel their notion.
How so?

By means of the decay of this body, [one realizes] that which is called the "interior space"—the Brahman in which everything is contained—does not decay; the meaning is that it does not undergo modification like the body.

Nor is this [Brahman] destroyed by its slaughter—that is, by the blow of weapons and the like—just as space is not; how much less so Brahman, which is subtler than even that, soundless, and intangible?

It might have been appropriate to state at this point that Brahman is not touched by the defects of the body, senses, and so forth; however, it is not stated here so that there may be no distraction from the subject at hand.
We shall explain this logically later in the story of Indra and Virocana.

This "city of Brahman" (brahmapura) is true and not false; it is Brahman itself that is the city, hence "the city of Brahman. However, what is called the body is the city of Brahman only in a figurative sense, for the purpose of indicating Brahman. In reality, however, it is indeed false.
According to the Śruti, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name";
thus, although the sprout-like body is unreal as a modification, Brahman is perceived within it, and so it is called the "City of Brahman" (brahmapura) in a conventional sense.
But the truly real City of Brahman is this very Brahman itself.

Because it is the locus of all worldly transactions, therefore, within this city of Brahman characterized by the white lotus, all desires that are sought after by you externally are contained right here within one's own self.
Thus, the intended meaning is: "Practice the very means for attaining that [Self] and abandon thirst for external objects."
This Self is your own true nature; hear its defining characteristic:
it is free from evil.
He whose evil—known as merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma)—has been struck away is "one whose evil has been struck away" (apahatapāpmā).
Likewise, he is free from old age (vijara) and free from death (vimṛtyu).
This was already stated previously: "He is not slain by the slaying of this [body]."
Why, however, is it stated again?
Even if he is not bound by old age and death that pertain to the body, there might still be another kind of connection with them; this is said for the purpose of removing such a doubt.
"Free from sorrow" (*viśoka*) means one whose sorrow has departed.
Sorrow (*śoka*) is a mental anguish caused by separation from those who are beloved and so forth.
Free from hunger (*vijighatsa*) means one whose desire for food has departed; free from thirst (*apipāsa*) means one whose desire for drink has departed.
But surely, by the quality of being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*), everything from old age up to sorrow is already excluded,
because their cause has been negated;
for they are indeed the effects of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

Alternatively, by the negation of old age and so forth, if there were an absence of effects for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), then even though they exist, they would be equivalent to non-existence; thus, their separate negation would be purposeless. True, this is so; nevertheless, one might suspect that just as there is natural bliss distinct from the effect of merit—as in the Vedic scripture, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma*)—so too, there might be a nature of suffering consisting of old age and so forth that is innate, even apart from the effects of demerit such as old age. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] proceeds.
Therefore, it is logical that, for the purpose of excluding those [qualities], there is a separate negation of old age and so forth from merit and demerit.
The mention of "old age and so forth" is intended as an illustration of all suffering.

Since the sufferings caused by evil are infinite, and since it is impossible to negate them individually, it is indeed appropriate to state "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) for the purpose of negating all suffering.
He whose desires are true and not false is Satyakāma;
for the desires of those in saṃsāra are indeed false,
whereas those of the Lord are the opposite.
Likewise, he whose volitions (saṃkalpa) regarding objects of desire are also true is "one of true volition" (satyasaṃkalpa).
These volitions and desires of the Lord have their cause in the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of pure being (sattva), like a painter;
they do not exist inherently, for it has been stated that He is "not this, not this" (neti neti).

Those who desire self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) must understand the Self exactly as it has been described—through the teachers, through the scriptures, and through its own direct realization (*ātmasaṃvedyatā*).
If it is not understood, what fault would there be?
Listen to the fault in this matter by means of an illustration.
For just as in this world subjects enter into and follow [the will of] others,
according to their instruction— just as subjects here, regarding another as their master, enter into and follow the various instructions of their own master—
what is it?
Whichever border region, frontier territory, or portion of land they desire, those seekers, in accordance with their own intellects, subsist upon that very border region and so forth;
this is the illustration regarding the fault of lack of independence in the enjoyment of the fruits of merit.

Just as here the world won by action perishes, even so there the world won by merit perishes. Therefore, those who depart from this world without having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is no freedom of movement in any worlds. But those who depart from this world having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds.

Now, there is another illustration regarding their destruction, beginning with "Just as here," and so forth. That is to say, just as in this world, for those very subjects who follow the commands of their master, the world won through service and the like is dependent on others for enjoyment and is exhausted—that is, it comes to an end—so now he concludes the point of the illustration: "In exactly the same way, in the next world, the world won by merit such as the Agnihotra sacrifice is dependent on others for enjoyment and is indeed exhausted. Thus, the defect of these [actions] has been stated; now he shows the scope [of this rule]: "That which..."
By these and other such statements [it is meant]:

those who, being qualified and competent for knowledge and action in this world—that is, in this very life—do not follow the Self as described by its characteristics, as taught by the scriptures and the teacher;
that is, without making it their own direct experience according to the instruction, they depart from this body, they pass away—those who [neglect] these aforementioned [teachings].

Without having realized the Truths and the desires established in their own Self—which are the effects of true resolve—they proceed [into the worlds]; for them, there is no freedom of will in all the worlds, a lack of autonomy, just as in the case of subjects who follow the commands of a king. This is the meaning.

Now, as for those others in this world who, having understood the Self through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, and having brought it to the state of being personally realized within themselves, proceed [to the worlds] and [attain] the true desires as previously described— for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds, just as that of a sovereign emperor in this world.
Thus ends the first section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers,
his fathers arise from his mere volition.
Endowed with that world of the ancestors, he is glorified.
"How does one come to have freedom of movement in all worlds?

It is said: he who has directly realized the Self within his heart according to the characteristics previously described, being endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) to be mentioned hereafter, and having [realized] the true desires residing therein—if, upon leaving the body, he desires the world of the fathers (*pitṛloka*), then the "fathers" are his progenitors.

Because they are objects of enjoyment by virtue of being causes of happiness, they are called "worlds" (*loka*). For one who has a desire for those worlds—that is, one who possesses a longing for a connection with those ancestors—the ancestors arise by his mere volition (*saṃkalpa*) and attain a state of connection with him.

Because he possesses true resolve due to the purity of his essence (*viśuddhasattva*), like that of the Lord (*īśvara*), he becomes endowed with that enjoyment of the world of the ancestors; "endowment" (*saṃpatti*) means the attainment of what is desired, and being enriched by that, he is exalted (*mahīyate*), meaning he is honored and prospers.
or experiences its greatness.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of mothers,
by his mere volition, mothers arise for him;
endowed with that world of mothers, he is magnified.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of brothers,
his brothers arise by his mere volition;
endowed with that world of brothers, he is magnified.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of sisters, by his mere volition his sisters arise;
endowed with that world of sisters, he is magnified.
Now, if he desires the world of friends,
his friends arise by his mere volition; endowed with that world of friends, he is glorified.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of perfumes and garlands,
by his mere volition, perfumes and garlands arise for him;
endowed with that world of perfumes and garlands, he is magnified.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of food and drink, by his mere volition food and drink arise for him;
endowed with that world of food and drink, he is magnified.
Now, if he has a desire for the world of song and instrumental music, by his mere volition, song and instrumental music arise for him;
endowed with that world of song and instrumental music, he exults.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of women, women arise for him by his mere volition;
endowed with that world of women, he rejoices.
The rest is the same.
The "mothers" are those who have passed away and served as causes for happiness by virtue of their capacity.

For it is not fitting that a yogi of pure being should have a desire for, or a connection with, mothers who were causes of suffering and the occasion for births such as village pigs; nor is such a connection logical.
Whatever end he desires,
whatever wish he wishes for, that arises for him by his mere volition alone.
Endowed with that, one is honored.

Whatever region he desires to go to, and whatever object of desire he longs for—even beyond what has been previously described—that destination is desired by him to be reached within, and that desire arises for him from mere volition (saṃkalpa) alone.
Thus, being endowed with the absence of frustration in his wishes and the attainment of his intended objects, he flourishes; this is the meaning already explained.
Thus ends the second section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
These true desires are covered by untruth;
for those true [desires] that exist, untruth is the covering.
For whoever departs from here, him one does not find here for the purpose of seeing.
In order to generate enthusiasm among practitioners for the practice of the means to meditate on the Self as described, [the author], out of compassion, says: "Alas, this is indeed a tragedy!

That these true desires, which reside within one's own Self and are capable of being attained, are covered by untruth. Although they reside within the Self and have the Self as their support, "untruth" refers to the thirst for external objects—such as women, food, drink, clothing, and so forth—and that which is caused by it.

And because it functions according to one's own whims and is caused by false knowledge, it is called "unreal" (*anṛta*). Since it is the cause for the non-attainment of true desires, it is like a covering; hence it is called a "covering" (*apidhāna*). How is it that their non-acquisition is caused by this unreal covering? [It is so] because...

It is said: Whosoever—whether a son, a brother, or a beloved one—departs from this world, goes forth, and dies, that beloved son or brother, though existing within the space of one's own heart, one does not obtain again here even while desiring to see him.
Now, whatever living beings belong to him here, and those who have departed, and whatever else he desires but does not obtain—all that he finds upon going there;
for here indeed are his true desires, covered by untruth.
It is just as if men ignorant of the spot were to pass repeatedly over a hidden treasure of gold and yet not find it.
In this very way, all these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it, for they are held back by untruth.

Furthermore, whatever living sons, brothers, or other relatives of this wise person are alive here, and whatever beloved kinsmen have passed away and died, and whatever else he desires in this world— be it clothing, food, drink, jewels, or any other object—
he obtains all that by going into this Brahman called the space of the heart, according to the method already described.
For here, in this space within the heart (*hārdākāśa*), these aforementioned true desires exist, unobstructed by a lid.

How could that be improper? It is explained thus: just as a treasure of gold—a "treasure" (*nidhi*) being so called because it is deposited (*nidhīyate*) by depositors for the sake of future retrieval—is buried beneath the earth, yet remains unknown to those who do not know the field (*akṣetrajña*).

Just as those who do not know the science of treasures (*nidhi-śāstra*) would not find a treasure—even though it is capable of being found—while walking back and forth directly over the site where the treasure lies;

even so, all these creatures, being possessed of ignorance, do not perceive that world of Brahman called the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*)—which is indeed Brahman itself—although they go there every day, at the time of deep sleep. They do not perceive it.
"May they obtain [this], thinking: 'Today I have attained the state of the world of Brahman.
For, as has been said, they are indeed excluded by untruth—that is, they are led away from their true nature by defects such as ignorance and are drawn outward.
Therefore, the intention is that this is a miserable condition for living beings, in that Brahman, though it is within their own reach, is not obtained."

This very Self is in the heart. Its etymological derivation is this: "He is here in the heart" (hṛdi ayam), therefore it is called "heart" (hṛdayam). Day after day, one who knows this goes to the heavenly world.

The word "vai" (indeed) serves to remind one of that very Self which was introduced as "the Self free from evil," so that it may be recognized as the Self intended here. That Self resides in the heart—that is, within the lotus of the heart—and is denoted by the word "ākāśa.
This is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of this very heart, and nothing else.

Since this Self dwells in the heart (*hṛdi*), it is therefore called the "heart" (*hṛdaya*); the intention is that through the well-known etymology of the name "heart," one should understand that the Self is indeed within one's own heart.
Day after day, indeed, every single day, one who knows thus—"This Self is in the heart"—attains the heavenly world, that is, the Brahman in the heart.
[Objection: But surely even one who does not know thus attains the Brahman in the heart at the time of deep sleep, since it has been said, "O dear one, at that time he becomes united with Being.
[Reply: Certainly it is so; nevertheless, there is a distinction.

Just as every living being—whether knowing or not knowing—is indeed the existent Brahman, yet the wise person, having been awakened by the instruction "That thou art," knows "I am only the Existent, I am nothing else," and thus becomes the Existent itself;
even so, although both the wise and the ignorant attain union with the Existent during deep sleep, it is said that "only the one who possesses such knowledge goes to the heavenly world.
This is the distinction, because the fruit of knowledge necessarily manifests even upon the fall of the body.
Then he said: "That serene being who, having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, appears in his own true form—this is the Self.
This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
And the name of this very Brahman is "Truth."

At the time of deep sleep, being united with his own self which is Being, he becomes perfectly serene; thus, by abandoning the turbidity born from the contact between the objects and the senses during the waking and dreaming states, he is called "serene" (*saṃprasāda*). Although this term is common to all living beings, nevertheless, because the context is "the knower of this goes to the heavenly world," the phrase "this serene one" refers specifically to him through a special effort directed toward what is proximate. Then, this body...
"Having left this body" means having risen up and abandoned the notion of the body as the self;
it is not appropriate here to understand "having risen up" as from a seat or similar object,
because of the qualification "in one's own form."
For one's own nature cannot be attained by arising from something else;
indeed, if it were to be attained, it would not be one's own nature.
This means that, having fully attained—that is, having reached the state of well-being—the light characterized as the Supreme Self, whose essence is consciousness.

One manifests in one's own true nature; prior to this attainment of one's own nature, however, through ignorance, one had identified with the body alone as another form, which is the self. It is with reference to that previous state that it is said, "in one's own nature. For bodilessness is the true nature of the Self—that which is its own supreme luminous essence. As it is said: "This serene being (saṃprasāda) is the Self; having attained its own nature, which is the supreme light, it becomes manifest.
He should say this—referring to the teacher who has been enjoined by the Śruti to instruct his disciples.

Moreover, this is the immortal and indestructible—the Plenum (bhūman). For it has been said: "That which is the Plenum is the immortal. Precisely for this reason, the Plenum is fearless, because of the absence of a second; therefore, this is Brahman.
Now, the name of this very Brahman is its designation.
"What is that truth?
Truth is indeed the non-false Brahman;
for it has been said, "That truth is the Self."
Now, for what purpose is this name stated again? It is for the purpose of praising the rule for its worship.
These, indeed, are those three syllables: *sat*, *ti*, and *yam*. That which is *sat* is immortal; that which is *ti* is mortal; and by *yam*, he holds both together.
Because he holds both together with this [syllable], therefore one who knows thus goes day by day to the heavenly world.

These, indeed, are the three syllables of the name of Brahman: *sat*, *tī*, and *yam*. In the word *satīya*, the *sa* and the *ta* [are two syllables], and *yam* is the third. The letter *ī* in *tī* is an *anubandha* (phonetic marker) used for the sake of pronunciation.
This is because they are subsequently referred to by means of short syllables alone.

In that regard, that which is the syllable *sa* is the immortal; because it denotes the immortal Brahman, the syllable *sa* is indeed the immortal, though it is pointed out as ending with the letter *t*.

Now, that which is the syllable *ti* is the mortal. Now, by that syllable which is *ya*, he restrains, controls, and subdues—meaning he brings under his own power—the two preceding syllables called the immortal and the mortal.
Because by this [word] "yam," one restrains both, therefore it is called *yām*. For by it, the two *yamas* (the twin gods) appear as if restrained.

This greatness—possessing attributes such as immortality and so forth—is attributed even to a single syllable of a name; how much more so for that which possesses a full name? Thus, it is praised for the sake of being an object of meditation (*upāsya*).
By the very etymological explanation of the name "Brahman," one who knows thus becomes a knower of the possessor of that name.
The statement, "Verily, day by day the one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world," has its meaning already explained.
Thus ends the third section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which is the Self is the bridge and the support for the non-confusion of these worlds.
Day and night do not cross this bridge; nor do old age, death, sorrow, merit, or demerit.
All evils turn back from here;
for this world of Brahman is free from evil.
Now, as for the statement "that which is the Self":

that serene confidence (*saṃprasāda*) whose characteristics have been described is further praised by means of the qualities about to be mentioned and those already stated, for the purpose of connecting it with the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
This Self, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, is like a bridge (*setu*).
*Vidhṛtiḥ* means the sustainer.

For by him, who ordains the entire world according to the agent through the regulations of distinctions such as caste (*varṇa*), stage of life (*āśrama*), actions, instruments, and results, it is sustained.
Indeed, if this universe were not sustained by the Lord, it would perish; therefore, he is the bridge (*setu*) and the sustainer (*vidhṛti*).

For what purpose is he a "bridge" (setu)? [The text] says: for the sake of the non-confusion, the non-fragmentation, and the non-destruction—meaning the non-disruption—of these [elements] beginning with earth, which are the substrates of agents and their objects.
And of what specific nature is this bridge? [The text] says: day and night—the two factors that delimit everything born—do not cross over this bridge, which is the Self (ātman).
The intention is that, unlike other transmigrating beings who are delimited by time characterized as day and night and so forth, this one is not delimited by time.
Because, according to another Vedic scripture, "the year revolves below by means of days," for this very reason, old age does not overcome—that is, does not reach—him;
likewise, neither death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds [overcome him]; here, "good and evil deeds" refers to merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
In this context, "attainment" (prāpti) is intended by the word "crossing over" (taraṇa), not "transcendence.
For the Self is the cause;
indeed, it is impossible for an effect to transcend its cause.
And everything, such as day and night, is an effect of that which exists;
for the attainment or the transgression of one thing can be effected by another,
but not by that very same thing itself.

For a jar does not reach or transcend clay; although the negation of evil and so forth was already stated previously by the passage beginning with "the Self which is free from evil," nevertheless, here this distinction is made: by the phrase "he does not cross over," the status of being an object of attainment is negated.
In that previous instance, the mere absence of old age and so forth was stated without such a distinction.

The sins already mentioned, such as day and night, and all others not mentioned, are said to be "evil" (*pāpman*); therefore, they turn back from this Self, which is like a bridge, without even reaching it—this is the meaning.
For this is the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), described as the world of Brahman because it is Brahman itself, free from evil (*apahatapāpmā*).
Therefore, having crossed this bridge, one who was blind becomes non-blind;
one who was pierced becomes unpierced;
one who was afflicted becomes unafflicted.
Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even at night one arrives at day alone;
for this world of Brahman is indeed always luminous.

And because the effects of evil, such as blindness and so forth, belong to one who possesses a body and not to one who is bodiless— therefore, having crossed and reached this Self which is a bridge, even though he was previously blind while possessing a body,

he becomes non-blind; likewise, even though he was pierced while possessing a body, upon the separation from the body, having crossed and reached the bridge, he becomes non-blind, even though he was previously blind while possessing a body.
Thus, one who was pierced while possessing a body becomes unpierced upon reaching the bridge—that is, upon attaining disembodiment.
Likewise, one who was afflicted, being subject to the afflictions of disease and so forth, becomes unafflicted.
Furthermore, because neither day nor night exist at that bridge, therefore, having crossed and reached this bridge, even the night—which is of the nature of darkness—becomes entirely day.
The meaning is that for the knower, this light of the self, whose nature is consciousness, becomes like the day—always of one form.
Shining once, it shines forever; always of one form, this world of Brahman exists by its own nature.
Therefore, those who find this world of Brahman through celibacy (brahmacarya)—for them alone is this world of Brahman;
for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds.

This being so, those who—by means of *brahmacarya*, that is, by abandoning thirst for the object of women—discover this aforementioned world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, bringing it to the state of being directly experienced by their own selves;

for those knowers of Brahman who possess the discipline of *brahmacarya*, this world of Brahman belongs, and not for others, even if they are knowers of Brahman, who remain possessed of thirst born from contact with the objects of women. This is the meaning.

"For them, there is freedom of movement in all worlds"—this has already been explained. Therefore, the intention is that this practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the supreme means for those who know Brahman.
Thus ends the fourth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which people call "sacrifice" is actually celibacy (brahmacarya);
for it is through celibacy alone that the knower finds That.
Now, that which they call "sacrifice" (iṣṭa) is indeed celibacy (brahmacarya);
for it is by means of celibacy alone that, having sacrificed, one finds the Self.

He states that for the sake of attaining that Self which has been praised through qualities such as being a bridge, another means of practice called *brahmacarya* (celibacy/study), acting as an auxiliary to knowledge, must be understood.

He praises it by means of sacrifice and so forth for the purpose of its performance: "Now, what in the world they call 'sacrifice'—that which the learned describe as the means for achieving the supreme human goal—that is indeed *brahmacarya*.
Since even the fruit of sacrifice is obtained by one who practices *brahmacarya*, therefore sacrifice itself should be understood as *brahmacarya*."

"How is celibacy a sacrifice? To this he says: because by means of celibacy alone, he who knows finds—that is, obtains—that world of Brahman which is the fruit of the sacrifice, albeit through a succession of stages; therefore, the sacrifice is indeed celibacy itself.
Because of the recurrence of the word "he who knows," the sacrifice is simply celibacy.
Now, that which they call "sacrifice" (iṣṭa) is actually celibacy (brahmacarya).
How so?
By means of celibacy alone as the instrument, having sacrificed to—that is, having worshipped—that Lord, or alternatively, having directed one's desire toward the Self, one finds that very Self.
Even that which is desired through seeking is indeed the practice of celibacy.

Now, that which they call the "sacrificial session" (sattra) is indeed celibacy (brahmacarya); for by means of celibacy alone does one find protection for the existing self. And that which they call "silence" (mauna) is indeed celibacy.
For it is indeed by means of the holy life (brahmacarya) that one, having discovered the Self, reflects upon it.

Now, that which they call *sattrāyaṇa* is indeed *brahmacarya*; for when one exists thus, through the means of *brahmacarya*, one finds protection (*trāṇa*) and preservation (*rakṣaṇa*) of the self from the Supreme Self; therefore, even the word *sattrāyaṇa* is truly *brahmacarya*.

Now, that which they call *mauna* (silence) is also *brahmacarya*; for being endowed with the means of *brahmacarya* alone, having understood the Self through the scriptures and the teacher, one subsequently reflects upon and meditates (*manute*) upon it.
Therefore, even the word "mauna" (silence) refers to celibacy itself.
Now, that which they call "the path of non-destruction" is indeed brahmacarya;
for this Self does not perish, which one finds through brahmacarya.
And that which they call "the path to the forest" is indeed brahmacarya.
Now, Ara and Nya, the two oceans, are in the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here;
there is the lake Airammadīya,
and there is the Aśvattha tree called Somasavana.
That is the invincible city of Brahmā, the golden hall built by the Lord.

Now, that which they call "the indestructible course" (*anāśakāyana*) is indeed celibacy (*brahmacarya*). For the Self that one finds through celibacy—this very Self does not perish for one who possesses the means of celibacy; therefore, even "the indestructible course" is simply celibacy.
Furthermore, that which they call "the forest course" (*araṇyāyana*) is indeed celibacy.

Because it is praised by such great means for achieving the goals of human life as follows: *araṇyāyana* (the journey to the forest) because one who practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*) journeys through the two "forests" (the ears); *yajña* (sacrifice) because it consists of knowledge; *iṣṭa* (the sacrifice of desire) because it is sought after; *sattrāyaṇa* (the sacrificial session) because it protects the virtuous; *mauna* (silence) because of its contemplative nature; *anāśakāyana* (the path of fasting) because of abstaining from food; and *araṇyāyana* (the journey to the forest) because of going to the two forests—therefore, celibacy is the supreme auxiliary cause and means for the attainment of knowledge. Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that it must be protected with effort by one who knows Brahman.
