For there, in that world of Brahman, there are indeed two well-known seas, Ara and Ṇya—likened to oceans or lakes—located in the third heaven from here, counting from this world;
that is, in the third celestial realm when reckoned starting from this earth and including the intermediate space.

In that very place is Lake Airammada, so called because its water is made of *aira*—that is, *maṇḍa*, a thick scum—and because it is filled with that; it intoxicates those who partake of it, producing joy. In that same place is the tree named Aśvattha, known as Somasavana, meaning "the distiller of Soma," or "the distiller of nectar" (*amṛta*).
And in that very same Brahmaloka is the city of Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha named Aparājitā, which cannot be conquered by others who lack the means of *brahmacarya*, as opposed to those who possess them.
And that which was specially measured out and constructed by the Lord Brahmā—that golden, i.e., made of gold, pavilion called "Prabhuvimita"—is the completion of the sentence.
Therefore, those who find these two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya)—to them alone belongs this world of Brahman;
for them, there is freedom of movement in all worlds.
For in that Brahma-world, those two oceans called Ara and Ṇya which were mentioned are found by means of the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya). This Brahma-world described here belongs only to them;
and for those knowers of Brahman who have perfected themselves through the practice of celibacy, there is freedom of movement in all worlds.
The meaning is that this does not apply at any time to others who are devoted to unchaste conduct and whose intellects are attached to external objects.

Now, some might argue: "In this context, just as someone is praised as highly worthy with words such as 'You are Indra,' 'You are Yama,' and 'You are Varuṇa,' so too, by words like 'desired' (iṣṭa) and so forth, it is not merely the cessation of thirst for objects such as women that is worthy of praise; rather, since knowledge is the means to liberation, it is that very knowledge which is praised by these terms. This is not so.
For those whose minds are carried away by thirst for external objects such as women and the like, the discriminative knowledge of the inner Self (pratyagātman) is impossible to attain.
This is established by hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts, such as: "The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self.

It is indeed appropriate to praise that [renunciation], because it must be enjoined as the means for achieving the cessation of thirst for objects such as women, which is an auxiliary cause for knowledge.
But is it not the case that, since celibacy is praised by means of sacrifices and so forth, it is understood that sacrifices and the like are means for achieving the goals of human life?
True, this is understood.

However, celibacy is not praised here by means of sacrifices and so forth with the intention of establishing sacrifices as the means for attaining the world of Brahman; rather, it is praised with reference to their well-known status as means for achieving the goals of human life.
Just as a king [is present] through Indra and others, yet it is not the case that the king's activity exists only where the activity of Indra and others exists; so it is here.

Are these oceans and so forth belonging to the world of Brahmā, and the enjoyments such as the fathers born of mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), material—consisting of earth and water as they are seen here in this world, such as oceans, trees, cities, and golden pavilions—or are they merely mental conceptions? What follows from this? If they were gross, consisting of earth and water, their containment within the space of the heart would be impossible.
Furthermore, the Purāṇic statement that in the world of Brahmā the body and other organs are composed of mind (manomaya) would be contradicted;
as would the Śruti passages beginning with "free from sorrow and great" (aśoka-mahiman).

[Objection: But would not the Purāṇic Smṛti—which states that oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells, sacrifices, Vedas, mantras, and so forth, being embodied, wait upon Brahmā—be contradicted if they were merely mental?
No;
for it is impossible for those things whose forms are well-known to possess corporeality to travel there.
Therefore, apart from their well-known corporeal forms, the oceans and so forth must assume another form, taken up by the oceans and others, which travels to the world of Brahmā.

In the case of mental construction (*kalpanā*), it is appropriate to conceive of forms such as male, female, and so forth, exactly as they are commonly known, because a connection with a mental body corresponding to them is logically possible;
for indeed, forms such as male, female, and so forth, which possess [mental] shapes, are observed to be purely mental in dreams.
[Objection: But surely those [desires] are indeed unreal;
if that were so, the scriptural statement "these desires are real" would be contradicted. [Reply: No, because it is possible for mental cognition to possess reality.
For mental cognitions in the form of women, men, and so forth, are seen in dreams.
[Objection: Surely those things seen in dreams are of the nature of impressions (*vāsanā*) from the waking state, and women and the like do not actually exist there in the dream.
[Reply: This that you say is far too little.

Even the objects of the waking state are produced solely from mental cognitions, because those waking objects consist of fire, water, and food, which are themselves produced by the power of true contemplation (*sadīkṣā*).
For it has been stated that "the worlds have their root in volition" in the passage, "Heaven and earth willed.

Furthermore, in all the Śrutis, the origin, dissolution, and subsistence of the internal Self (pratyagātman) therein are described in such passages as, "As the spokes are fixed in the hub," and so forth.
Therefore, it is indeed accepted that mental and external objects stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect, like a seed and a sprout.
Even though external objects are mental and mental objects are external, they never become unreal with respect to their own nature.
[Objection: But surely the objects perceived in a dream become unreal for one who has awakened?
This is indeed true;
however, that unreality is relative to waking consciousness and not intrinsic.
Likewise, the unreality of objects perceived in the waking state is relative to dream-consciousness and not intrinsic.

However, the mere appearance of specific forms is the cause of all false cognitions; thus, "modification is a verbal handle, a name, and is unreal; only the three forms [earth, water, and fire] are real.

Even these are unreal in terms of their specific forms, yet they are real in themselves as being of the nature of pure Being (*sanmātra*). Prior to the awakening to the Self that is Existence, everything—even within one's own sphere—is indeed real, like objects seen in a dream; thus there is no contradiction.
Therefore, the Brahma-world, the forests, the fathers, and the objects of desire are purely mental.

The meaning is that because they are free from impurity like the enjoyment of external objects, being produced by the volition of pure *sattva*, they are unsurpassed pleasures and real for the lords (*īśvara*).

Even when there is awakening to the existent, true Self, things such as snakes imagined upon a rope attain only the nature of the existent Self; thus, they are indeed real by virtue of the existent Self.
Thus ends the fifth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, those channels of the heart—white, blue, yellow, and red—exist for the sake of the subtle, tawny [light].
That sun is indeed tawny; it is white, it is blue, it is yellow, and it is red.

But for one who, endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and having abandoned the false thirst for external objects, worships the Brahman characterized by the aforementioned qualities situated within the lotus of the heart—for him, this departure by means of the channel (*nāḍī*) leading to the crown of the head must be explained; thus the section on the channels (*nāḍī-khaṇḍa*) begins:
"Now, those which are these channels connected to the heart, the site of the worship of Brahman, which is shaped like a lotus..."

Emerging from all sides from the lump of flesh that is the heart, like rays from the orb of the sun, these [channels] remain and exist filled with the essence of a subtle fluid (*aṇiman*) characterized by a specific color—namely, tawny (*piṅgala*); the meaning is that they persist in that very form.
Similarly, the phrase "filled with the essence" is to be supplied everywhere for white, blue, yellow, and red as well.

Due to contact with the solar heat known as *pitta*, which is produced by digestion, and with a small amount of *kapha*, the solar heat becomes tawny (*piṅgala*) and is designated as *pitta*. That same [heat] becomes blue due to a predominance of *vāta*, and it becomes white due to a predominance of *kapha*. When there is an equilibrium of *kapha*, it is yellow (*pīta*).
It is red due to an abundance of blood;
or rather, the specific colors should be investigated from medical science as to how they come to be.
However, scripture states that these specific colors belong to that light of the sun which has entered into the channels precisely because of its connection with the sun.
How so? This sun is tawny in color; yet this very sun is white, this is blue, this is yellow, and this is red—the sun itself.
Just as a great highway stretches out and goes to both villages—this one and that one—so too these rays of the sun go to both worlds—this one and that one.
They extend from yonder sun and have entered into these channels;
they extend from these channels and have entered into yonder sun.
Regarding how that [Self] is connected internally with the channels, he provides an illustration:

"In this regard, just as in the world a great path—a wide highway—stretched out and pervading, goes to both [villages], this one nearby and that one distant and far away; just as the illustrative example of the great path enters both villages, even so these..."
The rays of the sun go to both worlds— that solar orb and this person— having entered into both,
just like a great highway.
How so?
From that solar orb, they extend and become continuous.
They have crept—that is, gone and entered—into these internal channels (nāḍīs) of the aforementioned colors, such as tawny and so forth.
From these channels, they extend and proceed, existing as a continuous stream within that [orb].
Because rays possess both genders, they are referred to by the pronoun "te" (they).
When, being thus asleep, composed, and serene, one does not perceive any dream,
then he has entered into these channels;
no evil whatsoever touches him.
For at that time, he becomes endowed with splendor.
This being so, at that time and in that state when this living self (jīva) is asleep—
this qualification "entire" (samasta) is used because sleep is of two kinds;
it means that all the functions of the organs have been withdrawn.

Therefore, due to the absence of the turbidity produced by contact with external objects, he becomes perfectly clear and serene. For this very reason, he does not perceive—that is, he does not experience—the dream-cognition, which is mental and appears in the form of objects. This is the meaning.

When he has thus fallen asleep within these aforementioned channels (nāḍīs) which are filled with solar radiance, then he has "crept" or entered; the meaning is that, by means of the channels acting as gateways, he has gone to the space of the heart (hṛdayākāśa).
For there is no perception of dreams elsewhere than upon reaching Being (sat); therefore, by implication, the locative case in "in the channels" (nāḍīṣu) is transformed into an instrumental sense.
No one—meaning not even any evil in the form of merit or demerit (dharma-adharma)—touches him who has reached Being, because at that time the Self abides in its own true nature.

For evil touches one who is distinguished by a body and senses by bestowing the effects of pleasure and pain; however, no evil at all dares to touch one who has attained Being and abides in his true nature, because such a one is not an object [of evil]. Indeed, one thing becomes the object of another, but for one who has attained Being, there is no state of being "other" (anyatva) with respect to anything whatsoever.

We have already stated in the sixth chapter that the falling away from one's own true nature—the soul’s transition toward the states of waking and dreaming, and the perception of external objects—is caused by the burning of the seed of ignorance, desire, and action by the fire of the knowledge of Brahman; this should be understood here as well.
When one has thus fallen asleep, one becomes completely filled and pervaded on all sides by the solar light located within the channels (nāḍīs).
Therefore, at that time, his organs do not extend out through the channels of the eyes and other senses for the enjoyment of external objects;
consequently, it is logical that because of the cessation of the organs, he remains established in his own self and does not perceive dreams.
Then, when he has been brought to such weakness, those sitting around him say, "Do you know me? Do you know me?
as long as he has not yet departed from this body.
He knows only that much.

This being so, at that time, when Devadatta—having been brought to, or reached, a state of weakness, a state of frailty in the body caused by disease or the like, or a state of emaciation caused by old age and the like—that is to say, when he is about to die—his relatives sit around him, surrounding him on all sides, and say: "Do you know me, your son? Do you know me, your father? and so forth.
As long as that person who is about to die has not yet departed from this body—that is, as long as he has not gone out—he continues to know his sons and others.
Then, when he departs from this body,
he ascends upwards by means of these very rays;
he passes away either saying "Om" or simply "Hā."
As quickly as one might direct the mind, so does it go to the sun;
this indeed is the gate to the world, the path for the wise, and the obstruction for the ignorant.
Now, when he departs from this body— this being a qualification of the action—

he then ascends upwards by means of these very rays as previously described, toward the world acquired according to his karma, if he is ignorant; but the other, the wise one, endowed with the aforementioned means, meditating on the Self with the syllable *oṃ*, either proceeds as previously stated, or indeed just so.
The intention is that if he is a knower, he goes upward; otherwise, he goes horizontally.

"Is measured" (mīyate) means "is measured out" (pramīyate), which is to say, he goes. That knower, when about to depart, reaches the sun in as much time as it takes for the mind to be projected—that is, in the time required for the projection of the mind; the meaning is that he goes quickly, and not [in the manner previously described].
The intended meaning is "in that very amount of time.
For what purpose does he go to the sun? It is said: it is well known that the sun is the door to the world of Brahman; by means of that door, the knower goes to the world of Brahman.
Therefore, it is called the "means of entry" (*prapadana*) for the wise, because they enter the world of Brahman through this door.
"Nirodha" means cessation; it is so called because for the ignorant, cessation occurs from this sun.

The meaning is that, being obstructed by the solar heat within the body itself, they do not depart at all through the vein at the crown of the head, as indicated by the verse beginning with "viṣvaṅṅanyā."
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upward by that, one attains immortality; the others lead in all directions for departing, for departing."
Regarding this matter as it has been explained, there is this verse, which is a mantra:
"One hundred and one"—that is, one hundred and one principal channels connected to the heart, which is a mass of flesh;
for the channels of the body are infinite in number.

Of these, one has issued forth from the head; going upwards by that [path], one attains immortality, which is the state of being immortal. But the other channels—those spreading in various directions, moving sideways, and going upwards—are the gateways for wandering through saṃsāra;
they do not lead to immortality. Rather, the meaning is that they exist solely for the purpose of departing according to one's karma.
The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the section.
Thus ends the sixth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:

"That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand.
He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires," so said Prajāpati.

Now, regarding that which was said: "This serene being (saṃprasāda), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form—this is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman"—in this regard, what is this serenity, and how is it attained? And how is it to be thoroughly investigated as it departs from this body? This is indeed a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) and not an original injunction (apūrvavidhi).
The meaning is that he is to be sought after and desired to be known in this manner;
for seeking and desiring to know have a visible purpose.
And he will demonstrate this visible purpose more than once with the words, "I do not see anything here to be enjoyed."

Furthermore, since the visible fruit of attaining the true nature of the Self—which is being perceived through the attributes of the body and so forth by means of another's form—is the cessation of erroneous apprehension, it is proper that this injunction has the purpose of restriction (*niyama*); however, an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) like those concerning the *agnihotra* and other rites is not possible here.
Both the gods and the asuras became aware of this.
They said, "Come, let us seek that Self, by seeking which one obtains all worlds and all desires.
Of the gods, Indra set out; of the asuras, Virocana.
Agreeing with one another, they both approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands.
The purpose of the narrative beginning with "Then both" has been stated.
It is said that both—the gods and the asuras (the *devāsurāḥ*)—heard this speech of Prajāpati, which had come down through tradition and entered the range of their own ears; they understood it.
Having understood this speech of Prajāpati, what did they do? That is being told: the gods spoke thus to one another.
And the Asuras in their own assembly said, "Alas! If you have permission, let us seek that Self which was spoken of by Prajāpati;

let us perform the search for that Self, having sought which one obtains all worlds and all desires. Having said this, Indra indeed remained as king himself among the gods, and having established the other gods and all his enjoyments and possessions, he departed.
Virocana, the leader of the asuras, likewise departed toward Prajāpati with his physical body alone;
this demonstrates that teachers must be approached with humility,
for [the pursuit of knowledge] is weightier than even sovereignty over the three worlds.

Since the two kings of the gods and the asuras, though worthy of noble enjoyments, had thus accepted a teacher, they— reportedly being unaware of one another and not communicating with each other, yet displaying mutual jealousy regarding the fruit of their knowledge— approached Prajāpati with fuel in hand, carrying loads of sacrificial wood; they dwelt there for thirty-two years as religious students (*brahmacarya*).
Prajāpati said to them both: "Desiring what have you dwelt here? They replied:

"That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what must be sought, that is what one must desire to understand."
"He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires"—thus they declare the word of the Blessed One;
desiring that [Self], we have come hither.
Having gone there, the two of them dwelt as students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*), devoted to service for thirty-two years.
Prajāpati, knowing their intention, said to them: "Desiring what, with what purpose in mind, have you dwelt here? Being thus addressed, they both replied:
"The learned teach that which is the Self (*ātman*) and so forth according to the words of the Blessed One; therefore, desiring to know that Self, we have dwelt here."

Although they were previously possessed of mutual jealousy before approaching Prajāpati, nevertheless, having abandoned defects such as passion, hatred, delusion, and envy due to the gravity of the purpose for attaining knowledge, they lived the life of a student (brahmacarya) under Prajāpati;
by this, the greatness of the knowledge of the Self was proclaimed.
Prajāpati said to them both: "This person who is seen in the eye, this is the Self," he said.
"This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
Then [the two asked]: "Venerable sir, that which is perceived in the water and that which is in the mirror—which of these is it?"
"This very one, indeed, is perceived within all these ends," he said.

Having perceived that those two ascetics were pure of taint and fit [for instruction], Prajāpati said: "This person who is in the eye, seen by those whose vision has turned inward and whose passions have been worn away—this is the Self (Ātman) characterized by the qualities of being free from evil and so forth, of whom I spoke previously; through the knowledge of whom there is the attainment of all worlds and desires. This is the Immortal called 'Bhama' (Splendor); for this very reason it is 'Abhaya' (Fearless), and for this very reason it is 'Brahma,' the most ancient and great.
Now, having heard these words of Prajāpati, "The person in the eye is seen," the two of them took the person to be the reflected image.
Having grasped this, they asked Prajāpati for the sake of firm conviction:

"Now, O Venerable One, regarding that which is perceived all around in water, and that which is perceived as the form of one's own reflection in a mirror, in a sword, and so forth—which among these is the one spoken of by your honors? Or is it one and the same in all of them?"
Being thus questioned, Prajāpati said: "It is indeed this very one whom I have described as the seer in the eye.
Having kept this in mind, he said: "He is perceived within all these ends and in their midst.
Now, how is it appropriate for Prajāpati, being a teacher free from all defects, to permit such a contrary understanding on the part of his disciple?
That is true; it was not permitted.
How so?
Because Indra and Virocana had superimposed upon themselves the qualities of scholarship, greatness, and wisdom, and were thus renowned in the world accordingly.

Prajāpati considers that if those two were told by him, "You two are deluded and have grasped the matter incorrectly," then distress would arise in their minds; and from that mental dejection, there would be a loss of enthusiasm for further hearing, grasping, and internalizing the teaching. Therefore, he thinks that the two disciples must be protected.
"Take it for now; I shall remove it by means of the analogy of the water in the ladle.
[Objection: But surely it is not proper to speak such a falsehood as "this very one";
[Response: Yet no falsehood has been spoken.
How so?

Because Prajāpati himself stated that the person in the eye is more closely situated in the mind than the shadow-self grasped by the disciple, and because of the Vedic text, "He is within all, the innermost of all.
He spoke of that very one when he said, "This one indeed," and therefore nothing false was spoken by Prajāpati.
And thus, in order to eliminate their erroneous apprehension, he says:
Thus ends the seventh section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Look at yourselves in a bowl of water; whatever of the self you do not understand, tell that to me.
They both looked into the bowl of water.
Prajāpati said to them both, "What do you see? They replied, "O Venerable Sir, we see this entire self of ours exactly as it is, even to the hair and the nails."

"Having looked at yourselves in a water-filled bowl or similar vessel, tell me—that which you two do not recognize as the Self when seeing it there—explain that to me. Thus addressed, they both indeed looked into the water-bowl; they performed the act of looking.

When they had done so, Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see? To which they replied, "Tell me that. Having been thus addressed, they looked into the water-jar and did not report it to Prajāpati, saying, "This was not known by us. Since they had not reported it—the very cause of their ignorance—Prajāpati again asked, "What do you see? What is the intention behind this?
It is said in reply: the doubt did not arise for them that "this is unknown to us two," because the conviction regarding the self in the shadow-self was indeed certain;
for it will later state, "With their hearts calmed, they both departed.
For indeed, a state of having a calmed heart is not possible with respect to a desired object that is not certain.
Therefore, he did not say, "This was unknown to us both.
Furthermore, since disciples who grasp things erroneously must not be neglected, he himself asked, "What do you see?
and he will later say, "Well-adorned," and so forth, in order to remove their erroneous conviction.
The two of them said, "Venerable sir, we see this entire self of ours as it truly is, down to the very hairs and nails;
for just as we ourselves, O venerable sir, possess hair, nails, and so forth, even so do we see this likeness of ours in the water-jar, complete with hair, nails, and the rest."
Prajāpati said to them both, "Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, look into a pan of water.
Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, they both looked into the pan of water.
Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see?"
Prajāpati spoke to them again in order to remove their conviction that the reflection was the Self:

"Having become well-adorned, as you were in your own home—well-dressed, wearing costly garments, and well-groomed with hair and nails clipped—look into a vessel of water so that your grasping at the reflection as the Self may be removed. By this, it is understood that the capacity to produce a reflection belongs not only to adventitious things such as fine ornaments and fine clothes, but also to the body itself, just as it did previously when those items were attached to the body.
Furthermore, the parts of the body such as hair and nails, which were previously intended to be permanent and uncut, possessed the quality of casting a shadow;

however, when they are cut, no shadow of the hair, nails, and so forth is seen. Therefore, just like the hair and nails, it is established that the body is subject to coming into being and passing away.
Thus, it is established that the body—which is the cause of what is seen in a water-jar and the like—is not the Self. In a water-jar and the like... [the reflection is seen].
Because it casts a shadow, like ornaments and other such things attached to the body;

not only this much, but by this [reasoning], whatever is considered one's own—such as pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and delusion—is to be understood as non-self because it is occasional, like the nails and hair.
Thus, having heard the illustration of the well-adorned person given by Prajāpati for the purpose of removing all false attachments without exception, [the gods] understood accordingly.

Since even after they had performed the ritual, their misconception regarding the Self as being the reflection did not depart, it is understood that Indra and Virocana were thus obstructed by some inherent defect of their own, which prevented the discriminative knowledge [of the Self] from arising.
Therefore, he questioned them, as before, with firm conviction: "What do you see?"
The two of them said, "Venerable sir, just as we here are well-adorned, well-dressed, and groomed, even so these two, venerable sir, are well-adorned, well-dressed, and groomed.
"This is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
With their hearts at peace, the two of them departed.

The two of them accepted it exactly as it was stated, "This is so," and as before, they became even more firmly convinced of their misconception, thinking, "Just as we ourselves are distinguished by fine ornaments and the like, so too are these two shadow-selves.
Furthermore, while they were seeking further particulars regarding that Self whose characteristic was previously described as "the Self free from evil," [it was said]: "That which is this..."

When it was directly pointed out that "the person is seen in the eye," and even when the illustration of the water-jar and the well-adorned woman was given to remove the contrary grasp [of the Self], the contrary grasp did not depart due to the lack of awakening to the true nature of the Self.

Therefore, thinking that the capacity for discriminative knowledge was obstructed by some personal defect of his own, [Janaka] kept the Self exactly as he had conceived it in his mind and said: "This is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
Prajāpati is as before;
however, he did not intend that [specific] Self.

For both [disciples] had been refined by hearing the definition of the Self beginning with "That which is the Self," by the scriptural teaching of the Person in the eye, and by the logical reasoning concerning the water-vessel and so forth.

Thinking that by repeatedly remembering all his words, their discrimination regarding the Self would arise spontaneously through the destruction of obstacles, and desiring to avoid causing mental distress to them during the instruction on celibacy, Prajāpati overlooked them even as they departed with the conviction that they had already achieved their purpose.
The meaning is that those two, Indra and Virocana, had their hearts calmed and their hearts satisfied—that is, they were of the conviction that they had achieved their purpose.
However, this was not merely tranquility;
for if tranquility alone had arisen in them, their erroneous grasp would have vanished, yet they departed and went away.
Having observed them both, Prajāpati said:

"They depart without having perceived the Self and without having realized it; whichever of these two—whether gods or asuras—shall follow this teaching as their secret doctrine (upaniṣad), they will perish.
With a tranquil heart, Virocana went to the asuras.
To them he proclaimed this secret doctrine (upaniṣad): "The Self alone is to be magnified here; the Self is to be served.
By magnifying the Self alone here and by serving the Self, one attains both worlds—this one and the one beyond."

Fearing that once King Indra and Virocana had departed, their attachment to worldly enjoyments might cause them to forget what was said, and desiring to remove their mental distress through direct speech regarding that which is not directly perceptible, [the Teacher] observed them as they were traveling far away and thought: "Just as the passage beginning with 'The Self which is free from evil' reached their ears, so too shall this reach the range of their hearing."
Prajāpati said:

"Without perceiving the Self as described by its characteristics, without realizing it through direct personal experience, and having formed contrary convictions, these two, Indra and Virocana, are departing and going away.
Therefore, whichever of the two—whether gods or asuras—possess this *upaniṣad*, that is, the knowledge of the Self which has been grasped from them, they shall be those who have such a realization."
The meaning is that they will come to this certainty.
What will they do? They will be defeated; the meaning is that they will be defeated from the path to the highest good (*śreyas*), cast out, and destroyed.
Of the two kings of the gods and the asuras who were going to their own abodes, it was Virocana, the king of the asuras, who, with a peaceful heart, went to the asuras.
Having gone to those Asuras, he spoke this Upaniṣad—that secret doctrine concerning the body as the self—which had been taught to them.
[The Asuras thought: "The father has declared that the self is merely the body.

Therefore, in this world, the body alone is the self; it is to be honored, worshipped, served, and attended upon. By honoring and serving the self—the body—in this world, one attains both worlds: this one and the next.
And "this" refers to both this world and the next world; the king's intention is that all worlds and all objects of desire are included within these two alone.
Therefore, even today they say of one who does not give here, who lacks faith, and who does not sacrifice, "Alas, he is an Asura!
For this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Asuras:
they adorn the corpse of the deceased with alms-food, clothing, and ornaments.
For by this means, they believe they will conquer that world.

Therefore, because that tradition continues even today, the learned in this world, feeling distressed, say of one who does not give—that is, who fails to practice charity, lacks the habit of sharing, and is faithless—meaning devoid of faith regarding meritorious deeds—and who does not sacrifice according to his ability—that is, whose nature is not to perform sacrifices: "This man is truly asuric, for such is his very character; alas! they say.
For this is the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the Asuras, characterized by lack of faith and so forth.
Being consecrated by that secret doctrine, they prepare the corpse—the dead body—of the deceased through alms consisting of perfumes, garlands, food, and the like;
through clothing such as garments and the like, by way of covering it; and through ornaments, by means of making banners, flags, and so forth. It is by this [means] that they consecrate it.
By means of the funeral rites for a corpse, they think they will conquer that world which is to be attained after death.
Thus ends the eighth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, Indra, indeed, even before reaching the gods, perceived this fear:
"Just as this [Self] here becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, and well-dressed when it is well-dressed..."
"In a decorated [body], he becomes decorated; likewise, in this blind [body] he becomes blind, in a lame one he becomes lame, and in a maimed one he becomes maimed.
Following the destruction of this very body, he perishes.
I see no object of enjoyment here."

Now, it is said that Indra, even before reaching the gods, while traveling and repeatedly recollecting the words of his preceptor due to being endowed with divine fortitude and other such qualities, beheld— saw— this fear about to be described, which arose from the motive of grasping the Self.
A portion of that reasoning for which the illustration of the water-jug was stated by Prajāpati became manifest in Maghavan’s intellect.
And by what means did he perceive the fault in grasping the shadow-self?
How so?
Just as indeed, when this body is well-adorned, the shadow-self also becomes well-adorned, and when [the body] is well-clothed...

And just as one who is well-dressed becomes adorned when the body-parts such as nails and hair are removed— so that the shadow-self (*chāyātman*) also becomes adorned, being itself devoid of nails, hair, and so forth— in exactly the same way, this shadow-self, because its status as a body-part is equal to that of the nails, hair, and so on, becomes blind when the eyes are lost in a blind person, and lame when [the legs] are lame.
A *srāma* is said to be one-eyed because he has become blind in that eye;
or, one whose eyes or nose constantly discharge fluid is a *srāma*. A *parivṛkṇa* is one whose hand is severed or whose foot is severed.
When the body is wounded or mangled, the shadow-self likewise becomes so;
thus, following the destruction of this body, it perishes as well.
With sacrificial fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him:
"O Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart along with Virocana, desiring what have you come back?"

He said: "Just as indeed, O Venerable Sir, this [self] here becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-dressed when it is well-dressed, and well-groomed when it is well-groomed; even so, it becomes blind when this [body] is blind, lame when it is lame, and maimed when it is maimed."
"Following the destruction of this very body, he perishes; I see no enjoyment for myself in this."

"Therefore, I see no fruit of enjoyment here in this view of the self as a reflection, nor in this view of the self as the body. Having thus determined the defect in the views of the self as either a bodily reflection or the body itself, he returned with fuel in his hand to dwell in studentship (*brahmacarya*). Prajāpati said to him: "O Maghavan, since you have departed with a peaceful heart, having gone away along with Virocana, desiring what have you come back again?"
Even though he already knew, Prajāpati questioned him again in order to make Indra’s intention clear, just as one might say, "Come to me with what you know.
And so, Indra made his own intention manifest by saying, "As indeed this [body]...
and so forth; and Prajāpati approved, saying, "It is exactly so."
Now, since the report regarding the Person in the Eye was equal for both, why did Indra grasp the shadow of the body as the Self, while Virocana grasped the body itself?
Regarding this, it is considered as follows:

Just as in the case of Indra—who, while remembering Prajāpati’s words concerning the water-jar and so forth, had not yet reached the gods—there occurred, through the understanding of his teacher’s instruction, the grasping of the shadow-self and the perception of its defects.
It was not so for Virocana; rather, he perceived the body itself as the Self, nor did he perceive any defect in it.

In the same way, Indra’s and Virocana’s respective graspings of the shadow-self and the body depended on the relative smallness or greatness of the defects that obstructed their capacity to receive knowledge.

Because Indra had fewer defects, he accepted the literal meaning of the scriptural statement, "That which is seen," out of faith. The other [Virocana], however, set aside the body—which is the cause of the shadow—and grasped the literal meaning of the scriptural statement through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as it was spoken by Prajāpati.
"It is this [the body]," he thought, because of the preponderance of defects.

Just as when two garments, one blue and one not blue, are seen in a mirror, the one that appears blue is called "the precious garment" due to the reflection, yet it is the garment itself that is meant and not the reflection—such was Virocana’s intention.

For it has been demonstrated in another Vedic passage that the determination of the meaning of words depends solely on the qualities and defects of one's own mind, even when the hearing is identical: "Be self-controlled, give, and be compassionate," where the mere hearing of the letter *da* leads to different understandings.
The signs as well become auxiliary factors that are entirely concordant with it.
"Even so it is, O Maghavan," he said.
"But I shall explain this very matter to you further.
Dwell for another thirty-two years."
He lived there for another thirty-two years;
then he said to him:

"Prajāpati said: 'O Maghavan, it is exactly as you have understood; this is not the shadow-self. That Self which was introduced by me and spoken of is indeed that very Self; though it was previously explained to you, I shall explain it to you again.
For, although what was explained once reached the scope of comprehension for those free from defects, you did not grasp it due to some deficiency.'"
"Since you possess the capacity to grasp what is connected [to this knowledge], therefore dwell for another thirty-two years in order to exhaust those remaining defects.
Having said this, he spoke to him who had lived accordingly and whose defects were exhausted.
Thus ends the ninth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"He who moves about in sleep, being honored—this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
With his heart calmed, he set out.
Even before reaching the gods, he perceived this fear:
"Even if this body becomes blind, he remains sighted; even if it becomes lame, he remains able to walk."
This [self] is not defiled by the defect of that [body].
That Self, characterized by the qualities of being free from evil and so forth, which was explained in the passage beginning with "He who is in the eye," is this very one.
Who is he?
He is the one who, being honored—that is, being worshipped—by women and others while dreaming, moves about; the meaning is that he experiences various kinds of dream-enjoyments.
"This is the Self," he said; the rest is the same as before. Having been told this, Indra departed with a peaceful heart.
But even before reaching the gods, as before, he perceived fear in this Self as well.
How so?
Although this body runs while blind, the one who is the self in dream is not blind;
although this body is lame, he is not lame. Indeed, this self in dream is not defiled by the defect of this body.
It is not slain by its being slain; it does not waste away by its wasting away;
yet they do indeed slay it.
As if concealing it,
as if feeling aversion,
or even as if weeping, one thinks: "I see nothing here that can be enjoyed."
With fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him:
"O Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back?"
He said:
"Venerable sir, even if this body becomes blind, he [the self] remains sighted; if it becomes lame, he remains not lame.
Indeed, he is not affected by its defects."
It is not slain by his slaying;
it does not waste away by his wasting away. Yet, they seem to slay it.
It is as if covering [the mind];
it is as if experiencing what is unpleasant;
it is even as if weeping.
"I see no enjoyment here," [Maitreyi replied].
"It is just so, O Maghavan," he said.
"But I shall explain this very same thing to you further."
"Stay for another thirty-two years.
He stayed for another thirty-two years,
and then he said to him:

Nor is he killed by the killing of this [body], just as the shadow-self is not; nor does he suffer exhaustion through the exhaustion of this [body]. That which was introduced at the beginning of the chapter merely on the basis of scriptural authority—namely, "he does not age with its aging," and so forth—is here established by means of logical reasoning. To begin with, he is not possessed of the defects of the body like the shadow-self; however, they do indeed kill him.

The word *eva* has the sense of *iva* (as if). It should be understood as "certain people seem to kill him," because it is impossible for Prajāpati, who is being accepted as an authority, to be rendered a speaker of falsehood.
How could Indra, who regards Prajāpati as an authority, render false this statement of Prajāpati’s, namely, "This is the immortal"?
One might object: "But when Prajāpati spoke of the shadow-person, Indra pointed out the defect that 'when this body perishes, he perishes along with it'; would it not be the same here?
It is not so.
Why?
If one thinks, "This person who is seen in the eye [is the Self]," then how could he, having taken Prajāpati as his authority, go again with fuel in hand to hear [the teaching]?
And yet, he did go.
Therefore, one considers that the Self consisting of shadow was not what Prajāpati spoke of;
and thus it has been explained that "the Seer is seen in the eye.
Likewise, [the reflection] seems to obscure or seem to drive away [the original]; and similarly, due to the death of a son or other [relatives], it becomes as if it experiences what is unpleasant.
Moreover, it seems to weep of its own accord.
[Objection: But surely it experiences what is unpleasant; how then can it be said that it "seems" to experience it?
[Reply: It is said because the statement regarding its being immortal and fearless would otherwise be untenable.
And because of another scriptural passage stating, "It is as if it meditates.
If it is argued that this contradicts direct perception, we say no; for such a contradiction is possible through delusion, just like the perception of the body as the self.
"Let it be for now whether he experiences what is unpleasant or not;
I see no object of enjoyment here.
The intention is that even in the knowledge of the self as a dreamer, one does not obtain a desired fruit. "It is exactly so according to your intention"—this is the remainder of the sentence.

Because it was intended that the Self possesses the qualities of immortality and fearlessness, Prajāpati— thinking that although he had stated it twice, [the student] did not grasp it correctly due to reason, and therefore there must still be some obstructing cause for him as before— instructed him, saying, "Dwell for another thirty-two years in the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) in order to exhaust that [obstruction]."
To him who had dwelt there in such a manner and whose impurities were exhausted, I said:
Thus ends the tenth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"When one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream—this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
With his heart calmed, he set out.
But even before reaching the gods, he perceived this fear:
"Indeed, this one does not now truly know himself as 'this is I'."
"In this way, these beings simply go to their destruction;
I see nothing here that can be enjoyed."
With sacrificial fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him, "Maghavan, since you have gone forth with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back?
He replied, "Indeed, O Venerable One, even now this Self does not know itself thus: 'This is I.'"
"In this way, these beings do not exist;
they simply pass into destruction.
I see nothing here that can be enjoyed."

Having said "As before, but this one indeed to you... and so forth, he explained the passage beginning with "Now, when one is thus asleep... and so on: "He who is the seer in the eye and who moves about being honored in the dream state—he, when asleep, unified and serene, does not perceive any dream; he is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman"—thus expressing his own intended meaning.
Even there, Maghavā perceived a fault.
How so?
He said: "No; for even while in the state of deep sleep, this very Self does not, at present—that is, now—truly know itself; it does not know itself in this way."
How so?
"I am this" and "these are those beings"— it is not thus,
as it is in the waking state or in a dream.
Therefore, "destruction as it were" (vināśamiva) should be understood as "destruction itself" (vināśam eva), as explained previously.
The intended meaning is that he becomes as if gone away (apītaḥ), that is, as if destroyed (vinaṣṭaḥ).
For when knowledge exists, the existence of the knower is apprehended, but not when knowledge is absent.

And since no knowledge is perceived in one who is in deep sleep, the intention is that [the self] is as if destroyed; however, one who desires the authority of the scriptural declarations of immortality and fearlessness does not believe in the actual destruction of the self.
"It is even so, O Maghavan," he said.
"I shall explain this very same thing to you further, but not otherwise than this."
"May I dwell for another five years.
He dwelt for another five years;
thus they became one hundred and one.
This is what they say:
"For one hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) under Prajāpati;
to him, [Prajāpati] spoke."

Having said, "It is exactly as before," [the teacher replied]: "That very Self which I have described to you through three stages—do not think it is anything other than this; what else could it be? Rather, I shall explain this very same one. However, there remains a slight defect in you; therefore, dwell for another five years in order to exhaust that. Having been told this, he did accordingly. To him, Maghavan, whose defects such as the *kaṣāyas* had been rubbed away, he then spoke of the true nature of the Self—which is free from connection with the defects of the three states and characterized by freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth.
Those amounted to one hundred and one years; they became completed.

What the learned in the world say—that Maghavān indeed dwelt as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) with Prajāpati for one hundred and one years—is shown by this [passage] beginning with "thirty-two," etc.; thus, departing from the narrative form, it is stated by the Śruti.

Thus, he praises self-knowledge, saying that it is indeed even more weighty than the state of Indra himself; for even by the great Indra, with immense effort and the exertion of a hundred and one years, this knowledge of the Self was attained, and therefore there is no other goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha) higher than this.
Thus ends the eleventh section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"O Maghavan, this mortal body is indeed seized by death;
it is the substratum for this immortal, bodiless Self."
"Indeed, one who possesses a body is subject to the pleasant and the unpleasant.
For as long as one has a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
But when one is indeed bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him."
O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal and subject to death.
As for what you think— that the Self described by me as characterized by the eye, its support, and so forth, and characterized by supreme serenity, simply perishes when it has entered [the body]—
listen to the reason for that.
This body is indeed mortal and perishable;
moreover, it is constantly seized and swallowed by death.

When it is said that "it is mortal" in the sense that it dies only at some time or other, such terror does not arise as when it is said that it is "already swallowed" and "constantly pervaded" by death. This distinction is stated for the purpose of generating detachment (*vairāgya*).
"Seized by death"—
how indeed can one who has become detached from the identification with the body turn back?
Here, the term "body" is used to include the senses and the mind.

This "body" of this serene being (*saṃprasāda*) refers to that which is understood as having three stations, which is immortal, and which is devoid of the attributes of death and so forth pertaining to the body, the senses, and the mind.

Since its bodilessness is already established by the term "immortal," the further statement "of the bodiless one" is intended to ensure that the Self does not possess parts or material form like air and other elements.
Or else, for the Self who exists as the Seer, there has arisen a substratum produced through the sequence of fire, water, and earth.
"Adhiṣṭhāna" (the locus) means that which, having entered in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), presides over this [body].

This locus—which is of such a nature, eternally seized by death, and characterized by pleasure and pain because it is produced by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*)—is what one possesses when presided over by it; thus, one becomes "embodied.

For the Self, whose true nature is bodiless, that very state of being embodied arises from the lack of discrimination, thinking "I am this body" or "this body is I. Therefore, being embodied, one is "seized" or "devoured" by pleasure and pain.
This is well known:

for one who possesses a body and who, regarding the pleasure and pain caused by the contact with and separation from external objects, thinks "these belong to me," there is no removal, destruction, or cessation of those two as they exist in a continuous flow.

Furthermore, when that [Self], whose body of discriminative knowledge has been dissolved through the realization of its own bodiless nature by means of overcoming the identification with the body, exists in such a state, pleasure and pain do not touch it.

The verb "to touch" (*spṛś*) is connected with each [term] individually; thus, there are two statements: "pleasure does not touch it" and "pain does not touch it," just as in the rule, "one should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous."
For merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are indeed the effects of the body;

however, bodilessness (*aśarīratā*) is its true nature. Since merit and demerit are impossible there, the state of being their effect is even further removed; therefore, pleasure and pain do not touch it.

Now, if even pleasure does not touch the bodiless one, then what Maghavan said—that one situated in deep sleep has gone to utter destruction (*vināśam evāpītaḥ*)—has effectively occurred here as well.

This is not a fault, because what is intended to be expressed is the negation of pleasure and pain—which are the effects of merit and demerit and are connected with a body—by the statement, "pleasure and pain do not touch the bodiless one.

For the word "touch" (*sparśa*) is observed to be used for things that come and go, as in "the touch of cold" or "the touch of heat," but it is not said that "there is a touching by fire" of its own nature, namely heat and light; likewise, [this applies] to bliss which is the very nature of Agni or Sūrya, like their heat and light.

Even regarding that which is dear (*priya*), there is no negation here [of its existence], because of such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*) and "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahma*).
Furthermore, in this context as well, it has been stated that "only the Infinite (*bhūman*) is happiness.

Now, one might object: since the Infinite and the dear are one, it would follow that it is either unperceivable or, by its very nature, eternally perceived; thus, it would be devoid of distinctions, and this is not what Indra desires.
For it has been said: "Indeed, he does not now know himself as 'I am this,' nor indeed these beings; he has gone to utter destruction; I see nothing here to enjoy.
Therefore, that knowledge which Indra desired was that by which one knows both the beings and the Self, and perceives nothing unpleasant;
by that knowledge, one attains all worlds and all desires—this is the truth desired by Indra: "These beings are from me..."
"Other than me, all worlds and all desires are distinct; I am their master"—this was not beneficial for Indra. And that which is beneficial for Indra must be spoken by Prajāpati.

Prajāpati intended that what is beneficial for Indra should be taught as the attainment resulting from the realization of the self-nature of all beings and the world through being bodiless like space—
not, however, as something distinct, like a king’s acquisition of a kingdom.
This being so, when there is the oneness of the Self, how could one perceive "these beings" or "this is I"?

[Objection: "In this view, however, scriptural passages concerning sovereignty—such as 'If he is desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere will, fathers appear before him,' or 'He becomes one-fold through women or vehicles'—would be untenable. [Reply: No, because there is no contradiction, since it is possible for the Universal Self (sarvātman) to be connected with all fruits;
just as clay attains the state of all jars, bowls, pots, and so forth.
If it is objected that, if [the Self] were the self of all, there would also be a connection with suffering, we say no;
for since suffering itself is admitted to be the Self, there is no contradiction.
Sufferings have their cause in the imagination of ignorance within the Self, just as the imagination of a snake and so forth has its cause in a rope.
When that ignorance has been severed by the vision of the true nature of the identity of the body and the Self, the suspicion of a connection with suffering is no longer possible.

However, regarding desires caused by the volitions of pure *sattva*, the connection with the body of the Lord is as follows: He alone is the supreme enjoyer of mental objects within all beings through the medium of the adjuncts (*upādhi*) of all living creatures; thus, the Supreme Self alone is the locus for all transactions created by ignorance.
"There is no other" is the established conclusion of the Vedānta.
When Prajāpati said, "This person who is seen in the eye," he was referring only to the shadow-person;
and in the states of dreaming and deep sleep, it is indeed another.
Some maintain that the Supreme Self—characterized by such qualities as being free from evil—is not [the subject here] because of a contradiction;
they explain the purpose for teaching the selves consisting of shadow and so forth as follows:

if the Supreme Self were taught at the very outset, since it is difficult to comprehend, those whose minds are attached to extremely external objects might fall into confusion upon hearing of an exceedingly subtle reality. Therefore, [these intermediate selves are taught].

It is said that just as one desiring to show the subtle moon on the second day first points out a tree directly before him, saying, "Look, this is the moon," then another, then yet another, and finally a mountain peak situated near the moon, saying, "This is the moon," and only then does he see the moon;
in the same way, what was spoken by Prajāpati in three stages beginning with "That which is in the eye" is not the Supreme.
But in the fourth alternative, having risen from the mortal body and attained bodilessness, one becomes of the nature of light.
That Supreme Person in whom one exists eating, playing, and rejoicing with women and so forth—that Supreme Person is said to be the Highest; thus they say.
True, this interpretation is indeed pleasant to hear.
However, the meaning of this text cannot be understood in this way.
How so?
Having introduced the statement, "The person is seen in the eye," the two students grasped it as referring to the shadow-self; thus, there was a misunderstanding on their part.

If Prajāpati had taught that the reflection alone was the Self seen in the eye, then his presentation of the water-jar for its removal, his question "What do you see?", and his instruction regarding fine adornment would all be purposeless. Furthermore, if he had indeed taught [the reflection] himself, then a reason for the removal of that very understanding would also have to be stated.

He himself should have stated the reason for removing [the idea of the Self] even in the cases of grasping the Self in dreams and deep sleep; since he did not say so, we consider that the reflection-self in the eye was not what Prajāpati taught.
Furthermore, if the seer in the eye had been taught as "that which is seen," then this [objection] would be appropriate.
However, after saying "But him alone, indeed, to you," there is the teaching of the very seer even in the state of dream.
If it is argued that the seer is not taught [to exist] in a dream, we say no;
for there is the teaching: "He is as if weeping, as if experiencing what is unpleasant.
Furthermore, there is no one other than the seer who moves about being honored in a dream.
In this regard, it is established by reasoning and by other scriptural passages that "this person is self-luminous.
Although one possesses the intellect (*dhī*) during dream, nevertheless the intellect does not function as an instrument for the perception of dream-enjoyments.

Rather, like a painting on a canvas, the intellect is merely the object of sight, being supported by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state; thus, there is no sublation of the self-luminosity of the Seer.
Furthermore:
while awake and dreaming, one knows both the elements and the self, thinking, "These are the elements" and "I am this.
Since such cognition exists, a negation would be appropriate, as in the passage beginning with, "But he does not [perceive them as separate]," and so forth.
Thus, having stated that for the conscious self alone, while possessing a body caused by ignorance, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant,

it is logical that for that same self when it exists as bodiless— provided knowledge is present— there is a negation of the two states that were previously attained in the state of being embodied, according to the text: "Verily, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch one who is bodiless."

Furthermore, it is established in another scriptural passage that the single Self moves unattached between the states of dreaming and waking, like a great fish. As for the claim that the "serene one" (saṃprasāda), having risen from the body, rejoices with women and other objects— that which is designated as the locus where he rejoices is a different, supreme Person distinct from the serene one— that too is incorrect.
Because even in the fourth discourse it says, "He is indeed this very one";
for if another [entity] were intended there, Prajāpati would not have said as before, "He is indeed this very one," and thus he would be speaking falsely.

Furthermore, having shown the entry of the Existent (Sat), the creator of fire, water, food, and so forth, into the sprout-like body which is its own modification, the instruction "That thou art" given to the one who has entered would result in being false.
If the Supreme Person were other than the serene being (saṃprasāda), then the instruction "you will be terrified by women and the like" would have been appropriate.

Likewise, if the Bhūman were other than the individual soul (jīva), [the Teacher] would not have concluded with "this whole world is the Self alone," after having first taught "I am indeed the Bhūman.
This is also because of other scriptural passages such as, "There is no other seer but He."

Furthermore, the application of the word "Self" (ātman) to the Supreme in all the Vedas would not have occurred if the inner Self were not the supreme Self of all living beings; therefore, it is established that there is only one Self as the subject of this context.
Nor does the transmigratory state belong to the Self, because transmigration is superimposed upon the Self by ignorance (avidyā).

For it is not the case that snakes, silver, impurities, and so forth—which are superimposed through false cognition upon a rope, mother-of-pearl, the sky, and so on—actually belong to those things [the rope, etc.].
By this, it is explained that for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain.
And as for the established statement, "he experiences what is unpleasant," it is proven that he is *not* one who experiences only the unpleasant.

This being the case, in all these various modes of expression, Prajāpati’s statement— "This is the immortal, this is fearlessness, this is Brahman"— must indeed be true, whether it be the word of Prajāpati himself or the word of the Śruti appearing in the form of Prajāpati. Nor is it proper to render this false through the intellect of fallacious reasoning.
For no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) more authoritative than that is possible.
If it is argued that the perception of being an experiencer of unpleasantness such as suffering is experienced as non-erroneous, we say no;
for that [perception] is established just like the perceptual experiences: "I am aged though free from old age," "I was born," "I am long-lived," "I am fair," "I am dark," or "I am dead."

If it is argued that all of this is indeed true, it is certainly so; yet it is difficult to comprehend, for even the King of the Gods (Indra), despite being shown the reasoning regarding non-destruction through the example of the water-cup and so forth, was utterly deluded in this matter by thinking, "He has simply entered into destruction.
Likewise, Virocana, though highly wise and a son of Prajāpati, came to hold the view that the Self is nothing more than the body.
Similarly, the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) sank into an ocean of fear regarding the destruction of the Self, even while Indra was present.

Likewise, the Sāṃkhyas, although they have understood the seer to be distinct from the body and so forth, remain fixed in a perception of duality—which is the very domain of death—because they have abandoned the authority of the scriptures.

Similarly, others who follow the systems of Kaṇāda and others are engaged in purifying the substance of the self, which they believe is joined with nine qualities of the self, just as a cloth dyed with astringent color is cleansed with alkaline substances and the like.

Likewise, other ritualists, whose minds are carried away by external objects, even though they accept the Veda as authoritative, regard the oneness of the self—the ultimate truth—as if it were destruction, like Indra; and like a water-wheel, they are incessantly engaged in the process of ascending and descending.
[The mind] wanders about.
What else [could it do]? For other small creatures, being devoid of discrimination, have their minds naturally carried away by external objects.

Therefore, this [state] belongs only to those wandering mendicants who are supreme *paramahaṃsa*s, who have abandoned all external desires, who have no other refuge, who have transcended the stages of life (*atyāśramin*), and who are devoted to the realization of the Vedānta.
This work, which is to be experienced by those most worthy of worship and composed in four chapters by those following this tradition of the Prajāpati lineage,
teaches in such a way that even today they alone— and no others— are its true exponents.
The wind is bodiless;
the cloud, lightning, and thunder—these are bodiless.
Just as these, having risen from that space and having reached the highest light, manifest in their own forms.

In this context, it must be explained how that serene being (*saṃprasāda*), which is bodiless, yet having attained embodiment through its non-distinction from the body due to ignorance, emerges from the body and manifests in its own true form; therefore, an illustration is stated: "The wind is bodiless"—that is, it is bodiless because it lacks a body characterized by a head, hands, and so forth.
Furthermore, the cloud, lightning, and thunder— these are bodiless. This being so, when their purpose, such as rain,
has been fulfilled, just as the Vedic text, standing on earth, designates the region of space connected with the heavenly world by saying "from that" (amuṣmāt).

These elements, as previously described, having attained a form equal to space and being no longer perceived in their own forms as air and so forth, have come to be designated by the name "space. Just as the serene being (*saṃprasāda*), in the state of ignorance, attains the very nature of the body, so too these [elements], having become thus, emerge from that region of space connected with the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) for the purpose of accomplishing rain and other such effects. How?
At the end of the cold season, having reached the supreme, intense summer light of the sun— that is, having encountered the heat of the sun— they,
being separated from their own forms by the heat of the sun, abandon their state of stillness and appear in their respective forms as winds such as the *purovāta*,
as clouds in the form of earth, mountains, elephants, and so forth, and as lightning in its own flickering form of luminous creepers and the like.
Even the thundercloud manifests in its own form as thunder and lightning; thus, with the arrival of the rainy season, they emerge in their respective forms.
In just this way, this serene being, having risen from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form.
He is the Supreme Person.
There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, whether with women, or vehicles, or kinsmen, no longer remembering this body, which is subject to decay.
Just as a draft animal is yoked to a wagon, even so is this vital breath (prāṇa) yoked to this body.

Just as in this illustration, where [beings] attain a state of similarity with space and so forth through the wind and other elements, so too one who has attained a state of similarity with the body during the condition of transmigratory existence— thinking "I am the son of such-and-such," "I am born," "I have grown old," "I shall die"— is enlightened by Prajāpati, just as Maghavan was, through the aforementioned sequence, [with the words] "You are not the attributes of the body, senses, and so forth; thou art That" (*tattvamasi*).

This serene being, the individual soul (*jīva*), having emerged from this body—just as wind and other elements emerge from space—and having realized the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, abandons the identification with the body; this is what is meant.
It has been explained previously that it "manifests in its own form" as the very Self that is Being (*sat*).

By whatever own form that serene being (*saṃprasāda*) emerges after its previous state of delusion—that cause of error—it becomes a snake; just as a rope, once illuminated, emerges in its own true form as the essence of a rope. And so, he is the Supreme Person (*uttamapuruṣa*), for he is both supreme and a person; he alone is the Supreme Person—the one who was manifest in the eye and in the dream, and who is now unmanifest, merged in deep sleep, and serene.
"And the body by its own form.

This [Self] exists by its own form, having been designated as the "Supreme Person" (*uttama-puruṣa*) in the *Gītā* in relation to the perishable and the imperishable, the manifested and the unmanifested.
That serene one (*saṃprasāda*), by his own form, being established in himself within his own self, becomes the Self of all and moves about—sometimes in the form of Indra and so forth.
Eating—that is, laughing or consuming various desired foods—somewhere with objects produced by mere thought or by the will alone, belonging to the world of Brahmā;

and sporting, delighting with women and others through the mind alone; he does not remember this body, which is called "upajana" because it is born from the mutual union of a woman and a man, or because it is born in proximity to the self as its own manifestation. He does not remember that.
For upon remembering that, there would indeed be suffering, because its very nature is suffering.
[Objection: But if one does not remember what has been experienced, then the liberated one would lack omniscience.
This is not a fault.

For that which was produced by false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) and the like has been eradicated by *vidyā* (knowledge); therefore, it was never truly experienced, and thus there is no loss of omniscience due to the non-remembrance of it.

Indeed, what was experienced by one who is insane or possessed by a spirit need not be remembered even when the insanity or possession has ceased; likewise here, that which is experienced by transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*) who possess the defect of ignorance (*avidyā*) does not belong to the Self, which is bodiless and [all-pervading].
It does not touch [them],
because the cause of ignorance is absent.

However, those desires which are experienced by those whose defects are severed and whose impurities are crushed— desires that are real but have falsehood as their covering— are manifested by knowledge.

Thus, they are described as being connected with that which is liberated and has become the Self of all; this is taught for the sake of praising the knowledge of the Self. Therefore, it is rightly specified that "these are the worlds of Brahman.
For wherever they may be, they exist indeed in the world of Brahman alone; because Brahman is the Self of all, they are so called.

But is it not a contradiction that [the text says] "being one, he sees nothing else, knows nothing else; that is the Infinite (bhūman)" and also "he rejoices seeing the desires belonging to the world of Brahman"?
For it would be as if one were to see in one very same moment and yet not see in that very same moment.
This is not a fault.
Because this has been resolved in another Vedic scripture:
"Since the vision of the seer is never lost, he continues to see;
yet, because desires do not exist apart from the seer, he does not see."

Although that was stated regarding deep sleep, the absence of a second is the same for the liberated one as well because of the oneness of all; and it has already been said: "By what means could one see whom?
Yet, Prajāpati asked, "How is this person seen in the eye," referring to him whose true nature is bodiless and characterized by the removal of evil and other such qualities?
In this regard, since it must be explained how [the self] is directly perceived in the eye, this [section] is commenced.

As for the question, "What is the reason for seeing in the eye?", he provides an illustration: just as the word *prayogya* refers either to the act of yoking (*prayoga*) or to that which is to be yoked (*prayogya*), such as a horse or a bullock—being called "yokeable" (*prayogya*) because it is employed (*prayujyate*).
Just as in the world that by which one moves is called a "means of movement" (ācaraṇa), such as a chariot or a cart, and one is yoked to that means of movement for the purpose of drawing it along;

even so, in this body which stands in the place of a chariot, the five-fold vital breath (prāṇa) is yoked—conjoined with the senses, mind, and intellect; the conscious self (prajñātman), whose nature is a conflation of the two powers of knowledge and action; and who is appointed for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his own karma.
"In what, when it departs, shall I depart? Or in what, when it is established, shall I be established?
Thus [the self] is authorized over the operations of seeing, hearing, and movement by the Lord, like a prime minister by a king;
yet only a single part of that [Lord] is the faculty of sight, which serves as the gateway for the perception of form.
Now, where this space extends as far as the eye, that is the person in the eye; the eye is for the purpose of seeing.
Now, he who knows "let me smell this" is the Self; the nose is for the purpose of smelling. Now, he who knows "let me speak this" is the Self; speech is for the purpose of speaking.
Now, he who knows "may I hear this" is the Self; the ear is for the purpose of hearing.

Now, where the space characterized by the black pupil (kṛṣṇatāra) is entered into, joined with, and pervading the cavity of the body—therein is that aforementioned bodiless Self, who is "of the eye" (cākṣuṣa), meaning he exists in the eye. For the purpose of seeing—that is, for the perception of form—the eye is his instrument; because he is conjoined with the body and other elements, he exists here in the eye for the sake of the supreme Seer.
"The Supreme, who is bodiless and uncomposed, is seen by means of the sign of vision.
Prajāpati’s statement, "He is seen in the eye," is intended as an illustration for all the doors of the senses;
for He alone is indeed the perceiver of all objects.
In all the Vedas, the specific term "eyes" is used because they are the cause of clear perception;
and according to the Vedic scripture, "I saw"—this becomes true.

Furthermore, he who knows within this body, thinking, "How may I smell this, whether it be fragrant or foul? May I discern its odor?"—he is the Self, and the nose exists for his sake, for the purpose of smelling, that is, for the discernment of odors.
Now, he who knows, "I shall utter this speech," "I will speak"—that Self, for the accomplishment of the act of utterance, has the organ of speech as its instrument.
Now, he who knows, "I shall hear this"—that Self, for the purpose of hearing, has the ear.
Now, he who knows "I shall think this" is the Self;
the mind is his divine eye.
Indeed, with that divine eye, the mind, he beholds and delights in those desires which are in the world of Brahman.
Now, he who knows "I shall think this," [thinking] "I shall think" as a purely mental operation untouched by the senses—that is the Self; for the mind is for the purpose of thinking.

Since the expression "he who knows is the Self" is used everywhere in this manner, it is understood that knowing is its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Just as when it is said, "He who illumines the east is the sun; he who illumines the south, the west, the north, and above is the sun," it is understood that his essential nature is illumination.
The instruments, such as the eye, however, exist for the purpose of accomplishing actions such as seeing;
this is understood through the capacity of this self.
The self's status as the agent of cognition exists by its mere existence alone, and not through active exertion.
Just as the sun possesses the agency of illumination by its mere existence and not through any active exertion, so it is here:
the mind (*manas*) is the divine, non-material eye of this Self, uncommon to the other senses; it "sees" (*cakṣate*), meaning it perceives by means of this [eye].
And since the [other] senses have objects belonging to the present time, they are therefore "non-divine."

The mind, however, is called the divine eye because it is the instrument for perceiving objects of the three periods of time; when its defects are subdued, it is the instrument for perceiving all things, including those that are subtle or obstructed.

Indeed, he who is liberated, having attained his true nature, being separated from the body, senses, and mind produced by ignorance, and having attained the state of being the Self of all—being as pure as space and the Lord of all, with the mind as his limiting adjunct—he, by means of this very mind which is the Lord, [perceives] these desires, which are eternally extended like the light of the sun.
He rejoices by seeing them through vision.

To specify which desires these are, [the text] says: "those which, in the world of Brahman, are like a hidden treasure of gold—concealed by the untruth of attachment to external objects, yet obtainable by mere volition (saṃkalpa)"; this is the meaning.
The gods indeed worship that very Self;
therefore, all worlds and all desires are attained by them.
He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires.
Thus indeed spoke Prajāpati; Prajāpati spoke.
Since this Self was declared to Indra by Prajāpati, therefore, having heard of it from him, even today the gods worship that Self.
And through that worship, all worlds and all desires have been attained by them.
The intention is that the gods have obtained that very fruit for which Indra lived as a religious student (*brahmacarya*) with Prajāpati for one hundred and one years.
