It is appropriate that this applies to the gods because of their great fortune, but it is not possible for humans now, due to their short lifespan and their more limited intelligence; to this point, the following is said: "He attains all worlds and all desires even in the present.
Who is he?
"Prajāpati indeed spoke in general terms, saying that 'he who, like Indra and others, realizes and knows that Self'—
the meaning is that therefore the knowledge of the Self and the attainment of its fruit are exactly the same for everyone.
The repetition [of the concluding words] is for the purpose of marking the end of the section.
Thus ends the twelfth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"From the dark I go to the variegated; from the variegated I go to the dark."

"Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, I—being one whose self is perfected—attain the uncreated world of Brahman; I attain it! This [statement] is accompanied by the recitation of purifying mantras such as "From the dark I go to the speckled," intended for silent recitation (japa) or for meditation (dhyāna). "Śyāma" refers to a deep color; it is called "śyāma" because it is like that [color], namely the Heart-Brahman (hārda-brahman), due to its extreme profundity. That is the Heart.

Having known Brahman through meditation, from that dark [state] I shall reach the variegated; for the world of Brahman is "variegated" (śabala) because it is mixed with many desires such as those of the forest and so forth.
That variegated world of Brahman I shall reach with my mind—that is, I shall go upwards after the fall of the body.

Because I am departing from the variegated world of Brahman, I reach the dark [state]; the intention is: "I have entered the state of the heart. (The sense is: I have attained the nature of the *hārdam*.)
Therefore, the meaning is that one should resort to that very Self, which is variegated by nature.

How does one resort to the variegated world of Brahman? It is said: just as a horse shakes off its own hairs, thereby removing fatigue and dust from its coat and becoming pure through that shaking, so too [the seeker] shakes off [impurities] by means of the knowledge of the Brahman within the heart.
Just as the moon, which is [temporarily] eclipsed by Rāhu when its light is obscured by the conjunction of merit and demerit, becomes radiant again once it is released from that mouth of Rāhu;

even so, having shaken off the body— the abode of all misfortunes— right here through meditation, one who has perfected the self and accomplished his purpose attains the uncreated, eternal world of Brahman.
The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the mantra.

Thus ends the thirteenth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "That which is called space is indeed the revealer of name and form. That which is within them is Brahman; that is the immortal; that is the Self."
I enter the assembly hall and the dwelling of Prajāpati; may I become the glory of the Brahmins, the glory of the kings, the glory of the commoners.
I have attained glory;
indeed, I am the glory of glories.
The white, toothless one; the toothless, white, slippery one—may I not go toward it; may I not go toward the slippery one.
The passage beginning with "Or rather, space" is for the purpose of defining the characteristics of Brahman and for the sake of meditation.
Indeed, the Self is well-known in the Vedas by the name "space" (ākāśa),
because, like space, it is bodiless and subtle.

And that space is the sustainer (*nirvahitṛ*), the bearer (*nirvoḍhṛ*), and the manifester (*vyākṛtṛ*) of name and form—which reside within its own self, which constitute the seed of the world, and which stand in the relation of foam to water.
That Brahman exists "within" (i.e., in the midst of) those two, name and form;

or rather, that which exists in the midst of name and form, untouched by name and form—that is Brahman. It is distinct in nature from name and form and untouched by them, yet it possesses the quality of being their sustainer.
The meaning is that Brahman is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

This very point has been stated in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa; because pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) persists throughout, it is understood that everywhere there is only the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpatā*), and thus a single coherent statement (*ekavākyatā*) is established.
To the question "How is this understood?", he says: "That is the Self (*sa ātmā*)."

For the so-called Self (ātman) is well-known as the individual conscious principle of all living beings, directly perceivable by itself; it should be understood that the Self, when raised to its true nature as bodiless, all-pervading like space, is Brahman.
And that Self, which is Brahman, is immortal, having the nature of being deathless.
Hereafter follows the mantra.
I enter—that is, I go to—the assembly hall, the abode, the mansion built by the Lord, belonging to Prajāpati, who has four faces.
Furthermore, I am Yaśas, the Self named Yaśas; for I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas, since it is the Brāhmaṇas in particular who especially worship Him, and therefore I become their glory.
Likewise, [I am the self] of kings and of vaiśyas;
since they too are indeed [my] subjects, I am their self as well.
Therefore, I shall attain, and I desire to attain, that fame; for I am the self of those fames characterized by the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect.
To the question, "For what purpose am I thus approaching [her]?", it is said: She is white in color, like a ripe jujube fruit, and ruddy;

likewise, she is "adatka"—meaning toothless, yet also "adatka" in the sense of being a devourer, that is, one who destroys and annihilates the luster, strength, vigor, wisdom, and merit of those who indulge in her.
"That which has such characteristics—white, slimy, and slippery—may I not go toward it; may I not approach it.
The repetition [of the negative particle] is for the purpose of demonstrating that it is the cause of ultimate misfortune.
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
This very [knowledge] Brahmā spoke to Prajāpati; Prajāpati to Manu; and Manu to his progeny.

Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the rules, and having performed the duties for the teacher during the time remaining after [one's own studies], one should return home and dwell in a pure household.

Studying his sacred recitation in a suitable place, making others righteous, establishing all his senses within himself, and practicing non-violence toward all beings except at the prescribed sacred sites—
he, indeed, conducting himself thus throughout his life, attains the world of Brahmā.
And he does not return again, and he does not return again.

Now, this very knowledge of the Self, together with its ancillaries— including the meditations on "Om" as this syllable and so forth— and along with the text that expresses it, namely the eight-chapter work (the Aṣṭādhyāyī), Brahmā— whether Hiraṇyagarbha or the Supreme Lord through him— taught it to Prajāpati Kaśyapa.

He [Brahmā] imparted it to his son Manu, and Manu to the progeny; thus, the knowledge of the Upaniṣads, which has come down through this lineage of the traditional transmission of the meaning of the Śruti, is still understood among the learned even today.
Just as the knowledge of the Self revealed here in the three chapters beginning with the sixth is understood along with its fruit, so it is not the case for ritual actions.

When it might be concluded that there is no purpose [in this], with the desire to avoid the resulting futility, this meaningfulness of the rite performed by the learned is stated by way of its possession of a distinguished fruit: "Having studied the Veda from the house of a teacher" means having completed the study along with its meaning,
being endowed with the prescribed rules as declared in the Smṛtis.

Since every duty prescribed by the Smṛtis must be performed toward one's preceptor, the author says the following to demonstrate the preeminence of service to the teacher: "Having performed whatever work for the teacher is to be done, with the remaining time that is free from such work, he should study the Veda.
The intention is that the Veda studied in this manner by one who observes these rules leads to the attainment of the fruits of ritual action and knowledge, but not otherwise.

The meaning is as follows: having returned from the teacher’s house after completing the inquiry into the Dharma, and having lawfully taken a wife and established a household, one remains engaged in the duties prescribed for the householder stage (*gārhasthya*).

Even therein, in order to demonstrate the preeminence of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) among the duties prescribed for the householder, it is said that one should sit in a pure, secluded place free from impurities and the like, reciting the Veda according to the rule—both the daily (*nityaka*) and the additional portions.
Practicing the study of the *Ṛg-veda* and other scriptures according to his ability, making his sons and disciples righteous and endowed with dharma, and restraining them through righteousness;

having established and withdrawn all the senses into the Brahman within his own heart—that is, in the *Hārda*—and having renounced actions by the very mention of the senses; and practicing non-violence, meaning he does not cause injury or pain to others, nor does he afflict any living beings, whether stationary or moving.
Since even wandering for the sake of alms and so forth might cause suffering to others, he says: "Except at sacred sites" (*anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ*).
A "sacred site" (*tīrtha*) refers to a domain permitted by the scriptures; thus, the meaning is "other than that.
This applies equally to those in all stages of life (*āśrama*): except at sacred sites, there is indeed non-violence.

Others describe it thus: while performing all this within the household itself, he who is indeed authorized, conducting himself throughout his entire lifespan, for as long as he lives, in the manner just described, attains the world of Brahman at the end of the body and does not return again to assume a physical body,
because of the prohibition against returning once it has been reached.

The meaning is that, having reached the world of the effected Brahman by way of the path beginning with light, he remains right there for as long as the world of Brahman endures; until then, he does not return.
The repetition [of the final phrase] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the Upaniṣadic teaching.
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the teacher of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
